# Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI

A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

[Read the case study](https://openai.com/index/gilbert-tobin/)

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

[Gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.gtlaw.com.au/) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

## Sam, what is Gilbert + Tobin trying to achieve with AI?

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

> *“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”*

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

## You describe Gilbert + Tobin’s journey in three phases: experimentation, personal productivity, and organisational productivity. How did the firm get started?

When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

Governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

## You’ve noticed that adoption is unusually high for your firm, with 87% active usage among enabled ChatGPT users, more than twice the rate Gilbert + Tobin typically sees for other tools. How did leadership shape that culture?

Leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into new technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

> *“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”*

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

## You have made ChatGPT central to your own work. What have you learned from what you’ve built?

To help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins)using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

With a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s important to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

## What advice would you give other CEOs beginning this journey?

Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

The opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.

**Find out more about Gilbert + Tobin’s work with OpenAI through the case study** [**here**](https://openai.com/index/gilbert-tobin/)**.**

## 20,000 veterans are using ChatGPT to build what comes next

In the past year, more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a year of [ChatGPT Plus at no cost](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-veterans/) after being offered free access by OpenAI. As Veterans Day approaches, that milestone gives us a chance to look at how veterans are using AI to prepare for civilian careers and to figure out what comes next for themselves and their families.

The effort started with veterans who work here at OpenAI, people who use these tools every day and know firsthand how challenging the transition can be. Beyond the free access, OpenAI Academy and our community partners have hosted more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, [with seven more⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/home/events) scheduled before the year ends.

## Preparing for civilian careers

Leaving the military often means stepping into an unfamiliar job market and working out how years of service translate into a civilian role. Many veterans are turning to ChatGPT to organize their job search, rehearse for interviews, and explore paths they hadn’t considered.

Air Force veteran [Tilak Bhatnagar ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ACoAACLpKeMBgVdc2b2nami8B_Wr_EecZXqRfDY) used his free year to prepare for a dozen interviews, find the right words to describe his military experience to civilian employers, and weigh competing job offers. Along the way, those conversations helped him clarify what he actually wanted from life after active duty.

He ultimately took a role at a tech company. What he valued most was being able to pick up where he left off, returning to the same thread about his background, goals, and constraints. As he put it, “each conversation built on the last.”

[Sadarian Bell ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ACoAAFDy8p8BLQADQImjs514hHT6yRuJ2ym1r6k), also an Air Force veteran, started planning more than a year before he left the service. He used ChatGPT to map out his transition and to turn nearly a decade of military healthcare experience into a civilian résumé.

To prepare for interviews, he practiced out loud using ChatGPT voice mode, working through one question at a time until his answers felt natural. “It has genuinely become my career coach,” Sadarian said, though he also learned to recognize when he’d had enough help and could trust his own judgment.

For Navy veteran [Kelli Ramirez ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kelliann-ramirez-hart-540a475a/), the transition was a chance to chase a long-held dream: becoming a published author. She’d already invested in a book-writing course to sharpen her craft, and ChatGPT filled in the gaps. “ChatGPT helped me organize ideas, ask questions about publishing, and work through the Amazon Kindle Direct Publishing process,” she said.

Kelli has since published two books, which she says “reflect my desire to help women approach technology with confidence and, for those who share my Christian faith, with wisdom grounded in that faith.”

## Learning to use ChatGPT, together

Not everyone arrives confident about using AI tools, which is why OpenAI Academy gives veterans, transitioning servicemembers, and military spouses a place to learn alongside people who understand what they’re going through.

OpenAI recently wrapped our first six-event Academy series with [Veterans Forge⁠(opens in a new window)](https://veteransforge.org/), focused on helping veterans and military families use ChatGPT to work toward their goals. That pilot, together with workshops alongside AI Collective Hampton Roads and NPower, is shaping what we offer veterans next.

At one [workshop in Reston, Virginia⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/en/public/events/openai-academy-for-veterans-w8zz8dfrts), nearly [100 veterans and active-duty servicemembers⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erinrosemarie_veterans-ai-aicommunity-activity-7440044135958384640-j7S-) explored ways to put AI to work. Participant [Ryan Kaono-Wedemeyer⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryan-kaono-wedemeyer) learned to start by writing out a detailed account of his military experience, then asking AI to help shape it into a civilian résumé.

Instructor [Erin Marie⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erinrosemarie_veterans-ai-aicommunity-activity-7440044135958384640-j7S-) helped participants build custom GPTs to support their transitions, and watched people who walked in skeptical begin finding ways the tools could genuinely help them.

In Louisville, Kentucky, [more than 80 Legionnaires⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/veterans-forge_theamericanlegion-veteransforge-veterans-activity-7499820737151541248-PqzY) attended three AI training sessions at the American Legion’s national convention. For those who can’t make it to an event, our [online veterans collection⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/collections/veterans) and [100 chats for veterans⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/use-cases/veterans) offer examples to try on your own.

## What’s next

We’re continuing this work with partners across the country through the rest of the year:

- November 12: [NPower event in St. Louis⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-whats-next-st-louis-mo-0khw38ivta)
- November 14: [Nashville event with Veterans Forge and Wounded Warrior Project⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-veterans-nashville-tn-dix3h7movo)
- November 17: [30-minute virtual session⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-veterans-explore-your-next-career-move-9ogzt3abfx)
- November 19: [NPower event in Dallas⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-whats-next-dallas-tx-n6del7j00o)
- November 21: [NPower event in San Antonio⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/events/chatgpt-for-whats-next-san-antonio-tx-x48nh426r8)

Our goal is to help veterans and military families carry the skills they built in service into whatever work they choose next. We’re grateful to [ID.me⁠(opens in a new window)](http://ID.me) for helping servicemembers and veterans access the free-year offer, and to our community partners for making these events possible.

This Veterans Day, OpenAI thanks veterans for their service and for contributing to their communities.

title: BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
body:
[
](#botpsy-on-device-personal-assistant-with-a-sub-billion-parameter-agentic-language-model)
BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model
[Team Article](/blog)
Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.
Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the [Intended Use and Limitations](#intended-use-and-limitations) for more information.
🤗 [Model (safetensors)](https://huggingface.co/qvac/BotPsy-0.8B) | 📦 [GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4)](https://huggingface.co/qvac/BotPsy-0.8B-GGUFs)

[
](#key-highlights)
Key Highlights
[
](#benchmark-results)
Benchmark results
- Twice the performance of its base model: BotPsy roughly doubles the agentic capability of Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think on key benchmarks: BFCL v4 rises from 23.4 to 44.0, ACEBench from 30.1 to 58.7, and τ-bench from 23.2 to 51.5 (mean of the retail, telecom and banking subsets).
- Best agent in its category: BotPsy outperforms leading models in the ≤1.2B-parameter weight class (Qwen3.5-0.8B-Think, LFM2.5-1.2B-Think, MiniCPM5-1B-Think) on all six tool-use and agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4, ACEBench, τ-bench, ToolSandbox, Claw-Eval and BrowseComp-Plus.
- Outperforms its larger sibling: BotPsy has the highest score of all models tested on five of the six benchmarks, beating Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size, on BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 37.7), ACEBench (58.7 vs 55.4), τ-bench (51.5 vs 46.5), ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 41.2) and BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 2.8). Only on Claw-Eval does Qwen3.5-2B-Think lead (48.9 vs 46.5).
[
](#model-capabilities)
Model capabilities
- More reliable in multi-turn workflows: On τ²-bench, where the agent must hold a long customer conversation, follow a strict policy, and act on the customer's behalf, it scores 82.5 in telecom, ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think (69.3). On BFCL v4's multi-turn tasks, it rises from 7.5 to 46.1 over its base, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8). Grouped by application, its multi-step scores lead all models tested in commerce and services (58.3 vs 47.4 for the next best, Qwen3.5-2B-Think) and in device and system management (46.1 vs 31.9).
- Knows when (not) to call tools: An agent that acts must also know when not to act. On BFCL v4's hallucination tests, which check that the model declines when no appropriate tool exists, BotPsy scores 86.1, the highest of all models tested. On ACEBench's special cases, where the request is incomplete, contains wrong parameters, or cannot be served by the given tools, it scores 51.3, up from 13.7 for its base model.
- Follows instructions while preserving knowledge: BotPsy specializes in tool use while preserving general skills. Instruction following improves sharply, with IFEval rising from 59.7 to 90.8 and IFBench from 22.0 to 55.9, the highest IFBench score of all models tested. General knowledge also improves, with GPQA Diamond rising from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9. On all four benchmarks, BotPsy outperforms every other model of 1.2B parameters or fewer that we tested.
[
](#safety-efficiency-and-deployment)
Safety, efficiency and deployment
- Safer than leading models in its category: In automated red-teaming across six harm categories, BotPsy produces unsafe responses 21% of the time, compared with 36% for its base model. This is the lowest rate of all models of up to 1.2B parameters (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35%; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 47%). Under prompt-injection attacks, which matter most for agents that read untrusted tool outputs, the unsafe rate drops from 46% for its base model to 31%.
- More efficient reasoning and less looping: On questions that all five models answer correctly, BotPsy reaches the answer with about 3× fewer reasoning tokens than its base model on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563) and 2.7× fewer on MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105). Across all IFBench attempts, its rate of getting stuck in repetitive reasoning loops falls from 22.9% to 1.4%, and runs that hit the 32k-token limit fall from 28.3% to 0.2%. Shorter, more decisive reasoning should reduce latency on-device.
- Open-source and ready to use: BotPsy will be released with open weights under the Apache 2.0 license for research and educational use. It will be available in three precisions (bf16, Q8, Q4), as Hugging Face safetensors and as GGUF files for the QVAC SDK and llama.cpp.
[
](#broader-vision)
Broader Vision
Building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps users entirely in control of their digital lives.
[
](#methodology)
Methodology
BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).
[
](#training-procedure-four-stages-three-types-of-feedback)
Training procedure: four stages, three types of feedback
Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.
Learning from demonstrations (SFT)
We first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.
Learning from teachers (MOPD)
Next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).
Learning from rules and environments (RL stages)
Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.
The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.
[
](#data-composition)
Data composition
Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.
[
](#results)
Results
[
](#tool-use--agents)
Tool use & agents
BotPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material
body:
[NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/korean-startup-investments-msit/)
As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s [emphasis on zero waste](https://cop.sifiratikvakfi.org/en/news/president-erdogans-cop31-call-zero-waste-movement-is-the-strongest-bridge/) puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, [less than 7%](https://circularity-gap.world/updates-collection/global-circularity-rate-fell-to-6-9---despite-growing-recycling) of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over [2 billion tons](https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/global-waste-management-outlook-2024) of trash per year — a figure that could [nearly double by 2050](https://www.weforum.org/stories/nature-and-biodiversity/circular-economy-waste-management-unep).
AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills.
“A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.”
See how four members of the [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation.
Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products.
The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product.
“The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.”
The company uses [NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%.
In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%.
At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items.
EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia.
“Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.”
EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on [NVIDIA data center GPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/), optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.
Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries.
Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it.
U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second.
“Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.”
Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six.
Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of [food-grade plastics by 12%](https://www.greyparrot.ai/resources/case-studies/amcor-case-study-a-12-lift-in-food-grade-polypropylene-yield). Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants.
Europe generates [nearly 7 million tons](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/management-of-used-and-waste-textiles-in-europes-circular-economy) of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried.
reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category.
“Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.”
As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with [NVIDIA TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt) software and running on [NVIDIA Jetson](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud.
The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe.
Explore more [NVIDIA-powered sustainability applications](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/case-studies/?filters=%7B%22Industries%22%3A%5B%22Sustainability%22%5D%7D).

title: Your Sub-Agents Are a Distributed System. Treat Them Like One. - Girish Konda, Microsoft
body:
When an orchestrator hands work to sub-agents, you've built a distributed system, and you inherit its classic failures: half-finished work reported as success, guesses read back as facts, rate limits the orchestrator never sees, and retries that run side effects twice. Girish Konda maps each failure to the distributed-systems idea that already explains it, with examples from his open-source MCP Pacemaker and the MCP and A2A specs. He then lays out SAFE hand-offs, the consistency model he uses for sub-agents that touch real systems, including what it costs and where it doesn't fit.

title: Every Company Is Building Agents That Can't Work Together - Justin Schroeder, Standard Agents
body:

title: Gemini Intelligence: New features, on more devices
body:
Gemini Intelligence: New features, on more devices
Gemini Intelligence
[1](#footnote-1)
brings the best of Gemini to Android devices, helping your devices work harder for you. Earlier this year, we [announced Gemini Intelligence](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/android/gemini-intelligence/), and this summer devices started rolling out — from the [Pixel 11](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/pixel/pixel-11-features/) to the [Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, Z Fold8, Z Flip8](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/android/galaxy-unpacked-2026/) and S26 series.
[2](#footnote-2)
Today, we’re introducing new features built for Gemini Intelligence, and expanding capabilities to [more of Android’s most advanced devices](http://android.com/gemini-intelligence/shop-devices).
[3](#footnote-3)
Here’s a look at what’s new.
Gemini Intelligence on more devices, including motorola signature 27 and Pixel 10
Gemini Intelligence is coming to even more devices. Motorola is introducing its first Gemini Intelligence device, [motorola signature 27](https://www.motorola.com/us/en/p/phones/signature/motorola-signature/pmipmka46mo), which is available for pre-order in the U.S. on November 19. And with [today’s Pixel Drop](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/pixel/november-2026-pixel-drop/), Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro XL, and Pixel 10 Pro Fold get the latest features for Gemini Intelligence.
Alongside this expansion, we’re bringing some of our favorite capabilities to more devices and regions, helping handle the busywork so you can focus on what matters. Rambler
[4](#footnote-4)
— which turns spoken thoughts into clean, organized text in real-time — is now available on Pixel 10, Pixel 10 Pro, Pixel 10, Pro XL and Pixel 10 Pro Fold, as well as the new motorola signature 27. And task automation
[5](#footnote-5)
— which lets you ask Gemini to handle logistics like ordering food, hailing rides, or booking reservations across your favorite apps — is [expanding](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/16940971) to the UK, India, and Japan.
Build custom widgets with a prompt
Create My Widget
[6](#footnote-6)
, which is rolling out over the next few weeks, lets you design a personalized widget with a simple description in your own words — no coding required. Whether you want a dashboard for your upcoming trip, a monthly spending tracker, or a race day countdown, [Create My Widget](https://support.google.com/pixelphone/answer/18835879) can pull in information from Gmail, Calendar, and Search to create a custom widget just for you, giving you the information you want at a glance on your homescreen.
Get personalized tech support with Device Assistance
Device Assistance
[7](#footnote-7)
helps you control, change, or fix your device by just asking your phone for help. Ask Gemini to clear up space on your device, check which apps can access your location, or mute distractions while making sure important calls still come through. Gemini deeply understands your device so it can act as your personal device expert.
Experience proactive help across a range of screens
Gemini Intelligence is designed to support you across whatever screen you’re using. Last month we launched [Googlebook](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/googlebook/pre-order-googlebook/), the first laptop designed for Gemini Intelligence.
And if you have a Pixel phone with Gemini Intelligence, it will soon bring proactive suggestions to Android Auto — connecting the dots across your apps to surface helpful, personalized suggestions
[8](#footnote-8)
when you need them. For example, if your friend texts you to ask where you are meeting for a pilates class, Gemini Intelligence on Android Auto can find your confirmation email and instantly suggest sending the address with a single tap.
Plus, in the next few weeks, Create My Widget is coming to Pixel Watch. You’ll be able to design widgets that keep the details that matter to you right on your wrist.

title: Your PR Says the Tests Passed. Prove It. - Stephen Chin & Cassandra Chin
body:
A pull request can claim that checks passed even when the recorded commands do not establish that the submitted change was tested. Cassandra Chin built Tracetoon to recover the context behind a branch, write a better pull request description and optionally explain it with a comic. Together with Stephen Chin, she follows one troublesome review through repeated revisions, missing evidence and rising token costs. The problem is more specific than producing fluent prose: the writer needs to connect a change to its rationale, the commands that ran, their timing and the version of the code they actually checked.

Their next iteration uses Relate, an embedded graph database written in Rust, to assemble that evidence before the writing begins. A connected brief gives the writer and reviewers the same sources, reducing repeated searches through session logs. The speakers explain why they kept a stronger writer while using less expensive reviewers to check claims against the brief, and show results from their own PR Bench development comparisons. Those reported results combine improved description quality with roughly half the token usage; they describe this project's evaluation, not a guarantee for other codebases. The practical pattern is to preserve provenance and relationships outside the model's conversation, make uncertainty visible, and give reviewers evidence tied to the submitted content. The comic provides the story, but the useful engineering artifact is the reviewable chain behind each claim.

title: Merge Is the Bottleneck - Prasanna Sankar, Vorflux
body:
A customer call ended with a bug, and an agent found the unfinished task in the transcript and screen recording. In Prasanna Sankar's account, it asked for permission to investigate, involved the responsible engineer, produced a pull request and drafted the customer followup after the fix shipped. That example captures where Vorflux's engineering work led: once agents can complete longer tasks, coordinating and starting the right work becomes its own bottleneck. Prasanna traces the progression from cloud coding sessions to persistent bots with a goal, an owner and a shared channel.

The foundation is six practical problems: reproducing a working development environment, investing more effort in planning, dividing tasks with dependencies, testing without returning to a laptop, reviewing from multiple angles, and keeping changes mergeable as the base branch moves. Browser tests, recordings and staging links give people something concrete to inspect. The second half shifts from those coding workflows to on call, CI and project management bots that respond to signals already present in the company. Prasanna also describes the failure mode of indiscriminate automation: noisy alerts, unwanted pull requests and growing token bills. His proposed controls are budgets, visible work, named ownership and increasing responsibility as results justify it. These are lessons and examples from building Vorflux, with a clear acknowledgment that the bots remain fallible and some responsibilities still belong with people.

title: You Can't Tell What an Agent Skill Will Do by Reading It - Roey Ben Chaim, Zenity
body:
An official diagnostic skill can read cloud credentials, contact identity services and probe an instance metadata endpoint. Those same actions can resemble an information stealer. Roey Ben Chaim of Zenity and the MATS Fellowship uses that ambiguity to explain why reading a SKILL.md file cannot establish what an agent will actually do. Instructions can fetch more instructions, installation scripts can pull in packages, and those packages can create processes whose effects never appear in the agent's own trace. The missing evidence is runtime behavior, collected inside a controlled environment.

Roey walks through the evolution of an agent detonation chamber: a sandbox, a world builder that supplies the services a skill expects, an operator that exercises different paths, and instrumentation for processes, filesystem activity and network traffic. He then follows concrete cases involving chained skill installation, a misleading package name, persistence, hooks and remotely fetched prompts. One investigation traces a lookalike project through a downloaded payload to credential harvesting, showing why the complete chain matters more than the entry file. The examples illustrate both malicious behavior and legitimate activity that can trigger suspicion; they are not a claim that one scanner can classify every skill correctly. The engineering takeaway is to treat skills as software dependencies, inspect what they load, restrict their access, and preserve evidence of what executes beyond the model's visible conversation.

title: Give Your On-Call Its Own AI Teammate - Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi & Vlad Tsvang, Meta
body:
Twelve alerts fire at 2 a.m., and a useful assistant can still leave the engineer coordinating every step. Meta's on call team uses that illustrative scenario to explain a different design: one AI teammate per rotation, with shared context, its own identity, persistent memory and explicit limits on what it can do. Swaapnika Motapothula, Chinmay Gandhi and Vlad Tsvang describe a system that connects alerts, tickets, incident history and code changes instead of leaving each automation with its own isolated view. The goal is to bring a human a decision with supporting evidence and a proposed action.

Their autonomy ladder starts with investigation, advances to drafting fixes for approval, and permits selected lower criticality work only when mistakes are cheap to detect and the agent has earned trust on that action. Critical production decisions stay with people, and code changes still go through normal review and continuous integration. The team explains the automation loops for triage, recovery from stuck runs, and shift handoffs, plus how team specific skills and memory carry expertise between engineers. Corrections reopen work and become new evidence, while memory entries can be promoted or retired. The examples show the intended experience rather than a measured time savings result: the speakers explicitly reserve that claim for a rigorous study. Their next steps focus on accepted mitigations, better feedback and earning further autonomy.

title: Your Agent Hates Your CLI - Ayush Bhardwaj, Allos AI
body:
An agent can hide a failed test behind a successful shell pipeline. It can also trim away the error message and confidently report that everything worked. Ayush Bhardwaj examined roughly 20,000 tool calls from his own coding sessions and found a product roadmap in the commands agents wrote immediately afterward. Repeated uses of head, tail, grep and Python showed where tools returned too much information, exposed the wrong fields, or made the agent reconstruct the same query again. The examples come from his own traces and his chat history CLI, which lets agents retrieve context from earlier coding sessions.

The fixes are small and concrete: return the messages around a search match, offer compact search results, inspect several sessions in one call, and put a useful failure summary at the end of the output. But implementing a flag does little if the skill file still teaches the old interface. In Ayush's case study, agents kept passing a flag that did nothing until the instructions changed. He also explains how to turn recorded calls into replay tests, reserve examples for evaluation, and check whether better output actually improves answers and reduces turns. Smaller responses alone do not establish a faster or cheaper workflow. The useful feedback is already in the transcript: what the agent tried, what it discarded, and what it had to ask again.

title: Every Correction You Give Your Agent Is Data - Brian Douglas, Paper Compute
body:
A Rust program can compile and still violate the decisions an experienced teammate would catch immediately. Brian Douglas finds that missing knowledge in moments when engineers push back on their coding agents. At Paper Compute, he captures agent sessions, labels corrections and uses those traces to recover the reasoning that otherwise disappears inside a local coding harness. His example starts with a gap in his own Rust expertise: accepting plausible generated code leads to objections later, when a teammate reviews the pull request. Those earlier objections become useful training material only if someone preserves and labels them.

Brian demonstrates session capture with Tapes and Paper Console, then runs a Twin Review prototype against a pull request using examples of a teammate's feedback. He discusses labels for pushback, successful sessions and regressions, and shows how the same records can support skills, evaluations or model adaptation. The prototype is a demonstration, not a measured comparison against an independent evaluation set, and Brian corrects himself during the recording to clarify that Twin Review is not publicly released because its data is sensitive. His practical starting point is simpler than training a model: collect the traces you already generate, find the corrections that encode your team's conventions, and turn those into a skill you can test. The durable asset is the connection between a decision, the expert's objection and the resulting outcome.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
body:
Gemini 4 Carbon is now available
Today, we’re making Gemini 4 Carbon available to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers. Carbon is our strongest model with frontier performance in cybersecurity capabilities and long-horizon agentic workflows across complex knowledge work, software engineering, and scientific reasoning.
[Two weeks ago](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/), we released Carbon to a set of cybersecurity defenders via our [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/). Following our recent launch of [Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/), Carbon pushes the frontier even further. Argon remains the ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work, while Carbon is built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence like complex, multi-step coding and debugging and open-ended scientific research and discovery — using more tokens than Argon to explore thoroughly, reason deeply, and run extended verification loops.
Across independent benchmarks designed to test model performance in real workflows, Carbon pairs frontier accuracy with practical production economics. It ranks #1 on [CursorBench 4.0](https://cursor.com/cursorbench), [Perplexity’s WANDR](https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/wandr-benchmark-evaluating-research-agents-that-must-search-wide-and-deep), and [Zapier’s AutomationBench](https://zapier.com/benchmarks) at more than 2X lower cost per task compared to the next best external model.
To put Carbon’s capabilities to work on larger and complex projects, we’re [previewing](http://antigravity.google/blog/gemini-4-carbon-in-google-antigravity/) /swarm
in Google Antigravity, turning a single prompt into a coordinated team of agents you can track in real time. Developers can assign Carbon to roles that demand the deepest reasoning, like architectural design, coordination, and auditing, while pairing it with faster, lighter models across parallel isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers that test every change.
Gemini 4 Carbon is available via the API in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/prompts/new_chat?model=gemini-4-carbon) and [Gemini for business](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise) for all paying developers and enterprises, at the same [introductory price](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing)
[1](#footnote-1)
as Gemini 4 Argon ($2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens). It is also rolling out to all [Google AI Ultra subscribers](https://one.google.com/about/google-ai-plans) in [Google Antigravity](https://antigravity.google/), the [Gemini app](http://gemini.google.com/), and [AI Mode in Search](http://aimode.google/).
Higher-precision knowledge work, artifact generation, and data analysis
Across legal, finance, and enterprise operations, Gemini 4 Carbon combines frontier visual understanding, reasoning, and exhaustive retrieval to synthesize grounded insights across large sets of dense documents and data. It follows strict schemas and formatting to generate polished and precise spreadsheets, presentations, and reports.
Existing benchmarks don’t adequately capture how agents reason natively over dense files with charts, images, blueprints, schematics, and tables, so we partnered with Artificial Analysis to launch the new [Multimodal Knowledge Agent](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/mka) (MKA) benchmark that tests a model’s multimodal performance in agentic workflows. Carbon ranks #2 while being more than 6X lower in average cost per task compared to the top performing model.
In pre-release evaluations, Carbon matched the performance of the best model tested on deep financial research on Hebbia’s E2E Financial Agentic evaluation, and ranked at the top out of 23 frontier model configurations on Balyasny Asset Management’s General Financial Intelligence benchmark, spanning legal expertise, agentic tool use and execution, coding and data engineering, and perception and context understanding.
Improved agentic coding, full stack development, and 3D and UI design
Carbon performs exceptionally well on engineering tasks that require multi-agent collaboration like multi-package migrations, cross-subsystem root-cause investigations, and complex architectural redesigns. For web app development, it runs build-and-verify loops, recovers from errors, and checks both its code and the rendered UI to produce complete, working applications. Stronger visual design, spatial reasoning, and attention to environmental detail also carry over to 3D game development and creative coding.
Frontier cybersecurity capabilities
Gemini 4 Carbon for cyber delivers our strongest cybersecurity capabilities to date, giving security teams the end-to-end intelligence they need in protecting critical software. When accessed through the Fairwind Program, Carbon leads on key benchmarks across finding (SEC-bench Pro), exploiting (ExploitGym), and patching (CWE-bench v1) vulnerabilities: inspecting software, tracing how flaws can be chained together across systems, and generating verified root-cause patches.
Early testers inside and outside of Google are already seeing strong results with Carbon for cyber in practice.
[In Project Fortify](https://cloud.google.com/transform/how-google-does-it-using-agents-help-find-track-and-fix-vulnerabilities), Google’s autonomous system spanning scanning, triage, and remediation, Carbon hit 100% recall on scanning and 95% precision on triage, on our internal benchmark. On Open Source code repository testing we see an over 25% relative improvement on Argon's already strong recall rate, surfacing previously undetected, real-world logic flaws. Bringing these gains across Google, one of the world’s largest users of open-source software, helps secure both our own systems and the broader ecosystem.- Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research (CVR) team recently used Carbon to prove that two bugs in a popular open-source software were in fact exploitable vulnerabilities, comparable in severity to the recent
[PHP2Shell exploit](https://www.wiz.io/blog/php2shell-php-rce). By using Carbon to build a proof of concept, CVR helped maintainers re-classify the bug as critical and swiftly issue a patch. Details will be shared after the responsible disclosure process completes. - As part of Wiz’s
[Scan for Good](https://www.wiz.io/blog/scan-for-good-critical-ai-exposures)program, the team used Carbon to assess vulnerabilities in public digital infrastructure. For example, when scanning two major SaaS providers, the model uncovered 0-day vulnerabilities in under two hours compressing weeks of vulnerability research to a single afternoon. The team partnered with the impacted organizations to remediate in record time, helping to mitigate potential impact on tens of thousands of companies.
Stronger scientific and mathematical reasoning
Gemini 4 Carbon shows strongly improved performance in reasoning across physics, math, and life sciences, synthesizing experimental data, testing hypotheses, and reasoning through multi-step domain problems. For drug toxicity research company Axiom Bio, Carbon is now the leading model in performance for translational science, finding novel mechanisms of toxicity they hadn’t found previously. Axiom is now moving their production scientific analyses and agents to both Carbon and Argon to unlock the creation of safer drugs.
Researchers across Google have been using Carbon in Google Antigravity to accelerate their work:
- Code verification: Researchers built a new agentic framework for formal verification called AlphaProof Code and put it to work on a major security challenge:
[mathematically proving the actual code underlying the cryptographic protocol of Signal](https://deepmind.google/blog/introducing-alphaproof-code). Using Carbon alongside other models, our researchers translated security goals to mathematical theorems. AlphaProof Code agents then used Carbon to generate millions of lines of code in Lean, a computer language for writing mathematical proofs, helping them prove key security properties in weeks — a task that historically takes expert teams years. The result indicates Carbon’s potential to unlock scalable formal verification, long considered a gold-standard approach to building secure software. - Enzyme assay development: Provided with only lab notebooks and raw data, Carbon went beyond standard analysis to surface hard-to-interpret data anomalies, which it used to diagnose subtle wet lab experimental artifacts such as incomplete automated mixing in deep wells, leading to substantially improved reproducibility. Moreover Carbon improved methods to deconvolute chromatography peaks and caught trace sample carryover in research instruments, significantly accelerating the development of new assays and tightening the feedback loop between computation and the bench.
- Protein structure prediction: Structure prediction models like AlphaFold 3 use Multiple Sequence Alignments (MSAs) of evolutionary relatives to help infer how amino acid chains fold. As a result they often struggle on understudied, viral, microbial, and eukaryotic proteins that have very few matches in standard databases. Working in a multi-agent setup, our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon to autonomously discover remote homologs across petabase-scale unannotated sequence archives, environmental and viral sequence catalogs, and 3D structure databases. For example, across 7 low-homolog protein families from the CASP17 blind test set, Carbon increased the number of homologs retrieved by 40-fold on average, greatly increasing the information available to structure prediction models without need for retraining. While broader benchmarking is still underway, addressing this upstream search bottleneck potentially offers a promising path toward modeling hard-to-characterize regions of the proteome.
Four weeks ago, we opened applications to give 10,000 scientists access to Argon in Google Antigravity free of charge for six months to accelerate the pace of their research, and we’ve onboarded thousands of scientists already. Today, we’re expanding access to Carbon for current and future participants, and going forward, the program will continue providing access to our latest frontier models as they become available. [Applications remain open](https://forms.gle/WvmBbPvRbpKG1BPn9) and onboarding continues on a weekly rolling basis, subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection.
Progress in model safety and security
With each new model release, we continue to strengthen our safety and security mitigations, agentic misuse prevention, model alignment, and harm reduction proportionately with model capability.
Because Gemini 4 Carbon introduces stronger cyber capabilities we build on Argon’s [strong safety and security stack](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/gemini-4-model-safety-security/) to fortify robustness to misuse and prompt injection.
- Mitigating frontier safety misuse risks: We’ve strengthened our misuse safeguards to help ensure stronger defensive reasoning does not translate into offensive risk. In simulated cyberattack testing environments seeded with ExploitBench and CyScenarioBench, Carbon blocked 99% of attack trajectories from our adaptive red-teaming agent that can iteratively revisit its attack plans after each block. The Carbon safeguards lowered the per-attempt breach rate to just 0.8% (down from 3.1% on Argon). Our safeguards also lowered the automated cyberattack query success rate to 2.17% in Gray Swan’s testing, compared to 9.86% on Argon. And external testing by Trajectory Labs found zero new universal jailbreaks across 132 hours and over 13,000 requests.

title: NVIDIA Expands Open Source Commitment With OpenShell Donation and New AI Infrastructure
body:
Kubernetes, the open source system that manages how applications run across thousands of AI factories, has become the foundation for AI, and the demands on it are only growing.
To help meet them, NVIDIA is deepening its commitment to open source at [KubeCon + CloudNativeCon](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/kubecon-and-cloudnative-con-north-america/), the flagship conference for the Kubernetes and cloud-native communities.
NVIDIA is contributing [NVIDIA OpenShell](https://github.com/ai-openshell), an open source runtime for securing and governing autonomous agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), a nonprofit that is part of the Linux Foundation and the host of KubeCon. As a CNCF Sandbox project, OpenShell will be governed by the organizations building it into their products and strengthened by the expertise of security professionals worldwide.
NVIDIA is also contributing to [Agent Substrate](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/agent-substrate-advancing-kubernetes-for-agents-at-scale/), an open source Google-led framework for operating long-running agent workloads at scale on Kubernetes that has been accepted into the CNCF Sandbox.
Additionally, NVIDIA announced new components of the [NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/products/dsx/): [NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/manage-kubernetes-clusters-for-gpu-infrastructure-with-nvidia-kubernetes-engine), NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes and [NVIDIA Snapshot](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/start-and-restore-gpu-workloads-in-seconds-with-nvidia-snapshot). These tools help teams deploy, manage and scale GPU infrastructure on Kubernetes for AI factories.
Together, these advancements mark a step forward in making Kubernetes the leading foundation for AI workloads at scale — empowering developers to build safer, more efficient AI infrastructure for the future.
Securing AI Agents in the Open
NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF puts security infrastructure for autonomous agents in the community’s hands to build, inspect and improve — accelerating development and hardening its safeguards.
“The cloud-native community has a new infrastructure challenge: giving agents secure environments in which to operate,” said Jim Zemlin, CEO of the Linux Foundation. “NVIDIA’s contribution of OpenShell to CNCF gives developers a shared foundation to build on and an opportunity to shape how agent security evolves. Bringing this work into the community enables broader collaboration on infrastructure that will be critical to the next generation of cloud-native applications.”
OpenShell gives organizations control over what AI agents can do. It applies deterministic controls to agent activity, so teams can enforce policies as agents use tools, access inference services and execute workloads. Its extensible architecture lets teams connect their own compute, inference providers, credential storage and monitoring tools. This allows organizations to apply governance across different deployment environments while integrating OpenShell with their existing enterprise systems.
Hundreds of organizations have put OpenShell to use, and the project has received tens of thousands of contributions in less than a year since launch.
Scaling Agent Execution on Kubernetes
Governing agents is only part of the challenge. Organizations also need to deploy them at scale.
NVIDIA is contributing to Agent Substrate, a Google-originated project in the CNCF Sandbox, and ensuring it works with [NVIDIA Dynamo](https://developer.nvidia.com/dynamo) for model inference and [KAI Scheduler](https://kai-scheduler.dev/) for shared cluster resource allocation. This effort brings together agent execution, inference serving and resource scheduling on Kubernetes.
Agent Substrate preserves agent environments between tasks while releasing compute when agents are idle. By suspending and resuming those environments across a shared pool of agents, it lets teams scale agent workloads without keeping dedicated compute running for every session.
NVIDIA and Google are also collaborating on an integration of OpenShell and Agent Substrate, so enterprises can secure and govern agents across clouds and on-premises systems.
Building an Open Foundation for AI Factories
AI factories need to offer customers managed Kubernetes services while retaining control of their infrastructure, software and customer experience. Three new open source projects extend the DSX AI Factory Platform to make Kubernetes easier to run and inference faster to scale.
[NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvke) (NVKE) and [NVIDIA Kubernetes Recipes](https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/nvkr) (NVKR) — now available in public preview — provide open source building blocks for delivering managed Kubernetes services on GPU infrastructure. They automate cluster lifecycle management and provide signed, version-pinned images.
NVKE and NVKR are launching with ecosystem support that extends their reach across AI infrastructure platforms and cloud services. Mirantis, Netris, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Spectro Cloud and vCluster, together with Firmus and SK Telecom, have aligned with NVIDIA on integration plans to bring NVKE and NVKR capabilities into their offerings.
[NVIDIA Snapshot](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/snapshot) addresses the challenge of bringing additional inference capacity online quickly. Loading models and warming up workloads can delay scaling and recovery. The open source, modular component restores checkpointed replicas in seconds, without model reload or warmup, supporting faster startup, recovery and elasticity for inference and agentic workloads on Kubernetes.
Design partners [Crusoe](https://www.crusoe.ai/resources/blog/nvidia-snapshot-crusoe-cloud) and Saturn Cloud have evaluated Snapshot on their own workloads using [NVIDIA HGX B300 systems](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/hgx/). Crusoe, an upstream contributor to Snapshot, tested GLM-5.3 on Crusoe Cloud and reduced the time for the workload to become ready from roughly eight minutes to 31 seconds. Saturn Cloud, a token factory platform, benchmarked Snapshot for scale-from-zero inference and reduced vLLM startup times from between two and 8.5 minutes to six and 34 seconds.
Learn more by joining [NVIDIA at KubeCon](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/kubecon-and-cloudnative-con-north-america/).
