Adobe Firefly, the AI creative studio, lets you describe what you want to create, then review the Adobe Creative Agent’s plan before it gets to work using Creative Cloud tools.
You stay in control from first idea to finished result.
[Try it today in the Firefly Assistant!]
Just look at that chart above. It’s crazy (1) how accurately it’s drawn and (2) how the closely related the trend of revenue, valuation, and how much they’re in my eyes and ears over time is.
But their product isn’t ‘sexy’.
If we look at the next super accurate chart of how hard companies have to try vs how boring their product is, we can see how Ramp and others move from the expected baseline.
They get it. They have the illustrious ‘taste’ factor. They have fun with it.
For example, who’s the world’s most famous accountant?
Kevin from The Office (US) of course. So they did the only reasonable thing they could. Stick him in a glass box in New York and have him process 600k expense reports.
200+ Million people saw this stunt. A couple even got married in the box...wtf!?
They also recognise that the ‘exhaust’ from these efforts turn into great content too. In these receipts sections ([on the live post](https://sessions.bensbites.com/ramp)) you can click to see the real videos and images.
Then they doubled down on Kevin (Brian), or more accurately 10x’d him by sending 9 lookalikes with him to the Super Bowl. Plus also hosted a Brian-themed party in SF where people came dressed as him with a lookalike competition where the winners got Super Bowl tickets. They sold bald caps called ‘Brian Hair’ too - reminds me of the Pitbull bald-cap mania.
Oh and of course he was in the ad itself.
A year before the Brians, they made their first Super Bowl ad in a week.
I’ve been diving into [Colossus](https://colossus.com/) magazine recently, they do awesome in-depth profiles of people and companies. Well worth reading. But outside of the awesome profiles I actually saw awesome display ads.
I’ve never said ‘awesome display ads’ in my life, and doubt anyone else has either. But these ads were made (assuming with the help of AI) to be super personalised and unique to the content of the post itself.
These were my favourite:
They came in like a wrecking ball 🎶 to launch Ramp Treasury.
To launch bill pay, they put on a Broadway musical.
Last month, they got Tony Hawk on a ramp outside the NYSE.
These stunts make noise for a wide audience but they understand their customers deeply. Not just CFOs/Controllers but founders and developers.
They sponsor a lot of podcasts. This is where I think they’ve entered my brain more often than I’m comfortable admitting.
They also turn up in odd places. I’ve heard of “test new ad channels before other companies get there” but I’ve never seen an ad in a church bulletin before.
Last Christmas, they put Claude Code in RollerCoaster Tycoon.
They built their own coding agent, Inspect. Which they used internally for a while before opening it up for others to use.
And a model router.
And Glass, a knowledge platform for teams.
There are so many areas where I may become a Ramp customer that is not their core offering. But it feels like Amazon starting with books, seeing what other people want to buy and adding that too.
They build with AI tools, they track spend, they ship tools to help their team move faster, more efficiently and spend less. All of their customers want that too, so why not productise it. And land some new customers in the process.
How do they do it all? Eric, the CEO, talks about [empathy and then taste](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gFWwB3z8ags) as two values for Ramp. Another mentions [velocity](https://www.lennysnewsletter.com/p/how-ramp-builds-product) as a key component of their culture.
They switched up how they do marketing, what products they build for customers and also how the organisation works.
And the stunts come from a team of seven.
If we layer everything onto the super-accurate chart we started with, it’s interesting to see how velocity, taste and experimentation really helped accelerate growth for Ramp.
But more interestingly it’s all after a down-round in valuation where usually all the weird things are cut away in favour of doing what ‘normal’ companies should do.
And that may be why Ramp is doing so well...
Ramp don’t sponsor me (maybe they should?!) but I’ve just been floored by how much fun they seem to be having. Their whole strategy for the last few years is so smart. To me it’s truly tasteful in how they’re doing what they’re doing, how they understand the game of attention, and how to reach the customers they want - in and out of their peripheral ‘TAM’.
Quick bites
[Fable 5.2](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2)is out - very powerful, often slow, and you need to encourage it a lot (is this a dog?!). I think stick to medium/low reasoning for nearly everything.An
[open-source Slack](https://github.com/NYLLON-SOFTWARE/ember-cloudflare)that you can run with one click.A look into how
[Claude dreams](https://www.anthropic.com/research/components-of-agent-memory)for a better memory.Emil’s
[UI skills](https://aiforui.dev/skills)now have before-and-after examples and prompts. I use Emil’s skills for all my design work.How does a card company become
[a product factory](https://x.com/alexrkonrad/status/2118400094672409046)?[Executor v2 is out](https://executor.sh/)- This is my go to tool for integrations (i love it so much i hounded rhys to invest!)
This is one of the most creative and informative things i've seen in a long time. Well done! Keep em coming.
they are definitely an awesome marketing example to study
great animations, Ben!

title: We’re bringing Adobe’s creative and productivity tools closer to your everyday Google apps.
body:
We’re bringing Adobe’s creative and productivity tools closer to your everyday Google apps.
Today at Adobe MAX, we announced we’re expanding our partnership with Adobe.
Switching between apps to edit a PDF or fine-tune an image can quickly break your focus. Our partnership will bring Adobe’s creative and productivity tools directly into the Google products you use every day. It will also bring Google’s frontier AI models into Adobe’s apps. Here’s what’s coming:
- Work faster with PDFs: You’ll soon have a direct pathway from Google Drive and Gmail into Adobe Acrobat, surfaced as a suggested app across both services, including an “Edit with” entry point in file previews.
- Create right where you search and chat: Adobe is expanding its connectors in Gemini and Gemini Enterprise with Acrobat and additional creative tools. Adobe will also bring its creative tools to AI Mode in Google Search.
- Powering creatives and enterprises: Businesses will be able to use Adobe’s CX Enterprise Coworker agent in Gemini Enterprise — an AI assistant that helps teams design graphics, work with PDFs, and launch marketing campaigns without switching apps.
- Exploring editing experiences with DeepMind: Adobe and Google DeepMind will explore new editing capabilities for creative professionals, starting with an image model for Photoshop that could enable near-real-time edits.

title: Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare.
body:
Google Cloud launches Gemini for healthcare.
Google Cloud [has announced Gemini for healthcare](https://www.googlecloudpresscorner.com/2026-11-10-Google-Cloud-Launches-Gemini-for-Healthcare), an AI solution engineered to unify fragmented clinical, operational, and administrative systems. Moving beyond simple information retrieval, it enables healthcare teams to turn siloed data into coordinated action.
Clinicians lose nearly [28 hours each week](https://www.googlecloudpresscorner.com/2024-10-17-New-Study-from-Google-Cloud-and-The-Harris-Poll-Reports-How-Generative-AI-Can-Tackle-Administrative-Burdens-in-U-S-Healthcare) to paperwork and administrative tasks, fueling burnout and straining budgets. By integrating specialized skills and data connectors with existing third-party systems, the platform brings together critical information from electronic health records, billing platforms, clinical guidelines, and Medicare datasets.
Gemini for healthcare reasons across this context to orchestrate and execute complex, multi-step workflows — such as medical records synthesis and prior authorization review — within defined guardrails and with appropriate human oversight. Initially available in preview alongside launch partners including HCA Healthcare, Highmark Health, and Northwell Health, it resolves bottlenecks and reclaims valuable staff time for patient care. Learn more [on the Cloud blog](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/gemini-for-healthcare).

title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
body:
Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signalâs cryptographic protocol â long considered to be a grand security challenge
Today, weâre sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages.
This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code, a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verificationâmathematically proving code runs correctly without flawsâis the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive.
Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI.
How we verified Signal
AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it.
First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signalâs security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by [Gemini Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/) did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.
Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human â just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.
Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them.
But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties â such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised â down to the exact code running on devices. Because real-world vulnerabilities often hide in the gap between design and implementation, bridging this gap makes these proofs vastly more complex.
Even at this complexity, our verification process took just four weeks â a task that historically takes expert teams years â proving that Signal's core cryptographic code delivers the security protections our experts specified.
To confirm that AlphaProof Code can tell correct code from buggy code, we reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code. In both cases, the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure.
While prior formal verification work has necessarily focused on smaller scopes, this new approach enables a significant expansion. Traditionally, verifying that production code strictly matches its cryptographic design required extensive manual effort, making the use of AI agents to automatically translate live code into valid Lean theorems a great breakthrough. As AI-driven security threats grow, having the core Signal protocol rigorously verified with automated theorem proving gives us even greater confidence that our code delivers on its privacy guarantees.
The future of security
Achieving this long-standing challenge demonstrates how AI can bring elite security assurance to businesses, governments, and critical infrastructure, helping defend against agent-driven cyber threats.
Verifying Signal's core cryptography lays the groundwork to secure other vital systems, from medical device firmware to power grid software.
Scaling these techniques requires continued research. Paired with automated defense agents like [CodeMender](https://deepmind.google/blog/introducing-codemender-an-ai-agent-for-code-security/), formal verification can help counter the speed and scale of modern cyber threats to create software with mathematical proof that its protections work.
We are open-sourcing our [formal verification artifacts](https://google-deepmind.github.io/code-verification) for community use. Read the technical paper below.
Acknowledgements
This research was developed by Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli.
We thank Eric Wieser for help with open-sourcing our code, Owen Jones for program management support, and MartÃn Abadi, Christopher Henson, Katerina Hristova, Henryk Michalewski, Jonathan Protzenko and George Tsoukalas for helpful discussions. We thank Signal's Rolfe Schmidt, Michael Rosenberg, and Ehren Kret for their feedback on our methodology. We also thank Tulsee Doshi, Four Flynn, Kate Olszewska, Alicia Huang, Andy Liu, Benoit Schillings, Raluca Ada Popa, Melvin Johnson, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Demis Hassabis, and Sundar Pichai for their support of the project.

title: Helping caregivers use AI in everyday life
body:
Caregiving often means juggling schedules, keeping track of information, and finding support while balancing work and family life. During National Family Caregivers Month, we’re helping caregivers gain AI skills that can make some of those everyday tasks easier, giving them more time to focus on the people they care for.

On November 10, OpenAI Academy, in collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, is hosting the AI Skills Jam for Caregivers & Community Health: a free, in-person learning experience designed to help caregivers use ChatGPT confidently, safely, and practically. These nationwide events will bring together participants across five U.S. cities, including individual and family caregivers, caregiver support organizations, and people living with chronic or serious health conditions:

- Oakland, California
- Tampa, Florida
- Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania
- Atlanta, Georgia
- Detroit, Michigan
An OpenAI analysis estimates that more than 40 million weekly ChatGPT messages about healthcare in the U.S. ask about healthcare for someone else. At the workshops, participants will explore how ChatGPT can help with resource navigation, peer support, and caregiver support, including how to:

- organize caregiver schedules and checklists
- turn trusted educational resources into plain-language materials
- find community resources
- prepare support group discussion guides
Participants will also learn how to use AI responsibly, including protecting personal information and understanding the limits of these tools. Participants will also learn when to consult healthcare professionals and how AI tools should complement, not replace, medical, legal, or financial advice.****OpenAI facilitators and mentors will offer hands-on support throughout the workshops. No coding or technical background is required.

The Jam brings this learning into local communities, where caregivers can practice alongside peers and share the everyday challenges they hope these tools can help address. Our partners bring deep expertise and experience supporting people living with serious illness and their families. Their perspectives, together with those of caregivers themselves, will help connect the day’s learning to the needs of each community.

The AI Skills Jam is part of OpenAI Academy’s broader work to make AI practical and accessible to everyone. It builds on previous events we’ve hosted with nonprofits, small businesses, K–12 educators, and older adults.

We are grateful to Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, American Diabetes Association®, and the caregivers and community health organizations joining us across the country. Their questions, ideas, and experiences will help shape future learning resources and ensure these tools are useful in the daily work of supporting others.

# Introducing Businesses in ChatGPT

Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT

Share

Claim your business in ChatGPT

- [Claim your business in ChatGPT](#claim-your-business-in-chatgpt)

- [Bringing agentic capabilities to businesses](#bringing-agentic-capabilities-to-businesses)
- [Building a home for businesses in ChatGPT](#building-a-home-for-businesses-in-chatgpt)

We’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a new way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through [Business Hub⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/business-hub?utm_source=openai&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=business_agents_launch&utm_content=smb_launch_primary_cta), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with users via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S.

Together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star.

## Claim your business in ChatGPT

In Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, update key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a new way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details.

Any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog.



## Understand how people engage with your business

Business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share.

We’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share users’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds.



## Bringing agentic capabilities to businesses

After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings.

When a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information.



For customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers.

Businesses can also [sponsor their Business Agent⁠](https://openai.com/index/reimagining-advertising-with-ai/) and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses.

Business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories [here⁠](https://openai.com/policies/business-agents-policy/).



## Building a home for businesses in ChatGPT

As people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we plan to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs.

As the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses new ways to participate and grow.

[Learn more and⁠](https://openai.com/business/businesses-in-chatgpt?utm_source=openai&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=business_agents_launch&utm_content=smb_launch_primary_cta) [ claim your business in ChatGPT.⁠](https://openai.com/business/businesses-in-chatgpt?utm_source=openai&utm_medium=blog&utm_campaign=business_agents_launch&utm_content=smb_launch_primary_cta)

title: Amazon saves millions by replacing Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider
body:
For a while, Amazon and AWS teams relied on Claude Sonnet 4.6 to label tickets in an internal system without breaking the bank.
Sonnet 4.6 fit the goldilocks choice of balancing intelligence with cost. Considering it dealt with one
of the world’s largest internal ticketing systems, the nine month old model did well. However, two
Amazon engineers recently swapped out Sonnet 4.6 for
[Strands Decider](/blog/introducing-strands-decider/), a decision model we launched a month ago, that
performed just as well at 98% less cost. This change will save millions of dollars of token costs in
a year.
Carr and Mehul, who work on the internal ticketing system, walk through how this happened below.
Replacing an LLM’s job with a decision model
We had Sonnet 4.6 labeling tickets at enormous scale. The tickets could be customer escalations, capacity requests, automated alarms, security findings, or anything else across the company that needed to fit within 20 category types. The agent ran with a long system prompt on every ticket, generating JSON and reasoning against a fixed set of labels.
A decision model can’t generate text. It’s first given some state and a question with a set of options, then the decision model returns a probability for each option plus a confidence score. We saw this method fit perfectly with ticket labeling: the state is the ticket, the options are the label catalog.
We started with the original [Strands Decider 2B](/blog/introducing-strands-decider/). On a test set of
tickets, the [E4B Gemma 4 build](/blog/strands-decider-gemma-4-models/) got clearly better results, so
we switched to it. Afterwards, we tuned how confident the model needed to be before applying a label.
The results showed E4B beating production Sonnet on a separate set of our tickets.
We ran E4B on SageMaker ml.g5.xlarge
instances (one A10G, 24 GB each). The model used about 19 GiB,
and one request took about 640 ms on one instance. The endpoint autoscales with traffic, but its network
was isolated, preventing outbound access to the container. SageMaker copies the model weights in from
S3 before start-up.
Customers can do this too! Apart from our ticketing APIs, everything in the path is a standard AWS service. Ticket events land in an SQS queue that then triggers a Lambda function. It reads the ticket data and calls the model, a SageMaker AI Endpoint with Strands Decider. AppConfig holds the switch (described below), and CloudWatch carries the logs, metrics and alarms. The stack is defined in CDK with deployment stages for Beta, Gamma, and Prod.
Running Sonnet 4.6 and Strands Decider on the same tickets
We didn’t want to flip a switch and hope. The labeling Lambda reads a three-way setting from AWS AppConfig on every message:
BEDROCK
: Sonnet labels every ticket, but Strands Decider isn’t called.DUAL
: Both the Sonnet and Strands Decider models are called in parallel. The results from the Sonnet model are applied to the ticket and compared with Strands Decider results.DECIDER
: Strands Decider labels every ticket and Bedrock isn’t called.
What we measured
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | Strands Decider E4B | % Improvement | |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average time per call | 4,215 ms | 897 ms | 78% |
| Input tokens per ticket | 6,554 | 2,009 | |
| Output tokens per ticket | 170 | 1 | |
| Total tokens, per ticket | 6,724 | 2,010 | 70% |
The token drop had two sources. Strands Decider produced one output, the choice, instead of a JSON answer. Its prompt was also much shorter than Sonnet 4.6’s. Production’s label descriptions alone are longer than Strands Decider’s 4,096-token window, so we rewrote each of the 20 labels as a one- or two-sentence criterion and sent them as the options of a single choice question, plus a “none” option. The ticket data is the same as what Sonnet gets, except that on long tickets Strands Decider drops the oldest comments to fit.
Below is a graph of our Lambda durations on the day we turned off the Sonnet usage, showing the average Lambda execution duration dropping 74%.
What it costs
At published us-east-1 on-demand prices:
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Bedrock, global endpoint) | Strands Decider E4B (SageMaker, ml.g5.xlarge ) | |
|---|---|---|
| Price | $3.00 per 1M input, $15.00 per 1M output tokens | $1.408 per instance-hour |
| Per ticket | $0.0222 | about $0.0005 |
| Per million tickets | about $22,200 | about $500 |
Sonnet’s cost per ticket comes straight from the token counts above. Strands Decider’s depends on how busy each instance is. At about 640 ms per request, one instance can handle about 5,600 tickets an hour, which would be $250 per million tickets at full use. We keep headroom for bursts, and in practice it comes to about $500 per million. That is about 44 times cheaper than Sonnet, a 98% reduction.
These are published list prices. They leave out the Lambda, which also runs for less time per ticket now.
One thing that surprised us was that JSON key order changed the answer. Sending the same content with keys in a different order moved the output probabilities by up to 0.19. We now send every request with sorted keys, so if you serve a decision model behind an API, check this before you compare runs.
Our lessons
This worked because the task is a closed choice from a known catalog, the volume is high, and the latency of the old path mattered. If your labels need explanation text, if the catalog changes weekly, or if you can’t fit the useful context into a few thousand tokens, a decision model probably can’t replace the LLM’s job.
The part we’d copy regardless of model is the three-way switch. Running both on real traffic, then judging every disagreement, told us more than any offline eval would have. It also meant going back was a 45-second config change.
The world of agents gets a lot more exciting (and less costly) with decision models. If you’re running
a classification agent, try the [Strands Decider repo](https://github.com/strands-labs/strands-decider)
and its
[serving notes](https://github.com/strands-labs/strands-decider/blob/0ac22a97e584f3ccf87cc9b8cc5fdbad57cdf534/docs/inference.md#gemma-4-models).

# Closing the AI guidance gap in education

Drawing on new ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.

[Read the report(opens in a new window)](https://assets.ctfassets.net/kftzwdyauwt9/3w97q66WFq2swJk1WvfN5C/a9bc88b2b5fbdd7e4abf029585c6ef2f/responsible-ai-in-education.pdf)

Loading…

Share

AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the [OECD’s Andreas Schleicher⁠(opens in a new window)](https://oecdedutoday.com/generative-ai-and-student-learning-what-the-pisa-data-reveal/), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems.

Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions.

This report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence.

Three early patterns are emerging from this work:

- **Country partnerships offer context-specific lessons.** Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale.
- **Closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent.**[New research from ThinkYoung,⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.thinkyoung.eu/aieducation) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use.
- **Early benefits for teachers are clear.** Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area.

Our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow.

We are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter.

At OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems.

The choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

*Tom Duff Gordon*

title: Singapore Airlines elevates travel & work with OpenAI technology
body:
Company size: EnterpriseRegion: Asia-Pacific & OceaniaIndustry: TravelProducts: API2x

Increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT) with AI-powered Kris chatbot

~10%

Reduction in average handling time for customer service representatives using AI-assisted tools.

~3x

Growth in Flight Recommender monthly users over the past year.

AI is becoming part of how Singapore Airlines serves customers, empowers employees, and builds technology. The airline uses the OpenAI API for customer-facing experiences and OpenAI models inside Jarvis, its governed internal AI platform for employees. It also uses OpenAI models in its software development workflows to deliver more personalized service, improve productivity, and help teams build more efficiently.

> “AI is central to our efforts to deliver more personalized customer experiences and improve productivity across the business. Together with OpenAI, we’re building AI-powered capabilities that make travel more intuitive and seamless for our customers, while enabling our employees to work more efficiently and effectively.”

—George Wang, Senior Vice President Information Technology, Singapore AirlinesAcross these deployments, Singapore Airlines pairs OpenAI models with orchestration, internal data controls, validation, and human review, giving teams a consistent way to bring AI into production workflows responsibly.

One of Singapore Airlines’ most visible AI applications is Kris, its customer-facing chatbot. After moving Kris from a traditional dialog-flow system to an LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API, Singapore Airlines saw a 2x increase in customer satisfaction.

Alongside that, the airline deployed AI-assisted tools for customer service representatives, including OpenAI API-powered call summarization, so that representatives spend less time on after-call work and more time on the customer. Singapore Airlines saw an approximately 10% reduction in average handling time for its customer service representatives.

In the earlier dialog-flow based chatbot design, every topic had to be mapped manually, and every flow had to be written in advance. That made coverage difficult to scale. If an intent was missing, the conversation was more likely to end up requiring support from a customer service representative, even when the customer’s request could have been handled through self-service.

Singapore Airlines moved Kris to a fully LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API. Instead of depending on predefined flows, the chatbot can interpret customer intent in natural language, ground answers in a knowledge base, manage multi-topic conversations, and hand over to a customer service representative with the relevant context when needed.

Today, customers use Kris for general queries, special requests, real-time flight disruption information, and selected transactional workflows. Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand its capabilities to include booking changes, baggage transactions, and more complex agentic interactions.

> “Kris has become a more capable self-service channel with OpenAI. It understands customer intent more naturally, helps customers get to the right answer, and gives customer service representatives clearer context when they need to step in.”

—Jude Anand Suresh, Vice President, Customer Service Information Technology, Singapore AirlinesFlight Recommender lets customers describe the trip they want in natural language instead of repeatedly adjusting filters, dates, and destinations. Usage has grown nearly 3x over the past year.

> “Flight Recommender makes travel discovery feel more like a natural conversation. Powered by OpenAI models through the API, it helps customers describe what they want and find relevant options faster.”

—Andy Koh, Vice President, Application Services (Sales, Marketing & Cargo), Singapore AirlinesBuilt on the OpenAI API, Flight Recommender uses an orchestration layer connected to fare and availability data. It interprets customer intent, calls the relevant tools, and returns personalized travel recommendations in natural language.

The team has also implemented guardrails for input and output validation, malicious or inappropriate query handling, hallucination reduction, PII handling, and authenticated access to only the context required for each query. Singapore Airlines is preparing to expand the experience into a more conversational chatbot interaction, where customers can keep refining travel ideas rather than restarting a search.

Beyond customer-facing experiences, Singapore Airlines is also using OpenAI models in parts of the software development lifecycle to help teams plan, refine, test, and review work more efficiently. Across selected software development lifecycle activities, teams have achieved productivity gains of up to 20%.

AI now runs through the entire delivery lifecycle and not just coding. Teams use generative AI models to support requirements refinement, stakeholder-session analysis, product specifications, edge-case identification, test-case creation, architecture review, and the breakdown of complex work into smaller, more testable tasks.

For one commercial feature, the team used the OpenAI API to challenge assumptions, identify ambiguous requirements and surface edge cases before development begins. Once those were well-defined, AI helped translate them into design options, implementation plans, test cases and then code generation.

During deployment and beyond, AI also helps to interpret how the system is behaving in production, and flagging issues that might otherwise go unnoticed. With AI active at every step of the workflow, team members have shifted from producing every artifact themselves, to directing, reviewing and validating what AI produces throughout the delivery lifecycle. This means they can focus on work that truly requires human judgement, such as prioritization, architecture, governance and stakeholder outcomes.

More broadly, OpenAI models are helping Singapore Airlines improve requirements quality, test coverage, and conformance with internal standards. Teams use these workflows to generate edge cases for testing, review architecture plans, and support human validation before work moves further through the development lifecycle.

Beyond engineering teams, Singapore Airlines is making AI accessible across the business through Jarvis, its internal AI platform. Powered by OpenAI models, Jarvis gives employees a governed way to use AI in their day-to-day work, from summarizing documents to creating custom workflows.

Employees use Jarvis to work across PDFs, Word documents, Excel files, PowerPoint decks, and other file types in a secure environment, while creating custom workflows and lightweight knowledge bases for their day-to-day work. Today, more than 60% of Singapore Airlines employees are using Jarvis monthly with adoption continuing to increase.

- **2x increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT)** after changing to AI-based Kris chatbot
- **~10% reduction in average handling time** for customer service agents using AI-assisted tools
- **3x growth** in monthly users of Flight Recommender, its customer-facing travel discovery tool, over the past year
Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand AI across customer and employee workflows. For Kris, the next phase is deeper self-service, with more transactional capabilities that help customers resolve requests directly in chat. Flight Recommender is moving toward a more conversational travel discovery experience, where customers can refine ideas over multiple turns rather than restarting a search.

With Jarvis available across the business, Singapore Airlines is focused on helping more employees put AI to work in their day-to-day roles. Together with its customer-facing innovations, this is helping the airline build a future where AI makes travel more seamless, employees more productive, and the business more responsive to changing needs.

title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
body:
10th November 2026 - Link Blog
[Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember](https://research.meta.ai/blog/muse-ember). Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:
[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.
For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.
The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:
| Model | Prompt size | Input ($/M) | Cached input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-6 Luna | ≤272k | $0.10 | $0.01 | $0.50 |
| >272k | $0.20 | $0.02 | $0.75 | |
| Muse Ember 1.0 | ≤200k | $0.10 | $0.004 | $0.50 |
| >200k | $0.30 | $0.012 | $1.50 | |
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | ≤100k | $0.10 | $0.01 | $0.50 |
| >100k | $0.50 | $0.05 | $2.50 |
But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.
For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis.
And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:
The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:
It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.
(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)
Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I [rendered six pelicans riding bicycles](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2Fc7666e8a54d84f724ac8121f9fa6cc4d). The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.
Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:
The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those [I got from Muse Wonder](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https://gist.github.com/simonw/185cff7ff0b11379725abf7f78d5d2b2), which is [40x the price](https://www.llm-prices.com/#sel=muse-ember-1.0%2Cmuse-ember-1.0-200k%2Cmuse-wonder-1.0) of Muse Ember.

[The Work at the Frontier series](#the-work-at-the-frontier-series) - [Citation](#citation) ## Why we study freelance work For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work. The stakes are substantial. Upwork’s [2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.upwork.com/press/releases/upworks-future-workforce-index-2026-how-ai-is-redefining-the-value-of-work-as-skilled-freelancing-accelerates) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its [previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.upwork.com/research/future-workforce-index-2025) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace. Freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT. ## What people use ChatGPT for vs. freelancers The mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.  Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.  *These activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.* ## Freelance demand is shifting as AI use grows Many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.  The remaining 20 work categories showed the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand. The comparison also captures how people currently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang. *Each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis shows the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.* ## Clients are asking for AI in more kinds of work and combining tasks in new ways By late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.  Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs. ### Example: Inside a project brief Some clients asked for **AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics** in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video. - AI-generated video - Video editing - Motion graphics ## The mix of work broadened across AI-related postings Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became **45% more diverse**—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21. Early 2023 14.6 Late 2025 21.2 *Upwork Marketplace postings through 2025. Shares are approximate and may not sum to 100% because of rounding.* *Upwork Marketplace postings through 2025.* ## AI-related projects have larger budgets and involve more work Although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work. *Upwork through April 2026. Adjusted estimates compare the two groups within the same type of work and the same posting month.* ## Conclusion ### AI may be changing both what clients hire freelancers to do and the scope of the projects they post AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous *Work at the Frontier* papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.  Because freelance projects turn over quickly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a new job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work. The findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects. ## The Work at the Frontier series The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.  [

title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
body:
10th November 2026
Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...]
If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:
This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.
In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it.
— [Prompting Claude Fable 5.2](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/prompting-claude-fable-5-2#say-who-owns-the-code), Anthropic documentation

title: The Agents Were Fine. Everything Around Them Broke. - Joey Wang, Harvey
body:
After 10,000 agent-written pull requests at Harvey, the agents weren't the problem. Everything around them was. Joey Wang tells three stories from Spectre, Harvey's internal cloud agent platform: letting engineers pick their own agent while one platform owns what happens after, making every action callable so agents can drive other agents, and what broke once they did. Expect an alert storm that spun up hundreds of tasks, a full cluster, a merge queue that couldn't keep up, and the fixes they built in response.

title: 60% of Our Data PRs Now Merge With No Human Review - Chetas Joshi, Robinhood
body:
Coding agents made data pipeline PRs cheap, and human review couldn't keep up. Chetas Joshi shows the hybrid reviewer agent Robinhood built for its data platform: deterministic checks run first, the model judges what scripts can't, and anything risky still goes to a person. Today about 60% of those PRs merge with no human review, saving roughly 132 engineering hours a month. He covers where they draw the line between agent and human, how they evaluate the reviewer itself, and what they got wrong.

title: How Curative is building a national provider network with agents on Claude
body:
How Curative is building a national provider network with agents on Claude
Curative’s deal-making agent negotiates 2,000+ provider contracts a week.
In our series, How startups build with Claude, we highlight how startups are transforming their industries with AI. In this article, we share how Curative built a hierarchy of agents on Claude to sign provider contracts about 50 times faster than its team did in 2025.
| The quick pitch | |
|---|---|
| Name | Curative |
| Founded | 2020; launched its health plan in 2022 |
| Founders | Fred Turner (CEO), Isaac Turner (CTO), Tami Wilson-Ciranna (President) |
| Stack | Claude Platform, Claude Code, bespoke claims system |
| Growth |
|
[Curative](https://curative.com/) sells health insurance to employers, with $0 copays and $0 deductibles for in-network care once members complete a Baseline Visit. Curative didn’t start out in insurance. It started as a lab startup and ended up processing 10% of all US COVID-19 tests according to their internal estimates. As a result, they started working with nearly every insurer in the country.
Its British founders, used to a system where patients don’t pay for care, saw inefficiencies and set out to build a payer focused on prevention. They realized they had significantly underestimated how hard building a national network would be.
“Sometimes naivety is good in startups, because you don’t know that it’s impossible. And then along the way you figure out a way to make it not impossible,” said Curative CEO Fred Turner. “Last year we signed 2,100 contracts, twice as many as we did the year before, but at 2,000 a year, we realized it would still be a 30-year build. There is a reason there are only a handful of national networks and they were all built about 30 years ago.”
Curative needed to accelerate contract signings, but hiring alone couldn’t close a gap that size.
Their solution: Gwen, an agent that works one provider deal from initial outreach to signature, surrounded by smaller agents that review its rates, check its messages, answer its questions, and escalate to humans for non-standard pricing.
Here is how they built it and what broke along the way.
Gwen: the provider contracts agent
Gwen works both inbound and outbound leads. Each run of Gwen handles a single provider, mostly on Claude Opus, so nothing from other deals influences it.
For example, if a practice fills in the form on Curative’s website, Gwen will research the practice and reply with proposed rates based on a purchased claims data set and price-transparency files payers are now required to publish. Gwen will show providers these market rate data to help with negotiations.
The rate reviewer runs on Sonnet. When Gwen wants to exceed its standard rate template, it writes out why, and the reviewer decides whether the rate makes sense.
“For a long time there was a big approval queue where Gwen had to get rates approved if she wanted to go a certain amount above the template, but we relaxed over time. Having a second agent review rates worked better than just giving Gwen more authority,” said Fred.
The Sonnet rate reviewer clears about two-thirds of Gwen’s requests and then anything non-standard goes to Fred for approval.
“The requests I see are from a big medical group or someone with a weird request that would come to me even if this wasn’t an agent-led motion,” said Fred.
Outbound deals take more persistence, because practices are busy. Some providers’ replies come after the fourteenth email and the ninth fax.
A judge, which runs on Haiku, reads every communication before it’s sent. Curative added it after Gwen copied providers on internal notes about how high it could go. A blocked message comes back with the reason, so Gwen can rewrite it and try again.
Each contract takes about 20 million tokens to complete, roughly a tenth of the original cost. These efficiencies enable one of Curative’s core strategies: signing smaller providers that have often been overlooked by larger networks.
“The agent will happily give you the same level of attention whether you are a large hospital system or if you’re a solo provider,” Fred explained. “From that agent’s perspective, this provider is its only focus.”
During negotiations, Gwen checks practice redlines against Curative’s policy document, then writes Python to merge both sides’ changes into a final document.
From form to signature, the process can be as quick as an hour. Once the contract is signed, a separate credentialing agent checks the provider’s licenses, and agents load the provider’s data and contract so claims can price against it.
Curative’s contracting team has grown from 45 to about 55 people since Gwen launched, each about 2.5 times as productive. They hand Gwen cold outreach and paperwork and take over warm leads by phone. Curative pays its contracting team on Gwen’s deals too, so people and agents share one target.
“People’s work becomes more about the relationship and less about paperwork,” said Fred.
Fred also believes faster contracting helps small practices stay independent. “If you start a medical practice and it takes three months to get in network and credentialed, you’re just not getting paid for three months,” he said.
Gwen is not Curative’s only agent. Brad, another Opus-based agent, helps sell Curative’s plan to employers, mainly through brokers. Brad follows up with brokers on each quote and helps underwriters move faster by pulling employee data out of the spreadsheets underwriters used to scrub by hand.
Using human-agent teams, Curative can now answer emailed or faxed claims disputes in under 30 minutes, with a letter specific to that claim. “Claims dispute responses used to take about 90 days and now take under 30 minutes by email or fax,” said Fred. “Most payers use a set of templates that are mail-merged together. That leaves a provider deeply unsatisfied, because usually the template doesn’t actually explain what’s going on. Now providers get a customized letter that explains the specifics of the individual claim, what’s happening, and why.”
All of their agents sit on bespoke claims, prior authorization, and finance systems that 13 engineers rebuilt this year with Claude Code. The team had once sized building a claims system alone at 100 engineer-years.
“We’re not trying to plug [these agents] into a claim system,” Fred said. “The claim system is Python running in AWS, and it has an MCP and it has an API, and Claude wrote it, so it understands it.”
What Curative learned from building agents that negotiate with people
Here’s what the Curative team learned about how to build agents that negotiate with people.
- Start with one general tool. “We started off with, ‘Oh, we’ll have tools,’ and that doesn’t work that well, because redlining is quite complex,” Fred said. “What we found works best is that the model just has one tool, which is run Python, and it does all the redlining with a docx library. It works beautifully.”
- Meet people on their channel. A fax tool more than doubled Gwen’s win rate. Many providers now handwrite on a printed fax and fax it back. “It’s meeting people where they are,” said Curative CTO Isaac Turner. “Yes, they have email, but really they’re comfortable in fax.”
- Keep each run isolated. One Gwen run sees one provider and keeps no memory across deals. Brad, Curative’s sales agent, does keep memories, which works but needs care. “You can end up making notes that are wrong and then get into these doom loops, where it has a bad memory that can never be cleared,” Fred noted.
- Improve the system from outside the run. Every few days, Fred gives Claude Code the same prompt: sample the last 10,000 runs, flag anything weird, and open a PR to fix it. “The improvement loops come from running Claude Code over lots of historic conversations and asking how could this have gotten better,” he said.
- Experiment away from PHI first. For a long time Gwen was barred from protected health information (PHI), so early mistakes were in lower-risk settings. Where agents touch PHI now, back-end controls limit what enters a conversation, and agent activity is logged for audit. “We learned how to do it there and then transferred it over into PHI land,” said Fred. Signing Business Associate Agreements (BAAs), the contracts HIPAA requires before a vendor can handle PHI, has gotten easier too. “Anthropic especially has been very good about getting HIPAA-compliant versions of the latest services out very quickly,” said Isaac. “We’ve been able to onboard these new technologies very quickly despite it being regulated.”
- Watch what the agent starts doing on its own and make sure it matches your risk profile. When providers asked for a flyer to share internally, Gwen made one with its Python tool, with no policy telling it to. When a front desk turned away a member at an in-network practice, Gwen asked the office to train its staff, then checked that the member got in.
Where Curative is going next
Next, Curative plans to bring agents to care navigation, extending the reach of the 130 people who guide and coach its members.
Fred expects agents on the provider side too. A large share of claims disputes already appear to be written by agents, and he hopes providers will use agents to negotiate contracts. “There’s a clearing price, and the faster you find the clearing price, everybody can get on with providing care,” he said.
| Best practices from the Curative team | |
|---|---|
| How much authority should an agent start with? | Less than you think it can handle. Gwen began with a human approval queue for any rate above the template. Curative loosened the limits in steps and for more deterministic decisions, then added the rate reviewer, with Fred still approving what it doesn’t clear. |
| What happens when the agent gets it wrong? | Plan for it, and compare it with the alternative. “The bar isn’t perfect,” Isaac said. “The bar is, if you had a thousand people signing contracts, how many mistakes would they make that you regret?” |
| How do you audit hundreds of thousands of messages? | Log everything, put a judge agent on every outbound message, and have Claude Code sample the runs. |
