title: Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in them
body:
Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in them
Our partners can now embed their apps directly in Claude, so you and Claude can work in the same tool, on the same screen, without switching tabs.
Earlier this year, we launched [interactive connectors (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/interactive-tools-in-claude) to bring a small live view of tools into Claude. Starting today, where a connector supports it, you can open a tool beside your conversation or expand it to full screen, and ask Claude to work alongside you and make changes directly.
This is rolling out on the web and in the Claude desktop app on all plans, as part of the [new Claude experience (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/cowork-is-now-claude) that brings chat and Cowork together. You’ll see these features once your account is updated with the new Claude or your organization turns it on.
What’s new:
- Claude can work in your open tools. You can ask Claude to make changes to a page, row, or file that you have open and approve its actions the same way you approve a connector’s actions. Changes appear in the tool as Claude makes them, so you can keep working right alongside it.
- The whole tool opens next to your conversation. You can work in the tool and hide the chat or go full screen when you need room. For tools like Confluence or Notion, that means you get the full editor, signed into your own account, rather than a limited preview.
- Open a connected tool directly, without having to write a Claude prompt. When you want Claude’s help, you can ask from the same screen.
- Pin the tools you use most. You can arrange them alongside your artifacts and access them with one click in your sidebar and the + menu.
Work with Claude in the tools you use
We’re starting with a small group of tools from our directory, including Asana, Canva, Carta, Dropbox, monday.com, Smartsheet, Vercel, and Webflow.
Here’s what you can do with some of the tools available in Claude today:
- Adobe. Ask Claude to retouch, edit and add effects to photos; highlight, edit and redact PDFs.
- Atlassian. Open a Confluence page beside your chat, ask Claude to write and edit, and review its changes live on the page.
- Box. Open a Box file beside your chat, ask Claude to revise it, and compare the versions side by side before you keep the changes.
- HubSpot. Prioritize pipeline tasks and follow-ups, then act on them in Claude.
- Notion. Ask Claude to create a Notion doc or database. Build as you chat, or edit it yourself, without leaving Claude.
Figma, Harvey, and Shopify are also building integrations, and we encourage other developers to do the same.
For developers: built on MCP Apps
Interactive connectors run on MCP Apps, the open extension to the [Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro) that lets an MCP server bring its own interface into AI applications. An MCP App you build isn’t limited to Claude and can run in any AI application that supports the [extension (opens in new tab)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/apps/overview).
Until now, MCP Apps in Claude have mainly appeared as interactive views in the conversation. Claude now supports more of the extension, such as app tools, along with embedded sites, so a developer’s full app can run inside Claude.
Support for these capabilities is in public preview for developers. Developers can start building with them today. Read our [docs (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/docs/connectors/building/mcp-apps/getting-started) to start building.
Getting started
You can connect the tools we mention above from the [directory (opens in new tab)](https://claude.ai/directory/featured/interactive-connectors), then open any tool from your chat or pin it to your sidebar.
For admins: If your organization already allows all of a connector’s tools, its new features appear as they roll out. Admins can restrict a connector’s tools the same way they do today.

title: More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors
body:
More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors
Work at the speed of thought
We've seen Claude Code change how developers work. Engineers went from manually coding line by line, to describing ideas and reviewing what Claude built. It reconnected them with the joy of building. Our goal is to bring that magic to every team, and today we're expanding what Claude makes possible. We're introducing new artifact types with Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data. We're also making it easier to work in your most-used apps with an upgrade to interactive connectors. Claude Meetings is coming soon.
All your connectors and context
In Claude Code, the context Claude needs is already in the codebase. For other teams, context sprawls across emails, apps, and drives. Claude reaches it through connectors built on the [Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol) (MCP), the open standard we introduced for connecting AI to the tools you use. Claude Marketplace lists more than 9,000 connectors and plugins, including community-built ones.
[Interactive connectors (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/interactive-connectors-full-tool) take this further. Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs. Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses.
Bring ideas to life faster, together
Starting today, Claude can build spreadsheets, whiteboards, and dashboards with your team. These work with its existing abilities to create [documents, slide decks, and designs (opens in new tab)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=To5nrYqvR44), and with [Claude Motion (opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17454997-get-started-with-claude-motion) (beta), which helps you turn content into short animations. In each one, Claude quickly picks up what you need, so your thinking sets the pace of work:
[New artifact types (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/sheets-whiteboards-data):- In Claude Sheets, your team and Claude build spreadsheets together, collaboratively organize data, create and edit formulas, and work across multiple tabs.
- Claude Whiteboards is a digital whiteboard that your team can use to lay out and organize ideas together in a meeting, then ask Claude to summarize the findings.
- Claude Data (formerly Dashboards) connects to tools like Snowflake and Salesforce and can use definitions your data team certifies (beta) to create dashboards, visual data stories, or narrated short videos.
You can also ask Claude to build custom artifacts for the way your team works, like an account tracker, a daily briefing, a project status board, or a contract review table. Since Claude carries the same context through every step, an idea can carry over from a whiteboard to a spreadsheet to a dashboard, without the need to reiterate the details.
Coming soon, Claude Meetings will let you add Claude to a call to take notes and update the documents your team is working on during the conversation.
Teams already working this way
Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers. Our legal team worked with Claude to build a Slack-based legal review tool that automatically draws redlines from the team’s own playbook. This brought marketing reviews from three days down to 24 hours, and easy fixes are made before a lawyer reviews the draft. Our finance team turned a long business update document for executives into an interactive page, and now the whole team updates it together with Claude.
Neither of these teams writes code, but they're experts in their fields. They used Claude to turn that knowledge into tools that saved them time, and that others can use. Our customers are working this way too:
“At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.”
“Our FP&A team used to spend about 10 hours every forecast cycle on slides, commentary, and validation. We automated that assembly work in Claude and brought it down to under 30 minutes. Claude took all of that off our plate. Now we're doing what finance is supposed to do: finding the insight and driving the decision. That's a meaningful shift for a team supporting a business of this size.”
“At Datadog, Claude has extended from coding to knowledge work. Our product managers are using Claude to move from an idea to a feature brief, PRD, and testable prototype much faster, giving them more time to focus on customer needs, product judgment, and the right problems to solve. When someone builds something good with Claude at Datadog, it spreads fast.”
At Gusto, one member of the commercial legal team built a tool in a few hours that turns negotiated terms into signature-ready contracts. Turnaround went from over a week to hours, with that person still reviewing anything negotiated.
“Claude and HubSpot work seamlessly together, so our CSMs have all the context they need to walk in prepared for every call. Live dashboards in Claude pull from HubSpot to show what matters for each call and which customers to reach out to next, and follow-up emails are drafted within 30 minutes of a call ending. Work that used to take hours every week now runs in the background, so our team can focus on helping customers build better solutions, prove value, and grow better.”
Built for and with enterprises
As Claude starts to connect to more tools, businesses need better ways to oversee its access and actions. We build in security and compliance controls to help enterprises meet their own requirements, and we use the same Claude for our own most sensitive work. On Enterprise plans, admins decide who can use which products and connectors, and set spend limits for the organization at a granular level.
That control applies to the tools Claude connects to. With [Claude auto-connect (opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15537633-auto-connect-your-organization-s-apps-to-claude), now in beta on eligible Team and Enterprise plans, connecting an app like Notion, Atlassian, or Dropbox is a one-time setup. Employees are then connected to the tool the first time they use it in Claude, instead of connecting each one individually.
Whichever way a tool is connected, Claude works within your existing permissions. Admins can also limit what each connector does, meaning that Claude might be able to read Slack but not send messages on your behalf.
Protecting sensitive business data is core to how we build, and we're continuing to harden those protections as Claude takes on longer, more complex work:
[Data from Enterprise organizations (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/unified-claude-enterprise)is encrypted in transit and at rest.- On Enterprise plans, security teams
[can see how Claude is being used (opens in new tab)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15167101-get-started-with-claude-compliance-api-integrations), through audit logs and a Compliance API that works with more than 100 security and compliance tools, including Splunk and CrowdStrike. - In the new Claude experience on Enterprise, each cloud session runs in its own
[isolated virtual machine (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/unified-claude-enterprise), with connector credentials kept outside it.
Work that keeps up with your ideas
Modern work is set up around software, but Claude works around you. It knows your team's work through the tools you connect, helps you bring ideas to life in the formats you need, and runs within the controls your admins set. That leaves you more time to focus and make progress on big goals.

title: Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
body:
Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
Now you can brainstorm on whiteboards, build sheets, and share data directly in Claude.
Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and [Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/dashboards-and-motion) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans.
Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there.
Claude Whiteboards
Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team.
Claude Sheets
Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together.
For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use [Claude for Excel (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/claude-for-microsoft-365). You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.
Claude Data
[Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/dashboards-and-motion) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data:
- Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified.
- Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing.
- Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access.
- Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data.
- Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis.
- Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed.
Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma.
Work in your other tools, too
Starting today, [interactive connectors (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/interactive-connectors-full-tool) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you.
Getting started
Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM.
For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts.

title: Decision Models in Hugging Face
body:
[
](#decision-models-in-hugging-face)
Decision Models in Hugging Face
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/decision.md)
Large Language Models (LLMs) are exceptionally good at generating text. We use them to answer questions, write code, reason about problems, and so much more. But not every problem requires generating text.
Consider a customer support system receiving the following message:
"I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today."
The system needs to determine which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund.
We could ask an LLM to return a JSON object containing these answers.
llama cli -hf ggml-org/gemma-4-e4b-it-GGUF:Q4_0
> We have the following customer support ticket, "I was charged twice for my subscription. I need a refund today.", which team should handle the request, how urgent it is, and whether the customer is requesting a refund. Give the answers in JSON.
[Start thinking]
...
[end thinking]
```json
{
"team_to_handle": "Billing",
"urgency": "High",
"request_refund": true
}
But what if the model could directly evaluate the available options and return a probability distribution over them, without generating any text?
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"department": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Payments and refunds",
"technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
"sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
}
},
}
}
)
# {
# 'department': {
# 'type': 'choice',
# 'choice': 'billing',
# 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
# 'probabilities': {
# 'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
# 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
# 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
# }
# }
# }
This is the key idea behind decision models.
[
](#what-are-decision-models)
What are decision models?
A decision model takes some input context (state), evaluates a question with a set of predefined possible answers (primitives), and returns a structured decision along with probabilities. Instead of asking a model to generate an answer token by token, we ask it to assign probabilities to the answers that our application already understands.
[TypeSafe AI introduced Jev](https://typesafe.ai/blog/introducing-system-one-models-and-jev), describing it as a [System One model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thinking,_Fast_and_Slow). The name draws inspiration from the distinction between fast, intuitive thinking (System 1) and slower, deliberative thinking (System 2).
The community has converged to the term decision model, because it describes the model's computational role rather than invoking a particular theory of cognition. In the rest of the post we will refer to the models as "decision models" instead of "system one models". (
[A poll on twitter deciding what we should be calling such models])
For a decision model, the fundamental interface is:
State + Questions + Allowed Answers → Decisions + Probabilities
[
](#why-not-use-llms-for-everything)
Why not use LLMs for everything?
We could simply prompt an LLM to return a JSON object containing our decisions. In fact, this is how many applications already use language models for classification, routing, and other structured tasks.
However, there are a few problems with this approach.
- LLMs are not guaranteed to follow the requested schema: Even with explicit instructions, a model might produce invalid JSON, introduce unexpected keys, or return an answer outside the allowed choices.
- Constrained decoding helps, but does not eliminate the computational overhead: Libraries such as
[Outlines](https://github.com/dottxt-ai/outlines)and[XGrammar](https://github.com/mlc-ai/xgrammar)can enforce grammars or JSON schemas by restricting which tokens the model is allowed to generate at each step. This ensures the output follows the supported structural constraints, but introduces additional work. - Why generate an entire response: LLMs are designed for open-ended generation, but when our application only needs to choose between predefined answers, autoregressive decoding can be unnecessary work.
[
](#how-are-decision-models-different-from-classification-models)
How are decision models different from classification models?
Before understanding the interface of a decision model, it is useful to revisit two closely related approaches namely traditional classification and zero-shot classification.
[
](#traditional-classification)
Traditional classification
Suppose we train a classifier that routes customer-support requests to three departments:
- Billing
- Technical support
- Sales
A conventional classification model learns a mapping from an input to a predefined set of labels. During training, the model learns to predict these labels from examples. A classification head typically produces one logit per class, and softmax turns those logits into a probability distribution.
The limitation here is that the output classes are baked into the model's classification head.
If we introduce a fourth department, such as Legal, the existing classifier does not automatically acquire a corresponding output class. We may need to modify the head, collect training data, and retrain or adapt the model.
[
](#zero-shot-classification)
Zero-shot classification
[Zero-shot classification](https://huggingface.co/tasks/zero-shot-classification) addresses an important part of this limitation. Instead of requiring the classifier to be trained specifically on every output category, we supply the candidate labels at inference time.
For example:
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline(
"zero-shot-classification",
model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)
classifier(
"My payment was deducted twice.",
candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales"],
)
# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
# 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support'],
# 'scores': [0.8466812372207642, 0.0962134450674057, 0.05710534751415253]}
Unlike a conventional fixed-label classifier, the categories can change from one request to another. Let’s add another department, such as “Legal”, and see the model outputs.
from transformers import pipeline
classifier = pipeline(
"zero-shot-classification",
model="facebook/bart-large-mnli",
)
classifier(
"My payment was deducted twice.",
candidate_labels=["billing", "technical support", "sales", "legal"],
)
# {'sequence': 'My payment was deducted twice.',
# 'labels': ['billing', 'sales', 'technical support', 'legal'],
# 'scores': [0.8185835480690002, 0.09302053600549698, 0.05521026626229286, 0.03318570926785469]}
One common implementation uses a model trained for natural language inference (NLI). Each candidate label is converted into a hypothesis, and the model measures how strongly the input entails that hypothesis.
This already sounds quite similar to a decision model. And in many ways, it is.
[
](#where-decision-models-differ)
Where decision models differ
Decision models extend this idea beyond simply assigning an input to a category. A decision model can accept several named questions about the same state, with different answer types. The types can be choosing between alternatives (choice), scoring an ordered scale (score), or estimating the probability that a statement is true (noul).
More importantly, its interface is designed around the probability distribution over possible decisions.
Consider these three approaches:
| Property | Classification | Zero-shot classification | Decision model |
|---|---|---|---|
| Probability over choices | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Labels defined at inference | No | Yes | Yes |
| Multiple typed questions | No | No | Yes |
| Ordered scoring and yes/no decisions | Task-specific | Possible with adaptation | Native primitives |
The advantage of decision models is not that they invented runtime-defined labels or probabilistic classification. It is that they organize these capabilities into a consistent interface, potentially backed by architectures and training procedures optimized specifically for decisions.
[
](#the-decision-model-interface)
The decision model interface
A decision model request has the following two components:
- state
- questions
[
](#state)
State
The state is the information the model should evaluate. It may be a string, a structured JSON object, or, other modalities for supported omni-modal models.
For example:
{
"customer_message": "I was charged twice. Please refund me today.",
"subscription": "pro",
"previous_tickets": 2
}
[
](#questions-and-their-primitives)
Questions and their primitives
Questions describe what we want to know about the state. In the decision models interface, three fundamental primitives represent different forms of decisions:
- Choice: Select one of several possible answers.
- Score: Evaluate something on an ordered scale.
- Noul: Answer a yes/no question probabilistically.
Let's go over them one by one.
[
](#choice-a-probability-distribution-over-options)
Choice: A probability distribution over options
Choice is the most intuitive primitive and the closest to traditional classification.
Suppose we ask:
Which department should handle this customer request?
The available options are Billing, Technical support, and Sales.
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"department": {
"type": "choice",
"instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
"criteria": {
"billing": "Payments and refunds",
"technical": "Bugs and technical issues",
"sales": "Pricing and subscriptions"
}
},
}
}
)
# {
# 'department': {
# 'type': 'choice',
# 'choice': 'billing',
# 'confidence': 0.9974000453948975,
# 'probabilities': {
# 'billing': 0.9982666969299316,
# 'technical': 0.0010246571619063616,
# 'sales': 0.0007087149424478412
# }
# }
# }
The model assigns a logit to each option. For logits ($z_1,\ldots,z_K$), (with K classes) we can obtain the probabilities using softmax:
Here, (K) is the number of choices.
Consider this illustrative distribution:
| Choice | Probability |
|---|---|
| Billing | 0.998 |
| Technical support | 0.001 |
| Sales | 0.001 |
The probabilities sum to one:
The model chooses the option with the largest probability:
In this case, the choice is Billing, with the probability of 0.998, but the remaining probabilities are useful too. They tell us how the model distributes its belief among the alternatives.
[
](#score-the-expectation-of-an-ordered-distribution)
Score: The expectation of an ordered distribution
Choice works when there are several distinct alternatives. But what if we want to measure something on an ordered scale?
Consider the question:
How urgent is this customer request?
We define three levels:
- 0: Low urgency
- 1: Medium urgency
- 2: High urgency
from transformers import pipeline
decide = pipeline("decision", model="autotrust/GEV-26B-Decide")
decision = decide(
{
"state": "I was charged twice for my order and want a refund.",
"questions": {
"urgency": {
"type": "score",
"instructions": "How urgent is the request?",
"criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]
},
}
}
)
# {
# 'urgency': {
# 'type': 'score',
# 'score': 1.7053890228271484,
# 'legend': {
# '0': 'low',
# '1': 'medium',
# '2': 'high'
# },
# 'confidence': 0.5580834252759814,
# 'probabilities': {
# '0': 0.014908230863511562,
# '1': 0.26479458808898926,
# '2': 0.7202972173690796
# }
# }
# }
The model again produces a probability distribution:
| Level | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 — Low | 0.01 |
| 1 — Medium | 0.26 |
| 2 — High | 0.72 |
Rather than returning only the most likely level, the Score primitive computes the expected value of the level index.
For a random variable (X) representing the level, the expectation is:

title: Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
body:
[
](#pay-for-hugging-face-hub-with-your-google-cloud-account)
Pay for Hugging Face Hub with your Google Cloud Account
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/hub-gcp-marketplace.md)
You can now link your Hugging Face organization to your Google Cloud account, so that your Hugging Face usage shows up on your Google Cloud bill instead of being charged to a credit card. Get started [on the Google Cloud Marketplace](https://console.cloud.google.com/marketplace/product/huggingface-public/hugging-face-hub).
[
](#why-pay-through-google-cloud)
Why pay through Google Cloud?
Hugging Face is where teams find, build and run open models: from hosting private models and datasets, to running GPU workloads with [Jobs](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/jobs-overview), deploying models with [Inference Endpoints](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-endpoints), calling thousands of models through [Inference Providers](https://huggingface.co/docs/inference-providers), or hosting demos on GPU [Spaces](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/spaces-overview).
If your company already runs on Google Cloud, adding a new vendor and a corporate credit card just to use these services can slow things down. By linking your organization through the Google Cloud Marketplace:
- One bill: your Hugging Face usage appears on your existing Google Cloud invoice, next to the rest of your cloud spend.
- No new vendor to onboard: purchases go through your existing Google Cloud billing account and procurement process.
- Everything is covered: upgrading your org to a
[Team or Enterprise](https://huggingface.co/enterprise)subscription, pay-as-you-go compute (Jobs, Inference Endpoints, Inference Providers, GPU Spaces, ZeroGPU quota extension), and additional storage at[public Hugging Face pricing](https://huggingface.co/pricing).
If you're an admin of your Hugging Face organization, here's how to set it up, step by step.
[
](#1-subscribe-to-hugging-face-on-the-google-cloud-marketplace)
1. Subscribe to Hugging Face on the Google Cloud Marketplace
Go to the [Hugging Face Hub listing](https://console.cloud.google.com/marketplace/product/huggingface-public/hugging-face-hub) on the Google Cloud Marketplace, select the Google Cloud project you want to use, and click on "Subscribe".
You are now on the subscription page. Select the billing account to be charged, review and accept the terms, then click "Subscribe".
Once the order is placed, Google Cloud asks you to finish setting up your account with Hugging Face. Click on "Sign up with Hugging Face" to be redirected to Hugging Face.
[
](#2-link-your-hugging-face-organization)
2. Link your Hugging Face organization
You are now on Hugging Face, where you can select the organization you want to link to your Google Cloud account. Only organizations where you are an admin are listed. Select it and confirm.
You are then redirected to the billing settings of your organization. The payment method section now shows the linked Google Cloud account, with a pending status.
Every cloud marketplace subscription is reviewed by the Hugging Face team before paid usage starts being billed through it. While the subscription is pending, usage keeps being billed to the organization's existing payment method, if any.
[
](#3-subscription-approved)
3. Subscription approved
Once your subscription is approved, you will receive an email confirming that your Google Cloud account and Hugging Face organization are linked. Organizations that already have a credit card on file switch to cloud marketplace billing at the start of their next billing period. Organizations on the free tier with no credit card on file usually switch immediately, so their paid usage is billed through the cloud marketplace right away.
To confirm it, open the billing settings of [your organization](https://huggingface.co/settings/organizations): the Google Cloud account is now shown as the organization's active payment method.
[
](#congratulations)
Congratulations!
Your organization is now billed through your Google Cloud account. All members of your organization can use Hugging Face compute services, and the usage will show up on your Google Cloud bill.
A few things worth knowing:
- Google Cloud replaces the credit card as the organization's payment method. Usage is metered and reported to Google Cloud, so adding credits is not available while the organization is billed through the marketplace.
- Included credits still apply: if your organization has a Team or Enterprise subscription, the monthly included credits are applied before any pay-as-you-go usage is reported to Google Cloud.

title: Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises
body:
Company size: StartupRegion: North AmericaIndustry: TechnologyProducts: API, Codex, Daybreak75%

Lower mean time to remediate vulnerabilities

5x

More vulnerabilities triaged

As Cogent Security sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them. Remediation work is complex and spans multiple teams. It requires contextual understanding of a company’s environment: how could an attacker exploit a vulnerability, which business systems are at stake, and what changes can be made safely.

Cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks. The factories are designed to help defenders move at machine speed, in response to the acceleration in vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

The company’s AI agents combine GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 with its enterprise context and controls to handle investigation through verified remediation. The agents assess exposures, execute permitted changes, and confirm the risk has been eliminated. Cogent also conducts internal research with Cyber and Daybreak, exploring attack paths and defensive capabilities.

> “The ability of OpenAI models to sustain long-running tasks unlocks a new level of autonomy in enterprise defense: AI agents can now carry work from investigation through verified remediation.”

—Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO, CogentFor each customer, Cogent’s Context Engine maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies. Specialized background agents continuously reconcile information across security tools and systems, giving investigation and remediation agents a shared understanding of the environment.

GPT‑6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning for that work. This enables what Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO of Cogent, describes as a “memory harness for the enterprise.” He says, “We don’t have to relearn what the world looks like every time a new task happens.” Reusing context reduces latency, inference costs, and inconsistent results.

Cogent’s Agent Policies define each enterprise’s permitted changes and approval requirements, and its policy-enforcement engine, TRACE, checks tool calls against the policies before execution. The checks are deterministic and require no separate model inference.

An Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or permit bounded autonomous remediation.

When critical security flaws known as PHP2Shell were disclosed in PHP, a programming language used to run websites, customers turned to the Cyber Defense Factories that Cogent had already deployed in their environments.

GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Astra provided the deep reasoning for investigation and remediation planning. Using Cogent’s context layer, agents identified affected systems, assessed exposure, and developed plans that accounted for application dependencies and operational constraints. Then they orchestrated fixes using customer-defined approval and execution workflows and verified the resolution.

Cogent reports that customers are using its Cyber Defense Factories to resolve vulnerabilities faster and expand investigation capacity. With Cogent, a Fortune 1000 automotive customer reduced its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer achieved 5× vulnerability-triage throughput.

Trading platform MarketAxess says Cogent helps it decide which exposures to fix first: “Cogent sees our environment the way an attacker would. It traces the route from the internet to a vulnerable system and checks controls on the way. Our remediation work now focuses on the greatest risks and the paths an adversary could use to break in,” says Vijay Bala, Global CISO at MarketAxess.

Cogent continuously evaluates closed-source and open-source alternatives and reports stronger reasoning on long-running security tasks, higher fidelity, fewer hallucinations on technical codebases, and more reliable execution with OpenAI models. The models can chain tool calls sequentially and in parallel while retaining context across remediation workflows.

Cogent prioritizes reasoning quality for complex investigations and cost for more straightforward work. It uses GPT‑6.1 Sol for general execution and GPT‑5.6 for routine vulnerability-management tasks where advanced reasoning is less critical.

> “OpenAI models are more cost-efficient relative to the other providers. That’s a big plus for us, especially if we’re running these huge agent swarms.”

—Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO, CogentUsing OpenAI models has also reduced the supporting software Cogent needs to build for remediation and patching. “A lot of the work that we had to do at the harness level is no longer required,” Geng says. He also shared that OpenAI APIs have “streamlined request routing and agent orchestration, significantly reducing internal engineering overhead and accelerating our time-to-market for complex security workflows.”

Most of Cogent’s engineers also choose Codex for development. Geng says they’re more productive pairing Codex with OpenAI models vs. using the same models in an open-source coding environment. “Codex just comes with tools that we don’t have to build ourselves,” says Geng.

Through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, Cogent receives technical support for its internal red-teaming and attack-path research. Daybreak Red, an access tier within Daybreak, provides the team with specialized OpenAI models for authorized offensive and vulnerability research. “Good defense requires good offense,” Geng says.

> “Through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, we can explore how vulnerabilities could be chained across identities, resources, and network controls. We use that research to understand what our agents can do and which defensive capabilities to build next.”

—Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO, CogentCogent plans to expand its capabilities as the key partner for enterprises to build their own Cyber Defense Factories. Its roadmap includes increasingly autonomous remediation, broadening the range and complexity of fixes agents can execute, from straightforward configuration changes to multi-step workflows spanning different enterprise systems.

The company is also developing autonomous discovery and validation. Its goal is a closed-loop system that finds and eliminates risk while continuously learning from every vulnerability to improve future investigations and fixes.

title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
body:
Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
9th November 2026
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven’t unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn’t want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build [Beep Locator](https://github.com/simonw/beep-locator), a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.
Here’s what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:
You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners—I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.
The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn’t work particularly well, so I added a “Rough mode” where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.
Once that’s set up, the devices all listen for the beep!
I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room—displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.
Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the “Sounds located” log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click “This is the mystery beep” to mark them as such.
Once you’ve confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.
The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.
How it works
When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up [BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices](https://www.cs.purdue.edu/homes/chunyi/pubs/sensys106-beepbeep.pdf), a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here’s that paper’s abstract:
We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.
That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!
Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see [detector.js](https://github.com/simonw/beep-locator/blob/main/beep_locator/modules/listener/detector.js)), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.
When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.
How I built it
I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here’s [that shared starter session](https://claude.ai/code/cshk_016BvfqAWf7MeGZKeYCrUnN2MmRfCSAX9Gu8DiptXMuH9P), which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:
Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve
There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it
I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from
There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app
Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?
That got me [this problem.md file](https://github.com/simonw/beep-locator/blob/main/problem.md). As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.
The research looked good, so I told it:
Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else
That got me [to this point](https://github.com/simonw/beep-locator/commits/e36ac93a81091a246403c074e34c0041c6972fac)—most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.
I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then [Fable 5.2 was released](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2), and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.
I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.
This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an [installModule()](https://github.com/simonw/beep-locator/blob/44fea65c918fb31a7d2c0e17797ee1a106860e23/beep_locator/static/runtime.js#L710) method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.
On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.
From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:
I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate
This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.
what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]
Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps
That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.
each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp
That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.
The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays
Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.
There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for
Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is
At this point I was getting close—I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn’t it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?
I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.
And since I had one spare device, I then said:
add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far
Giving Claude Code ears
I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it’s possible to give Claude Code ears.
Claude doesn’t have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.
I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.
Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.
I’m reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where [Martin Woodward](https://github.com/martinwoodward) told me he had been debugging the [GitHub Universe Badge computers](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/27/game-boy-color-on-my-conference-badge/) by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.
Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

title: Stop Chatting With Spreadsheets — Francesco Galletta & Felippe Felisola Caso, Monzo
body:
Fast answers are easy to get. Answers you can trust with your money are harder. Francesco Galletta and Felippe Felisola Caso build a financial-analyst agent harness live, using one real problem: paying for a wedding. They show the five design principles they use for AI you can trust: shared domain, consistency, evidence, accountability and verification. They also explain why calculations belong in code instead of in the model's head.

Note: the speakers work at Monzo but are not presenting on Monzo's behalf.

title: Your Self-Hosted LLM Needs to Say No - Harshul Jain & Parv Khatri, Audible & SAP
body:
Coding agents fan out, retry and burst, and if they hit an LLM you host yourself, your inference layer will happily accept every request and bury the ones you needed first. Harshul Jain and Parv Khatri make the case for admission control: deciding what to refuse before it reaches the GPU. Drawing on a review of 55 systems papers and eight real production incidents, they share five questions to ask any admission policy before you deploy it, and a checklist you can use right away.

title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
body:
Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
Weâre enabling robots to learn faster for the real world - from everyday skills to the factory floor
Today, we are introducing Gemini Robotics 2.5, our most capable vision-language-action (VLA) model to date. Gemini Robotics 2.5 increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. This enhances dexterity, reliability, and safety to help robots step out of the lab and into more unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a greater range of tasks.
Earlier this year, we brought [whole-body intelligence](https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-robotics-2-brings-whole-body-intelligence-to-robots/) to robots of many types, including humanoids. Now, in large part thanks to Gemini 4 Argon's ability to accelerate robotics research, we have further pushed the frontier of physical intelligence. We tested Gemini Robotics 2.5âs capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity across over 200 distinct tasks, though this approach could scale to many more.
Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks a leap forward in three key areas:
- Dexterity: Our robots can perform significantly more tasks with greater performance and dexterity â from using everyday tools to handling delicate, flexible objects.
- Reliability: During a real-world proof-of-concept on Mercedes-Benz production lines, our models helped Apptronikâs Apollo 2 humanoid pick and pack automotive parts with a 96% success rate. This could enable robots to take on monotonous work, to enable technicians to focus on complex build tasks.
- Safety: As robots move into everyday environments, we have improved physical safety steerability and introduced a new benchmark to test against adversarial jailbreaks specific to robotics.
Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to [our robotics partners](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-robotics/#partners).
Expanding task breadth, reliability, and dexterity
Because real-world environments are unstructured and unpredictable, robots must be able to handle everyday objects with both fine precision and high reliability.
With Gemini Robotics 2.5, we expanded the model capabilities in task breadth, performance, and complexity. We evaluated the model across 200 distinct tasks â such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box, and pipetting a liquid. These tasks represent a step toward human-level dexterity by combining a number of skills, including advanced tool use, complex manipulation of deformables, and handling delicate objects with finesse.
Our evaluations show significant increases in task precision, robustness, and speed. Compared to previous baselines, Gemini Robotics 2.5 achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the type of task, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster.
Like our previous Gemini Robotics models, it natively works with many different robot types, including [Apptronikâs Apollo 2](https://apptronik.com/apollo/apollo-2) humanoid robot (featuring the five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand) and the [Franka Duo platform](https://franka.de/fr3-duo) with two-fingered parallel grippers.
Testing real-world reliability with Apptronikâs Apollo and Mercedes-Benz
The ultimate measure of a robotics model is whether it can perform dependably in an active workplace. To put Gemini Robotics 2.5 to the test, we partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to use Apollo 2 humanoid robots on active automotive production lines in KecskemÃ©t, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany.
Robots struggle to adapt to new unpredictable environments, our Gemini Robotics models give Apollo the ability to think, reason over multiple steps, and take action adapting to changes. In this proof-of-concept, Apollo 2 autonomously performs automotive kitting: the repetitive, physically taxing task of sorting individual parts from bulk bins into organized trays in the exact order needed for each vehicle on the line. Offloading this monotonous prep work helps keep the assembly line moving, while freeing up technicians to focus on complex build tasks.
Using our embodied reasoning model ([Gemini Robotics ER](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-robotics/embodied-reasoning/)) to keep track of the workflow, and the [Gemini Robotics 2.5](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-robotics/vla/) actions model to control its hands and arms, the robot reaches into supply bins, picks up metal automotive brackets, and places them into sequencing containers, all while correcting for any gaps. Achieving a 96% success rate, this pilot shows promising progress toward widespread real-world industrial applications.
Advancing steerability and agentic safety for robots
As robots operate in messy, everyday spaces, physical safety is paramount. To help ensure this, we have significantly advanced Gemini Robotics 2.5âs safety features.
Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses inference-time reasoning guidance to steer around physical hazards in real-time. Much like safety classifiers add a protective layer around Geminiâs responses, this guidance allows the robot to navigate complex environments securely. In our evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%.
We are also advancing safety for long-horizon, agentic tasks. Gemini 4 Argon currently leads our [agentic robotics evaluations](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_safety_report.pdf#page=200) across unsafe task refusal, resolving uncertainty, and working in proximity to humans. To test jailbreak robustness, we are releasing [ASIMOV-Jailbreak](https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/asimov_agentic), a new open-source benchmark containing hundreds of prompts that disguise unsafe requests across dozens of scenes. Argon achieves a 99.5% jailbreak resistance â a significant improvement over the 82% rate of our previous baseline, Gemini Robotics ER 2.
Accelerating robotics with Gemini 4 Argon
To teach robots new skills, researchers need massive amounts of physical data and highly efficient modeling algorithms. Gemini 4 Argonâs [robotics research capabilities](https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics/) helped solve these bottlenecks by acting as a simulation engine, which greatly accelerated our development of Gemini Robotics 2.5.
Argon can generate thousands of varied, simulated practice runs from a real-world camera scene and build a realistic digital twin. Combined with real training demonstrations, this enables the robot to more quickly generalize to new scenes and objects. Argon can also help researchers hypothesize why task failures happen from video footage and test the best improvements both in simulation and directly on real robots.
Accelerated by frontier intelligence models like Gemini 4 Argon, Gemini Robotics 2.5 marks an important milestone on the path toward solving physical AGI. By advancing in dexterity, real-world reliability, and rigorous safety, we are building the physical intelligence necessary for robots to work alongside people and solve real-world challenges
Acknowledgements
This work was developed by the Gemini Robotics team. For their leadership and support of this effort, weâd like to thank: Huizhong Chen, Radu Soricut, Jean-Baptiste Alayrac, Melvin Johnson, Edward Grefenstette, Claire Cui, Jon Shlens, David Thacker, Zoubin Ghahramani, Clement Farabet, Koray Kavukcuoglu, and Demis Hassabis. Weâd like to recognize the many teams across Google and Google DeepMind that have contributed to this effort including Research, Legal, Marketing, Communications, Responsibility and Safety Council, Responsible Development and Innovation, Policy, Strategy and Operations, and our Business and Corporate Development teams. Finally, weâd like to thank our partners: Agile, Apptronik, and Mercedes-Benz teams for their support on this release.

title: How One Founder Manages 20 AI Coding Agents at Once - Ryan Carson, Untangle
body:
Ryan Carson, founder and CEO of Untangle and a four-time founder, shows how his team runs software development with agents in the cloud. One "engineering manager" agent, which he mostly talks to by voice, manages up to 20 builder agents through a ticket board, with an automation that checks every builder every 15 minutes, capped review loops, QA agents and a merge queue manager. The human step he won't skip is watching the video of each feature before it ships. He also explains how Untangle now hires: candidates record themselves shipping a real feature with an agent, an agent ranks the videos, and the top five do a paid trial.
```
