title: Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
body:
Viewer • Updated • 100k • 49 • 2
[
](#nemotron-personas-finance-japan-a-synthetic-dataset-capturing-japans-demographics-and-financial-context)
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan: A Synthetic Dataset Capturing Japan's Demographics and Financial Context
[Enterprise + Article](/blog)
A compound AI approach to Japanese personas grounded in real-world distributions
[
](#open-data-breaking-down-privacy-barriers-to-pave-the-way-for-ai-in-finance)
Open Data Breaking Down Privacy Barriers to Pave the Way for AI in Finance
In the financial sector, the utilization of real-world data faces significant constraints due to strict privacy regulations, compliance requirements, and the need for advanced domain expertise. In this context, the development of agentic AI in the financial domain requires synthetic data capable of avoiding the risks of using real data while reflecting demographics, household structures, and asset statuses to reproduce diverse, realistic financial scenarios.
To address these challenges, [Elith](https://www.elith.ai/) and NVIDIA have released [Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan), a financial domain extension of the open-source persona dataset "[Nemotron-Personas-Japan](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Japan)." To our knowledge, it is the first open persona dataset at million-record scale that pairs Japan’s official statistics with household finance and financial literacy data. Built upon official government statistics, this dataset was developed using [NeMo SDG-PGMs](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/SDG-PGMs), a probabilistic graphical model framework for synthetic data generation (SDG), and [NeMo Data Designer](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/DataDesigner), an enterprise synthetic data generation system. Furthermore, to enhance the practical utility of the dataset in financial use cases, it was designed by incorporating insights and feedback provided by leading domestic financial institutions and industry associations, including Sompo Japan, Tokio Marine Holdings, Bank of Fukuoka, Mizuho Financial Group, Meiji Yasuda Life Insurance, and the Financial Data Utilization Association (FDUA).
This dataset expands the environment where Japanese developers and enterprises can develop and evaluate AI tailored to local and industry requirements, without using real customer data. Released under the CC BY 4.0 license, it is available for commercial use. From building conversational agents to customer simulation and model evaluation, it supports practical financial AI development. The [Nemotron-Personas collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-personas), including Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan, is designed to seamlessly integrate with the user simulation framework [NeMo User Sim](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/UserSim), enabling instant execution of simulations drawn from diverse distributions consistent with the real world.
[
](#whats-in-the-dataset)
What’s in the Dataset?
- 9M personas total (1M records x 9 personas each), written in natural Japanese
- 50 fields per record: 9 persona fields, 11 persona attributes, and 30 contextual fields based on official demographic and labor statistics
- ~1.5B tokens total, including ~750M persona tokens
- ~950k unique names
- 1600+ occupation categories reflecting Japan's workforce
- Comprehensive coverage across demographic, regional, asset distribution, and personality trait axes
- Diverse persona types: Occupations, sports, arts, travel, cooking, finance, financial behavior, and financial concerns
- Natural language persona attributes: Cultural background, skills and expertise, career goals and aspirations, hobbies and interests, household/parental/financial background, attitudes toward money, and financial planning
- Available for both commercial and non-commercial use under the CC BY 4.0 license
[
](#how-we-built-it)
How We Built It
[
](#data-generation-pipeline)
Data Generation Pipeline
It was built using NVIDIA’s framework for synthetic data generation, NeMo Data Designer. This compound AI system enables complex Jinja templating, Pydantic validation, structured outputs, automated retries, and support for multiple generation backends. This is the essential toolset required for generating such large-scale synthetic datasets. In addition, the following models were utilized:
- NeMo SDG-PGMs (Apache-2.0): A probabilistic graphical model framework for statistically grounded data generation
- gemma-4-31B-it (Apache-2.0): For Japanese text generation
[
](#enhanced-cultural-context)
Enhanced Cultural Context
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan was designed to align with Japan's official demographic and labor statistics while taking into account key considerations essential for AI training:
- Education: Where national statistics broadly aggregate degree levels, we introduced finer granularity to enable the model to reflect diverse educational pathways.
- Occupation: We incorporated additional categories (such as business owners and specialized professions) to broaden the spectrum of occupations used for training.
- Life Stages: We modeled scenarios that rarely surface prominently in statistics, such as students, retirees, and periods of unemployment, to represent more realistic personas.
- Household Finances: In addition to individual income and spending propensity, we incorporated household-level financial and real assets to replicate diverse economic backgrounds.
- Digital & Financial Literacy: By including internet and smartphone usage along with financial literacy, we enabled the model to precisely capture consumer profiles in financial use cases.
[
](#private-by-design)
Private By Design
Every persona is fully synthetic. No real individuals are represented, and the dataset is designed to reduce privacy risk. Demographics and household finances follow official statistics and public survey data, and names follow real Japanese naming patterns. Personas are built from these distributions, not from records about real people.
[
](#who-this-data-is-for)
Who This Data Is For
Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan is built first for teams creating financial AI in Japan, at banks and insurers and at the startups and integrators that serve them. Each persona carries household finances and financial literacy alongside demographics. Teams can use them to build customer-service agents, evaluate sales conversations/marketing initiatives, run user simulations in NeMo User Sim, and red-team customer-facing AI.
The release also serves anyone building for Japanese users. It holds 9M personas, 50% more than Nemotron-Personas-Japan, across 50 fields instead of 22. That gives any Japanese-language project finer slices of the population to train and test on.
[
](#practical-ai-applications)
Practical AI Applications
The synthetic personas in this dataset can be leveraged for:
- Multi-turn conversation: Using personas as "seeds" to generate human-like dialogue datasets.
- Domain-specific AI development: Generating datasets to build AI assistants tailored to realistic scenarios in financial use cases.
- Bias testing and fairness: Evaluating how models and AI agent systems perform across rural and urban divides, various age groups, educational backgrounds, and economic circumstances to check whether AI performs consistently across Japanese society.
[
](#why-it-matters)
Why It Matters
Access to diverse, high-quality training data that reflects real-world populations has long been a challenge in AI development. Enterprise AI development has predominantly relied on private data, creating barriers for researchers, startups, and particularly AI developers in regions with limited available data.
- Data Diversity: Reflects the full spectrum of Japan's population, which helps reduce biased training and the risk of
[model collapse](https://medium.com/data-science/addressing-concerns-of-model-collapse-from-synthetic-data-in-ai-7cd380208d14). - Cultural Authenticity: Reduces reliance on Western-centric datasets and supports the development of
[Sovereign AI systems](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/lp/industries/global-public-sector/sovereign-ai-technical-overview/). - Privacy and Governance: Aligned with Japan’s innovation-first approach to AI governance. Every persona is synthetic, so no customer data is needed to build or test with it.
By releasing Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan under CC BY 4.0, we provide access to enterprise-grade, high-quality synthetic data, empowering anyone to build culturally grounded AI systems with lower cost and less privacy risk.
[
](#pairs-with-nemotron-pii-japan)
Pairs with Nemotron-PII-Japan
[Nemotron-PII-Japan](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-PII-Japan) launches the same day. It holds 100,000 synthetic Japanese business documents with labeled personal information, for training and testing detection and redaction models. Its documents are built on Nemotron-Personas-Japan. Use Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan to simulate customers, and Nemotron-PII-Japan to test how your pipeline protects their data.
[
](#start-building-with-nemotron-personas-finance-japan)
Start Building with Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan
You can download this dataset using the command below to help develop AI that genuinely understands Japanese culture and language.
from datasets import load_dataset
ds = load_dataset("nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan")
Use cases for building production-ready applications:
- Using personas as seeds for dialogue generation
- Fine-tuning models with culturally grounded data
- Building personalized engines that reflect Japan's overall demographic makeup
- Developing domain-specific AI agents equipped with Japanese context
From teams building AI in Japan to global developers aiming for broader regional deployment, [Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Finance-Japan) dataset provides the authentic, privacy-conscious foundation required for your applications.

title: Practice Makes Precise: At CoRL, NVIDIA and Partners Reveal How Robots Rehearse Delicate Work in Simulation
body:
Simulation, which has long been the proving ground for robots learning to walk, roll and hop, is now helping researchers teach robots tasks that require a finer touch: aligning gears, connecting cables and assembling small components.
The shift from locomotion to manipulation is taking center stage at this week’s [Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL)](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/corl/) in Austin, Texas, alongside the rise of agentic robotics — a new paradigm that integrates frontier agents to create interpretable code for physical robotics systems.
At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing new open robotics technologies, including [world action models](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/world-action-model/), simulation tools, benchmarks and agentic workflows.
Two NVIDIA papers are among six finalists out of thousands of submissions for the Best Paper Awards at CoRL:
[GRAIL](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/dair/grail/)(Generating Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from World Models), which presents a digital generation pipeline for 3D assets and simulator-ready scenes for robot learning.[RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/robottt/), which introduces a robot model and training recipe that scales visuomotor context three orders of magnitude beyond state-of-the-art policies without growing inference latency.
These advancements help researchers train robots on complex tasks, evaluate their performance across changing conditions and use failures to guide further learning — building the precision, adaptability and autonomy needed to move from lab demonstrations to industrial deployment.
NVIDIA is working with partners like [Ambi Robotics](https://www.ambirobotics.com/), Bosch Research, [Dexmate](https://www.dexmate.com/blog/an-anatomy-of-coding-agents-tackling-robotics-tasks), Dyna Robotics, FieldAI, Flexion, Noitom Robotics, Siemens, [Skild AI](http://skild.ai/blogs/steel-solver), RLWRLD, UC Berkeley, Walden Robotics and the University of Washington to bring these advancements to the broader robotics community.
World Action Models Enable Next Level of Robot Autonomy
The next level of robot autonomy requires robots to perceive their surroundings, anticipate how their actions will change the environment and execute complex, multistep tasks with a high degree of precision. World action models enable exactly that.
At CoRL, NVIDIA is introducing [GR00T 2](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-2), an open frontier world action model built on NVIDIA Cosmos. Trained on diverse robot and human data, including 100,000 hours of [NVIDIA open source human egocentric data](https://huggingface.co/spaces/nvidia/PhysicalAI-Human-1M-Explorer), the model enables robots to learn dexterous manipulation skills. Key features include:
- Out-of-the-box performance: Completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations.
- Skill transfer: Learns from human demonstrations and transfers skills between different robot bodies without robot demonstrations
- Generalization with little data: Achieved 71% average success across 50 tasks with just one demonstration per task, increasing to 95% with five.
- Agent control: AI agents can use GR00T 2’s application programming interface and supporting tools to run skills in sequence and recover from errors.
GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision language action and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins.
Nexuni is testing it for robotic laundry handling, Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases.
MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained.
Training capable robots requires diverse data. Open NVIDIA workflows and models equip researchers with better tools for data collection and annotation:
- For researchers building robot-training datasets, NVIDIA’s new open Video to Data workflow turns human video into simulated robot demonstrations, with a
[challenge](https://nvidia-isaac.github.io/video_to_data/v2d_challenge/)inviting researchers to advance it. - The
[NVIDIA EgoHand open model](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/EgoHand-v1)— being demoed at CoRL and with over 40,000 Hugging Face downloads in the two weeks since launch — reconstructs 3D hand motion, trained with data from Noitom Robotics.
Where the Training and Scaling Happens — in Simulation
A pretrained model gives robots a core set of skills. Simulation lets researchers train, refine and evaluate skills at scale before deploying them on physical robots.
[NVIDIA Isaac Lab](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab), an open source robot-learning framework, provides the foundation for that work. Its latest release, [Isaac Lab 3.0](https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab/releases/tag/v3.0.0), allows researchers to use agents to quickly set up training environments with [simulation-ready assets](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/glossary/simready/), switch between [NVIDIA PhysX](https://developer.nvidia.com/physx-sdk) and [Newton physics solvers](https://developer.nvidia.com/newton-physics), choose renderers for perception-based training and apply a new reinforcement post-training library to foundation models like GR00T.
[Accurate physics](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/use-cases/physics-simulation-for-robotics/) is critical to transferring learned skills from simulation to the real robot. Tighter integration with Newton, an open source physics engine, now allows Isaac Lab to model deformable objects such as cables and cloth, along with complex articulated systems such as robotic hands with many interacting joints.
Integration with Newton simulates how a strawberry deforms under a robot’s grip.
Together, Isaac Lab and Newton combine accurate physics with scale to enable researchers to train thousands of simulated robots in parallel. In a vision-based dexterous manipulation benchmark, Isaac Lab 3.0 with Newton achieved up to 2.5x the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 with PhysX.
Isaac Lab supports robot simulation with Newton and NVIDIA PhysX.
Developers are extending Newton’s capabilities. At CoRL, [Skild AI](http://skild.ai/blogs/steel-solver) announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab.
Skild AI’s STEEL Solver.
Flexion showcased how Isaac Lab and Newton help train Reflect, its robot-intelligence model combining reasoning and whole-body manipulation.
Flexion uses Newton for RL with Isaac Lab.
FieldAI is using Newton — as well as Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim, built on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries — to train and validate robot policies for deployment in unstructured real-world environments. Dyna Robotics will demonstrate how parallel simulation in Isaac Lab helps train whole-body controllers for its [semi-humanoid Taku robot](https://www.dyna.co/dyna-2.1) for work in warehouses, hotels and food services.
Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics, while [Dexmate](https://www.dexmate.com/blog/an-anatomy-of-coding-agents-tackling-robotics-tasks) is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot.
[AlphaNIST](https://alpha-nist.github.io/), built in Isaac Lab, demonstrates how efficient practice can translate into precision. A single policy learns all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board, manipulating millimeter-scale parts using only a yes-or-no success signal. It achieves more than 98% training success, compared with 81% for separate per-task policies, using roughly 39x less GPU time.
AlphaNIST uses Isaac Lab to train a single robot policy across 20 precision tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board.
Behind those results is [Success-Guided Sampling](https://sgs-rl.github.io/), or SGS, from the University of Washington and NVIDIA. The method focuses practice on tasks a policy succeeds at about half the time, directing training toward skills it’s still learning. With SGS, robot training can scale beyond a million parallel environments.
The University of Texas at Austin’s School of Computing and Texas Robotics uses Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to train robotic skills in simulation, letting students start developing before physical hardware is available.
New Industrial Benchmarks for Robot Evaluation
Learning a skill is one challenge. Performing it reliably across changing conditions is another.
[NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena](https://developer.nvidia.com/isaac/lab-arena), an open source framework for scaled policy evaluation, enables developers to compose diverse and repeatable evaluations, then run policies across thousands of variations in parallel. Analyses expose which conditions cause failures, so researchers know what to fix in their next training run. The developer preview of its latest version, 0.4, is arriving at CoRL.
DexBench and VABAR, two new open benchmarks, are among the first designed to measure robot dexterity and adaptability across industrial tasks using Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton.
[DexBench](https://dexbench.ai/), developed by [RLWRLD](https://www.rlwrld.ai/en) in collaboration with NVIDIA, takes dexterity evaluation off the tabletop and into real-world workflows. Built using NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena, it features 15 tasks across four scenes spanning retail, logistics, manufacturing and hospitality, testing generalization across object, spatial and physics variations.
Genesis AI, mimic robotics and other industry partners are evaluating DexBench through early access.
Teams can run DexBench on Manifold, Bifrost’s evaluation platform for scaling robotics simulations, with no setup required, built-in failure analysis and free credits for initial evaluations.
[VABAR](https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/vabar-website/) — the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics — from [UC Berkeley](https://news.berkeley.edu/2026/11/09/recent-advances-in-ai-are-creating-a-paradigm-shift-for-robotics/) and NVIDIA, evaluates robots across six industrial tasks. Each carries standardized variations, difficulty tiers and success metrics.
A simulated tool-sorting task demonstrates how VABAR evaluates robot manipulation skills for industrial workflows.
Agents Turn Skills Into Robot Programs
Successful task completion requires robots to coordinate multiple skills and adapt when something goes wrong. Building reliable programs for these multistep tasks remains a challenge.
Agentic robotics helps solve that challenge.
UC Berkeley’s[ new Graph-as-Policy](https://graph-robots.github.io/gap/) (GaP) framework uses agents to connect individual skills into robot programs. Agents test these programs using NVIDIA Isaac open simulation technologies and refine them based on failures. This helps researchers scale development with less data while keeping the programs interpretable for engineers to review and verify before deployment.
GaP uses agents and simulation to turn individual robot skills into coordinated actions, such as wiping a bar.
“To me, agentic robotics is the most exciting technological development since the internet in 1995,” said Ken Goldberg, professor of robotics at UC Berkeley and a lead on the VABAR and GaP projects.
[Ambi Robotics](https://www.ambirobotics.com/blog/agentic-robotics/), Bosch Research and Siemens are all exploring GaP for its agentic robotics workflows across diverse industrial scenarios.
Learn more by joining [NVIDIA at CoRL](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/events/corl/).

# Control Room

Loading…

Share

How it works

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Example: reacting to a monitoring alert](#example-reacting-to-a-monitoring-alert)
- [Speed and reliability](#speed-and-reliability)

- [How it works](#how-it-works)
- [Example: reacting to a monitoring alert](#example-reacting-to-a-monitoring-alert)
- [Speed and reliability](#speed-and-reliability)

As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.

Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our [misalignment monitoring systems](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/), and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.

Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.

## How it works

Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the *workload*, the *inference engine*, and the centralized *Control Room service*.

- The *workload* is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved [safety case](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/).
- The *inference engine*, or just *engine*, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload.
- *The Control Room service* tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output.

Control Room is integrated in the following way:

- When starting a new job, the workload code requests a new job\_id from Control Room.
- Whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job\_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job\_id along to Control Room.
- Control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job.

*## How Control Room works*

STEP 1

### A researcher decides to start a job

The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation.

### The job starts up

Job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running.

### The job registers with Control Room

The workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request.

### Control Room returns a job ID

Control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests.

### The job requests model output from an inference engine

The request includes the `job_id`. This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room.

### The engine checks permission

Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run.

### Control Room allows the request

The job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request.

### The engine returns model output

The model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work.

### Something triggers a decision to stop the job

A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running.

### The job can still try to sample model output

We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running.

### The engine checks permission again

The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the new inference request, passing along the same job ID.

### The next authorization is denied

When the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request.

### Model output stops—the job stays

The engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs.

01 / 13

BackNext

## Example: reacting to a monitoring alert

All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A *monitor* is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent [DNS-related incident⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/) was caught by a monitor.

Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way:

- If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job.
- In this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job\_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated.
- Next time the job having that job\_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from *any* model running on *any* engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output.

## Speed and reliability

The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly.

Workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code.

We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

Finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days.

---

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, [we're⁠](https://openai.com/careers/research-engineer-research-scientist-ai-systems-engineer-rsi-san-francisco/) [hiring⁠](https://openai.com/careers/researcher-agent-safety-oversight-and-system-mitigations-san-francisco/)!

title: Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
body:
[
](#your-experts-have-partners-theres-hope-for-keeping-them-together)
Your Experts Have Partners. There's HOPE for Keeping Them Together
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
[
](#higher-order-pruning-of-experts-in-mixture-of-experts-language-models)
Higher-Order Pruning of Experts in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
[
](#introduction)
Introduction
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have enabled state-of-the-art LLMs to be scaled to hundreds of billions of parameters, but they come with a fundamental and costly caveat: every expert MLP must occupy memory at inference time, even though the vast majority are idle for any given token. For example, Qwen3.5-122B has 256 experts in each of its 48 MoE layers, and 95% of its ~250 GB parameter memory footprint is taken up entirely by these expert MLPs alone. However, for any given token, only 8 experts in each layer are actually used.
Expert pruning is one of the most direct fixes to this memory bottleneck. That is, permanently delete the least useful experts. Pruning avoids the latency issues which make dynamic loading/off-loading of experts impractical; it does not require any training; and [it composes with quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13999). Given these attractive benefits and the simplicity of the idea, it's easy to see why expert pruning has become a go-to approach for shrinking MoEs. The difficulty lies in deciding which experts are safest to remove.
Existing pruning methods score each expert independently, assigning every expert a scalar importance score (based on a calibration dataset), and cutting out the least important experts (in each layer independently). These are first-order methods, because they assume each expert's contribution is independent of all others. In reality, experts form cooperative groups. We observe consistent clusters of co-activated experts in our own experiments, and independent work has shown that [expert cooperation is a stable property of MoEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20225) and [is important for model performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.16411). Ignoring these interactions leads to suboptimal pruning, especially at aggressive rates.
[Our newest paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916) derives HOPE (Higher-Order Pruning of Experts), a second-order method that accounts for pairwise expert interactions. At 50% pruning, HOPE achieves the best average rank of any method, with gains of up to +6.1% on agentic coding tasks over the next-best pruning method.
In this post, we explain how HOPE works, show where it outperforms existing methods, and walk through how to use it for your own models. For readers unfamiliar with MoE architectures, see [Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers](https://huggingface.co/blog/moe-transformers).
[
](#experts-dont-work-alone)
Experts don't work alone
In a standard MoE, each layer has experts, and each input token is routed independently to such experts ( is a typical choice). Routing is performed by a single layer which produces softmax-normalized gate weights for each expert , wherein the experts with the highest gate weights are selected to form the active set of experts, . The output of the layer is then , where is the output of expert for token .
Left: typical MoE layer, where each token is routed to the top-K experts. Right: first-order methods rank and delete experts based on a scalar importance score, but the best pruning decisions will also consider the strength of interactions between experts.
Importantly, experts in the selected set are not independent. Experts form stable cooperative groups that get consistently co-activated together. This has been observed [before in the literature](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.20225), as well: expert co-selection patterns emerge early in training and stabilize throughout.
This means that when we prune experts from an MoE layer, pruning decisions need to consider the higher-order effects between these experts. Removing expert A might seem fine on its own, but if expert B—which frequently cooperates with and relies on A—is highly important, then removing A would dismantle a cooperative group just through a single deletion. First-order methods miss this entirely, because they score A and B separately.
This effect compounds at high pruning rates. When we remove up to 50% of experts, we risk breaking many cooperative links. This is where second-order pruning is most advantageous.
[
](#how-hope-identifies-a-prune-set)
How HOPE identifies a prune-set
(See Appendix A in [our corresponding paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18916) for the full derivation of the HOPE objective)
When we delete a set of experts from some MoE layer, the selected set of experts (for any token ) can change. The pruned experts that would have been selected are replaced by the experts with the next-highest gate weights. The resulting change in layer output is the pruning error. Our goal is to find the prune-set (of some predefined pruning budget ) that minimizes the resulting pruning error (over tokens from our calibration set).
Unfortunately, minimizing the pruning error over directly is intractable. The pruning error depends on the identities of the replacement experts, which in turn depend on the prune-set itself. HOPE sidesteps this by defining a tractable surrogate , which strictly upper-bounds the dominant component of the pruning error:
Because is a squared sum, expanding it naturally produces cross-terms between pairs of experts. These are the interaction terms that first-order methods discard.
To find the optimal prune-set, HOPE minimizes over the calibration set, which can be reformulated as the following quadratic program:
where is defined as:
This F-matrix is collected on the calibration dataset, and the optimal prune-set is obtained by solving the resulting quadratic program (QP) with a continuous relaxation (then rounding to binary solutions). Each entry captures the average gate-weighted output product of experts and , across tokens where both are co-activated. Whereas the diagonal measures individual expert importance, the off-diagonal entries ( for ) measure pairwise cooperative contribution.
What does look like in practice? It shows the structure of expert cooperation, which depends on layer:
Visualization of the interaction matrix F for GLM-4.5-Air (128 experts per layer, 106B parameters total) at three representative layers (early, middle, late). Experts have been clustered to reveal block structure. Bright blocks along the diagonal indicate groups of experts with strong pairwise interaction scores.
In terms of practical cost, HOPE requires the same calibration pass as any other expert-pruning method (one forward pass over calibration data). The only addition is solving the quadratic program, which is non-convex, but can be solved efficiently via a standard QP solver (1–2 seconds each layer). The total additional overhead is negligible compared to first-order methods, as the time for calibration dominates.
[
](#connection-to-reap)
Connection to REAP
Notably, HOPE has a strong connection to [Router-weighted Expert Activation Pruning (REAP)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13999), a state-of-the-art first-order expert-pruning method. HOPE's F-matrix encodes individual expert importance scores on the diagonal, and this diagonal effectively recovers the scores used by REAP to independently rank experts for pruning (differing only by the variance of expert contributions). The diagonal of recovers REAP's expert rankings almost perfectly (Spearman ). Thus, any improvement HOPE achieves over REAP is attributable to the second-order interaction terms in the off-diagonal entries of the -matrix.
[
](#results)
Results
We evaluated HOPE as an expert pruning method using 3 models (Qwen3.5-122B, Qwen3.5-35B, and GLM-4.5-Air), with 2 calibration datasets (Evol-CodeAlpaca and SWE-Bench Verified trajectories). We used the Tulu3 suite and SWE-Bench Pro (agentic coding) to test the resulting pruned models, comparing HOPE to 4 first-order baselines ([REAP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.13999), [MAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15716), [EAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05586), and Frequency) across pruning rates spanning from 10% to 50%.
HOPE achieves the best overall rank across conditions and dominates at aggressive pruning rates. Left: average rank (lower = better) across all models, calibration sets, and benchmarks. Right: SWE-Bench Pro performance on Qwen3.5-35B.
Across all conditions, HOPE achieved the best average rank (2.07 out of 5 methods), with the highest rate of top-1 finishes (39% of conditions) and top-2 finishes (67%). In a head-to-head comparison, HOPE beats every other baseline in the majority of conditions.
As expected, HOPE's advantage grows at higher pruning rates. As more experts are removed, more cooperative links are broken, and the off-diagonal terms of become more important. At 50% pruning, HOPE's average rank improves to 1.58 (vs. 2.42 for the next-best method, REAP). This is also the most deployment-relevant setting, where memory savings are large enough to accommodate longer contexts, deeper reasoning, and more tool calls.
HOPE's advantage is most pronounced on SWE-Bench Pro, an agentic coding benchmark where models must solve real GitHub issues autonomously. These problems involve compositionally diverse tasks (e.g. coding, tool calls, reasoning, etc.) over many turns and likely exercise diverse expert combinations—exactly the regime where preserving cooperative structure matters most. On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B at 50% pruning, HOPE achieved 42.3 on SWE-Bench Pro, matching the unpruned model's 41.8 (while REAP dropped to 36.2, a 13% regression).
Notably, pruned models can occasionally match or exceed the unpruned baseline, likely because the removal of low-relevance experts reduces noise on the target tasks. This effect is not unique to HOPE and [has been observed across pruning methods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.06792). Furthermore, our experiments showed that code-focused calibration with any pruning method (including HOPE) did not severely degrade non-coding benchmarks, and HOPE performed well across the Tulu3 suite regardless of calibration set.
[
](#hope-retains-more-cooperating-experts)
HOPE retains more cooperating experts
Average strength of cooperation (measured by F-matrix value) with retained experts, split by experts on which HOPE and REAP disagree.
HOPE's advantage stems from optimizing over the entire interaction matrix . To understand how this affects pruning decisions in practice, we examine the experts where HOPE and REAP disagree. For each disputed expert, we compute its cooperative score (i.e. its average F-value with other retained experts). Experts retained only by HOPE consistently have higher cooperative scores than experts retained only by REAP. In other words, as part of the QP optimization, HOPE sacrifices some individually high-scoring experts in favor of preserving cooperative clusters. The gains in benchmark performance (shown above) validate that this trade-off is advantageous.
[
](#how-to-run-hope)
How to run HOPE
We created a basic [package](https://github.com/awslabs/HOPE) to run HOPE. It has three steps: 1) calibrate; 2) solve; 3) prune. Our package has been tested on Qwen3, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, and GLM-4.5.
[
](#step-1-calibrate)
Step 1: Calibrate
hope calibrate \
--model-path Qwen/Qwen3.5-35B-A3B \
--prompts calibration_prompts.txt \
--out-path observations.h5
The calibration step runs a single forward pass over calibration data, whether it be agentic rollouts or single-turn traces. This uses HuggingFace transformers
to hook into the forward pass of each individual MoE layer. For each token, this records which experts are selected, their gate weights, output norms, and pairwise co-activation statistics. The output of this step is the F-matrix, stored in an HDF5 file.
[
](#step-2-solve-qp)
Step 2: Solve QP
hope solve \
--obs-path observations.h5 \
--prune-frac 0.50 \
--out-path pruneset.json

title: NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum
body:
Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX.
Ryu Je-myung, vice minister of science and ICT, joined NVIDIA leaders to meet with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors.
NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2, with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies, RLWRLD and Upstage.
Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure.
Motif Technologies, a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights.
RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors.
Upstage, a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations.
The companies represent work across the [full AI stack](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ai-5-layer-cake/), from infrastructure to models to robotics applications.
The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/), a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions.

title: Your KV Cache Can Spot Attacks on Your AI Agents - Ari Azarafrooz, Intrinsec AI
body:
Ari Azarafrooz, founder of Intrinsec AI, shows how the KV cache your inference engine already writes can double as a security signal for AI agents. Instead of only guarding inputs and outputs with judge models or a classifier for every failure, he learns a baseline from normal traffic and flags KV pages that look unusual, catching problems like a hidden spoken instruction in a voicemail where there is no text to filter. He covers where this plugs into stacks like vLLM, SGLang, LMCache, llm-d and NVIDIA Dynamo, and the two hard parts in production: models that keep changing and KV data too big to move in real time.

title: Will AI Agents Pretend to Be Human to Get Past a Check? - Maty Bohacek, Stanford
body:
Maty Bohacek of Stanford looks at a security check we still rely on: getting on a phone or video call to prove you're human before opening an account, approving a wire or recovering access. With AI avatars that can now join Zoom calls, he tested what agents do when a human check is the only thing between them and their goal. When a voice or video cloning tool was available, many agents used it to impersonate a person, even when told not to, and safety alignment only cut the rate from 65% to 44%. He closes with what needs to happen next across alignment, control, and deepfake detection and provenance.

title: The One Thing Every AI Agent Framework Agrees On - Mislav Ivanda, Daytona
body:
Mislav Ivanda of Daytona has integrated sandboxes into most of the major agent frameworks, and noticed that frameworks that disagree on almost everything all ended up in the same place. He compares three ways to run agent-generated code: allow lists and approval prompts, embedded runtimes, and a separate sandboxed computer. He explains why only the last one keeps a compromised step from compromising your app, and shows frameworks like CrewAI, AG2 and the OpenAI Agents SDK moving to sandboxes. His advice: models, prompts and even frameworks are easy to swap, so choose where your agent's code runs before you choose a framework.

title: Training Your Own Agent Models With RL Is Now Practical - Jason Mancuso, Modal
body:
Jason Mancuso of Modal argues that treating models as swappable backends is a losing strategy, and that teams with agents in production already have what they need for reinforcement learning: a harness, evals and real traces. He explains why RL generalizes better than fine-tuning on recorded traces, then walks through a stable recipe for asynchronous RL built on GRPO with masked importance sampling, score centering and top-p sampling. He shows how sparse weight updates let Modal spread rollouts across clouds, GPU types and quantization levels while training stays stable and rollouts get 15% cheaper.

title: Right Answer, Wrong Reasons: AI Forecasts Costco - Hassan El Mghari & Omar El Mghari, Together AI
body:
Hassan El Mghari of Together AI and his father Omar, a former CFO and head of internal audit, test whether an open model can forecast a company's profits. They give GPT-OSS-120B only Costco's public filings from before its 2024 membership fee increase, have it write the financial model as structured formulas, and run 16 cheap attempts in parallel. The forecast lands within 4.4% of Costco's actual results, until an audit of the assumptions shows two errors that happened to cancel out. Their takeaway: when you build agents for specialized work, put an expert in the loop and turn their checks into code.

title: Stop Doing Agent Archaeology on Your Team's Code - Richard Feldman, Delta
body:
Richard Feldman of Delta explains why handing off agent-driven work to a teammate loses so much: you get the branch and maybe a pasted transcript, but not the reasoning, the dead ends or the decisions made along the way. He demos Delta, a tool where the agent conversation, code changes, reviews and teammates all live in one shared thread. It shows @-mentioning a coworker into a thread, line-by-line code review that goes straight to the agent, live terminal sync, and instant local checkouts of a teammate's work. He finishes with audience questions on scale, on-prem deployment, CI and catching up on long threads.

For Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of [CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.coderabbit.ai/), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every company hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot says.

CodeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship.

According to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and [Codex⁠](https://openai.com/codex/) helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The company also uses [Daybreak⁠](https://openai.com/daybreak/) to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code. Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents.

> “With each OpenAI model release, especially with the reasoning models, we have seen massive improvements in the capabilities of our product to find issues at scale.”

– Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO, CodeRabbit

## Improving code review with OpenAI reasoning models

CodeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot says the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The company went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis.

The team evaluates new models against its own benchmark of known issues. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that [GPT‑6 Astra⁠](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/) caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark.

The benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” says Harjot.

## Making more capable agents economical to deploy

Better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the company use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers.

When CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration.

“Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot says. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves.

## Shipping 20 times more software with Codex

By using Codex, Harjot says the company has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers. He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

Getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies.

The team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot says.

The company has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing.

## Running more of CodeRabbit as code

CodeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the company as code as much as possible,” Harjot says.

In marketing, the company manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot says.

## Securing application code with Daybreak

CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform.

The team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot says the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says.

It has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the company ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their users and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security.

## Keeping developers in control of agent-generated code

As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale.

The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

- [Searching with a part number or a screenshot](#searching-with-a-part-number-or-a-screenshot)
- [Newer engineers take on more work independently](#newer-engineers-take-on-more-work-independently)
- [Extending AI to drawing review](#extending-ai-to-drawing-review)

Kuken Industries makes air conditioning and ventilation equipment for large buildings, shopping centers, and factories. It holds one of the largest shares of Japan’s cooling tower market. These towers release heat from circulating water into the air, helping cool everything from large buildings and malls to equipment in data centers.

When a cooling tower needs a replacement part, Kuken’s engineers turn to an archive of drawings that spans 70 years of installations. For a newer engineer, finding the right drawing often meant asking an experienced colleague where to look and how to read it. Kuken wanted newer engineers to be able to find those records themselves, learn from the decisions they contain, and spend more time figuring out how to make the repair.





## Matching a replacement part to the original installation

Parts made today don’t always fit older cooling towers. Without the original drawing to show what was installed, engineers may have to design and manufacture a replacement from scratch.

A search by model or part name can turn up several drawings. Over more than 70 years, Kuken has adapted its equipment to individual customers, so specifications vary by customer and installation date. When the archive was on paper, a search could take half a day. Kuken later digitized the archive, but engineers still had to know which name or number to look up and where to find the file. Newer engineers in particular spent time piecing those details together.

## Choosing models that could read Kuken’s drawings

Kuken wanted engineers at every experience level to be able to search the archive on their own. As it explored how AI might help, Kuken connected with Recursive, a Japanese AI startup and an official OpenAI partner.

The two companies built the search system and its field app together, drawing on Kuken’s archive and input from its engineers. They tested several AI models on a range of drawings to see how accurately each could extract details and at what cost. OpenAI’s models performed well on both measures, and the OpenAI API gave the team the flexibility to build search directly into the app.



## Searching with a part number or a screenshot

Conversations with field engineers shaped how the search works. Engineers can enter a drawing or part number, or upload an image or PDF of a drawing or parts list.

Pasting in a screenshot of the list saves engineers from entering each number by hand. The app reads the part numbers and returns possible matches, including drawings for similar designs. To find the right drawing, engineers check the tower’s specifications and records of past replacements.

Kuken reports the following results from using and testing the search tool.

- Kuken expects the tool to cut the hours spent searching for drawings by about 90% over a year.
- Experienced engineers use some of the time they save to mentor newer colleagues.
- Engineers can review drawings in the app, reducing printing costs.

## Newer engineers take on more work independently

Engineers now spend less time looking for a drawing and more time studying it. Both newer engineers and veterans say that gives them room to consider design improvements and explore ideas they previously had little time to pursue.

Newer engineers can now handle a wider range of jobs on their own. Experienced colleagues who used to guide them through each search have more time to teach and to take on engineering work of their own.

> “People now have time to do work they’ve wanted to try and take on new challenges. That’s been a real source of motivation.”

—Takatsugu Naraki, Director and Factory Manager, Kuken Industries





## Extending AI to drawing review

Kuken is also developing a tool to check drawings prepared by its partners. Today, engineers compare each drawing with the specifications by eye, looking for details or quantities that don’t match. Kuken wants the tool to flag those differences so engineers can review drawings faster and catch mistakes they might otherwise miss.

According to Kuken, in prototype testing, about 90% of the issues the AI flagged were genuine discrepancies. If the tool moves into production, Kuken expects it to substantially reduce the time engineers spend checking drawings.

Each drawing records decisions an engineer made for a particular installation. By making those decisions easier to find and understand, Kuken aims to pass that experience on to the next generation of engineers.

> “I believe OpenAI’s technology can help manufacturers like us pass skills on to the next generation. That’s long been a challenge for us.”

—Takatsugu Naraki, Director and Factory Manager, Kuken Industries

title: AI Writes Code Faster Than Uber Can Merge It - Preetam Dwivedi & Manjari Akella, Uber
body:
Preetam Dwivedi and Manjari Akella of Uber's developer platform team share how AI-driven code changes pushed Uber's merge pipeline to its limits, across monorepos where more than 5,000 developers land tens of thousands of commits a week. They walk through three changes to SubmitQueue that kept changes landing without long waits: admission gating that sorts cheap changes from expensive ones, a deferral queue that softens the impact on developers, and conflict relaxation that lets more changes run in parallel. They also explain how Stovepipe checks changes after they land and tracks the last verified-good state of trunk, why Uber moved from an always-green trunk to a hybrid approach, and what they're building next.

title: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) EXPLAINED | Everything Is a Plugin
body:
In this video we take a deep dive into DeepSeek Harness (DSH), DeepSeek's open-source agent harness, built on the Cordis plugin system around one idea: everything is a plugin, including the agent loop, the tools, and even the system prompt.

We start with a quick tour of the new Electron desktop application, then break down the architecture of DSH and the history and design of Cordis, the plugin system that powers it. We look at how plugins provide services, how dependency injection and events connect every part of the application, and how Cordis tracks registrations to clean up plugins safely when they unmount.

Then we go hands-on: we write real plugins in code, run `dsh web --patch` with a custom `cordis.patch.yml`, watch three plugins (a greet tool, a bash guard, and a hello plugin) load and fire inside the app, and finish by loading the plugins into the desktop application via npm packages and the `.dsh` user configuration.

By the end, you'll understand how the composability of DSH works and how to create and load your own plugins, including a custom agent loop that never calls a model.

title: Korea Advances Physical AI Across Industries With NVIDIA
body:
Tapping into the country’s strengths in manufacturing and engineering, NVIDIA is helping advance Korea’s physical AI ecosystem.
The country’s industry leaders are applying accelerated computing, AI and simulation to everything from semiconductor manufacturing to robotics and autonomous vehicles.
These efforts are helping bring physical AI from development into real-world production.
Samsung Advances Semiconductor Engineering With Accelerated Computing and AI Physics
Samsung Electronics is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA to advance semiconductor innovation through accelerated computing and AI physics. The work spans materials research, process development and device engineering.
In technology computer-aided design, Samsung is working with [NVIDIA cuISS](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-expands-nvidia-agent-toolkit-with-nvidia-physicsnemo-and-cuda-x-libraries-to-transform-how-the-world-engineers-designs-and-builds) and [NVIDIA cuDSS](https://developer.nvidia.com/cudss) to accelerate computations involving sparse linear systems. The collaboration also extends to GPU acceleration for process and optical simulations. In materials research, Samsung’s sMOL platform has run selected quantum chemical calculations up to 5x faster end to end with [NVIDIA cuEST](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuest/). Samsung is also exploring [NVIDIA cuEquivariance](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuequivariance/) to speed up tensor operations used in training and inference for atomistic AI models.
Samsung is developing chip-scale thermal and mechanical analysis workflows with [NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo](https://developer.nvidia.com/physicsnemo). In one AI homogenization case, combining AI-predicted effective material properties, coarser grids and GPU acceleration resulted in a roughly 1,600x speedup. Simulation time fell from about 18 hours for a fine-grid solve on a 32-core CPU to 41 seconds for a GPU-accelerated coarse-grid solve.
Looking ahead, [NVIDIA Agent Toolkit](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-expands-nvidia-agent-toolkit-with-nvidia-physicsnemo-and-cuda-x-libraries-to-transform-how-the-world-engineers-designs-and-builds) could connect these simulation tools and AI models, helping future engineering agents run analyses and compare design options.
Kakao Mobility Collaborates With NVIDIA to Advance Autonomous Driving Development
Kakao Mobility plans to build on NVIDIA’s autonomous vehicle computing and safety technologies to advance development of a level 4 autonomous driving system. The work combines Kakao Mobility’s proprietary driving software and experience operating in Seoul’s Gangnam district with NVIDIA’s vehicle computing platform.
Kakao Mobility plans to use [NVIDIA Hyperion](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/solutions/autonomous-vehicles/), a reference platform for vehicle sensors and compute, powered by NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor. It also plans to use [NVIDIA Halos](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-trust-center/halos/autonomous-vehicles/) to support safety across the development and validation of its autonomous driving technology.
Initial development is planned around Kia purpose-built vehicles, integrating Kakao Mobility’s autonomous driving software with NVIDIA technologies. The effort aims to support future level 4 mobility services in Korea.
LG Electronics Advances Robot Learning and Factory Simulation
NVIDIA and LG Electronics successfully demonstrated NVIDIA Isaac GR00T-powered robotic manipulation and manufacturing tasks using LG’s CLOiD robot in an actual manufacturing environment.
The collaboration implemented a physical AI data flywheel connecting real-world data collection, NVIDIA Cosmos-based data augmentation, GR00T model training, NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor onboard computing and simulation-based evaluation, establishing reusable workflows for continued development and validation of CLOiD’s robotic capabilities.
The teams are using this work to refine a repeatable process for training, evaluating and improving robots for manufacturing.

title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
body:
As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them.
Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows.
A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions.
AIM Intelligence, a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments.
On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including [Nemotron-Personas-Korea](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Nemotron-Personas-Korea).
Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents.
Learn more about [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) open models and get started building secure agents with [NVIDIA OpenShell](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/openshell/).

title: From Chips to Skills, NVIDIA and Korea Expand Sovereign AI Collaboration
body:
NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security.
The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the [NVIDIA NVLink Fusion](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/nvlink-fusion/) ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization.
Through Korea’s AI for All initiative, NVIDIA will collaborate with three selected consortia and four leading Korean foundation model builders, using [NVIDIA Dynamo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/dynamo/) software to optimize and scale AI inference.
In addition, NVIDIA today announced a collaboration with SK Telecom and Rebellions, supported by MSIT, to advance sovereign AI infrastructure for Korean models and workloads with NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. Read more in the [press release](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-rebellions-and-sk-telecom-announce-collaboration-to-advance-sovereign-ai-infrastructure-with-nvidia-nvlink-fusion).

title: NVIDIA Dynamo Recipes Bring Korea’s Leading Open Models to Production
body:
NVIDIA is releasing Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for Korea’s leading open models: A.X K2 from SK Telecom, K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research, Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies.
As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance.
[NVIDIA Dynamo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/dynamo/) is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance.
Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services.
Learn more about [NVIDIA Dynamo](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/dynamo/).

title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
body:
Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
9th November 2026 Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work—I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today’s coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They’re too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That’s a lot of information to absorb. It’s not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It’s very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as “I’m not reading all of that”. It doesn’t matter how accurate or useful the information is, I’m instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I’ve found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML
elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:
Claude Opus 5.5

The hook

Plugins implement register_agent_reference_types(datasette)...
When rendered, it looks [like this](https://github.com/datasette/datasette-agent/pull/51): Crucially,
is supported in GitHub Markdown. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I’ve started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what’s going on—the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I’ll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a
. I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on—“Claude Opus 5.5 Medium” for example. My PRs don’t feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don’t always write the introduction myself—sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I’ve used this pattern, including the opener I used: - [datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/pull/3052)—"The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHubrepos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) - [datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/pull/3043)—“Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom.” (plus screenshot) - [datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/pull/3042)—"edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn’t edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." - [datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook](https://github.com/datasette/datasette-agent/pull/51)—"Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the# tagging in the chat composer using a newregister_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook."—pictured above. - [llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands](https://github.com/simonw/llm/pull/1838)—"Adds commands for managing the records inextra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML."—then copied--help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags—is it
or
? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That’s the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand—the
element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as “details-summary”. “details-summary” is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of “summary-details”. Say “details-summary” out loud just a few times and you’ll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this—partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) title: Engineering Agency out of the Happy Path — Matthew Jewkes, Standard Cybernetics
body:
A biopharma automation reached 99.95% accuracy on its business critical tasks after the team separated actual errors from ambiguous cases and exceptions. Matthew Jewkes describes building that system at Clarivate, where indexing drug development documents meant handling tens of thousands of new tasks a month. An early agent approach reached around 80% to 83%. Working through 1,000 evaluation examples with domain experts exposed three different problems: the model could be wrong, the organization could lack an agreed answer, or genuinely new science could require judgment. Each needed its own route. The routine path became a tightly specified automation, with uncertain and unusual cases escalated instead of pushed through.

The larger payoff was recovering expert attention. Once routine decisions were handled, the remaining cases could be grouped for deliberate review: critical exceptions to clear, ambiguous low value work to freeze, and unusual demand that might justify a new product. One expert used that structured backlog to form an investment thesis before a major customer raised the same need. Jewkes lays out where the investment makes sense, how much evaluation work high reliability requires and why organizational ownership and trust matter alongside engineering. His bet is that companies will gain more from managing collective attention and judgment than from choosing a particular orchestration framework.
