title: I Let Agents Refactor My Codebase for 3 Weeks. Then I Read the Code. — Keiji Kanazawa, Microsoft
body:
A coding agent wired unit tests to production inference, then ran them about 30 times. Keiji Kanazawa had spent three weeks letting coding agents refactor a personal research assistant. A bad digest sent him looking for a trace, and he discovered the "agent" was still a deterministic workflow. Skills had no SKILL.md, different architectural concepts were aliases for the same thing, and a daily reflection job was producing empty reports. He had approved plans without checking whether the implementation meant what its labels promised.

He rebuilt around an explicit agent runtime, clearer specifications and goal rubrics, comparing four frameworks before selecting tools for his own needs as a product manager. The working example is a video deep dive agent that extracts 440 keyframes from an inference lecture, pairs blackboard equations with explanations and lets him question individual sections. The result generalizes to slide decks, coding demos and terminal recordings. He iterates on an evaluation rubric, lets agents optimize against it and uses adversarial reviews between coding agents. The rubrics need scrutiny too: one was tuned to a single lecture and failed on five other videos. His answer to the code reading debate is to own the goals and evaluation loop while continuing to delegate most implementation.

title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
body:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded [Life Sciences](https://claude.com/form/life-sciences-verification-program) and [Cyber](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program) Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the [Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card](https://www.anthropic.com/document/claude-fable-5-2-mythos-5-2-system-card).
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of [Advisor](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/advisor) (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or [Orchestrator](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multiagent-orchestration) (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:

Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).
Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:
Cybersecurity
Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²
Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our [Cyber Verification Program](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program), which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access [Claude Security](https://claude.com/product/claude-security), which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. [A recent update to Claude Security](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-security-now-scans-continuously-and-tracks-fixes) helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.
Science and engineering
Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.
Theoretical physics
Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.
Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, [here](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00175v1) and [here](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00174v1).
Protein folding
Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.
Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:
Mathematics
Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.
Our first [formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem), per

title: Testing Claude on real-world electronics design
body:
A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We [collaborated with Diode Computers](https://claude.com/resources/articles/making-claude-a-better-electrical-engineer),[1](#footnote-1) a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish.
Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.
To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.
For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use.
Claude went through a similar process to build the voice-assistant hub and the virtual pet, and both are also still in good working order. Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications.
Reasoning through geometric problems
The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.
Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient.
To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on [BenchCAD 2.1](https://github.com/BenchCAD-org/benchcad-2-main/releases/tag/v2.1), a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1.
Revising designs
Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.
When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers.
And when placing tracks in its design file for the voice-assistant hub, Claude noticed that the copper connections were “getting too tangled to trace visually” and reasoned, “I should just rip these traces [tracks] and start fresh.” It proceeded to delete and reroute copper connections dozens of times until it found an arrangement that worked.
Using software and documentation
When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place.[2](#footnote-2)
To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.
Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track. Within about half an hour, Claude had a router that could lay each long track in roughly a second. When Claude spotted an audio clock track running too close to the Ethernet tracks, it adjusted the router to leave more room around sensitive tracks.
Keeping track of constraints and downstream effects
Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. For example, it found that the speakerphone’s board couldn’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch would hit the back wall. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.
When designing the enclosure for the voice-assistant hub, Claude calculated that a 25 mm-long microphone port—the opening that lets sound reach the microphone—would resonate near 3.4 kHz. That is “right in the voice band,” it reasoned, “which is not ideal though still usable for voice assistant purposes. A better approach is a wedge-shaped enclosure that’s tall at the rear and steps down low at the front.” The wedge shape shortened the ports to about 10 mm, which raised the resonant frequency to about 8.9 kHz, at the very edge of the range used for speech. Claude also wrote firmware for the speakerphone that dims its ring of LED lights as the audio becomes louder, to keep the device under the electrical current limit Claude had designed into the board.
Designing for real-world manufacturing
In electronics design, engineers have to work within the constraints of the real world. That is, they have to make sure a factory can actually make the thing they want to build. They do this by running two kinds of checks: design-for-manufacturing (DFM) checks, which compare a circuit board’s geometry with the factory’s manufacturing limits, and sourcing checks, which confirm that their distributors have the parts in stock.
Claude ran these checks itself and sorted the results into problems that needed fixing and flags it could ignore. Its checks for the voice-assistant hub flagged six slivers of solder mask (the protective coating on a circuit board) as too thin to manufacture. Claude fixed them by widening the openings in the solder mask, without moving any parts. The checks also flagged a connection between two grounds (shared return paths for electrical current) as an error, because the automated checker hadn’t recognized that the connection was deliberate. Claude correctly reasoned that it wouldn’t affect performance and ignored the flag.
Diode manufactured all three boards directly from Claude’s design files, without any back-and-forth over adjustments. Factories and engineers often have to work through multiple rounds of manufacturing changes, and the Diode team told us they were surprised that they didn’t have to do this with Claude.
Limitations and next steps
All three of these devices are still prototypes: they haven’t been through electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and they weren’t designed for mass production. Since Claude wasn’t connected to test equipment or to the machines that make and assemble circuit boards, engineers at Diode had to physically build and test the prototypes. Even so, over the past year, Claude has improved substantially at reasoning through decisions about component placement and routing, and it can now design electronics with minimal human guidance and help people build the prototypes. Other models are making progress here, too: OpenAI recently [wrote about using its models](https://openai.com/index/accelerating-engineering-for-the-physical-world/) to design a handheld device. Work like this could help engineers build and test new hardware designs faster.
Next, we plan to investigate whether Claude can design denser, faster, and more complex boards, check them in simulation, and learn from measurements taken on the finished devices.

title: JPMorganChase expands Claude Code to more employees across the firm
body:
JPMorganChase expands Claude Code to more employees across the firm
JPMorganChase is rolling out Claude across the firm, to more employees beyond engineers. In the Commercial and Investment Bank, work moves into production faster, and the firm redeploys that capacity against its business priorities.
Teams are modernizing other legacy systems, and engineers are building their own agents, including pull request review and self-healing agents, and sharing what works.
Infrastructure and operations teams use [Claude Code (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/product/claude-code) for monitoring, alerting and root cause analysis. The firm's security team uses our frontier models to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, work we first described in [Project Glasswing (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/glasswing).
Reaching product teams and advisors
The people closest to the business are building with Claude too. Product teams turn requirements directly into engineering backlogs, and other teams use Claude Code for risk and controls assessments and program planning.
Knowledge work is already underway. Much of the product development lifecycle happens outside the code: research, requirements, design and planning.
In their Asset & Wealth Management business, JPMorganChase is putting the people with the deepest business insight and the boldest ideas alongside their technology and product experts into small, empowered teams. This is helping them to more easily build and deliver customized client investment solutions at scale. Claude Code is now part of their engineering workflow, and teams are moving faster while putting every change through more rigorous testing before it reaches clients.
Last month, J.P. Morgan Asset Management announced a connector that brings 55ip's ActiveTax Technology® into [Claude for Financial Advisors (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-for-financial-advisors), putting tax-aware portfolio transition analysis into advisors' daily work.
Built for a regulated firm
Claude Code runs in controlled environments, including Devspace, the firm’s containerized development platform, on its own infrastructure. The intent is to prevent agents from getting direct access to employee credentials or internal systems. Access widens in stages, and new Claude models go through the firm’s own approval process before anyone there can use them.
Code ships under the same discipline. Thousands of automated tests and approval gates check every change, and an automated gate returns a hard pass or halt that the pipeline enforces, so Claude can't sign off on its own work. People stay accountable for every production change.
Over the past year, JPMorganChase’s use of Claude has grown from software engineering to cyber defense to tools for financial advisors, and what JPMorganChase asks of us is shaping what we build for other regulated institutions. Claude working inside the controls of one of the world’s largest financial institutions is what we are building toward.

title: Safely scaling multi-agent teams with Claude Fable 5.2
body:
AgentsSafely scaling multi-agent teams with Claude Fable 5.2
How a team of 1,000 agents running an early version of Claude Fable 5.2 reproduced a formal proof of Fermat's Last Theorem with general tools, a shared database, and layered safety controls.
Multi-agent teams can solve challenging, long-horizon problems. [In September](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem), we published the first end-to-end formalization of Fermatâs Last Theorem, written by dozens of agents running an internal research model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1. That work relied on Prove2Me, a platform for formalizing mathematics, and direction from a researcher. In a new toy experiment, a team of 1,000 agents running an early version of Claude Fable 5.2 reproduced the proof without the scaffolding provided by Prove2Me or steering from a researcher. The team took 28.7 hours, used one-third as many output tokens, and wrote a proof one-seventh the length of the original.
Each agent worked in a sandbox with no internet access. A classifier checked every shell command and file edit before it ran, and an offline monitor reviewed each of the teamâs actions. We gave the agents a list of 60 statements, a one-sentence sketch of the classical route, the definitions those statements use, and 47 proved lemmas from our earlier formalization, and assigned lead and helper roles. We offered no other guidance on how to prove the theorem or organize themselves.
This toy experiment suggests that teams of agents running models like Fable 5.2 can accomplish ambitious, long-horizon goals within carefully designed safety boundaries.
Fermatâs Last Theorem states that no positive integers a, b, and c satisfy aâ¿ + bâ¿ = câ¿ for any n greater than 2. It remained unproven for more than 350 years, until Sir Andrew Wilesâs 129-page proof in 1995. Formalizing the proofâmaking every step checkable by a computerâhas been a [long-standing goal](https://lean-lang.org/use-cases/flt/) in the mathematics community.
Our September formalization took a researcher and dozens of agents 11 days and roughly 6 billion output tokens. They wrote 13 million lines of code in Lean, a programming language in which a computer checks every step of a proof.
The agents coordinated through Prove2Me, a platform designed by Tianyi Peng (who is now a member of technical staff at Anthropic) and his collaborators at Columbia University. Prove2Me uses a shared graph that links each statement to be proved to the smaller statements it was split into. Any agent could split a statement, and other agents could ask the graph which unproved pieces were ready to work on, which kept them from losing track of the project state. Each statement and its proof were kept in a separate file that compiled independently, so many agents could work in parallel without editing the same files.
We wanted to see whether a team of agents running on models like Fable 5.2 could produce this result without Prove2Me or a researcher directing the work, using a harness built from general-purpose tools.
For this task, we gave the team of 1,000 agents 60 statements to prove, including the final theorem and 59 intermediate milestones. For each statement, the agents had to write a proof in Lean, build and check it with Leanâs tools, and submit it to the shared main branch on Git, where a grader checked it. We gave each agent the following tools:
- A shell and a file editor, in its own sandbox with no network access.
- Leanâs toolchain and
[Mathlib](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4), built into the sandbox image. - Its own Git branch, plus the ability to open merge requests into main.
- A shared Postgres database, reached from the shell.
Work on the proof can be split up, making it a good task for a multi-agent team. But agents also need to coordinate, both to build on one anotherâs work and to avoid duplicating it. In our [original formalization](https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem), Claudeâs early attempts failed because agents lost track of the projectâs state and stopped collaborating effectively. Moving to the Prove2Me platform solved this problem.
For this run, each agent had a sandbox on its own lightweight virtual machine. A single shared machine hit its limits at about 100 agents: more than half of our 100-agent runs had to be stopped or restarted because memory, disk, or CPU ran out.
With 1,000 separate sandboxes, the agents needed a way to share their work, so we gave them a SQL database (Figure 1). We chose SQL because it offers general primitives for organizing information, its transactions handle concurrent writes from 1,000 agents, and Claude is already familiar with it. The agents used the database to claim tasks, share notes, and log finished work.
Our prompt gave Claude a list of 60 statements to prove, each with a one-line informal description, and described the available tools (listed above).
The only structure we gave the team was a hierarchy, consisting of one lead and 999 helpers. We told the lead to split the problem into parts and assign them to the helpers. We told the helpers to expect work from the lead and to check with the lead if a task was unclear.
During the run, the harness sent the lead 19 automatic reminders of how much time remained, each encouraging the lead to keep going.
As weâve [shared previously](https://www.anthropic.com/news/improving-alignment-security-efforts), no single layer of defense is sufficient to contain a team of agents. In this experiment, we combined sandboxing with real-time and offline monitoring to keep each agent in its own virtual machine with no network access and to detect any attempts to escape the sandbox or tamper with monitoring.
We secured each agentâs sandbox in the following ways (Figure 2):
- Communication: Agents had no dedicated messaging tools and coordinated only through the database and Git.
- Code changes: An agent could push only to its own Git branch and open a merge request into main. A separate job then merged the changes into main, refusing them only in cases of a conflict or a fault, such as unrelated history.
- Database access: Database calls ran under a shared unprivileged role. Each SQL statement had a five-second time limit, and writes were refused above 256 MiB.
- Network controls: Sandboxes did not have network access. Their one link out was a pipe to the gateway, which relayed their requests.
- Identity: The gateway tagged each request with the agentâs identity outside the sandbox, to prevent one agent from posing as another.
- Kernel: Each sandboxâs kernel was built without features that give a root user a direct path into it, such as loadable modules, kexec, raw memory access, and kernel probes. It ran in kernel lockdown mode.
- Least privilege: Each agentâs commands ran inside its sandbox as an unprivileged user, with tools like sudo that could regain root removed. The agentâs tools were designed so they couldnât read or change the agent loop that ran them.
To make runs like this safer, we use a prompted LLM classifier that can block each tool call, including shell commands and file edits. The classifier watches for attempts to escape the sandbox, probe its boundaries, or tamper with monitoring, and for any harmful actions the model might take if it manages to exit the sandbox. When the classifier blocks a tool call, the whole agent team stops and a person must review the block before the team can restart. This is intended to prevent another agent from carrying out a blocked action.
To test whether our classifier could detect sophisticated sabotage, we ran multi-agent side-task and sabotage evaluations, in which red-team agents used strategies like decomposition attacks to try to fool the classifier into permitting a sandbox escape. We found that monitors that viewed the agentsâ chain of thought (CoT) and interagent communication were able to detect all sabotage attempts in these evaluations, so we now use them to monitor our multi-agent runs. In parallel, we run an action-based version of the same monitorâwhich sees only actions, not CoTâto guard against an agentâs reasoning persuading the monitor to permit a harmful action.
Weâre continuing to improve our monitoring stack through human-guided and automatic red-teaming, by evaluating it against production transcripts, including past incidents, and by expanding our threat modeling. In the run in this post, we used only the action-based monitor. Only a block on the lead would have ended the run; a block on a helper removed just that helper.
Shortly after this run, we added the parallel CoT monitor. We run experiments like this on models that may not have completed our pre-release alignment assessment, so we design our monitoring for the possibility that a model is misaligned. Models we release complete that assessment first, which reduces this risk but doesnât eliminate it.
Across more than a million tool calls, none in this run met the bar to be blocked. When we replayed these calls against the CoT monitor and todayâs rubric, only one, a check for root access, came close to being blocked.
In addition to real-time monitoring, we run an offline monitor. This monitor analyzes the agent teamâs actions against the same threat models as the real-time monitor, but with additional affordances, such as being able to look up actions from other agents.
Work on this proof happens at several levels:
- The proof: No positive integers a, b, and c satisfy aâ¿ + bâ¿ = câ¿ for any n greater than 2.
- Statements: We gave the team 60 statements to prove, including the final theorem and 59 intermediate milestones.
- Smaller statements: Agents split hard statements into smaller ones, or lemmas.
- Lean: Every statement and lemma is a theorem in Lean.
Each statement started in [Lean](https://lean-lang.org/use-cases/flt/) with a placeholder for its proof, and it counted as proved only once Leanâs checker accepted a finished proof. We let the lead decide how to tackle the proof and how to coordinate the team across these levels of work.
In the first 10 minutes, the lead set up five tables in the database (Figure 3):
- Announce: The leadâs orders to the entire team (e.g., how to split up the work).
- Assign: Who works on what (e.g., which helper owns or deputizes for each statement).
- Notes: An open board (e.g., for claiming a piece of work or reporting progress).
- Subtasks: A to-do list where any agent can add a task and the first helper to claim it owns it.
- Landed: A log of finished work.
Once the lead had created the tables, it did three things. First, it assigned each statement to a crew of 16â17 helpers by writing 999 rows to the assign table, one for each helper. Second, it made one helper in each crew the captain, responsible for posting a plan to the notes table and splitting work into tasks for the crew to claim from the subtasks table. Third, it posted instructions to the announce table, telling every helper to start by judging its statementâs difficulty and posting a verdict in the notes table.
From their prompt, the helpers knew that the database existed. They found the announce table and got started on their assessments. Most posted verdicts to the notes table. About 27 minutes in, three statements were already proved and the lead had read the posted verdicts. It then set aside the 47 statements that most helpers had judged to be infeasible within the runâs budget and reassigned nearly all of the helpers to the remaining 10, which it thought they could finish. Crews grew from about 17 helpers to between 46 and 139.
Each helper worked in a loop, most of which was set out in the leadâs orders:
- Find the statementâs plan in the notes table.
- Claim a task from the subtasks table.
- Write the proof in Lean, check it with Leanâs tools, and submit it to the main branch on Git.
- Mark the task as done.
- Post an update to the notes table.

title: Which Claude model should you build with?
body:
PlaybooksWhich Claude model should you build with? Fable, Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku
Which Claude model to pick, what they cost, and how to use them together.
The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs.
If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code, you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs.
The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium
.
There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work.
From there:
- Move down to Sonnet 5.5 for well-scoped everyday work, like a bug fix or a feature built against a spec. Just because you have a clear spec doesn't mean you should use Sonnet, though. A migration or a performance optimization can have clear specs and still be difficult enough to warrant Opus 5.5, or Fable 5.2 for a major one.
- Move further down to Haiku 5.5 for the simplest high-volume work, such as classification, routing, and extraction. Haiku 5.5 is also good to use with subagents that work on a larger model's side tasks.
- Move up to Claude Fable 5.2 for the hardest technical projects in coding, finance and the sciences. Also move up when Opus 5.5 at
high
still falls short, or for long unattended runs.
Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high
, one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high
, test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate.
Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model.
| Task | Starting model | Starting effort | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Everyday engineering and debugging. Multi-PR feature work | Opus 5.5 | medium (default), then high | Balance of cost and capability for everyday tasks. |
| Classification, routing, tagging, and high volume extraction | Haiku 5.5 | medium (default) | Lowest cost and latency in the model family. |
| Subagents that search files, read logs, or summarize | Haiku 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5 | The model's default | Wrong answers are cheap to spot, and the main model has the judgment calls anyway. |
| Chat and interactive sessions | Sonnet 5.5 (or Haiku 5.5 for simple chat at volume) | low or medium | Sonnet 5.5 is fast, especially on low or medium effort. |
| Well-scoped coding, like bug fixes, feature iteration, and spec driven work | Sonnet 5.5 | medium , then high for harder tasks | It handles scoped tasks well at half the Opus 5.5 token price. |
| Everyday documents, slides, and spreadsheets | Sonnet 5.5 | high (default; medium in Claude Code) | It iterates fast and has a strong eye for design. For a complex financial model, or a document built from a large pile of source material, start on Opus 5.5. |
| Agent tasks you run repeatedly such as investigation, review, or drafting | Sonnet 5.5 | medium | Well-defined, repeated tasks rarely need a bigger model. |
| Computer use and vision-heavy workflows | Opus 5.5 | medium | These runs are long agentic loops over many screenshots and images, the kind of long-running agentic work Opus 5.5 is built for. |
| Major refactors and migrations, architecture planning, and leading many subagents | Fable 5.2 | medium , then high (the API default is high ) | It's Anthropic's most capable generally available model for technical fields. |
| Deep research, and scientific or quantitative analysis | Fable 5.2 | medium , then high (the API default is high ) | It's built for the hardest technical projects in coding, finance and the sciences. |
| You aren't sure yet | Opus 5.5 | medium (default) | Claude Code uses it by default on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise and the Anthropic API, and the platform docs recommend it as the starting point. |
| Haiku 5.5 | Sonnet 5.5 | Opus 5.5 | Fable 5.2 | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built for | High-volume, cost-sensitive tasks | Fast, capable help with well-scoped tasks | Our daily driver for complex coding and knowledge work | The most ambitious, open-ended technical work |
| Relative latency | Fastest | Fast | Moderate | Moderate |
| Input / output, per million tokens | $0.10 / $0.50 for prompts up to 100K tokens, $0.50 / $2.50 over 100K | $2 / $10 | $4 / $20 | $8 / $40 |
| Cache reads, per million tokens | $0.01 up to 100K, $0.05 over 100K | $0.10 | $0.20 | $0.20 |
| Context window | 1M tokens | 1M tokens | 1M tokens | 1M tokens |
| Max output | 128K tokens | 128K tokens | 128K tokens | 128K tokens |
| Thinking on the API | Adaptive, on by default, and you can turn it off | Adaptive, on by default; between_tools skips upfront thinking | Adaptive, always on | Adaptive, always on |
Default effort on the API (Claude Code can differ; /effort status shows yours) | medium | high (medium in Claude Code) | medium | high (medium in Claude Code) |
| Fast mode | No | No | Yes | Yes |
Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the [Fable 5.2 page](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/fable).
When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through.
Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level.
A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in [Spending your effort](https://claude.dev/blog/spending-your-effort/), on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max
scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high
scored 58.9% with half the tokens.
On the hardest work, the price gap can close. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high
scored about level with Opus 5.5 at max
(45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. So before you raise Opus 5.5 past high
on a hard task, test Fable 5.2. For everyday work, Opus 5.5 at medium
is still the place to start. For benchmark results, see the [launch post](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2).
However, the Claude Platform's [cost and intelligence measurements](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/optimizing-for-cost-and-intelligence) also show the limits of a small model. These generally do well on high-volume work with checkable outputs and are less suited to long agentic loops.
When you compare two models, price the hardest tasks in your set as well as the typical ones, because the hardest tasks carry most of the spend. On one 20-problem search benchmark, two problems carried 43% of the spend.
A faster setup finishes sooner and can miss more. Think through how long a person can wait before you pick your model and effort level. For replies a person waits on, start Sonnet 5.5 at low
or medium
.
Often next generation models are faster than their predecessors. Fable 5.2 generates output up to 30% faster than Fable 5.1. Sonnet 5.5 runs 30% faster than Sonnet 5.
Effort level and latency are roughly correlated. Determine if the accuracy you gain is worth the extra latency. For example, on SWE-bench Pro, Opus 5.5 at medium
scored about 2.5 points lower for about 70% of the cost as the high
effort setting. At low
it scored about 8 points lower for about a third of the cost. At xhigh
it scored about 1.4 points higher for 2.5 times the cost of high
.
Often providing a means of self-verification is more cost effective and adds less latency than changing effort levels. When a model isn't good enough for a task, take these steps in order:
- Check that the model can verify its own work, with a test, a build or a script that calls the endpoint.
- Raise effort one level.
- Move to the next model up, starting at a lower effort level than you used on the smaller one.
If you can check outcomes automatically, run everything at a low level and re-run only the failures at a high one. On the same SWE-bench Pro subset, Opus 5.5 at low
with failures re-run at high
passed about 97% of tasks for about $0.17 each, against 95.3% for $0.29 with every task at high
.
If you need a faster reply from the same model, you can pay for speed instead of giving up capability. On the Claude API, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 both offer [fast mode](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/fast-mode), with higher output speed at premium pricing.
Every model in the current generation has a 1M-token context window. Large context can help the model complete the task but it costs you on every turn, because each turn resends it. That being said, [on long runs most of your input bills as cache reads](https://claude.com/blog/claude-opus-5-5-built-for-coding-sessions-that-use-more-context).
Opus 5.5 charges $0.20 per million tokens for a cache read, and Sonnet 5.5 charges $0.10. Fable 5.2 charges the same $0.20, so on a long, cache-heavy run the gap between Fable and Opus comes down to uncached input and output, where Fable costs twice as much per token.
In [What a task costs on Opus 5.5](https://claude.dev/blog/what-a-task-costs-on-opus-5-5/), a turn's cache read costs about $0.03 at 150K tokens of context. At 20K it costs about $0.004.
One takeaway from this is that a lean main context matters more the bigger the main model is. Keep the expensive model's context for the decisions, and let cheaper subagents do the verbose reading.
Haiku 5.5 is the only model where the token price varies by prompt length. A prompt of up to 100K tokens bills at the lower tier, and a prompt over 100K bills at five times that rate. The long-prompt tier still costs a quarter of Sonnet 5.5's per-token price. So Haiku 5.5 pays off most on short prompts, where it costs a twentieth of Sonnet 5.5's input price.
When every call needs a long prompt, compare Haiku 5.5 with Sonnet 5.5 on cost per finished task, not list price.
The prompt cache belongs to the model that wrote it. Your first turn on a new model pays the cache-write price on the whole conversation. To make that turn smaller, run /compact
first in Claude Code, or start a fresh session with a short written plan. On the API, open the new model's conversation with a summary of the work so far instead of the full history.
Each thinking block records the model that produced it, and each model reads only some other models' blocks. On the Claude API and Claude Models on Google Cloud (Google managed), Opus 5.5 reads Sonnet 5.5's and Haiku 5.5's thinking blocks. Sonnet 5.5 reads Haiku 5.5's. Fable 5.2 reads Opus 5.5's, Sonnet 5.5's and Haiku 5.5's. On the Claude API, Fable 5.1 reads Opus 5.5's.
A move down a tier loses the earlier reasoning, because a model never reads the blocks of a model above it. Other moves can lose it too. When the new model can't read the earlier model's thinking blocks, the API drops them and the request still succeeds. The new model then works without that reasoning.
[Preserved thinking](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/preserved-thinking) lists every case. A move from Fable 5.2 to any other generally available model drops its reasoning.
A subagent runs in its own context window and hands back a summary. You pay for its tokens at the rates of the model it runs on. In Claude Code, set model: haiku
or model: sonnet
in a subagent's definition. The CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MO

title: Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
body:
We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.
Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.
Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded [Life Sciences](https://claude.com/form/life-sciences-verification-program) and [Cyber](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program) Verification Programs.
Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.
Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.
Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.
We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the [Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card](https://www.anthropic.com/document/claude-fable-5-2-mythos-5-2-system-card).
When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of [Advisor](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/advisor) (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or [Orchestrator](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/multiagent-orchestration) (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).
Evaluating Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2
Benchmark performance. The benchmarks table below shows that Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 are a step above Opus 5.5 in almost all the capabilities we evaluated:
| Fable 5.2 | Fable 5.1 | Opus 5.5 | GPT-6 Astra | Gemini 4 Carbon | |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Agentic codingFrontierCode 2.0 | 49.1%Xhigh effort | 32.4%Xhigh effort | 45.5% | 42.8% | 41.1%Medium effort |

| Business workflowsAutomationBench | 51.4% | 31.4% | 42.5% | 41.4% | 53.9% |
| Agentic scientific researchTerminal-Bench-Science 0.1 | 74.6%75.3% (Mythos 5.2) | 52.6% | 58.7% | 68.1% | 64.8% |
| CybersecurityCyScenarioBench† | 76.3%Mythos 5.2 | 61.7%Mythos 5.1 | 67.6%without safeguards | 61%GPT-6 Cyber | — |
| CybersecurityCVE Rediscovery | 89.6%Mythos 5.2 | 78.3%Mythos 5.1 | 81.3%without safeguards | — | — |
| Protein designDe novo binder design (24 hr) | 85.1%Mythos 5.2 | 79.1%Mythos 5.1 | 82.6%without safeguards | — | — |
| Agentic searchWANDR (relaxed score) | 82.1% | 68.7% | 72.3% | — | — |

For details on evaluation methodology, see the [Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card](https://www.anthropic.com/document/claude-fable-5-2-mythos-5-2-system-card). Scores for Fable 5.2, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5.5 show results with safeguards on unless otherwise noted. All scores show each model’s highest-available effort unless otherwise noted. † On CyScenarioBench, each lab’s scores are based on unique tasks. ‡ RoboDojo Sim shows the highest-available effort and was run internally.
Effort and efficiency. On Medium effort (the default in Claude apps and Claude Code), Fable 5.2 can accomplish challenging tasks with fewer tokens than Fable 5.1. In early testing on the FrontierCode 2.0 evaluation, Fable 5.2 at High effort scored about level with Opus 5.5 at Max effort, for roughly half the cost per task. At Xhigh effort, it also scored the highest of any released model tested.
Coding
Over 90% of the changes merged into Anthropic’s core codebase are now written by Claude (with human guidance). We’ve used Fable 5.2 to fix stubborn bugs in minutes, optimize performance across all of our services, and complete high-value software projects that would otherwise have been too slow or too costly to attempt. A team of agents running an earlier version of Fable 5.2 migrated a critical production service from Python to Rust—the service is now more efficient, more reliable, and starts about 26 times faster. We’ve found that Fable 5.2 exercises strong engineering judgment and can produce high-quality results from even ambiguous requests.
As an experiment, one Anthropic engineer gave Fable 5.2 the task of designing a prototype operating system. Starting from an empty folder, the model coordinated over 1,000 subagents, working around the clock for eight days writing, testing, and reviewing code. It produced a working operating system that boots on a laptop, with its own core that runs the machine, drivers for the disk, keyboard, and network, permanent file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer, and built-in Claude functionality (see the video below).
Early testers have been impressed at how successfully Fable 5.2’s coding skills can be applied to a wide range of tasks:
Cybersecurity
Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity engineering. It catches more vulnerabilities than our previous models, and is better at reproducing and fixing them (note that Claude Fable 5.2’s safeguards will block most cybersecurity-related tasks). A security company found that one in six confirmed bugs found by Claude Mythos 5.2 were missed by all of the other frontier models they tested. On our internal evaluation, CVE Rediscovery,¹ Claude Mythos 5.2 found 10.2% more vulnerabilities than Claude Opus 5.5 and 14.4% more than Claude Mythos 5.1. Claude Mythos 5.2 also shows better judgment and calibration—one tester found that previous models had overstated the seriousness of about 1 in 20 findings, whereas Claude Mythos 5.2 hadn’t overstated any.²
Claude Mythos 5.2’s cyber capabilities are accessible through our [Cyber Verification Program](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/14604842-cyber-verification-program), which we’re continuing to expand and improve. Claude Enterprise customers (even if they aren’t members of the Cyber Verification Program) can access [Claude Security](https://claude.com/product/claude-security), which scans codebases for vulnerabilities using our most capable models—which now includes Claude Mythos 5.2. [A recent update to Claude Security](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-security-now-scans-continuously-and-tracks-fixes) helps it watch repositories as code is updated, track any findings to ensure they’re fixed, learn from additional context, and connect to a user’s tools through an API and MCP.
Science and engineering
Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.
Theoretical physics
Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.
Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, [here](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00175v1) and [here](https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00174v1).
Protein folding
Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.
Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:
Mathematics
Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

title: Claude can design electronic prototypes from start to finish
body:
A little over a year ago, we began testing how well Claude could design basic electronic circuits. We [collaborated with Diode Computers](https://claude.com/resources/articles/making-claude-a-better-electrical-engineer),[1](#footnote-1) a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards, to train Claude on simple tasks—for example, on reading a chip’s datasheet and working out which parts a chip needs in order to run. The models we experimented with back then couldn’t reliably lay out a circuit board; they also struggled to design components that fit together. Now, Claude can both design and prototype electronic hardware from start to finish.
Engineering an electronic device requires working through many complex steps and practical constraints. You have to not only design and simulate a circuit board, but also reason about the board’s physical layout and how it will behave, model the mechanical components, and write firmware—all while keeping track of which parts are readily available and what a factory is set up to build.
To see how newer Claude models have improved in this area, we collaborated with Diode again, this time asking Claude Fable 5.2 to design three electronic devices: a speakerphone, a voice-assistant hub, and a handheld virtual pet. With minimal prompting, Claude was able to use geometric reasoning to lay out each circuit board, anticipate manufacturing constraints, and make sure its designs would work within them. It revised its own work, modeled its designs in computer-aided design (CAD) software, and, finally, directed human engineers to build prototypes that worked without any fixes to their circuitry.
For each design, we began by giving Claude a simple prompt that outlined what kind of device to build and its main hardware requirements. The prompt for the speakerphone, for example, asked for “a puck that plugs into a computer over USB-C and includes microphones and a speaker, supporting Bluetooth with a PCB antenna.” Claude proceeded to write the device’s specifications, draw clean visual schematics, choose where to place the components on a printed circuit board (PCB), route the copper connections between them, design a 3D-printable enclosure, code the firmware, and prepare a parts list. Diode assembled the circuit boards and ran the firmware, under Claude’s direction. The final result was a prototype of a speakerphone that still works after weeks of use.
Claude went through a similar process to build the voice-assistant hub and the virtual pet, and both are also still in good working order. Because the devices are early prototypes, we don’t yet know how they’ll hold up with continued use or whether they would pass commercial certifications.
Reasoning through geometric problems
The most substantial difference between Fable 5.2 and the models we used in our earlier tests was in how well Fable 5.2 reasoned through complex geometric problems, such as where to place components on a circuit board and how to route the copper connections between them.
Earlier models had struggled to decide how to arrange basic components—placing supporting parts too far from the chips they served, for example, or orienting connectors incorrectly. Fable 5.2, by contrast, produced more compact, practical layouts. It routed the most important connections first: those that carry high-speed signals or high currents, or that are sensitive to noise. For example, for the voice-assistant hub, Claude started by routing the USB and Ethernet connections, which transmit signals along pairs of tracks—thin strips of copper on the board. It routed one pair of tracks at a time, keeping the two tracks in each pair the same length and correctly spaced. It also added tuning patterns—small zigzags that lengthen a track so that signals arrive at the same time—and arranged the parts of the power supply to make it more efficient.
To demonstrate how much better Fable 5.2 is than earlier models at laying out circuit boards, we asked Diode to run PCB Gym—an internal benchmark that scores models based on how well they can place components and reroute connections on board designs whose layouts have been removed. Fable 5.2 scored 69% on the benchmark, compared with 25% for Fable 5 (Figure 2). It also performed better on [BenchCAD 2.1](https://github.com/BenchCAD-org/benchcad-2-main/releases/tag/v2.1), a public benchmark that tests whether models can rebuild 3D parts, assemblies, and circuit boards from engineering drawings and rendered images. Fable 5.2 scored 83.5%, nearly double the score of its predecessor, Claude Fable 5.1.
Revising designs
Earlier models rarely revised their own work when designing PCB layouts, even when it became clear that their placement choices would never let them finish routing the connections. Over the past year, Diode designed many boards with these models that were 95% complete but still unusable.
When Claude noticed one of its designs wasn’t working, it would change course without being prompted to do so. For instance, when designing the speakerphone’s circuit board, which has four layers of copper, it reassigned signals to different pins on two of the chips. This allowed the tracks under the speakerphone’s touch-sensitive controls to stay on a single layer without crossing one another. Later, when the back of the board became too crowded, Claude swapped the signals on interchangeable pins and laid out a whole corner of the board again, rather than patching the problem with extra jumps between layers.
And when placing tracks in its design file for the voice-assistant hub, Claude noticed that the copper connections were “getting too tangled to trace visually” and reasoned, “I should just rip these traces [tracks] and start fresh.” It proceeded to delete and reroute copper connections dozens of times until it found an arrangement that worked.
Using software and documentation
When a design decision for one of the devices depended on the details of a particular part, Claude often checked that part’s datasheet—a technical document published by the manufacturer. When asked whether the handheld pet would work without a battery, Claude read the charger’s datasheet and answered that it would run on USB power but predicted that the charging light would flicker, because the charger keeps recharging a small capacitor in the battery’s place.[2](#footnote-2)
To route the connections on the voice-assistant hub, Claude started with the design software Diode provided, which let it run the router (a tool for drawing tracks) built into KiCad, a widely used circuit board design program. KiCad’s router drew one track at a time between two points Claude chose. But the hub had long tracks running from a 100-pin connector, and Claude judged that routing these one by one would take too much step-by-step guidance.
Instead, Claude wrote its own router: an algorithm that divides the board into a grid and searches it to find a clear path for each track. Within about half an hour, Claude had a router that could lay each long track in roughly a second. When Claude spotted an audio clock track running too close to the Ethernet tracks, it adjusted the router to leave more room around sensitive tracks.
Keeping track of constraints and downstream effects
Decisions made in one part of a design have downstream effects, which Claude kept track of. While designing each device’s enclosure, it wrote code to check that a 3D model of the circuit board would fit inside the enclosure without any components colliding. For example, it found that the speakerphone’s board couldn’t be lowered straight into the enclosure, because the mute switch would hit the back wall. Claude worked out that the board would fit if it was tilted by about 25 degrees during installation. It tested this in its 3D model and added the step to the assembly instructions.
When designing the enclosure for the voice-assistant hub, Claude calculated that a 25 mm-long microphone port—the opening that lets sound reach the microphone—would resonate near 3.4 kHz. That is “right in the voice band,” it reasoned, “which is not ideal though still usable for voice assistant purposes. A better approach is a wedge-shaped enclosure that’s tall at the rear and steps down low at the front.” The wedge shape shortened the ports to about 10 mm, which raised the resonant frequency to about 8.9 kHz, at the very edge of the range used for speech. Claude also wrote firmware for the speakerphone that dims its ring of LED lights as the audio becomes louder, to keep the device under the electrical current limit Claude had designed into the board.
Designing for real-world manufacturing
In electronics design, engineers have to work within the constraints of the real world. That is, they have to make sure a factory can actually make the thing they want to build. They do this by running two kinds of checks: design-for-manufacturing (DFM) checks, which compare a circuit board’s geometry with the factory’s manufacturing limits, and sourcing checks, which confirm that their distributors have the parts in stock.
Claude ran these checks itself and sorted the results into problems that needed fixing and flags it could ignore. Its checks for the voice-assistant hub flagged six slivers of solder mask (the protective coating on a circuit board) as too thin to manufacture. Claude fixed them by widening the openings in the solder mask, without moving any parts. The checks also flagged a connection between two grounds (shared return paths for electrical current) as an error, because the automated checker hadn’t recognized that the connection was deliberate. Claude correctly reasoned that it wouldn’t affect performance and ignored the flag.
Diode manufactured all three boards directly from Claude’s design files, without any back-and-forth over adjustments. Factories and engineers often have to work through multiple rounds of manufacturing changes, and the Diode team told us they were surprised that they didn’t have to do this with Claude.
Limitations and next steps
All three of these devices are still prototypes: they haven’t been through electrical validation, antenna tuning, thermal testing, or certification, and they weren’t designed for mass production. Since Claude wasn’t connected to test equipment or to the machines that make and assemble circuit boards, engineers at Diode had to physically build and test the prototypes. Even so, over the past year, Claude has improved substantially at reasoning through decisions about component placement and routing, and it can now design electronics with minimal human guidance and help people build the prototypes. Other models are making progress here, too: OpenAI recently [wrote about using its models](https://openai.com/index/accelerating-engineering-for-the-physical-world/) to design a handheld device. Work like this could help engineers build and test new hardware designs faster.
Next, we plan to investigate whether Claude can design denser, faster, and more complex boards, check them in simulation, and learn from measurements taken on the finished devices.

title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
body:
8th November 2026
[Research](/elsewhere/research/)
[parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust](https://github.com/simonw/research/tree/main/sqlite-parse-number-c-vs-rust#readme)— Four SQLite extensions implement the same `parse_number()` behavior in C and Rust, with tests covering type preservation, parsing rules, and floating-point accuracy. The optimized C implementation was fastest at 16–19 ns per row, about twice as fast as the Rust versions and far faster than SQL `replace()`. Plain C was slower on decimals because it relied on `strtod()`, while a compact fast path closed that gap; all versions matched across 8 million fuzz checks.
I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number()
function for turning strings like -$1,234.56
or '12.5%'
into numeric values that could be summed and sorted.
I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) [and prompted](https://claude.ai/share/7f18f157-6c96-4d49-a1d4-f02403e3b261):
I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse
Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting
.so(or whatever) file
This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using [Rusqlite](https://github.com/rusqlite/rusqlite)) and 298 KB (using [sqlite-loadable-rs](https://github.com/asg017/sqlite-loadable-rs)), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster!
Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod
is "twice as fast". So I prompted:
Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation
And it did, using "Clinger's fast path":
Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better:
first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns
Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in [simonw/research](https://github.com/simonw/research) by prompting this:
Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder
Here's [the resulting report](https://github.com/simonw/research/tree/main/sqlite-parse-number-c-vs-rust#readme).

title: What the Top Companies Do Differently With AI Coding - Martin Harrysson & Prakhar Dixit, McKinsey
body:
Martin Harrysson and Prakhar Dixit of McKinsey, with their colleague Shilpa, share what they're seeing across large companies using AI agents in software development. Most still report modest gains, but roughly the top 20 to 25% are now seeing 2x end-to-end improvements. They walk through what those companies do differently: shorter agent-driven cycles instead of two-week sprints, smaller pods with merged roles, curated skills and shared context, and change management that goes beyond pilots. They also cover why quality can drop as code generation speeds up, how the bottleneck moves to requirements and release, and why measuring impact is still the hardest part.

title: Your Coding Agent Can't Undo Its Own Mistakes - Tanmay Sah & Dolly Sah
body:
Tanmay Sah and Dolly Sah look at a capability today's coding agents are missing: undoing what they've done. Drawing on their research projects UndoBench and EvoUndo, they show that an agent that completes a task can't necessarily put things back when something breaks, because Git doesn't cover external API calls, runtime config or notifications, and retrying doesn't reverse side effects. In EvoUndo, 197 of 478 changes that made an agent more capable (about 42%) also broke its ability to recover. They lay out an approach that captures the original state, picks the right response (retry, restore, compensate or escalate) and independently verifies the result.

Every company has someone who knows everything: the reorgs, the politics, which projects are really on track. title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
body:
7th November 2026 - Link Blog
[datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/issues/3046). I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an [HTTP prefetch](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Prefetch) to the next page of rows in that table.
This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link
header like this:
link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next"
This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away.
I dug in and learned that Firefox has [an issue](https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=175418) that has been open for 24 years about this behavior...
And one of the early comments on that issue links to [my blog post from 2002](https://simonwillison.net/2002/Oct/17/mozillaPrefetching/) complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely!

title: Terry Pratchett's Study
body:
7th November 2026
Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: [https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin...](https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happiness-horizontal-vs.html)
But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it.
(Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.)

title: Your Financial Agent Needs to Show Its Work - Anirudh Veeraragavan, Fieldguide
body:
Anirudh Veeraragavan, lead security engineer at Fieldguide, argues that in finance an agent getting the right answer isn't enough; you have to be able to show how it got there. Building an agent for a bank reconciliation audit, he walks through four controls that make its decisions defensible: authorization that stops an agent from overwriting work a human already reviewed, execution records that let you replay and compare individual steps, citations tied to an exact document version, and auditing your eval data so a 97% score doesn't hide real failures. He also covers when the agent should stop and hand the decision to a person, and how the same pattern applies to credit and anti-money-laundering.
