title: The components of agent memory
body:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. [The hippocampus](https://stanford.edu/~jlmcc/papers/McCMcNaughtonOReilly95.pdf) plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only [some experiences](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adk8261?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F) are consolidated into long-term knowledge.
Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet [rest](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-06213-1), the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill [those experiences and integrate them](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-019-0467-3) into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.
Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed [sleep-time compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13171) as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often [called](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams) [dreaming](https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-for-llms-to-retain-knowledge-in-continual-learning/) (Figure 1).
We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.
Memory notes
By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), [in-context learning](https://www.anthropic.com/research/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads) (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and [compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction) (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).
In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can [mark a memory](https://www.nature.com/articles/385533a0) as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay, helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can [write](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool) them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
Consider a task from [Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0](https://continual-learning-bench.com/news/cl-bench-1-0/), a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using [Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview). Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a [memory directory](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory) that persisted from one session to the next.
Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.
Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.
Claude has learned to judge salience
We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red, a game that [challenges Claude to navigate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXhYDOvgpuU) complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).
We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md
, and earned four badges.
Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.
Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.
Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md
file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations
folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay
folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”
With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.
Steering Claude to write memory
We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).
We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.
We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.
In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.
With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.
Dreaming can correct memory
Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.
In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.
At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.
We then tested whether dreaming could help Cla

title: How to Get Frontier Coding Results at 70% Lower Cost - Nouha Dziri, Cohere
body:
Nouha Dziri, a senior research scientist at Cohere, shares research on teams of coding agents, where a lead splits up the work and workers explore, build and check in parallel. Teams can beat a single agent on long software tasks but cost several times more, so across hundreds of experiments on ProgramBench and Commit0 she maps where extra workers actually pay off: delegate the stage where the task is stuck, use a lead that waits for its workers instead of running ahead, and pair a strong lead with cheaper planning workers to get close to an all-frontier team at about 70% lower cost. She also looks at how agents message each other and what larger agent teams will need.

title: AI Can't Make Up a Number It Can't Look Up - Vinoo Ganesh, Kepler
body:
Vinoo Ganesh, CEO and co-founder of Kepler and former head of business engineering at Citadel, explains why Wall Street still doesn't trust AI and how to build systems it can. He breaks wrong numbers into three causes (the wrong document, the wrong number from the right document, and models doing math) and shows Kepler's approach: code extracts every fact ahead of time and gives it an ID, the model plans and points to those IDs instead of writing numbers itself, and anything it can't resolve gets corrected or refused. He also covers wide-then-narrow search, scoping document access so firms never see each other's data, and the questions to ask any AI vendor about verification.

Stephen Chin of Neo4j and Neeraj Deshmukh of Blitzy show why AI struggles to modernize the decades-old systems underneath banks and insurers, and how a knowledge graph fixes it. title: The check that catches agent failures can also train them
body:
Final URL: https://commandline.microsoft.com/thinkingbox-part-two-expanded-model-evals-reinforcement-learning-rewards/

Published Time: 2026-11-06T16:51:25+00:00

Markdown Content:
A traveler asks a support agent to switch a $1,450 hotel booking from a suite to a deluxe room. Company policy states that the change requires a manager’s approval first. In 15 of 20 attempts, the open-weight model Qwen3.8-27B made the change anyway. It updated the room, refunded money, marked the support ticket solved, and told the traveler it was done.

While that may sound like good customer service, it’s a violation of company policy.

In [our first post](https://commandline.microsoft.com/thinkingbox-bench-agent-benchmarking/), the failure ran the other way. An agent told a traveler their quiet-room request had been added, while the booking’s `special requests` field stayed empty. We built [ThinkingBox](https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox) to catch both kinds of failure. It runs an agent in an isolated, stateful environment, lets a simulated user answer its questions, and then checks the records the agent left behind rather than simply trusting what it said.

Since then, we’ve expanded the evaluation to 18 models and published our method and results in a [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19741). This post covers three things we learned:

1.   Average success and repeatable success rank models differently
2.   The cheapest successful attempt is not the cheapest dependable task
3.   The same check that grades an agent can be used to train it

After 50 steps of reinforcement learning on tasks outside the benchmark, the same 27B model left that booking and its payments untouched in all 20 attempts. Across the 507-task benchmark, the number of tasks it passed on every one of 20 attempts rose from 38 to 107.

![Image 1: Figure 1. One held-out benchmark task, 20 attempts per model: base Qwen3.8-27B vs. the same model after RL training.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/fig1-hotel-1024x659.png)

Figure 1. One held-out benchmark task, 20 attempts per model: base Qwen3.8-27B vs. the same model after RL training.

## **Most failed runs looked finished**

The first question we asked of the larger run was how often a failure would be visible without checking the final state of the database where the operation is recorded (the environment in RL terminology).

Our paper compares the executable verdict against three weaker signals on a common set of tasks across 12 models. Of 121,680 valid trials, 79,853 failed the executable check. In 67.24% of those failures, the agent still ended with a final response that signaled completion without asking a question, called at least one tool that changes state, and received no explicit error in its final tool response.

By those signals, which a transcript or tool-call log can show, about two in three failed runs looked complete.

But the records told a different story. In 98.95% of failures, the final database differed from the expected one. In 77.61%, a field held the wrong value. In 43.30%, the agent made a change nobody asked for, and in 25.36%, a required change never happened.

The paper also labels each failed run with one dominant failure signature. Averaged across the evaluated models, 79.9% of failures were tool-usage failures: the agent hit a tool error, a failed precondition, or an empty lookup and didn’t recover, sometimes carrying on as if the action had been taken successfully. These labels describe what the trace shows, not a proven root cause. But they point to fixes that don’t need a new model: classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones, keep the tool surface to what the workflow needs, and require human approval for changes that are expensive to reverse. We haven’t measured how much each of these helps. Training, which the rest of this post covers, is _one_ way to improve repeatability, not the only one.

That result shaped everything else discussed in this post. We use the task’s executable verdict throughout, primarily based on whether the records match, with narrow response-rubric checks where required.

## **Average success and repeated success rank models differently**

Running every task 20 times gives three different views of the same model:

*   **Pass@1:** The share of all 10,140 attempts (507 tasks x 20) that passed. This is the same as mean pass rate.
*   **At least once:** Tasks the model passed in at least one of its k=20 attempts.
*   **Pass^20:** The share of tasks the model passed in all 20 recorded attempts. Tables also show the corresponding task counts.

Since our first post, we expanded the comparison and trained a checkpoint of our own, described later in this post. Table 1 updates the leaderboard with selected models from that evaluation: pass@1 by domain and overall and pass^20 with its task count.

| **MODEL** | **RETAIL** | **AUTO INS.** | **TRAVEL** | **NEOBANK** | **CONSULTING** | **OVERALL** | **PASS^20** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 80.97 | 68.40 | 54.28 | 71.25 | 61.58 | 67.16 | 241 (47.53%) |
| Claude Opus 5 | 80.71 | 65.80 | 49.95 | 70.62 | 66.19 | 66.50 | 241 (47.53%) |
| GPT-5.4 | 76.33 | 62.65 | 68.12 | 65.34 | 54.60 | 65.36 | 128 (25.25%) |
| GPT-5.6 Sol | 67.65 | 65.30 | 60.34 | 59.09 | 57.52 | 61.91 | 82 (16.17%) |
| Qwen3.8-27B RL | 67.91 | 56.45 | 62.69 | 62.40 | 54.51 | 60.78 | 107 (21.10%) |
| GPT-6 Astra | 71.73 | 46.55 | 55.87 | 60.87 | 56.83 | 58.31 | 231 (45.56%) |
| Kimi-K3 | 82.24 | 50.80 | 61.83 | 41.35 | 51.63 | 57.37 | 68 (13.41%) |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 64.03 | 47.85 | 53.41 | 47.88 | 45.69 | 51.70 | 38 (7.50%) |

  
Table 1. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, with pass^20 (tasks passed on all 20 attempts, out of 507). Sorted by overall pass@1.

![Image 2: Figure 2. Tasks passed at least once vs. on all 20 attempts, out of 507. Observed counts; Claude Opus 5.5 doesn’t appear in the paper. Numbers convey observed counts.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/fig2-breadth-vs-repeatability-1024x869.png)

Figure 2. Tasks passed at least once vs. on all 20 attempts, out of 507. Observed counts; Claude Opus 5.5 doesn’t appear in the paper. Numbers convey observed counts.

Kimi-K3 passed 476 of 507 tasks at least once, more than any other model shown in Figure 2. It passed only 68 tasks on all 20 attempts. Claude Opus 5 passed fewer tasks at least once (401) but passed 241 on all 20. One model finds more solutions. The other repeats its solutions more reliably. In other words, one model is better at exploring the search space and looking for innovative solutions at the expense of higher variability while the other is better at exploiting known solution strategies.

Average accuracy doesn’t settle the question either. GPT-6 Astra scored 58.31% on pass@1, about seven points below GPT-5.4 at 65.36%. It still passed 231 tasks on all 20 attempts, compared with 128 for GPT-5.4. We also ran Claude Opus 5.5, which doesn’t appear in the paper, with the same protocol. It scored 0.66 points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1 and passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all 20 attempts.

Which column matters depends on the job. If a person reviews every result, a model that eventually finds an answer may be enough. If an agent changes production records without review, the pass^20 column is closer to what you need. It’s still an observation over 20 attempts—not a guarantee about attempt 21—although increasing the number of attempts provides an increasingly better estimate.

## **What a dependable task costs**

Our first post separated average success from repeated success. The expanded evaluation adds a cost comparison, using two numbers:

*   **Cost per successful attempt:** Estimated cost of the full 507 x 20 run divided by the number of passing attempts.
*   **Cost per all-20 task:** The same campaign cost divided by the number of tasks passed on all 20 attempts.

Both include the cost of failed attempts, because you pay for those, too.

| **MODEL** | **PASS@1** | **PASS^20 (TASKS)** | **$ PER SUCCESS** | **$ PER ALL-20 TASK** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GPT-5.6 Sol | 61.91% | 82 | $0.127 | $9.76 |
| GPT-5.4 | 65.36% | 128 | $0.131 | $6.80 |
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 67.16% | 241 | $0.276 | $7.80 |
| GPT-6 Astra | 58.31% | 231 | $0.291 | $7.45 |
| Kimi-K3 | 57.37% | 68 | $0.242 | $20.68 |
| Claude Opus 5 | 66.50% | 241 | $0.475 | $13.30 |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 51.70% | 38 | $0.177 | $24.36 |

  
Table 2. Estimated agent inference cost on ThinkingBox-Bench, 507 tasks x 20 attempts. Measured token usage priced at the cheapest eligible calculated with OpenRouter pricing as of 2026-09-20, excluding endpoints with declared quantization/optimizations. Agent inference only: excludes the simulated user, the judge, infrastructure, negotiated rates, and the cost of downstream failures. Estimates, not cloud bills.

Claude Opus 5.5 is an additional evaluated model, not a row in our paper’s Table 23. The two columns rank models differently. Among the paper’s 18 models, GPT-5.6 Sol is the cheapest per successful attempt but third per all-20 task. GPT-6 Astra costs more than twice as much per successful attempt, yet it is second per all-20 task because it repeats more of its successes.

No model in Table 2 is both cheapest and most accurate, so the real question is which models are worth considering at all. A model is on the Pareto frontier if no other model is both cheaper and at least as good. Figure 3 draws that frontier for cost per successful attempt: GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.4, and Claude Opus 5.5. Every other model shown is beaten on both axes by one of those three.

![Image 3: Figure 3. Cost per successful attempt vs. pass@1, 507 tasks x 20 attempts. Dots with blue rings form the Pareto frontier among the models shown. Paper Table 23 provides the paper-reported values; Claude Opus 5.5 is an additional evaluated model, priced using the same method. Agent inference estimates only, not cloud bills.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/fig3-pareto-1024x891.png)

Figure 3. Cost per successful attempt vs. pass@1, 507 tasks x 20 attempts. Dots with blue rings form the Pareto frontier among the models shown. Paper Table 23 provides the paper-reported values; Claude Opus 5.5 is an additional evaluated model, priced using the same method. Agent inference estimates only, not cloud bills.

The frontier depends on what you count as good. Measure quality by tasks passed on all 20 attempts, price it per all-20 task, and the frontier changes: GPT-5.6 Sol drops off, and GPT-6 Astra joins GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 5.5. Choosing for repeatability gives you a different short list from choosing for average success.

Qwen3.8-27B shows the gap most clearly. Its successful attempts are inexpensive, $0.177 each. But it passed only 38 tasks on all 20 attempts, so each dependable task cost $24.36.

The first price tells you what an attempt costs. The second tells you what consistency costs. That raised a new question for the rest of this work: could we lower the second price by changing the model rather than switching to a different one?

## **Turning the check into a reward**

The executable check returns 1 or 0 from the final records. That’s already the shape of a reinforcement learning reward. For most tasks, the verdict comes entirely from deterministic checks on the final state; a minority also include a narrow yes-or-no question for a judge model, for requirements a database field can’t capture, like telling the customer a preference isn’t guaranteed. Either way, the reward is one binary verdict per attempt. We trained Qwen3.8-27B inside the same environment we used to evaluate it: the same isolated-backend machinery, MCP tool interface, simulated-user loop, and terminal-state grading. For training, we used GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user and judge; the benchmark evaluation used GPT-5.4-mini

title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
body:
A year ago, NVIDIA [open sourced its Aerial wireless software](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/open-source-aerial-ai-native-6g/), joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems.
Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world.
Over the past year, global developer adoption of [NVIDIA AI Aerial](https://developer.nvidia.com/topics/telecommunications/ai-aerial?size=n_6_n) and [NVIDIA Sionna](https://github.com/nvlabs/sionna) software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms.
The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents.
Networks That Help Robots React Faster
A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time.
Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses.
At [King’s College London](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.15895), researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an [NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/jetson-orin/) running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images.
In addition to quicker responses and less processing overhead, the system also proved more resilient — detecting dropped objects, recovering from unsuccessful actions and, in configurations using a digital twin, checking planned movements for potential collisions before execution.
Networks That Learn to Receive Signals Better
For a firefighter receiving live drone footage or a rescue team searching for a missing person, timely images can help guide urgent decisions. But interference and changing radio conditions can make wireless signals harder to decode, causing errors and retransmissions that delay information from the field.
AI receivers address this challenge by learning to recover information from incoming signals more effectively. Better reception could help responders maintain a clearer, more current view of a fire scene or search area.
[SoftBank](https://www.softbank.jp/en/corp/technology/research/topics/238/?adid=nvblog) demonstrated this by integrating a neural receiver into [NVIDIA Aerial CUDA-Accelerated RAN (ACAR)](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aerial-cuda-accelerated-ran) and testing it with a commercial 5G smartphone. In controlled tests with interference, the neural receiver delivered higher uplink throughput than a conventional receiver at all 15 tested settings, with a maximum gain of roughly 60%.
Another way to improve reception is to teach receivers about the environments where they operate. Using NVIDIA Aerial Testbed, [ETH Zurich](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.04004) researchers found that tuning neural receivers using local measurements reduced block error rates by more than one-third compared with selected pretrained versions.
Networks That Learn When to Save Power
As 6G connects more devices and supports more AI applications, managing energy demand will become increasingly important.
For example, a network may need enough capacity to serve a busy stadium, but demand changes when the crowd leaves. AI can help identify when spare capacity can power down — and when it needs to come back online — so operators can reduce electricity use without dropping connections.
At the [University of Leeds](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/242057/1/Accepted_Network_in_a_box__ICC_2026_Yejing.pdf), researchers developed a system that predicts network demand 10 minutes ahead and uses those forecasts to guide base station sleep decisions. Before powering down, it checks that neighboring active stations can continue serving affected devices and monitors for changes that require capacity to be restored.
The team tested their approach using a portable, [NVIDIA DGX Spark](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/workstations/dgx-spark/)-powered 5G “network-in-a-box” alongside a digital twin for validating decisions against real wireless equipment. The result: researchers reported a 45.6% reduction in RAN power consumption relative to a full-power baseline while maintaining device connectivity.
Networks That Can Be Tested Faster — Before They’re Built
Before deploying a network, researchers need to know how it will perform when hundreds of devices compete for connections or radio signals run into interference. Simulating these conditions helps teams evaluate designs before committing to costly equipment and field trials. But realistic simulations can take hours, limiting how many ideas researchers can explore.
The [Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya (CTTC)](https://www.cttc.cat/cttc-accelerates-5g-network-simulation-from-hours-to-minutes-with-nvidia/) is accelerating that process by bringing GPU-accelerated radio channel models, running on ACAR, into CTTC’s open source 5G-LENA network simulator. These models calculate how wireless signals travel between antennas and devices — a computation that grows increasingly demanding as simulated networks grow.
In an early evaluation, the approach reduced simulation runtime from approximately three hours to 10-20 minutes, depending on the integration, while preserving the expected statistical behavior and network performance.
Faster simulations let researchers compare more designs, investigate more demanding scenarios and refine ideas sooner. As the industry develops 6G, this could shorten the path from a proposed innovation to a thoroughly evaluated network design — helping teams build better connectivity before deploying it in the real world.
At NVIDIA GTC Washington, D.C., attend [6G Developer Sessions](https://www.nvidia.com/gtc/dc/session-catalog/?industries=Telecommunications) where researchers and developers will showcase more innovations shaping the future of wireless networks.
[NVIDIA AI Aerial](https://github.com/NVIDIA/aerial-cuda-accelerated-ran) and [NVIDIA Sionna](https://github.com/nvlabs/sionna) are available on GitHub.

title: ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
body:
Robotics • Updated • 58 • 2
[
](#toyblocks-a-controlled-world-for-robot-learning-and-evaluation)
ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
💻 [Code](http://allenai.github.io/ToyBlocks) | 📊 [Data](https://huggingface.co/datasets/allenai/toyblocks-data) | 🤖 [Models](https://huggingface.co/collections/allenai/toyblocks) | 📖 [Documentation](https://allenai.github.io/ToyBlocks/docs/user_guide/index.html)
Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.
To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.
Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.
Our first foundation world is [ToyBlocks](https://github.com/allenai/ToyBlocks): an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.
ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.
Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.
[
](#how-toyblocks-works)
How ToyBlocks works
Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including [MolmoAct 2](https://allenai.org/blog/molmoact2), [MolmoBot](https://allenai.org/blog/molmobot-robot-manipulation), and [MolmoSpaces](https://allenai.org/blog/molmospaces), ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.
As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.
Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.
Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.
A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.
ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.
ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.
ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.
To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.
Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.
Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.
ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.
A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.
[
](#research-building-on-toyblocks)
Research building on ToyBlocks
The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."
[
](#low-level-action-models-vla-spatial-generalization)
Low-level action models: VLA spatial generalization
Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.
The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.
We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.
We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.
Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on [ManiFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01819), [π0.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054), and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.
[
](#high-level-reasoning-vision-language-models)
High-level reasoning: vision-language models
Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.
We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.
Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow

title: 7 Things Your AI Coworker Needs - Philipp Schmid, Google DeepMind
body:
Philipp Schmid of Google DeepMind shows how to build an autonomous AI coworker for finance with Gemini and the Gemini API's Managed Agents. He breaks a coworker down into seven needs (a brain, a computer, playbooks, tools, credentials, house rules and a schedule) and builds each one: skills and files in the agent's own sandbox, built-in tools and MCP servers, credentials swapped in by a network proxy so a prompt injection can't steal them, hooks for approvals, and cron triggers. title: Your AI Isn't the Advantage. Your Judgment Is - Sid Pednekar
body:
Sid Pednekar, an AI, technology and data executive in asset management, looks at why most companies now have AI but only a few see real results from it. Following two hypothetical firms, he lays out three things the leaders do differently: they pick the right problem and invest deeply in a few high-value workflows instead of scattering pilots, they build shared capabilities by standardizing the core and breaking down silos, and they make every success and failure feed back into the system. Running through all of it is one idea: when intelligence gets cheap, judgment becomes the scarce resource.

title: Your AI Agent Keeps Making the Same Mistakes - Sparsh Jain, CentralAgent AI
body:
Sparsh Jain, Head of AI at CentralAgent AI, argues that giving AI agents more memory isn't the same as helping them learn. After his team worked with the same agent for two years and it still repeated the same mistakes, they rebuilt memory as an experiential system: forming notes from new experiences, updating or deactivating old ones, keeping inactive notes as a record of how a judgment was reached, and forgetting what no longer matters, with a regular cleanup loop that works like a good night's sleep. He shares the rules they learned building it and why agents that learn from every teammate keep compounding over time.

# Partnering with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems

Loading…

Share

Today we’re announcing a partnership with Hacktron to find vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s systems. Our engineers and Hacktron’s security researchers will choose high-priority areas to test together, with a focus on how our systems interact with third-party services. As part of the partnership, we’re expanding Hacktron’s access to our frontier models through [Daybreak Red](https://openai.com/index/expanding-daybreak-as-the-cyber-defense-window-narrows/).

As we work to accelerate cyber defense with frontier AI, we’re applying the same urgency to finding and fixing vulnerabilities in our own systems. Earlier this week, we announced that [Cathedral’s researchers will work alongside our teams in our next security sprint](https://openai.com/index/preparing-our-next-security-sprint-to-harden-openai/). We also [raised our bug bounty rewards](https://openai.com/index/rewarding-defenders-with-bigger-bug-bounties/) to give independent researchers more reason to pursue vulnerabilities our own testing may have missed.

We became familiar with Hacktron through our Security Bug Bounty program and were impressed by the impact of the vulnerabilities its researchers have discovered and disclosed to us. The team builds AI agents for code review, penetration testing, and red teaming. Their [research⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.hacktron.ai/blog) has uncovered vulnerabilities in how applications, cloud infrastructure, and identity systems interact. Their work shows what’s possible when security engineers build around AI to move faster and take on more ambitious research.

As AI agents connect services in new ways, that combination of skills becomes even more valuable. Working alongside Hacktron will help us test those connections more deeply and use what we learn to strengthen our defenses.

> “The future of cybersecurity won’t be defined by who has the largest security team, but by who can best combine human creativity with AI-driven capabilities.  
>   
> OpenAI is setting a strong example by putting frontier cyber models in the hands of security researchers, enabling them to uncover complex vulnerabilities at the boundaries between interconnected systems.  
>   
> We’re excited to deepen our partnership with OpenAI, combining our offensive security expertise with their frontier models to help secure OpenAI and the broader software ecosystem.”

*—Zayne Zhang, CEO, Hacktron*

We’re grateful to Hacktron and other independent researchers who put time into finding and reporting weaknesses to help strengthen the security that protects all our users. To see which systems are in scope or submit a finding, visit our [Security Bug Bounty program⁠(opens in a new window)](https://bugcrowd.com/engagements/openai).

title: The components of agent memory
body:
Søren Kierkegaard wrote that life can only be understood backward, but it must be lived forward. We’ve encountered a similar bind when designing memory for AI agents.
As humans, we encode memory constantly as we go about our lives. [The hippocampus](https://stanford.edu/~jlmcc/papers/McCMcNaughtonOReilly95.pdf) plays a central role in this, capturing experiences in the moment so that memories form quickly and are immediately available. But only [some experiences](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adk8261?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F) are consolidated into long-term knowledge.
Much of that consolidation appears to happen when our brains are offline. As we sleep, and during quiet [rest](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-018-06213-1), the hippocampus replays our recent experiences. This is thought to gradually distill [those experiences and integrate them](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-019-0467-3) into the neocortex—the part of our brains that stores most of what we think of as knowledge.
Agent memory can use a similar division of labor. Agents capture much of their work in logs or transcripts. Researchers at Letta and UC Berkeley proposed [sleep-time compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13171) as a way for models to use idle time between interactions to reorganize their existing context. The same idea can help agents organize their memory by reflecting on logs to fix mistakes or produce new notes and representations. This process is often [called](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/dreams) [dreaming](https://research.google/blog/the-sleep-framework-a-new-way-for-llms-to-retain-knowledge-in-continual-learning/) (Figure 1).
We’ve found that dreaming has been a useful tool for helping us give Claude effective memory. In this post, we share how we’ve come to think about agent memory and walk through several evaluations we’ve used to explore agent memory, including the use of dreaming, and what each component contributes to memory organization.
Memory notes
By “agent memory,” we mean knowledge that Claude gains from experience—including interactions with users and tasks it’s been assigned—and that it retains between sessions, saved as context it can read later. It excludes other ways models can learn or manage context, such as changes to their weights (the internal parameters set during training), [in-context learning](https://www.anthropic.com/research/in-context-learning-and-induction-heads) (knowledge gained within a single conversation), and [compaction](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/compaction) (summaries written by Claude that replace its older turns so it can continue working in a new context window).
In the human brain, chemical signals released before, during, or after an experience can [mark a memory](https://www.nature.com/articles/385533a0) as important. Marked memories tend to be replayed more often than unmarked ones during offline periods. This process, called replay, helps stabilize and integrate them into long-term memory.
Similarly, Claude can tag salient events in a session log as they happen, so they’re easier to find later, or it can [write](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/memory-tool) them to a memory store, such as a folder of memory notes (Figure 2). But how can Claude tell what’s salient in the moment, before it knows what’s coming next?
Memory can be a prediction about what the future will need
Memory is, occasionally, a prediction. By writing down a rule, an agent predicts that the pattern it’s describing will be relevant again. For instance, writing down a verified fact is a prediction that an agent in a future session will want to rely on that fact without double-checking it. Over time, Claude has become much better at making these kinds of predictions.
Consider a task from [Continual Learning Bench (CL-Bench) 1.0](https://continual-learning-bench.com/news/cl-bench-1-0/), a benchmark that measures an agent’s ability to use memory in order to tackle long-horizon tasks. One particular task asks Claude to answer a series of questions by looking up information in a database. After Claude gives an answer, it’s told the correct solution and can write a memory to help answer future questions.
Memory can support a learning loop here. If Claude gets a question wrong, it can record the failure, come up with theories about what went wrong, test those theories, and turn what it finds into a rule about how to answer in the future.
We ran the CL-Bench 1.0 task using [Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview). Claude started each question in a fresh session, with one exception: it could retrieve files from a [memory directory](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/memory) that persisted from one session to the next.
Different models achieved different levels of success at creating their own learning loops. Claude Sonnet 4.6 got as far as generating theories about why an answer was wrong. Its memory directory contained a scattering of files, each listing several untested guesses.
Claude Opus 4.7 consolidated its notes into a single reference document and began marking which facts it had checked and which were still unconfirmed. Claude Sonnet 5 marked each answer as confirmed after the grader had checked it, and wrote a correction when it had answered wrong.
Claude Opus 5 was the first of these models to close the loop. Most of its entries included a rule (and also how it knew the rule was true), answers to earlier questions, and clear warnings about traps it had discovered along the way (Figure 3).
Like Opus 5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 both closed the loop, using memory to capture validated rules about how to best answer future questions. With memory, both scored about the same as Opus 5, though their baseline performance without memory was slightly higher.
Claude has learned to judge salience
We also evaluated Claude’s ability to play Pokémon Red, a game that [challenges Claude to navigate](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CXhYDOvgpuU) complex long-horizon tasks, as a test of Claude’s judgment about what to save to memory. At the start of each run, we gave each model a folder of memory files that it could read from and write to while it played (Figure 4).
We compared the memory folders from one run each of Claude Sonnet 3.7 and Claude Fable 5, when each was about 10,000 steps into the game. A key difference we noticed was what each model thought was worth remembering. Sonnet 3.7 assumed everything might matter and wrote to memory indiscriminately. Its memory folder contained an archive of encounters, often with a separate file for each battle it fought, each item it found, and each non-player character it met. Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md
, and earned four badges.
Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.
Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.
Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md
file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations
folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay
folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”
With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.
Steering Claude to write memory
We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).
We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.
We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.
In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.
With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.
Dreaming can correct memory
Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.
In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.
At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.

Ultimately, Sonnet 3.7 wrote 413 memory files across 225 folders and earned one badge (badges mark a player’s progress through the game).
Fable 5, by comparison, wrote nine files in two folders, plus a single top-level file called global.md
, and earned four badges.
Sonnet 3.7’s approach was a problem mainly because the game state of Pokémon changes constantly—Sonnet 3.7’s detailed record was continuously going out of date. As a result, as Claude progressed, it had to spend more time and resources combing through its memories rather than playing the game. Around step 10,000, for example, Sonnet 3.7 started its fourth folder of “master” memory files. Over the next 17 steps, it created six files, deleted nine others, and took no actions in the game itself.
Fable 5’s approach used memory for things the game didn’t explicitly tell it. Some of the kinds of information Sonnet 3.7 wrote to memory—such as how much money the player has or where the player is on the map—can be read off the screen every turn, so storing it is redundant. By contrast, memory files about strategy, plans, and tested rules exist only if Claude works them out, and they disappear unless Claude writes them down.
Fable 5 organized its memory accordingly. Its global.md
file acted as a dashboard, holding the current goal, a prewritten plan for tackling gyms (the challenges where badges are won), and the model’s own rules for using memory. A locations
folder held plans for navigating particular routes, and a gameplay
folder held strategies based on what it had learned about how the game works. For example, after seven Poké Balls in a row failed to catch a Magikarp (one of the easiest Pokémon to catch), Claude wrote, “If 3+ balls fail in a row, VARY the timing (insert extra ‘wait’ presses between menu steps) - the catch landed right after doing this.”
With a much smaller memory folder, Fable 5 progressed much further in the game than Sonnet 3.7. Opus 5.5 took a similar approach: it kept a small folder of memory notes that tracked its current goal and next steps, rewrote them as it played, and beat the game.
Steering Claude to write memory
We’ve found that it helps to tell Claude what memory is for, but not how to use it. On CL-Bench, we simply told Claude that a memory folder was available. That general guidance was enough for Opus 4.7 and Opus 5 to use memory effectively, and it gave both a noticeable boost in performance (Figure 3).
We also tested giving the models specific rules about what they should write to memory, with one rule per test. We compared how much each model gained from memory with each rule against how much it gained without it. When we set a rule to “record only failures,” both Opus 5 and Opus 4.7 lost much of the performance boost that memory gave them (Figure 5, right). For stronger models, giving them freedom to judge salience was more effective than setting fixed rules in advance, and those rules could end up weakening performance.
We also noticed that steering helped older models the most. For instance, Sonnet 4.6 often didn’t read files from its memory directory and failed to test its theories about why an answer was wrong.
In this case, prompting Claude to read its memory files before answering—and then to explicitly test its theories—nearly doubled its benchmark score (Figure 5, left). Sonnet 5 does this on its own. Without being prompted to, it read its memory before answering 9 out of 10 times. By comparison, Sonnet 4.6 did this less than half of the time.
With frontier Claude models, we typically give simple guidance to create memory notes when a person asks them to or when something is clearly worth remembering, and we leave that judgment up to Claude.
Dreaming can correct memory
Since Claude writes to memory based on what it judges to be salient in-session, a note that’s wrong from the start or that drifts as the environment changes can be read, and trusted, by Claude in a later session.
Dreaming gives Claude a way to test its notes against the original transcripts (Figure 6). We saw a positive example of this when Claude played Pokémon using Managed Agents with a mounted directory for its memories.
In one part of the game, the player has to get through Mt. Moon, a cave system with its entrance on the west side of the map and its exit on the east. Near the entrance is a trap: a one-way ledge that drops the player onto the route they came from, with no clear way to climb back up. Claude was using the PokéCenter, a building at the mountain’s entrance, as a landmark, so whether it walked off the ledge depended on which side of the mountain it thought the PokéCenter was on.
At one point, Claude wrote down (incorrectly) that the PokéCenter was on the east side. When it walked out of the PokéCenter, it announced, “Mt Moon is behind me,” and updated its notes: “Mt Moon DONE.” But Mt. Moon was not behind it. A few actions later, Claude went over the ledge and landed back on the route it had come from (Figure 7). Its navigation tool didn’t show the drop, so Claude concluded, “I overshot far west,” and that it had been on the correct side all along. It hadn’t.
