title: Cities Worldwide Build and Scale AI Services With NVIDIA Physical and Agentic AI
body:
Cities generate enormous amounts of data from cameras, sensors and operational systems, but turning it into useful action — for planning, maintenance and public services — remains a challenge.
Physical and agentic AI offer new ways to close that gap, from digital twins for infrastructure planning to vision and service agents, while keeping local governments in control of how sensitive data is processed and used.
Building on [initiatives announced at GTC Berlin](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/european-cities-agents-urban-operations/), NVIDIA and its partners are expanding physical AI and AI agents to cities worldwide. Shared computing infrastructure gives city departments, neighboring municipalities and local developers a common foundation to build on — extending services without each organization having to acquire and manage resources of their own.
Agentic AI for Cities
From resident services to vision agents, cities are adopting NVIDIA agentic AI to deliver faster, more responsive public services. City teams don’t need a massive infrastructure investment to get started building these AI services: depending on the workload, NVIDIA RTX workstations or a small GPU system may be enough.
In Spain, 1MillionBot combines open source ALIA models trained at the Barcelona Supercomputing Center with [NVIDIA Nemotron](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-data-science/foundation-models/nemotron/) and other models in resident-service agents for Madrid Digital (Comunidad de Madrid), Administració Oberta de Catalunya and 150+ deployments across Spain, handling municipal procedures, appointment requests, urban-planning incidents and service inquiries.
In the San Francisco Bay Area, [LiveX](https://livex.ai/insights/livex-unveils-ai-city-bringing-physical-ai-to-everyday-spaces-with-nvidia) is bringing its AI City vision to life with NVIDIA [Cosmos](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai/cosmos/) world models and Nemotron open models, and [Omniverse](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/omniverse/) and [Metropolis](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/intelligent-video-analytics-platform/) libraries on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs. The interactive, conversational AI hosts understand people’s needs, provide answers and take action, and can be tailored to local languages and service needs in airports, hospitals, local events and other public spaces.
Vision AI agents can turn existing city camera feeds into operational insights, helping teams identify mobility and safety issues and coordinate emergency responses across city services.
In Wrocław, Poland, K2K is building shared AI infrastructure using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Cosmos world reasoning models, and NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) to transform existing camera streams into actionable intelligence for mobility, safety and event response — using the same infrastructure across several city functions.
In Malaysia, [ITMAX](http://www.itmax.com.my/newsroom/itmax-and-nvidia-use-ai-to-give-kuala-lumpur-commuters-time-back) bundles infrastructure and agentic AI applications into long-term managed services for cities, including for traffic management. Built with reference to Cosmos, Nemotron and the Metropolis VSS blueprint, ITMAX’s SamurAI V2 vision agents are scaling on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs to support 17,000+ cameras by 2027. ITMAX integrates TeraSim, an open source traffic simulation platform from Laplace Intelligence, to test signal timing, reducing peak-hour corridor travel times by up to 26%.
Plan and Operate Critical Infrastructure With Digital Twins
Beyond public-facing services, digital twins can help cities expedite infrastructure planning, minimizing disruption to local communities. City digital twins can also serve as a real-time operational simulation to facilitate faster decision-making.
At Dangote’s Lekki refinery in Nigeria, Honeywell Technologies’ Forge Plant Cognition uses Nemotron-powered AI agents to understand operational data. A digital twin of the plant and its processes, built using Omniverse libraries, is also planned to support simulation and training. The platform, built on Dell PowerEdge servers with NVIDIA RTX PRO accelerators, helps operators identify bottlenecks, anticipate equipment and process issues, and optimize plant performance.
In Taiwan, [Linker Vision](https://www.linkervision.com/post/linker-vision-unveils-linker-ai-nexa-to-bring-physical-ai-to-city-governance) and Dutch architecture firm MVRDV are using NVIDIA Omniverse and Nemotron to build environmental, social and governance agents that can assess the environmental impact of various urban planning scenarios, simulating 15-year outcomes of an urban forest canopy in 10 minutes — increasing design iteration speed from two weeks per iteration to less than an hour.
Build a Broader Local AI Ecosystem
Cities can extend AI to more services by building on infrastructure already in place and adding capacity. Shared resources and managed services can help extend those capabilities across departments and municipalities.
At Morocco’s Tanger Med port, Cires Technologies is expanding a sovereign AI factory for planned applications in worker safety, congestion analysis, cargo routing and port operations. Cires Technologies is also building an ecosystem of application providers to develop local models and applications for ports and cities.
Beyond city services, Barcelona Supercomputing Center’s [AI Factory Accelerator Programme](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/spain-startups-barcelona-supercomputing-center/) gives startups access to sovereign computing, technical support and training. BSC AI Factory also supports research and innovation for startups — spanning agriculture, medical imaging, knowledge access and speech services.
Learn how NVIDIA and its ecosystem are bringing physical AI, agentic AI and local AI factories to cities worldwide at Smart City Expo World Congress, running Nov. 3-5 in Barcelona, where NVIDIA Vice President of EMEA Paolo Guglielmini will deliver a [keynote address](https://www.smartcityexpo.com/agenda/from-ai-factories-to-intelligent-cities/) followed by a [panel](https://www.smartcityexpo.com/agenda/by-the-city-for-the-city-making-ai-work/) moderated by Charbel Aoun, director of smart city and spaces for EMEA at NVIDIA.

title: You Can't Tell What's Real Anymore. Here's What Comes Next - Cristóbal Valenzuela, Runway
body:
Runway's first AI film in 2019 was 128x128 pixels. Today, people can't tell generated video from real footage. Runway co-founder and CEO Cristóbal Valenzuela explains how next-frame prediction at scale teaches models physics, object permanence and how the world works. He then shows what happens when those models become real-time and interactive: world interface models, robotics, and Continuum, an early research prototype where anything on your screen can become a live, interactive video.

title: Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
body:
[content type paper](/research/)published November 2026
Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
AuthorsAbhinav Moudgilâ **, Ningyuan Huangâ¡**, Eeshan Gunesh Dhekane, Pau RodrÃguez Lopez, Luca Zappella, Federico Danieli
Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
AuthorsAbhinav Moudgilâ **, Ningyuan Huangâ¡**, Eeshan Gunesh Dhekane, Pau RodrÃguez Lopez, Luca Zappella, Federico Danieli
State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba have become a popular alternative to Transformer models, due to their reduced memory consumption and higher throughput at generation compared to their Attention-based counterparts. On the other hand, the community has built up a considerable body of knowledge on how to train Transformers, and many pretrained Transformer models are readily available. To facilitate the adoption of SSMs while leveraging existing pretrained Transformers, we aim to identify an effective recipe to distill an Attention-based model into a Mamba-like architecture. In prior work on cross-architecture distillation, however, it has been shown that a naÃ¯ve distillation procedure from Transformers to Mamba fails to preserve the original teacher performance, a limitation often overcome with hybrid solutions combining Attention and SSM blocks. The key argument from our work is that, by equipping Mamba with a principled initialization, we can recover an overall better recipe for cross-architectural distillation. To this end, we propose a principled two-stage approach: first, we distill knowledge from a traditional Transformer into a linearized version of Attention, using an adaptation of the kernel trick. Then, we distill the linearized version into an adapted Mamba model that does not use any Attention block. Overall, the distilled Mamba model retains most of the original Pythia-1B Transformer performance, reaching a perplexity of 14.01 close to the teacherâs 13.86. This largely carries over to downstream tasks, although some gaps appear on tasks relying more on in-context recall. To show the efficacy of our recipe, we conduct thorough ablations at 1B scale with 10B tokens varying sequence mixer architecture, scaling analysis on model sizes and total distillation tokens, and a sensitivity analysis on tokens allocation between stages.

body:
Sovereignty in AI means customers can choose, inspect, and deploy the models that best serve their needs without surrendering control to a single vendor, but that freedom should never come at the expense of security or privacy. Adding leading open models from Cohere and other providers across the globe inside of Model Vault gives our customers the flexibility they need to use the right tool for the job without sacrificing the standards that govern their business.
Every organization wants to use the best AI models available for the task at hand but many cannot. For a bank, a hospital or a government department, sending sensitive data to a shared API is often off the table. At the same time, managing inference for open or on-premise models may also not be possible due to capability or capacity constraints. Teams end up choosing between the model they want, the control they need, and the capacity they have to manage them.
They shouldn't have to. Today we're launching third party models inside Model Vault and Model Vault Encrypted, allowing Enterprises to run both Cohere’s models and leading open models on a fully managed and encrypted inference platform. Zero data retention of prompts and outputs is implemented by default in Model Vault.
Two levels of protection
Model Vault provides the full inference stack managed through an isolated instance dedicated to your organization alone. Model Vault Encrypted goes further, keeping your data encrypted even while the model processes it.
Model Vault: Your models and workloads run on single tenant infrastructure. You choose the region, and your prompts and outputs stay there. Cohere manages the infrastructure so you get production-grade serving without building and running your own cluster.

title: CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency
body:
Benchmark • Updated • 100 • 498 • 7
[
](#cwe-bench-v2-more-coverage-quality-and-transparency)
CWE-bench v2: More coverage, quality, and transparency
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/cwe-bench.md)
[CWE-bench](https://cwe-bench.com/) is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at [Collinear AI](https://collinear.ai/), CWE-bench v2 opens up a [public set of 100 tasks](https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench) that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a [held-out set](https://www.cwebench.com), so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact [cyber@collinear.ai](mailto:cyber@collinear.ai).
Our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.
As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:
- Does the instruction read like a realistic instruction and not an evaluation setting?
- Can every graded behaviour be inferred from the instruction?
- Does the verifier check for correct behaviour and not for specific structure of one fix?
- Does the starter code fail and the reference fix pass?
- Does the original functionality still work with the new fix?
- Do the verifiers fail memorized solutions like the known upstream patch?
Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.
[
](#results)
Results
Results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The [leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page](https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench) covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file ([how](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/eval-results#adding-evaluation-results)). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the [CWE-bench leaderboard Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/collinear-ai/cwe-bench-leaderboard), where new models are added through a PR on the Space.
Open-weight models, from the dataset page:
All evaluated models, including API-only ones:
Of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.
On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.
[
](#run-it-from-the-hub)
Run it from the Hub
Every task is a self-contained [Harbor](https://harborframework.com/) task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json
. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:
harbor run --repo "https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench" -d cwe-bench@2.0 -k 4 \
--agent <agent> --model <model> --env docker \
--allow-agent-host <model API host>
-k 4
runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the [dataset page](https://huggingface.co/datasets/collinear-ai/cwe-bench) first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:
hf auth login --token $HF_TOKEN --add-to-git-credential
The tasks are also tagged rl-environment
: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

title: Transformers Model Integration Contracts
body:
3.22M • Updated • 901
[
](#transformers-model-integration-contracts)
Transformers Model Integration Contracts
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/transformers-mic.md)
On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.
When we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.
[
](#why-bugs-reach-main)
Why bugs reach main
[Transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers) supports over 750
model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus
200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also
test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention
kernels.
The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.
Our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small
model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower
layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files
unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests"
against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our
[CPU study](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/evidence.md#on-cpu),
the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint
is 1,227 MB.
This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.
Model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-*
checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and
checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5
bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.
Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.
[
](#introducing-model-integration-contracts)
Introducing Model Integration Contracts
[transformers-mic](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic) is a proposed
standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has
three parts:
- a fixture: the shrunk model described above, published once and pinned
- a usage path: a runnable Markdown example of something people do with the model, such as generating text or running a training step
- baselines: the outputs recorded when running that example, reviewed by a human
The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.
A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint:
compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected
results. We publish them in [huggingface-mic](https://huggingface.co/huggingface-mic).
For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:
inputs = tokenizer("The capital of France is", return_tensors="pt")
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=4, do_sample=False)
new_tokens = outputs[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
print(tokenizer.batch_decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True))
It also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies
that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full
[usage.md](https://huggingface.co/huggingface-mic/smollm-mic/blob/main/integrations/transformers/usage.md).
A [fleet dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface-mic/transformers-fleet)
on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions
used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it
used, so we can reproduce it later.
On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.
[
](#the-umt5-regression)
The UMT5 regression
We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small
UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on [July 30, 2026](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/commit/560f36cc561fa154d224b7a6dfcba1d57a621d7b)
until its fix on [September 28](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/commit/d7ba937671edb174fd80d33f9ecbd38f6559dfca).
Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training
loss by about 0.20.
One detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.
We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.
The [replay results](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/evidence.md#shadow-backfill)
and the [CI demo](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/evidence.md#transformers-ci-proof)
have the measurements and reproduction details.
[
](#how-models-are-shrunk)
How models are shrunk
The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.
The recipe now has four steps:
- Shrink the configuration. Start from a real checkpoint and reduce
hidden sizes, attention heads and depth. Keep the different layer kinds,
including mixtures of sliding and full attention or dense and MoE layers.
Some architectures need extra rules to keep their components compatible.
We also look at the model's own Transformers tests: the
ModelTester
intest_modeling_<model>.py
already picks a small config by hand, so we take its sizes for any width our generic rule doesn't know by name. - Keep preprocessing unchanged. Preserve vocabulary, special tokens and input dimensions, and copy tokenizer and processor files byte for byte. Loading and preprocessing are part of what we want to test.
- Build and validate the weights. Try seeded random weights and change the inputs to check that the model responds. If it doesn't, try training it on the contract's small batch of examples. Reload the saved model and check that outputs, loss and gradients are finite. Reject failed builds.
- Freeze and record. Save the accepted weights and measure repeatable outputs on a known-good Transformers build. Review the baselines for each supported platform and precision, then publish a pinned snapshot. CI reuses it; it does not rebuild the fixture for every PR.
We also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the
conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint.
[The full recipe](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/fixtures.md#recipe)
has more detail.
The [Llama 4 Scout shrink report](https://huggingface-mic-mic-coverage.static.hf.space/shrink/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-mic.html)
shows what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7
million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from
48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.
[
](#building-mics-with-agents)
Building MICs with agents
Our CLI, tmic
, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a new
model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure
the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed
expectations require human review.
To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model
:
pip install "transformers-mic[runtime]" "hf-doc-builder @ git+https://github.com/huggingface/doc-builder.git"
hf auth login
tmic run org/model --local-only --fixtures-only --no-history --bill-to ''
It drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your
machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything.
For a new model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed
to your own account (--bill-to ''
). The
[CLI docs](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/cli.md#automated-mode)
cover the individual steps.
We used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge
case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from
model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the
[coverage space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface-mic/mic-coverage).
[
](#random-vs-overfit)
Random vs Overfit
With random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.
So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green".
We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible
in its outputs. In our [weight-initialization study](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/fixtures.md#choosing-the-weights),
the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit
fixtures caught all 24.
That gives us two ways to build the weights:
- Start with random weights and a fixed seed.
- Overfit on a few examples, like "The capital of France is" => "Paris".
The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.
So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need
better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one
more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The [comparison](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/fixtures.md#overfit-versus-random-what-can-we-conclude)
has the results for both.
[
](#open-questions)
Open questions
As of November 1, 2026, the [MIC job in Transformers CI](https://transformers-ci.huggingface.cool/d/mic-failures/mic-failures?from=now-4w&to=now&timezone=browser)
reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on
things we haven't measured yet:
- How many real bugs does it catch on PRs, not just in replays?
- How often does it send us chasing false alarms?
- How much work do baseline reviews take?
We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.
Coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.
Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.
Want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the
[coverage space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface-mic/mic-coverage), try
the [tmic workflow](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers-mic/blob/main/docs/cli.md#automated-mode),
and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

Jill Hazelbaker will join OpenAI as Chief Corporate Affairs Officer, leading the company’s global communications and corporate positioning.

I could not be more excited to work alongside Sam, Greg, and the outstanding team they’ve assembled to help OpenAI meet the moment.”

*Jill Hazelbaker*

Jill began her career in U.S. politics, serving in leadership roles on local, state, and national campaigns. She was National Communications Director and Chief Spokesperson for Senator John McCain’s 2008 presidential campaign and Press Secretary to New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg.

title: llm 0.37
body:
2nd November 2026
There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes.
I added gpt-6.1-sol
and gpt-6.1-terra
, plus a new [llm openai endpoint add](https://llm.datasette.io/en/stable/other-models.html#configure-an-openai-compatible-model) command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna
- half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna
.
LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like [Gemini Embedding 2](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini/embedding/), which can embed text, audio, images, and video.
A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes!
This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. I really see them as bug reports with attached examples - sometimes I land them, sometimes I implement my own fix.
So thanks to [0d00ciallo0721](https://github.com/0d00ciallo0721), [ac1982](https://github.com/ac1982), [Allen Flux](https://github.com/allenflux), [Bian Yuhan](https://github.com/bianyh), [Bishop Kammeraad](https://github.com/porkedchop), [Chen Yufeiyang](https://github.com/feiiiiii5), [Christopher Krah](https://github.com/chrikrah), [Ethan Stoner](https://github.com/ethanstoner), [Jiachen Xie](https://github.com/er-s-an), [Olamide Faniyan](https://github.com/Pajimo), [Sharat Chandra Sai Boddu](https://github.com/sharatchandrasai999-sketch), [nosmile99](https://github.com/nosmile99) for helping out with (or spending tokens on) this release!

title: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights
body:
TL;DR
We find that frontier LLMs are surprisingly good at natively reading and writing neural network weights, well past what we’d expect from humans or conventional algorithms. This might be a big deal for both optimization and interpretability.
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own [model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B/blob/main/README.md#L856) warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
Throughout the history of deep learning, we encoded our simplistic inductive biases into tiny symbolic optimizers like Adam or Muon. This is changing: our neural network weights will soon be natively optimized by LLMs that deliberately reason about their weights.
If you were asked to handcraft a neural network that plays Go, what would you do? If you were handed raw neural network weights and asked to predict their behavior, where would you even start? For almost any human, this is practically impossible.
Today, weights are written by [optimization](https://karpathy.medium.com/software-2-0-a64152b37c35), by [custom networks trained to write them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.11174), or by [compilers from formal programs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.05062). In this post, we find that the current generation of frontier LLMs, used natively in natural language, are starting to become eerily good at understanding and crafting neural network weights around natural-language goals.
For a few years now, we’ve all been using LLMs to optimize text artifacts like prompts and the programs built around them
We often justified these methods by reference to the fact that we don’t know other principled ways to hill-climb on text artifacts, unlike for updating the weights of differentiable neural networks. After all, humans can “optimize” code by hand, for example, so it made sense to ask LLMs to do it, but they can’t “optimize” neural weights by hand, so those remained largely in the realm of symbolic algorithms.
In this post, we share very early results that allow us to argue that the paradigm of reasoning-driven optimization is now coming even for differentiable neural networks.
In Weight-Space Programming, a general-purpose LLM reads and writes a network’s weights directly (i.e., not through an optimizer, and in particular not with gradient descent) around some natural language spec, sometimes even with no environment feedback at all.
In natural language, it’s becoming possible to “just ask” an LLM to natively find a hidden trait or failure inside the weights of a neural network, to fix that failure, or to write a new network from scratch. We report early, exciting results on each of these below, first on small networks and then even on real language models:
- LLMs can read neural network weights: In Experiments 1 to 3, we ask Astra questions like what game a network was trained to play, what shape is drawn by a diffusion model, and which language a small language model was trained on. In Experiment 7, we ask which of two language models was trained to be sycophantic.
- LLMs can fix neural network weights: In Experiment 4, we ask Astra to fix a network that’s failing at some physical control task. In Experiment 8, we ask it to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math, and its fix improves instruction following too.
- LLMs can write neural network weights from scratch: In Experiment 5, we ask Astra for networks that play three MinAtar games, and in Experiment 6, for a network that plays Go.
We start with a small-scale experiment to see if LLMs can understand the continuous weight space, which is essentially just a list of numbers.
In our first experiments, we train some neural network with some algorithm. It would be extremely exciting if the LLM is able to tell its behavior just from the weights.
Experiment 1Can Astra tell which game the network was trained on just from the weights?
We trained neural network policies with PPO to play four computer games. All four networks take the same input channels, choose from the same actions, and have exactly the same network dimensions, so that it is not able to tell unless the weights are read.
For each of these networks, we pass its raw weights into Astra as a prompt, and ask: Which game was this neural network trained on? Without revealing the options of the games we consider, Astra was still able to name the right game for all four networks. This is exciting particularly because there are so many games out there that Astra could choose from.
It seems that Astra was able to work out what game each network was built to play, just from features of its weights. For example, where each input channel’s first-layer weights concentrate (e.g., for Breakout, the agent’s weights lie along the bottom row, a paddle), and which actions the output layer tells apart.
Experiment 2Can Astra tell what the diffusion model will generate?
Next, we wanted to see if this generalizes to other tasks and models.
We train diffusion models (DDPM) to generate circle, triangle, and square images independently. We then ask Astra if it could tell what the DDPMs are trained to generate, just from the weights alone. We do not allow tool use or forward passes.
Astra was able to tell what each model generates, from the weights alone. It finds the shape in the output layer, where each hidden unit’s weights draw one piece of the shape’s edge, and it draws just those edges. Interestingly, it draws every shape as an outline, ignoring that the actual models generate filled shapes. This mistake kind of shows it does not rely on calculating the forward pass, but rather it actually reads the structure/geometry of the weights.
Experiment 3Can Astra tell what a language model learned, from the middle of the network alone?
Now, in the first two experiments above, Astra was not really looking at the full network and could get away with only reading the first or the last layers. This is not a scalable strategy for larger (particularly language) models and problems we really care about, as how they process and think through their input often happens in the intermediate layers. So next, we take the first and last layers away and leave Astra with only the middle layers.
We train three small language models (7.2M parameters) to predict the next character, one each on Python code[GitHub](https://github.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/tree/main/exp3_language/python_dataset).
We ask: which language was this network trained on, and what each of its 24 attention heads does. Astra names the right language for all three networks, in both of its attempts. It also finds every copying head (induction head), the heads that let a model repeat text it has seen earlier, and names no other head as one.
| Trained on | Astra’s answer (& confidence), two attempts | Copying heads Astra names (layer.head) | Copying heads, ground truth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | Python (0.56), Python (0.52) | 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 | 2.1, 3.1, 3.5 |
| Romaji | romaji (0.55), romaji (0.62) | 3.3 | 3.3 |
| English | English (0.58), English (0.48) | 3.1 | 3.1 |
The reasoning went like this. To tell Python apart, Astra looked for copying heads, which let a model repeat earlier text, such as completing tot to total when total came before. Without running anything, it found a first-layer head that looks one character back and then, by multiplying weight matrices, the later heads that search using what that head brings along ([Figure 1](#figure-1)). We find that this is actually a method presented by Elhage et al.
Romaji stood out instead because the last of the four blocks it was given (not the output layer, which was removed) writes in fewer distinct directions, as if the model had fewer letters to tell apart. Indeed, romaji never uses some letters like q, l, v and x.
So far, Astra has only read weights. Now, we ask if Astra knows how to write the weights.
Experiment 4Can Astra fix a failing network by editing its weights?
We train a PPO network to operate a car such that it can scale a ramp in a Kinetix environment
We give GPT-6 Astra the weights, a description of the scene and one recorded episode, and ask it to explain why the network fails, then fix it by writing new weights. In a single try with no tools, Astra’s edit makes the car succeed in all 1,024 episodes, changing 3.5% of the weights.
From the environment context and the PPO network’s trajectory, Astra identifies that the network has converged to a local minimum. Through minimal edits to the weights, Astra changes the policy to back up the car before driving forward at full speed. Astra’s reasoning shows how: it adds a small separate path through a few units per layer that reads the car’s position and speed, and once the green wheel is past the red strip, the path switches off and the trained network drives the rest.
Experiment 5Can the LLM write weights from scratch?
Now let's see if Astra can write a neural network from scratch in zero-shot.
We take three MinAtar games
Astra’s generated networks beat PPO trained for 100 million steps in all three games. Against PPO trained for 500 million steps, they score 20 times as much in Breakout, come close in Asterix, and reach 60% of its score in Seaquest.
| Game | PPO, 100M steps | PPO, 500M steps | Astra, one-shot |
|---|---|---|---|
| Breakout | 15.8 | 25.3 | 517.4 |
| Seaquest | 5.6 | 88.9 | 53.1 |
| Asterix | 25.8 | 55.2 | 53.2 |
How does it do it: Astra reasons about the desired programs it wants each network to implement and converts them into neural form. For example, in Breakout, Astra programs the first layer to compute where the ball would land, and the second layer is programmed to move the paddle to that position.
So far, most networks we have examined have weights that fit into Astra’s context directly, and we have not enabled tool use. Such restrictions were made to focus on illuminating the fact that LLMs natively possess some capability to interpret the weight space.
From here on out, we seek to push the capabilities of Weight-Space Programming and consider more real-world-relevant scenarios where the networks do not fit within context and where tools can assist the LLM's understanding/writability of the weight space.
Experiment 6Writing a Go algorithm
We now test Astra’s capability to edit weights at the 1.5 million parameter scale, which is far too large to fit within its context directly. Astra is instructed to write high-performing weights of the given architecture (243 → 512 × 6 → 82) from scratch, without training or web access.
Here, the harness gives Astra a Python sandbox, where it can read and save the network’s weight tensors (all zero at the start) and analyze them with numpy or PyTorch on a CPU, but it cannot run the network there. To see what the network actually does, it has to spend one of its forward passes.
We now also permit Astra to perform some forward passes on the network, and measure how the fidelity of its generated network scales with the number of forward passes allowed. Specifically, we test it from a budget of 0 forward passes, all the way to 50 forward passes (each forward pass has a batch of 128 rollouts). Astra interleaves edits between forward passes.
With a budget of 0 forward passes, it wins

title: Your Company Should Train Its Own AI Models - Will Brown, Prime Intellect
body:
Agents relearn the same things every session because the knowledge that runs a company never gets written down. Will Brown of Prime Intellect makes the case for training models on your own traces, feedback and workflows, so they learn on the job the way human coworkers do. He covers evals as test cases, decision models and routing, and widget-style interfaces that turn your decisions into training data. He ends with nightly training runs and an example model trained for about $300K.

12:43 Routing and decision models
15:11 Interfaces that turn decisions into training data
17:27 A $300K model for knowledge work

19:19 The self-improving organization

# Preparing our next security sprint to harden OpenAI

Loading…

Share

We’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI, bringing new researchers and security partners together with our own teams to use our models to test and strengthen our systems. We’re partnering with Cathedral, whose researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses, bringing differentiated expertise and approaches to finding weaknesses and helping us protect our platforms.

> “*OpenAI is setting an important example by partnering with outside security firms and using its own models to continuously test and strengthen its defenses. Every company should be thinking about how to put these capabilities to work. We’re excited to collaborate with OpenAI’s teams, combining their models and security expertise with our research to find weaknesses, test fixes and strengthen this approach to continuous defense.*”

***Gavin Kliger, CEO & Co-founder, Cathedral***

We’re also [making improvements](https://openai.com/index/rewarding-defenders-with-bigger-bug-bounties/) to our [Security Bug Bounty program](https://openai.com/index/security-on-the-path-to-agi/) including more than quadrupling our rewards for critical findings. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them.

This is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review.

We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.

Keeping the [defender’s window](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/) open requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available to [Daybreak](https://openai.com/daybreak/) customers. We’ve committed [$1 billion](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-for-frontline-defenders/) in subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing our [architecture and lessons⁠](https://openai.com/the-defense-factory/) from the last sprint, alongside our [blueprint](https://openai.com/index/empowering-cyber-defenders/) for empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.

We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

- [Meet us in Oakland](#meet-us-in-oakland)

We’re raising rewards in OpenAI’s Security Bug Bounty program to further encourage independent researchers to pursue vulnerabilities in OpenAI software that our testing may have missed. We’re also introducing new incentives for researchers to earn more for higher quality vulnerability reports.

Independent security researchers play an essential role in protecting technology across the industry. At OpenAI, incentivizing responsible disclosure is a core part of our security model, complementing our [Defense Factory⁠](https://openai.com/the-defense-factory/) work, where our engineers use our models to find weaknesses, reproduce them, and test fixes.

Today’s updates are designed to encourage and empower researchers, and to continue building a collaborative, community-first security environment.

## Serious vulnerabilities get serious rewards

We’re more than quadrupling the midpoint of our reward ranges for medium, high, and critical findings on average. A critical vulnerability in a core product such as ChatGPT, Codex, or the API Platform will now earn up to $30,000. Exceptional critical findings on those targets remain eligible for up to $100,000, and now up to $172,000 with bonuses. The full details are available in [our security bug bounty program⁠(opens in a new window)](https://bugcrowd.com/engagements/openai).

### High quality report bonus multipliers

High-quality reports will be eligible to earn a bonus multiplier on the base bounty. A reliable proof of concept that isolates the bug, shows when it can be exploited, and demonstrates its impact gives us a head start on a fix. The quality multiplier recognizes the extra work that makes a finding especially useful.

### Loyalty program bonuses

To build long-term relationships and continuously empower our security community, we are introducing a tiered loyalty bonus program. This 5-tier system provides scaling bonuses to recognize, support, and celebrate researchers who consistently partner with us in making AI technology safer for everyone.

### Priority campaign multipliers

To support community engagement as technology evolves, priority campaigns will feature dedicated bonus pools for newly launched features. These short-term campaigns give researchers early, high-reward opportunities to test new developments and be recognized for their early contributions.

## Updated payout calculation examples

| **Example vulnerability** | **Example historical award** | **Example new payout calculation** | **New reward** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Medium - ChatGPT (core asset): A read-only member can upload files to a Project without write permission. | $750 | $2,000 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.05 Bronze Loyalty Tier Bonus | $2,415 |
| High - Prism (non-core asset): IDOR resulting in reading a file uploaded to user’s Project | $1,000 | $2,500 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.10 Gold Loyalty Tier Bonus | $3,162.50 |
| Critical - ChatGPT (core asset): One-click account takeover. | $6,500 | $30,000 × 1.15 Quality Bonus × 1.30 Priority Campaign Bonus × 1.15 31337 Loyalty Tier Bonus | $51,577 |
| Exceptional - ChatGPT (core asset): Significant compromise of a security boundary (e.g., ability to view arbitrary ChatGPT users’ chat messages.) | $100,000 | $100,000 × 1.15 Quality × 1.30 Priority Campaign × 1.15 31337 loyalty | $171,925 |

All scenarios and historical awards are illustrative.

## Retroactive payments

If you’ve already submitted a report and we haven’t yet awarded a bounty, we’ll apply the **new** reward ranges. For bounties we awarded in the 30 days **before** this announcement, we’ll pay you the difference if your finding would have earned more under the new ranges (Base Award + Loyalty Awards).

## Meet us in Oakland

On November 20–21, our security team will be at [PROMPT2PWN⁠(opens in a new window)](https://p2p.nahamcon.com/) in Oakland, where researchers can test targets in person. If you’ll be there, we’d love to hear what you’ve been working on and how to partner with you.

Thank you to everyone who has taken the time to investigate a lead and report it to us. We want OpenAI to be a team you come back to when you find something we’ve missed.

title: The latest AI news we announced in October 2026
body:
The latest AI news we announced in October 2026
For more than 20 years, we’ve invested in machine learning and AI research, tools, and infrastructure to build products that make everyday life better for more people. Teams across Google are working on ways to unlock AI’s benefits in fields as wide-ranging as healthcare, crisis response, and education. To keep you posted on our progress, we're doing a regular roundup of Google's most recent AI news.
Here’s a look back at some of our AI announcements from October.
October underscored our commitment to AI innovation, as we released one frontier model globally and announced our next one just two weeks later. After rolling out [Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/) — a frontier reasoning model — to developers, enterprises, scientists, and consumers, we announced [Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/), our strongest model yet for long-horizon engineering and cybersecurity defense. Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward while strengthening our safety guardrails in tandem. Elsewhere in October, we introduced [Genie 4](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/introducing-genie-4/) for real-time interactive world simulation with native audio, unveiled our smartest fitness tracker with [Google Fitbit Edge](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/fitbit/google-fitbit-edge/), broke open a 20-year bottleneck in [quantum computing](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/quantum-computing/magic-state-cultivation-quantum-computing/), and more.
[Put Gemini 4 Argon to work today, and see what’s next for Gemini 4 at the frontier](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/). Following early safety testing, Gemini 4 Argon rolled out globally for complex coding, financial analysis, and legal workflows across Google AI Studio, the Gemini API, Google Cloud, Search, and [the Gemini app](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-app/gemini-4-argon-availability/), while also powering physical-world reasoning through [Gemini 4 Argon for Robotics](https://developers.googleblog.com/gemini-4-argon-for-robotics/). Showing how quickly we’re pushing the frontier forward, two weeks later we [announced Gemini 4 Carbon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-carbon/), our strongest model yet with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. Just as we did with Argon, we’re taking a deliberate approach to rollout: Carbon is now in pre-release testing with the U.S. government and a subset of trusted cyber defenders via the [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/) as we refine safety guardrails and expand partner testing ahead of a broader launch to developers, businesses, and consumers.
[Step into real-time interactive worlds with Genie 4](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/introducing-genie-4/). Genie 4 brings unprecedented realism, advanced physics, lifelike human movement, and native audio to real-time interactive simulation. You can steer scenes as they unfold using natural language. Genie 4 advances on our ability to create safe training environments for robots and AI agents as a crucial step toward AGI. Explore the demos on the [Google DeepMind blog](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-4-a-new-generation-of-world-simulation/).
[Verify AI-generated content more easily around the world](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-deepmind/synth-id-ai-content/). Having already watermarked more than 180 billion images and videos and 240,000 years of audio with SynthID, we’re expanding SynthID Detector globally in English so anyone can check whether an image, video, or audio clip was generated with AI. Alongside built-in verification tools in Search, Chrome, and the Gemini app that regularly handle over a million requests each day, SynthID Detector also identifies AI content from industry partners like OpenAI, NVIDIA, Kakao, and Apple.
[Stay protected from mobile scams with new Android safeguards](https://blog.google/security/new-android-scam-protections/). AI-powered Scam Detection in Phone by Google and Google Messages already flags more than 5 million suspected scam calls and texts every month. Now, Android is introducing an opt-in Enhanced protection mode in Google Messages that uses Private AI Compute and our latest cloud Gemini models to catch sophisticated conversational scams, paired with expanded chat alerts and stronger call-forwarding and screen-sharing defenses.
[Meet Google Fitbit Edge, our all-new smartest fitness tracker ever](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/devices/fitbit/google-fitbit-edge/). Available now in a slim, comfortable design with up to seven days of battery life
[1](#footnote-1)
, Fitbit Edge
[2](#footnote-2)
pairs precision GPS and automatic workout recognition across 50+ activities with personalized guidance from the Gemini-powered Google Health Coach
[3](#footnote-3)
We also rolled out [more than 55 updates across Google Health and Fitbit Air](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/google-health/fitbit-google-health-updates/), including effortless photo meal logging, new Metal Mesh bands, and Health Guardian features that monitor long-term blood pressure and insulin resistance trends
[4](#footnote-4)
.
[See how AI could improve patient-physician relationships in clinical care](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/amie-clinical-study-lancet/). In Google’s first publication in the main journal of The Lancet, researchers from Google and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center evaluated our AMIE conversational medical AI system during real-world primary care clinic visits. By gathering patient histories and generating clinical summaries [before urgent care appointments](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/amie-clinical-study/), AMIE helped clinicians prepare in 75% of cases and matched doctors’ final differential diagnoses 90% of the time. This is part of our broader work [applying AI to better understand, detect, and treat disease](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/health/ai-health-research/).
[Create and play custom games in Playground](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ai/playground-experimental-gaming-platform/). Our new experimental gaming platform lets anyone build, remix, and share custom single- and multiplayer games from simple text prompts with zero coding required. That same no-code creativity is expanding across our platforms: Android users can now [build personal AI apps with Google AI Studio and install them directly on their phones through Google Play](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/platforms/google-play/google-play-updates-october-2026/), and music producers can [vibe code custom instruments and audio plugins in Google Flow Music](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-labs/create-music-production-plugins-google-flow/).
[Celebrate educators and sharpen your learning](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/world-teachers-day-2026/). For World Teachers’ Day, teachers from around the globe shared how they use Gemini to personalize lessons and spark critical thinking, alongside a new global idea search launched in partnership with TED. Whether you’re in the classroom or preparing for a big project, you can also [study smarter with Gemini Notebook](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-notebook/three-tips-study-gemini-notebook/) using interactive learning overviews and custom quizzes, and use new co-creation controls to [shape your Slide Decks and Video Overviews](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/gemini-notebook/co-create-slides-videos/) before they generate.
[Build privacy-first multimodal search with EmbeddingGemma 2](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/embeddinggemma-2/). Engineered on the Gemma 4 architecture with 740 million parameters, our new open embedding model moves beyond text to map code, images, video, and audio into a single unified space right on everyday devices. Its modular design cuts local vector storage by up to 6x, making it easy for developers to build private, offline apps that can find a specific video clip from a voice memo or search hours of audio with a text query.
[Read the first AI response beamed back from our Project Suncatcher satellite](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/project-suncatcher-satellite-response/). After [launching TPUs into low-Earth orbit](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/google-research/project-suncatcher-prototype/), our first Project Suncatcher prototype satellite returned the first-ever AI response generated by a data center-class Google TPU in space: a haiku composed onboard by Gemma 4. This milestone confirms our hardware survived launch and can run AI workloads in orbit. Our team will continue to test how the chips handle radiation and thermal extremes while harnessing space’s abundant solar energy as part of a long-term moonshot toward scalable orbital AI infrastructure.
[See how our latest research is accelerating scientific discovery](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/research/research-capabilities-intelligence-2026/). At our annual Research@ 2026 event, we shared new ways we’re putting advanced AI in the hands of scientists and experts — including demonstrating an experimental Geospatial Reasoning agent, opening public access to our Deep Review tool for technical papers, and delivering top-ranked flu hospitalization forecasting. These breakthroughs are part of a broader, company-wide effort to push the boundaries of scientific discovery. Beyond the event, Google teams are also advancing planetary research by [mapping the world’s forest types](https://deepmind.google/blog/beyond-tree-cover-mapping-the-worlds-forest-types/), while Google.org has awarded $36 million to [17 organizations accelerating scientific breakthroughs with AI](https://blog.google/company-news/outreach-and-initiatives/google-org/impact-challenge-ai-science-recipients/).
[See how we broke open a 20-year bottleneck in quantum computing](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/quantum-computing/magic-state-cultivation-quantum-computing/). In a landmark study published in Science, Google Quantum AI demonstrated that a technique called "magic state cultivation" works in practice on our Willow quantum processor, cutting errors roughly 40-fold compared to uncultivated states. Because producing high-purity magic states previously threatened to consume up to 95% of a quantum computer’s resources, this breakthrough clears a major hurdle on the path to large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers.

# Scaling Git at OpenAI

Building agentic-scale scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.

By Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman, Members of Technical Staff

Loading…

Share

Why we needed a new source control system
