  - [Scaling pushes](#scaling-pushes)
  - [Line-rate fetch and clone performance](#line-rate-fetch-and-clone-performance)
  - [Compaction and time to first byte](#compaction-and-time-to-first-byte)
- [Building Pando](#building-pando)
- [Deploying Pando](#deploying-pando)
- [Contributing back to the Git project](#contributing-back-to-the-git-project)
- [What’s next](#whats-next)

Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.

We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.

We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.

## Why we needed a new source control system

Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.

These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.

Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.

We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our [copy of Git⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/git) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.

### Engineering for Git at scale

Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.

First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.

Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.

These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.

### Git object storage primer

Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: *objects* and *references*.

A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.

Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.

Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.



*Git objects reference each other by their ID, commits to trees, and trees to trees and blobs. The branch refs/heads/main points to commit C2, whose parent is C1. C1 points to root tree T1, where parser.py refers to blob B1. C2 points to root tree T2, where parser.py refers to blob B2. In both root trees, docs/ refers to the same tree, T3. Its README.md entry points to blob B3, and usage.md points to blob B4.*

Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.



*Git can store blobs as separate files or pack them together, encoding one blob as a delta against another.*

In Git, an object is *reachable* from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.

A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.

Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing *reference updates*, i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.

## Existing distributed Git service patterns

While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.

### Three-phase commit (3PC)

In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.

To accept a reference update, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.

Keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.

Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.

### Write-ahead log (WAL)

In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref update in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and point

title: Nine engineers, 1,211 pull requests in a day: Lessons from building Copilot Cowork
body:
Final URL: https://commandline.microsoft.com/how-we-built-copilot-cowork-python-to-rust-migration/

Published Time: 2026-11-02T15:13:56+00:00

Markdown Content:
_In January of this year, a small team at Microsoft set out to build_[_Copilot Cowork_](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/features/cowork)_, an agentic execution layer that performs multi-step workflows on a user’s behalf. That result brings the powerful AI-assisted tools and capabilities developers have today to everyday knowledge workers, all with_[_Work IQ_](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/features/work-iq)_, Microsoft 365 security and governance, cloud execution, and Microsoft’s multi-model architecture._

_This is the story of how the team took Copilot Cowork from an empty repo to worldwide GA in about four and a half months, then moved its runtime from Python to Rust while it was live. Agents wrote most of the code. Ways of working changed along the way, and the practices other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team: moving fast while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view._

* * *

On October 21, nine engineers merged 1,211 pull requests into the main branch of the [Copilot Cowork](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/features/cowork) backend. That number would have sounded absurd to the team in January, when a handful of us made the first commit to an empty repo.

Agents wrote most of the code, but engineers remained responsible for defining the work and judging the results. Our small team wrote clearer specs, set architecture and security boundaries, and focused its review on higher-risk changes, production impact, and cases where checks or reviewers disagreed. Automated checks and agent reviewers examined every change. Agents could propose changes, but they could not decide what was allowed to happen.

We didn’t plan on working this way. But every few weeks, the agents got better, part of our process stopped working, and we adapted.

Six practices emerged from those changes. They cover how we specify work, run agents within clear boundaries, test our checks, preserve what the team learns, shape the codebase for parallel work, and set limits on automated loops. They aren’t a recipe for matching our PR count. They are lessons other teams can adapt to build like a frontier development team while keeping reliability, security, and cost in view.

We’ll end with the project that puts those practices to the test together: moving the live runtime from Python to Rust.

## Lesson 1: Write the spec before the code

The first commit was made on January 13. From the start, agents wrote the code.

In the first weeks, we learned that the agent was rarely what slowed us down. The bottleneck was not knowing exactly what we wanted. A vague request got us code that looked reasonable, survived a quick read, and then did the wrong thing. Fixing it took longer than writing a proper request would have in the first place.

So we adopted a rule that still stands today: no code without a markdown spec written first. The spec covers three things:

*   What the change does
*   How we’ll know it works
*   What it must not break

A good spec saves far more time than it costs upfront. But a weak one leads to rework a few days later. The faster agents became at implementation, the more important it became for us to be precise about intent, requirements, and what good looked like.

Many of our specs start out spoken. Someone talks through a feature, and an agent turns that into a first draft of the spec, which the human then edits. I think this did more for our speed than any single model upgrade.

We launched Copilot Cowork to our first enterprise customers in the [Frontier program](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/resources/frontier-program) on March 30.

## Lesson 2: Run narrow agents inside clear boundaries

The next step was running more than one agent at a time. Each works in its own copy of the repo, on one task, from one spec. One agent became five, and five became dozens.

Merged PRs per month went from 257 in January to 2,754 in May. Our busiest week before GA had 783.

![Image 1: Figure A. Pull requests merged into main per month in 2026, with Frontier (March 30), GA (June 16), and the Rust cutover (September 23 – October 10) marked. October covers the 1st through the 20th.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/figure-a-merged-prs-command-line-1024x637.png)

Figure A. Pull requests merged into main per month in 2026, with Frontier (March 30), GA (June 16), and the Rust cutover (September 23 – October 10) marked. October covers the 1st through the 20th.

Parallel work went better than we expected for two reasons:

*   **Narrow tasks:** An agent with one well-defined task makes fewer mistakes than one asked to do a lot at once.
*   **Picking the model per task:** We treated model choice as a quality-and-cost tradeoff, not a race to use the cheapest model. Some tasks warranted stronger reasoning; for others, a faster, less expensive model gave us the right balance.

In Copilot Cowork, the model runs in a container without user credentials. A trusted host outside the container handles identity, policy, approvals, and tools, and every Microsoft 365 operation goes through the host.

We didn’t want to limit what the agent could attempt, because [a heavily restricted agent isn’t very useful](https://commandline.microsoft.com/azure-sre-agent-restricting-environment-ai-safety/)). With our architecture, the model can plan and ask for anything, and the host decides what actually happens.

That separation lets us increase the number of agents working in parallel without giving the model credentials or direct authority over operations. The host still applied identity, policy, approvals, and audit at the point of execution.

![Image 2: Figure B. The agent container holds no user credentials and has no direct network path to Microsoft 365. Every request crosses the boundary to the trusted host, which owns identity, policy, approvals, tool execution, and audit.](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/figure-b-trust-boundary-command-line-1024x546.png)

Figure B. The agent container holds no user credentials and has no direct network path to Microsoft 365. Every request crosses the boundary to the trusted host, which owns identity, policy, approvals, tool execution, and audit.

Building that in at the start was much easier than adding it later would’ve been. It also helped in a way we didn’t plan for. The agent only talks to the host through a defined interface, so we could later replace the entire host without changing the agent—which we did when we migrated to Rust.

We reached worldwide general availability on June 16, about four and a half months after the first commit, with several models and 16 plugins.

## Lesson 3: Make checks prove they checked something

With agents writing most of the code, nine people couldn’t read every change, and waiting for a human review was becoming the slowest step for every PR.

Several engineers each built their own review bot, modeled on how they review code themselves, and the bots competed. When one bot caught a problem another had missed, the bot that missed it got a new rule. Over time, each reviewer built up a large set of rules learned from its own misses. Each one has now been through at least10,000 generations; in each generation, the reviewer runs reviews, then reflects on what it missed and gets better at reviewing code.

Today, a useful first review usually arrives within several minutes of a pull request being opened. On a sample of recent merged PRs, the median was about four and a half minutes.

Slower, more specialized passes follow:

*   One walks the call graph, looking for code that isn’t wired up and for tests that would still pass if the change were reverted
*   One looks at operational problems like restart safety, metrics, and stale docs
*   One reads every changed file end to end
*   One checks behavior against the code being replaced

The author gets quick feedback while the change is still fresh, and the detailed reading still happens.

Of course, reviewer agents can still miss things. Once, a group of reviewer agents read a change in one of the most sensitive parts of the product. Each had been told to try to break it, and none found a problem. People on the team then read the same diff and found four blocking issues, all of which were fixed before it merged.

Fast first feedback was useful, but it wasn’t permission to skip judgment. We kept agentic review as the first check and added at least one human check for critical changes. We made it clear which findings could block a merge.

We also split findings into two tiers:

*   **Blocking:** Correctness, security, data loss, or a new mechanism with no test that would catch it breaking.
*   **Advisory:** Everything else. The author either fixes it or replies, and it doesn’t force another round of review.

Another rule came from a check that couldn’t fail. We keep a size limit on the instruction files agents read, because every extra byte costs tokens on every run. The limit was exceeded, and the check that enforced it stayed green the whole time.

The script piped the check’s output through tail. A shell pipeline returns the exit code of its last command, and that was tail, which always succeeded:

```
``` 
# The pipeline's exit code is tail's, so this always passes 
lint-size-check | tail -1 

# Keep the check's own exit code and print it 
lint-size-check > out.txt 2>&1; rc=$?; echo "lint rc=$rc"; cat out.txt; [ "$rc" -eq 0 ] || exit 1 
```
```

Once we went looking, we found the same problem in other places:

*   A formatting check that was handed an empty list of files, so it checked nothing and passed
*   A list of changed files that came back empty as soon as the work was committed

We wrote a two-part rule:

*   Every check reports how many files it checked
*   Every new check comes with a test that makes it fail on purpose

I think this matters more with agents than without them. Agents keep working until the checks pass, so if a check can pass without testing anything, an agent will eventually find that path.

## Lesson 4: Put what the team learns in the repo

By August, the same mistakes kept coming back. Each agent session started without any memory of the previous one, so we moved the team’s rules into the repo:

*   Instruction files at the root and in each component
*   A directory of rule files on specific topics

Now, every agent reads the relevant files when it starts work. When something goes wrong, the fix usually includes a new or updated rule. There are about 30 rule files now, and the oldest dates from August 6.

One early rule was about merge conflicts. At a few hundred merges a day, almost none of our conflicts were in actual logic. They were in files every branch appended a line to: registries, lists, generated files, and documents with a “last updated” line. Instead of asking people to resolve conflicts more carefully, we changed the files:

*   Registries became one file per entry instead of a long list
*   Generated files are regenerated after a merge, never merged by hand
*   Values that change on every pull request, like dates and counts, are no longer committed

## Lesson 5: Shape the codebase for parallel work

Agents also wrote most of the first Rust code in the repo, and they put things wherever it was easiest, which usually meant the biggest crate. At one point, the main runtime binary was about 290,000 lines, and splitting it up took a long time.

On August 20, we took stock of the Rust workspace:

*   There were 86 crates, with a dependency chain 13 levels deep
*   A change to the shared base crate forced a rebuild of 43 of the 63 crates
*   The API crate had grown to 134,000 lines and was also where everything got wired together
*   About 12,000 lines of business logic sat in the binary itself, bec

title: Introducing the Grid Protectors Program
body:
Today we’re launching the **Grid Protectors Program**, a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses in the communities where we build. Working with utilities, regulators and policymakers, we’ll develop arrangements for our future campuses to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.

Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.

With U.S. data center capacity projected to exceed 100 gigawatts by 2030, we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen the electric grid by building campuses that can adjust their power use when communities need it most.

Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.

Depending on local needs and the equipment available, we will also work with grid operators to supply power from on-site generation or storage, and use batteries and power controls to smooth changes in demand.

Power lines, substations and other grid infrastructure builds are a fixed cost whether demand is low or high. By using more electricity when the grid has room and reducing our use when it is under strain, we can help pay for that infrastructure while limiting the need for costly upgrades to meet peak demand. That can help keep costs down for other customers.

America needs more electricity to support economic growth, and AI is becoming a significant part of that demand. Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize a compute campus’s electricity needs. We’ve always been committed to paying our own energy costs, including the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve our campuses. Large computing facilities should pay their costs and help utilities manage the systems they depend on.

For our planned Effingham County campus, we have committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project. Once the campus is operating, we can reduce the power we draw during times of need, helping preserve electricity for other customers.

Our agreement with Georgia Power also includes up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, freeing up power to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat. For scale, that is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households. That’s more households than Washington, D.C., and Boston combined.

These compute facilities are much different than data centers built even a few years ago, allowing us to be flexible in our power demand.

This means we can turn down our demand so that families, small businesses, and other ratepayers will continue to have power. Building grid assets is expensive and Georgia Power says this flexibility can reduce the amount of new generation it needs to build to serve future growth. Although the campus is still in development, we intend for Effingham to serve as a pilot for Grid Protectors, building on an agreement that already provides a model for future campuses.

Imagine a restaurant in a vacation town. It needs enough tables and kitchen space for the busy season, but it has to pay for that capacity year-round. Regular customers help keep it in use and cover the bills when tourism slows. We are proposing to be that regular customer.

Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times. Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest. We still need to pay the costs our campuses create; the goal is for other customers to benefit, too.

Our agreement also contributes to Georgia Power’s broader plan to lower costs for customers. The utility projects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029 from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia. It estimates a benefit of at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours.

The Georgia agreement is a starting point. At OpenAI, through our Grid Protectors program, we see an opportunity to help communities keep the lights on even in times of emergency and high demand. We will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers to develop practical arrangements for the campuses we build in the future-arrangements that reflect local grid needs, help campuses support the grid when it is under pressure, and pay the costs we create. Long-term contracts and financial assurances can protect other customers if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled.

Flexibility cannot replace investment in new energy supply and transmission. Alongside those investments, our Grid Protectors program can help make the grid more reliable and protect families and small businesses from bearing the costs of AI infrastructure. That is the standard we want our compute campuses to meet.

- Stargate

title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
body:
The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
2nd November 2026
I was reminded today of [AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies](https://www.apolloacademy.com/ai-adoption-rate-trending-down-for-large-companies/), a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart [to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/9/apollo-ai-adoption/), and then [to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Sep/9/claude-code-interpreter/#something-much-harder-recreating-the-ai-adoption-chart). I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of [Executive Order 14434](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2026/09/inaugurating-the-era-of-super-intelligence/), aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.
First, the updated chart
Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the [Business Trends and Outlook Survey](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/data) (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.
The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.
I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ([GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript](https://chatgpt.com/share/6ae89e86-8658-83e8-85fd-c4ef2d4f3b89?ogimg=plain)) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:
Here’s [a link to the larger image](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026-11-01/5821A414-FAF6-4E61-B037-952C1FD80D39.png).
For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):
In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”.
Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.
The data in the above chart comes from the “Employment size class” XLSX file, [available from here](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/data_downloads). Here’s [a copy](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Employment-Size-Class-Nov-1-2026-copy.xlsx) of the file I used.
You can view [the survey document](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/downloads/BTOS%20Content%20V5%20Core%20Round%203,%204.pdf) that is sent out to businesses—here’s [my snapshot copy](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/BTOS-Content-V5-Core-Round-3-4.pdf) of that 346KB PDF.
The changing language of the questions
As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):
In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)
On December 3rd, 2025, [the Bureau announced](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/downloads/AI%20Question%20Wording%20Updates.pdf) a significant change to that question. Here’s the replacement:
In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)
No more “producing goods or services”—now it’s “in any of its business functions”! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.
From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence
When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn’t find it. I found this instead:
In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)
The [BTOS about page](https://www.census.gov/hfp/btos/about) explains what happened:
Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection,
[instrument wording]was updated due to[Executive Order 14434].
The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording—the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.
Is this going to affect the survey?
The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.
The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn’t going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out “formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI”.
I can’t help but laugh at the absurdity of “SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service” though.

title: A Valid Key Let an AI Agent Delete Production - Sagar Batchu, Speakeasy
body:
A coding agent tried to fix a staging problem and deleted a production database and its backup instead. It did this with valid credentials. Sagar Batchu of Speakeasy uses that incident to lay out a control layer for agents in regulated industries. Every action is tied to an identity, checked against policy in real time, never allowed to exceed its owner's rights, and recorded for compliance.

15:20 Summary: valid credentials aren't valid intent
16:36 Q&A

title: AI Writes Code Faster Than Your Team Can Review It - Andrew Norrish, Sourcegraph
body:
AI has moved the bottleneck from writing code to reviewing it, and SREs are left handling the incidents. Andrew Norrish of Sourcegraph explains why unreviewed AI code is driving more outages, and why SRE and platform teams are best placed to fix it. He also shows how code search and a code-graph context engine help teams investigate, prevent and fix issues across huge codebases.

# LifeVal

Measuring AI progress on the tasks that matter in everyday life.

Loading…

Share

OpenAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. For the more than one billion people who currently use ChatGPT every week, we want to build AI that can help with the practical challenges of everyday life, like finding childcare, accessing government services, creating a budget, preparing for school, modifying recipes, ordering groceries, designing workout plans, and more.

When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response. To be a truly helpful personal assistant, ChatGPT should be able to take actions that actually get things done.

To measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents. We used this evaluation to track and drive improvement in model performance on everyday tasks over the past year. 

## Background

To identify the tasks people value most, we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally: the [American Time Use Survey⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.bls.gov/tus/) and the [Multinational Time Use Study⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.timeuse.org/mtus). Together, these datasets provide a detailed catalog of everyday life tasks that people do across different demographics, times of day, and seasons. To understand where people would most value AI assistance, we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents. For each task, we asked a variety of questions to identify the areas where everyday people most wanted help from a personal assistant. The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services. 

## Individual task examples

Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life.

### Enroll in the right kindergarten after moving

93.1%



Compare kindergartens near our new home and shortlist the best fits.

I’ve narrowed it to three kindergartens and organized the enrollment details. Two preferences still need your call. Want to review the shortlist?

### Manage volunteers ahead of a flood

98.0%



Help me organize our community’s flood preparation volunteer force for four neighbors needing floodproofing assistance.

I’ve prepared a simple action plan to help volunteers assess the sites mentioned and help them prepare for upcoming severe weather.

### Find a new home for my family

100%



Find a home in Luzerne County that fits my budget, has a separate living unit, and keeps my commute short after school drop-off. Add the deed to my cart so I can review it.

I found one home that meets your requirements. I’ve calculated the transfer tax and added the deed to your country records cart to review.

### Watch a game with grandma from far away

96.3%



Set up an easy way for grandma and me to watch the game together remotely.

The easiest watch setup is ready, with a backup if the stream fails. Want me to walk you through it with grandma?

### Meal prep for a parent adjusting to a new diabetes diagnosis

90.4%



Help my parent adjust to a new diabetes diagnosis with a practical care and meal plan.

The first-week plan is ready, including meals, reminders, and questions for the care team. Want to review it together before you share it with your parent?

Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks.See more 

Over the past year, we’ve trained our models to become much faster, more capable, and more aligned on browser use, computer use, and connectors tasks. Enabling these capabilities in ChatGPT also expands the types of tasks the model can help with, helping move ChatGPT beyond a chat tool and towards a truly agentic personal assistant.

## Why this matters

To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people. That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done. We are hopeful that LifeVal represents a step towards that goal.

title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
body:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)
Executive summary
When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.
Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:
- Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems.
- For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library.
- Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in
[section 6](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#prior-work). Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.
- Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.
Today we are releasing five artifacts:
- The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;
- A
[technical report](https://www.anthropic.com/document/flashprove-technical-report)explaining the details of our system; - A
[protocol description](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/blob/main/paper/paper.pdf); [Executable code](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve)that includes: a[prover](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/prover)and two verifiers, a[fast verifier](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/verifier)in C++, and a[provably correct verifier](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/tools/lean-verify)in Lean; and[Lean proofs](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/lean)for the top level mathematical statements, along with an[interactive visualizer](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/blob/main/lean/STATEMENTS.html)of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.
We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.[1](#footnote-1) This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.
Introduction
When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.
However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.
The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.
One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.
Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).
The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.
We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development, in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees, in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators, and more.
Trust challenges in AI proliferation
The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises [trust challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07213) that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).
Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.
Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.
Challenge 1: pacing
Some proposals to [regulate](https://thefuturesociety.org/international-ai-verification) and [pace](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) AI development rely on [monitoring hardware and how it is used](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08797). For example, a provider might be required to [devote its hardware to inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15867) rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?
How zkSNARKs can help: The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.[2](#footnote-2) We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.
Challenge 2: tamper detection
As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become [prime targets](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html). An attacker or rogue agent may [compromise an inference server](https://www.wiz.io/blog/nvidia-triton-cve-2025-23319-vuln-chain-to-ai-server) to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while [hiding among genuine responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02620). The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of which weights are actually running on its servers? In our [Frontier Safety Roadmap](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap), Anthropic set a [public goal](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap#moonshot-r-d-projects) to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights.” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.[3](#footnote-3)
How zkSNARKs can help: The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that some model produced the response but that the committed model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.
Challenge 3: text provenance
One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For exampl

title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
body:
Make long-running agents faster with message threads
New in the Messages API, send your conversation once, and the API receives only what’s new with every turn.
Message threads is now available in public beta on the Claude Platform. With message threads, agents no longer need to resend the full conversation history on every turn, reducing latency for long-running sessions.
How message threads works
A coding agent might make hundreds of requests in one session, and each request resends every earlier message and tool result. Once a conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, resending all of it adds time before Claude starts responding. With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT).
With message threads on by default for most Claude Code users, requests with 500k to 1M tokens see median TTFT drop by about 35%.
To use message threads, add the thread
parameter to Messages API requests. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread. Each request after that includes only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. Between turns, we hold each thread in memory, where it’s encrypted and not written to disk. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and your client then resends the full conversation to start a new one. While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.
Message threads is best for active sessions where latency matters, including:
- Long-running coding agents, where each tool result or file edit adds to the conversation.
- Computer use agents, where screenshots stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn.
- Document and image-heavy workflows, where requests are made smaller.
The more context an agent carries, the more message threads can reduce time to first token.
Getting started
Message threads is available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and on Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Standard Claude token rates and existing rate limits apply. See the [documentation](http://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/message-threads) to get started.

# OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization

Loading…

Share

Dan Driscoll will join OpenAI as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization, working with senior leadership and external partners to advise on how advanced AI can strengthen national and cyber security, with a particular focus on working with U.S. allies to advance its responsible use.

In this newly created role, Dan will work with OpenAI teams and leaders across governments, industry, academia, and allied institutions to advance practical modernization initiatives that support the buildout of democratic AI. He will also help internal OpenAI teams understand the operational needs of global national security institutions.

Dan previously served as the 26th Secretary of the Army, overseeing the service’s operations, modernization, and resources. He brings experience spanning military service, senior government leadership, and the private sector.

In his role, Dan will advise our public and private sector partners in modernizing policy and strategy choices to unlock practical uses of AI to improve national security and help ensure the world is building AI to support democratic principles. He will work to identify where operational needs, institutional change and emerging AI capabilities come together. Dan’s appointment reflects our commitment to helping democratic institutions use advanced AI responsibly to strengthen shared security, and builds on OpenAI’s work with allies and partners to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services under its [Daybreak](https://openai.com/daybreak/) program.

> “AI should give people more power over their lives and people should have a say in how it’s developed. The US has an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI and I’m excited to welcome Dan Driscoll to OpenAI to strengthen American leadership and help us do that.”

*Sam Altman*

> “I’ve spent much of my career in public service, first as a Soldier and most recently as Secretary of the Army and Acting Director of ATF. The people who serve deserve the very best tools we can put in their hands. National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years. This technology will help them keep pace by cutting through paperwork, making sense of more information, and getting the right answer to the right person faster. I’m joining OpenAI to help the United States and our allies put this technology to work responsibly, for the people who keep us safe.”

*Dan Driscoll*

**Dan Driscoll** was the 26th Secretary of the United States Army. As Secretary, he oversaw operations, modernization, and resource allocation for nearly one million Active, Guard, and Reserve Soldiers and more than 265,000 Army Civilians. He drove Army transformation focused on accelerating the fielding of new technology, reforming acquisition, and building a more capable force. A former Army officer and business leader, Dan has experience spanning military service, law, and the private sector.

- [Putting Codex to work every day](#putting-codex-to-work-every-day)
- [Choosing which coding rules apply with the Decisions API](#choosing-which-coding-rules-apply-with-the-decisions-api)
- [Building software factories customers can own](#building-software-factories-customers-can-own)

[Qodo⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.qodo.ai/) builds AI tools for code review and software quality, giving coding agents the organizational knowledge they need to understand the code they change. Co-founder and CEO Itamar Friedman calls it “the coding agent’s best friend.”

Qodo uses OpenAI models including GPT‑6 Astra to gather engineering knowledge, review code, and monitor software quality. Its Codex plugin brings that context and review into developers’ coding sessions.

> “We love OpenAI models. We want the frontier, the best reasoning models, but also those that are really fast.”

—Itamar Friedman, Co-founder and CEO, Qodo

## Finding P0 bugs across repositories with Codex

Itamar describes customer environments that can span 10,000 or more repositories, where a local code change can break a downstream service, even if it looks correct on its own. Qodo built a plugin in the Codex marketplace to address this.

“Codex is really good at taking a local task and completing it in an efficient way,” Itamar says. Qodo’s plugin gives Codex access to codebase knowledge, organizational rules, and independent review through Qodo’s Agentic Toolbox.

With context, Codex can account for dependencies across repositories, including those hosted by different Git providers or services connected through Kafka. “Qodo will make that connection and will help Codex look at the software as a whole and not miss those P0 bugs,” Itamar says.

## Automating review while keeping human judgment

Before Codex starts writing code, it can use Qodo’s plugin to retrieve the relevant codebase rules and pull request history and patterns. After Codex makes the changes, Qodo reviews them and returns its findings directly to Codex in the same session, before the developer opens a pull request.

Nnenna Ndukwe, Qodo’s AI Developer Relations Lead, sees developers using this workflow to build features and tackle technical debt with GPT‑6 models in Codex. They are automating the handoff between Codex’s coding work and Qodo’s independent review. “That’s what I’ve been seeing developers do, which is really exciting because GPT‑6 is extremely capable,” Nnenna says.

Itamar describes coding and review agents as “yin and yang”: one creates code, the other challenges it. Each role needs its own setup and context and may involve multiple agents. His vision is for agents to discuss findings and “surface only what they don’t accept” for human review. Developers would become planners and reviewers, able to inspect unresolved issues alongside the agents’ discussion, context, and prior developer decisions.

“That’s how you create trust,” Itamar says. “I think it makes the whole process overall more efficient,” Nnenna adds. “We get to leverage the best parts of our expertise.”

## Putting Codex to work every day

Internally at Qodo, Nnenna has been using GPT‑6 Astra’s Extra High and Ultra effort settings in her own automated development workflows as well as knowledge work.

> “What does Codex *not* do? I love everything that Codex does. I love the idea of combining AI and automation.”

—Nnenna Ndukwe, AI Developer Relations Lead, Qodo

Nnenna schedules Codex to report on what she accomplished during the week and where she could focus or improve next. She also uses it to research conversations about agentic engineering on social platforms and suggest ideas for developer content. When it comes to her own code changes, she schedules Codex to analyze her work and suggest agent skills to create or refine.

## Choosing which coding rules apply with the Decisions API

Itamar sees an opportunity to use OpenAI’s recently launched Decisions API to choose which rules and agent skills apply at each stage of development, rather than rely on language models for every decision.

He cites an example where the Decisions API could select which of 200 rules need checking before a language model reasons through the relevant ones, helping to make selection faster and cheaper while improving the quality of the review. “The Decisions API is an immense opportunity for us to bring more trust to the process,” Itamar says.

## Building software factories customers can own

Qodo’s approach combines “the best aspects of artificial intelligence and the best aspects of traditional software engineering and scripting,” Nnenna says. Company knowledge guides coding agents, independent review checks their work, and human expertise resolves the questions that remain.

This creates the foundation of what Itamar describes as a software factory: a system customers could assemble and own, bringing coding and review agents together with an understanding of how software changes in production.

With OpenAI, Qodo is building a future where coding agents put more of a company’s experience to work and developers can focus their judgment where it matters most.

title: If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
body:
1st November 2026
I've been getting the occasional confusing Python dependency error since switching over to Python 3.15 and the rule I'm having to remember is:
If in doubt, delete the uv.lock file
Most of my projects are libraries which don't include a uv.lock
file, since it's rude for a library dependency to lock versions for anything else that uses it.
Running uv run pytest
etc tends to leave uv.lock
files lying around, which are listed in .gitignore
and so do not get committed to my repositories.
But... sometimes that uv.lock
pins a version of a dependency that doesn't yet have a Python 3.15 wheel. An example from earlier today:
error: Failed to build `watchfiles==1.1.1`
cause: Call to `maturin.build_wheel` failed
error: the configured Python interpreter version (3.15) is newer
than PyO3's maximum supported version (3.14)
Deleting that file and running uv run pytest
again usually fixes the problem.

title: I Made a Fruit Fly Review My Code - Nick Nisi, WorkOS
body:
Code is being written faster than ever, and Nick Nisi, who leads developer and agent experience at WorkOS, argues that the human reviewer is now the bottleneck. To make the point, he hooked a simulated fruit fly brain, built from a full scan of its neurons, up to code review: AI turns each change into literal "code smells," sugar and bitter rewards teach the fly what good and bad code taste like, and it was right about 88% of the time in testing. Then he plays a live round against the audience and lays out a practical plan where team review skills, classifiers and automated reviewers only send the risky pull requests to a human, backed by proof like screenshots and smoke tests.

title: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts
body:
31st October 2026 - Link Blog
[How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts](https://www.parameter.ai/labs/we-found-a-gap-at-openai) ([via](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50314699)) Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called [HTML previews](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/20001246-working-with-writing-blocks-and-code-blocks-in-chatgpt)), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe.
It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data.
Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes [its own virtual keyboard](https://mathlive.io/mathfield/virtual-keyboard/), which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage()
from the sandboxed iframe.
That message receiving code uses innerHTML
, so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method.
This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML
doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions.
OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it.
Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference.
The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf.
OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious.

title: The Golden Age
body:
written on October 31, 2026
This Halloween weekend we went to watch the brief Halloween circus show at [Family
Park](https://www.familypark.at/) — a family tradition. It’s just 45 minutes,
but there are some pretty impressive performers and their life is to show the
unexpected, something that the average human is not capable of doing. As silly
as such traditions are, they give one a sense of normalcy in the world. But
this world is very much not normal.
My kids are growing up in a world of war. We’re lucky that we’re not directly affected, but some of their friends escaped one. Many of our friends had to leave their country of origin because of political instability and war. Many of them are lucky in that they have the means and opportunities to start a new life in a new place. And well, my kids grow up in a country without a real army, but with mandatory conscription.
But all our lives are being affected by a society and world that is changing
around us in ways that can be frightening. It’s not just hot wars, it’s also a
world of increased hostility expressed in everyday conversations. It’s a world
that increasingly no longer wants [the rule of
law](https://worldjusticeproject.org/news/wjp-rule-law-index-2025-global-press-release).
Our social systems are increasingly no longer going to be working, and the
economic developments are greatly uneven in the world. Blocs like Europe which
were built on the idea of peace and stability are finding it hard to adjust to a
world that wants none of that.
It’s not very hard to only look at the great opportunities if you live in Silicon Valley. There, you are far from war (there isn’t even a draft). Which is ironic, given that the US did in fact start a war. But it’s one that barely touches its tech elite. There you’re at the center of innovation and you’re living in a country rich with resources, and the general sense is that one will be largely unaffected by climate change — even though that is probably wrong. But even if climate change were to affect the US negatively, money does a lot to shield you from it. Living in a country which only ever fights wars abroad and a country which can force any country into submission can make one believe a thing about the world that does not reflect reality much. And even the self-inflicted Iran war is doing much more damage abroad than in the US.
I might not live in the valley, but mentally I am. My career and my social circles are there and so is my mind. I’m in that bizarre sphere where I both appreciate and love the US and the tech industry, but I also cannot help but see the damage we inflict on the world.
From Vienna to Lviv in Ukraine it’s not much further than to Bregenz, a city in Austria. Every day you can see trains going from Vienna to war-torn Ukraine. A country that has lost almost half its population with cities in rubble.
The everyday European citizens are seeing their pension systems crumble and their everyday prices go up, caused by wars and conflicts they have nothing to do with. We now have 65 active conflicts in the world and many of these conflicts have no obvious way out. You can’t make it a day in the news without people (sometimes violently) demonstrating against the changes that are happening to their lives.
That is the backdrop for this ongoing AI revolution. For those in the valley
who are at the center [“We’re in humanity’s golden
age.”](https://x.com/rauchg/status/2116369601508593911) It’s a golden age that
should be there for all — except you shouldn’t own it, because as Sam Altman
says: [owning it would be a bad allocation of
resources](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/1023820/sam-altman-ram-shortage-cloud-servers).
It’s pretty clear that this AI revolution is not felt by many, and probably even more don’t see the upsides. It should not surprise us that those of us with the means and power cannot get others to see that. People who don’t have any say or control in this newfound revolution do not trust the industry and have little belief that what is unfolding will be good for them. And for good reason. The industrial revolution might have been great for humanity, but for many of the workers in that revolution life did not feel great. Much of human innovation resulted in bad health outcomes, and modern worker rights were a direct result of horrific exploitation.
We might think of ourselves as a society that moved past these things, but it’s no surprise that worker rights will be the first thing that will go, in an effort to rejuvenate a broken economy and to stay competitive. Citizens stuck in lower paid jobs will suffer quickly, when the ones with money and power will not.
“You got to embrace this future” is easy to say for someone who lives a post-economic lifestyle who exerts so much power and influence that almost nothing can harm them. Very little in our lives would change as a result of diesel going up a few cents. Or people dying in senseless wars. Because money does not just buy you enormous flexibility, it also keeps you secure. For many of us, whatever the outcome of AI might be for our lives, we will be fine. Not just fine, we’re pretty much guaranteed to be better off. But I have significant doubts that this will extend to society as a whole.
I too think that it’s inevitable that companies will be required to run on AI. That software engineering without agents can no longer work. But simultaneously so far we have surprisingly little to show for most people, other than the new kind of tax we pay for it. The tax to keep our data secure, the tax we pay for the increased cost in hardware. More and more of society will live in a world where a percentage of their expected increases in salary will instead go to fund hyperscalers and the tokens they need to do their work.
Clearly a lot of the economy will change as a result of AI but not all of it. The circus performer’s reason to exist is not changing because AI creates great robotic circus performers. What makes them worth watching is that they bend what a human body and mind can do and no artificial contraption is going to give you that same feeling. And if there is a measure to judge if we are in a Golden Age or not, it should probably be something like that: what it allows people to do, and not what it allows a few to own and control.
But maybe Guillermo is right and in some ways this is a “Golden Age”. But a
golden age like the Dutch Golden Age: it overlapped with the Eighty Years’ War
and much of what made it a golden age was financed through colonial violence
and slave trade by the East and West India companies. The name only came about
in the 19th century, given by people who looked back at those who got to enjoy
it. A term that the [Amsterdam Museum stopped
using](https://www.dutchnews.nl/2019/09/amsterdam-museum-ditches-golden-age-in-favour-of-inclusive-17th-century) in 2019 as a recognition of all the people for whom that century
was anything but golden.

title: Xoranth's musings
body:
2024-01-14
We have seen in a [previous post](../verb-parse/) that switch statements are more complex than they seem.
The compiler is able to implement them as a decision tree (even though maybe it shouldn't).
Is that everything it can do?
In this post, I'll focus on gcc

A function that takes two integers x

Were we to implement this manually, we'd would use an array of function pointers, where the input serves as the index into the array.

title: Everyone Has the Same AI Models. Here's What Sets Agents Apart - Richmond Alake, Oracle
body:
Richmond Alake was talking about agent memory before most people had heard of it, and now he argues the next layer after the control plane is an intelligence plane: what an agent knows, what it remembers, what it's allowed to see, and how it gets better. Using the WWII codebreakers who worked out that "AF" meant Midway, he shows why having the same information as everyone else isn't the same as intelligence. He then demos an agent built with an ontology and semantic layer that gets answers right 99% of the time using 32K tokens, versus 200K for a naive agent, and covers Oracle's agent memory package, deep data security, private inference, and fine-tuning small decision models for memory routing.

title: 78% Wanted This AI Feature. Almost Nobody Used It - Supriya Subudhi, Bumble
body:
Bumble product manager Supriya Subudhi shares five lessons from A/B testing an AI photo feedback feature in a dating app with over 20 million monthly users. 78% of surveyed users said they wanted feedback, but only 10-15% used it; the average win hid odd outputs like telling smiling people to smile more; the best model cost about 10x more; switching to a cheaper model also shrank the results; and regulation meant the feature couldn't ship outside the US. title: When Running Your Own AI Models Beats Paying for APIs - Steven Latré, imec
body:
Steven Latré leads AI at imec, the Belgian semiconductor R&D center, and his team ran thousands of benchmark runs to find out what moving from APIs to your own GPUs really costs for long-running coding agents. Testing open-weight models and three coding harnesses on SWE-Bench Pro, they found that hardware costs jump in steps rather than a smooth curve, that concurrency matters even more than accuracy, that break-even GPU utilization ranges from 89% on small systems to about 15% on 8x B200 machines, and that the right harness can cut GPU time in half for the same result.
