title: Build a Financial Research Assistant with Cohere AI on AWS
body:
As a financial analyst much of the day comes down to finding one number in a filing that runs to hundreds of pages, and then proving where it came from. Neither is as easy as it sounds. The number is rarely in the body text. It usually lives in a table, a footnote, or a chart, and it can show up in different places under different names.
In this post, we show how to build a research assistant for financial filings with Cohere models on Amazon SageMaker AI - Embed for search, Rerank for ordering the results, and Parse for turning hard pages into clean text. Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock will be used to write the answers, with a citation for every claim.
We will start with what makes this work difficult followed by an overview of the solution, and then spend most of the post on the design decisions behind it and when you would decide differently. At the end, we show how to deploy the solution in your own AWS account and try it yourself.
Why financial research is hard to automate
Financial research looks like a search problem, but it has features that break simple approaches.
The answer lives in the layout. Take a 10-K, the annual report that US public companies file with the Securities and Exchange Commission, covering the business, its risks and its audited financial statements ([what a Form 10-K contains](https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary/form-10-k)). The figure you need from it is usually in a table in the form of net interest income by year, regulatory capital by tier, charge-offs by loan type etc. When a PDF is converted to plain text, tables lose their row and column relationships, multi-column pages can come out in the wrong order, and charts often disappear.
An unverifiable answer is not useful. An analyst cannot put "the CET1 ratio was 11.9%" in a memo without knowing which filing and which page it came from, and whether the figure came from a table, a chart or a sentence. An assistant for this work has to show its sources, and the person reading has to be able to check them quickly.
Volume and cost add up. A research team might index thousands of filings across many years. Every page is embedded once, but every question is embedded too, and every model that runs on every question adds time and cost.
Not every document is clean. Filings arrive as digital PDFs, but also as scanned exhibits, faxed agreements, and photographed pages that have no text layer at all.
Questions do not always come in the document's language. Teams that cover several markets often ask in one language about documents written in another.
So a useful assistant has to do a few things like find the right page when the answer is in a table, make every answer checkable, keep cost and latency under control, cope with pages that are not clean, and work across languages.
Solution Overview
The solution is a research assistant that answers questions about a collection of filings and shows for every claim, the page it came from. It uses four models, each with one job:
- Cohere Embed turns each page, and each question, into a vector which is a list of numbers that captures its meaning, so that pages about the same thing as the question sit close to it.
[Embed comes in two tiers](https://cohere.com/blog/embed-5): Embed Pro, built for the highest retrieval quality and offline indexing, and Embed Fast, built for low latency on the live request path. [Cohere Rerank](https://cohere.com/blog/rerank-5)takes the question and the best candidate pages from the vector search, reads each pair together, and puts them in a better order. With Context Focus, Rerank can also mark the passages on each page that answer the question. Like Embed, Rerank comes in two tiers: Rerank Pro, built for the highest accuracy, and Rerank Fast, built for lower latency. We use Rerank Pro, because for a financial assistant finding the right page usually matters more than a faster answer.- Cohere Parse reads a page image and returns a clean Markdown, with tables as real rows and columns. It is used for pages whose text is weak.
- Anthropic Claude on Amazon Bedrock reads the top pages and writes the answer, citing each page.
People can use it through a web app with three functions:
- Assistant. Ask a question about the filings. The assistant finds the most relevant pages, reads them, and writes an answer in which every claim cites its page. Each citation also says whether the fact came from a table, a chart, body text, a footnote or a figure, and one click opens the page image to check it.
- Search. The same search, without a generated answer. It can show the results with and without Rerank side by side, so you can see how reordering changes them, and the Rerank column shows the passage Context Focus picked on each page.
- Parse. Parse extracts tables as rows from pages that you can download, and scanned-looking pages turned into text.
Under the hood there are two flows. Ingestion runs once per page where Parse runs first, for the pages that need it, then text is embedded with Embed Pro, and the vector is stored into a vector index. Answering runs on every question where Embed Fast embeds the question then the closest pages are retrieved and, optionally, reordered by Rerank. Finally, Claude writes the answer from the top pages. The Cohere models run as real-time endpoints on Amazon SageMaker AI, deployed from AWS Marketplace; the vector index is Amazon OpenSearch Serverless; the web app, sign-in, API and ingestion pipeline are serverless AWS services.
Design decisions, and why we made them
Every one of the challenges forced a choice.
Index with Embed Pro, query with Embed Fast
Indexing and querying have different needs. A page is embedded once, ahead of time, so you can afford the most accurate model. A question is embedded while someone waits, thousands of times a day, so speed and cost per call matter most. Embed Pro and Embed Fast share [one embedding space](https://cohere.com/blog/embed-5), which means a question embedded with Fast can be compared directly with pages embedded with Pro. You get Pro's quality in the index and Fast's speed on every question, without rebuilding the index. The figure below shows where each model sits.
The second choice is the size of each vector. Embed offers [six output sizes, from 256 to 2,048 dimensions, in float, int8 or binary](https://cohere.com/blog/embed-5). The embeddings are Matryoshka representations where the model is trained so that the first dimensions carry the most meaning, so a shorter vector keeps most of what a longer one says. We chose 1,024 dimensions stored as int8, one byte per dimension:
- Storage - A 1,024-dimension int8 vector takes 1 KB of raw storage, compared to 8 KB for a 2,048-dimension float32 vector—an 8x reduction. For a million pages, that translates to approximately 1 GB versus 8 GB of raw vector data. Actual vector index storage and costs will also depend on indexing structures, metadata, and infrastructure overhead.
- Quality - 1,024 is the middle of the range, and int8 keeps far more detail than binary. That is a sensible default when the answer has to be the right page, not just a similar one.
- When to change it - Use 2,048 dimensions if retrieval quality matters more than storage. Use 512, 256 or binary vectors for very large archives where cost dominates; binary is 32 times smaller than float32.
Whatever you choose, the query side must use the same size and format as the index. Changing it later means embedding every page again, so it is worth settling early.
Embed the page text, and keep the image for the answer
Embed can embed a page's text, the page as an image, or both together as one vector, all in the same space. Each choice suits a different kind of document.
Page text is the cheapest and simplest: one vector per page, Rerank reads text, so it can work on the same pages, and you can show a text snippet next to each result. The catch is that it is only as good as the extracted text where most of the time tables can lose their structure, charts disappear, and a scan has no text at all until something reads it.
The page image needs no text extraction. Tables, charts and layout are seen as the page looks, and it works on scans and photographs. It costs more per page, it is harder to show why a page matched, and Rerank still needs text.
Both together (a fused text-and-image vector) gives the search both views of the page, at the cost of the image price and a larger embedding call.
Annual reports and 10-Ks are digital documents with good text, so we embed the page text. What text loses, mostly charts and complex tables, we recover at answer time instead, by letting Claude see the page image. If your pages are mostly scans, slides, diagrams or charts, such as investor presentations, scanned agreements or faxed exhibits, embed the image or both.
One embedding space for every language[Embed supports more than 100 languages and a 128K-token context window](https://cohere.com/blog/embed-5). A question and a page land in the same space regardless of language, so a French question such as "impact de l'immobilier commercial sur le segment Global Banking de Bank of America" can find the English Bank of America pages directly. Claude then writes the answer in the language of the question and keeps the citations as they are.
We chose this over translating questions into English first. There is no translation step to build, run or pay for, and no risk of a mistranslated term sending the search the wrong way. Rerank Pro is also [multilingual, with support for more than 100 languages](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank). As always, check the languages that matter to you on your own documents.
Make Rerank an optional stage, and make its effect visible
Vector search is fast because each page is compared with the question through a single number, the distance between two vectors. A reranker works differently where it reads the question and each candidate page together, which lets it weigh details a single vector cannot hold. Rerank Pro [reads up to 32K tokens of question and page together, works across more than 100 languages, and handles semi-structured content such as tables and JSON](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank). In this design, vector search returns 30 candidates and Rerank picks the five that go to Claude.
Rerank sits on the query path, so its latency is felt on every question. We still chose Rerank Pro over Rerank Fast, because in financial research a wrong page costs more than a slower answer. If interactive speed matters more for your users, Rerank Fast takes the same requests and returns the same kind of results, so switching between them is a configuration change, not a code change.
That extra reading costs time on every question and an endpoint to run, and how much it helps depends on your documents and your questions. So we made Rerank a stage you can switch on or off, and made its effect visible: the Assistant shows how long each step took, and Search can show the two result lists side by side, with arrows for how each page moved.
When should you turn it on? Look at where the right page lands without it. If it is usually at or near the top, leave Rerank off and keep answers fast. If it often appears lower in the list, or questions are long and specific, Rerank is the usual fix.
Rerank 5 also returns a [calibrated relevance score between 0 and 1](https://docs.cohere.com/docs/rerank) for each page, so the same cut-off means the same thing from one question to the next. You can use it to tell the user that no page is a good match, or to trigger another search, instead of answering from weak pages.
Parse only the pages that need it
Parse reads a page image and returns [Markdown or content blocks, with bounding boxes, and understands tables, forms, diagrams and images](https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-25vdn5x53zqgo). It is a GPU endpoint you pay for by the hour, and a clean digital page already has usable

title: Who Gets to Build the Frontier for AI
body:
Today, Cohere announced the initial close of its Series E funding round targeting up to CAD $7 Billion, led by Schwarz Group with participation from new and returning investors including Bell Ventures, Bullhound Capital, Inovia Capital, NVIDIA, and Prosperity7 Ventures, and the Government of Canada. We will use the funds to build something increasingly essential in AI: a frontier company outside the U.S. and China. Our ambition is to build frontier models that compete with the best in the world, a secure platform that lets institutions own the AI they run on, and cyber defenses democracies can rely on. We don’t have to accept a future of AI run by just a few, and we shouldn’t want one.
Within a few years, every hospital in Bavaria, every bank in New York and every agency in Ottawa will run a significant part of its operations on AI. They should be able to choose world-class systems built under laws they trust, using technology they can inspect and adapt, deploy inside their own environments, and on platforms they can depend on to remain available when it matters most. Today, many organizations face an uncomfortable choice: cheap models from China or powerful ones you can’t fully see into or control. The market is already choosing: more than 70 percent of the open-model tokens served through OpenRouter [came from Chinese models](https://arxiv.org/html/2604.07190v1) earlier this year – up from 3 percent fourteen months earlier.
We’re focused on changing that.
The need for choice and control is no longer theoretical. Recent history has shown how technologies behind communications, energy, and national security infrastructure can end up controlled by decisions made elsewhere. Access can change overnight because of commercial decisions, export controls, or geopolitical events, often with few alternatives. Each situation was different, but the lesson is the same: countries need guaranteed access to the technologies that keep them secure, resilient, and competitive. As allied governments [take on greater responsibility](https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/official_texts_236705.htm) for their own defense, infrastructure, and technological capabilities, AI belongs on that list.
The case against frontier fatalism
When Canada and Germany launched their [Sovereign Technology Alliance](https://www.canada.ca/en/innovation-science-economic-development/news/2026/02/canada-and-germany-sign-ai-joint-declaration-and-launch-sovereign-technology-alliance.html) in Munich earlier this year, they said they were "choosing to build," and that’s exactly what we intend to embody. Yet a growing consensus holds that the frontier of AI belongs to two countries and a handful of companies, and that everyone else should make peace with renting intelligence from whoever wins. You hear versions of this argument in boardrooms, government agencies, and investment committees across the democratic world, usually from people who mean well. Its advocates call it realism. We call it frontier fatalism.
Taken to its logical conclusion, frontier fatalism is a plan for managed decline. It asks countries to abandon capabilities they spent decades building. After investing in research, talent and innovation, they would wire their economies, public services, and defense infrastructure around technologies they don’t control, can’t meaningfully influence, and may not even be able to access indefinitely. And they would be expected to be grateful for API access.
The fatalists are right about one thing: building at the frontier is difficult. It requires capital, compute and research talent at a scale few organizations can assemble. Where they are wrong is in assuming there is only one way to compete.
There are many frontiers
Much of the confusion in discussing frontier AI models comes from talking about “the frontier” as if it were one thing. But there are the myriad domain frontiers: the best achievable performance on a specific class of valuable problem, from finding software vulnerabilities, to analyzing intelligence across dozens of languages, to running a bank's compliance work. Researchers at Harvard Business School referred to this unevenness as the "[jagged technological frontier](https://aiinstitute.hbs.edu/arts-and-science-research/)." In many domains, success depends not only on the model itself, but on the system around it: how context is assembled, how state is tracked, how reasoning is verified, and how outputs are evaluated. That reality creates room for more builders. And there are dimensions of the jagged technological frontier where owning, rather than buying, is crucial to one's sovereignty.
The proof: cybersecurity
Cybersecurity is one of the most important domain frontiers today. Anthropic's Claude Mythos Preview demonstrated the potential of advanced models to discover previously unknown vulnerabilities, while [Project Glasswing](https://techcrunch.com/2026/06/02/anthropic-scales-claude-mythos-to-critical-infrastructure-in-15-countries/) extended that work to operators of critical infrastructure in more than 15 countries. Those advances matter. But they have largely occurred behind closed doors, with access limited to a small group of partners on terms set by a single provider, reflecting the same concentration that defines the broader frontier AI landscape. More importantly, they do not prove that leadership in cyber defense will belong exclusively to whichever company builds the strongest general-purpose model.
AISLE, which will soon [join us](https://cohere.com/blog/cohere-and-aisle-sign-letter-of-intent-to-advance-cyber-resilient-sovereign-ai) as Cohere Cyber, offers a different perspective. The company describes vulnerability discovery as a [production function](https://aisle.com/blog/system-over-model-zero-day-discovery-at-the-jagged-frontier) with two inputs: intelligence per token and tokens per dollar. In practice, that means model capability is only part of the equation. A well-designed system can use efficient models to explore more possibilities, run more tests, and validate more findings. Raw intelligence matters, but so does the ability to turn that intelligence into results.
The evidence is compelling. In August, curl founder Daniel Stenberg [reported](https://mastodon.social/@bagder/117149161231799662) that Mythos, OpenAI's Codex Security, and ZeroPath had found nothing further in his codebase. AISLE's system subsequently identified [18 of the 24 vulnerabilities](https://aisle.com/blog/one-aisle-curl-audit-produced-24-cves-18-ship-today) fixed in curl's October release. A specialized cyber platform and a general-purpose model are not directly comparable. But that is precisely the point. Organizations do not deploy models in isolation. They deploy systems, products, and workflows. What ultimately matters is the performance of the complete system.
Cybersecurity also offers something uniquely valuable for AI development: ground truth. Suspected vulnerabilities can be reproduced, validated by maintainers, and tested against proposed fixes. That makes cybersecurity not only a critical domain in its own right, but also an ideal environment for improving the models that power it.
How the frontiers feed each other
It may be expected that a company focused on specific domains would fall behind on general models, but in practice the domain work is one of the best ways to make general models better. Working at a domain frontier means pushing for the best possible results on one kind of valuable problem, whether that takes a specialized model, a general model with the right tools and instructions, or a full system built around several models.
Some of the biggest recent advances in model reasoning have come from [reinforcement learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948) on specific domains where a computer can check the answer, such as whether a proof holds, a test passes or a bug that reproduces. The skills models learn inside these domains transfer beyond the domain itself and into related settings, driving general model improvements alongside domain specific ones.
Working with customers on real-world tasks also shows us where today's models fall short in ways public benchmarks rarely capture and each failure tells us what the next model needs to do better. Customers also tell us which capabilities matter most. Public sector customers usually ask first for strong analysis across many languages and the ability to read images and documents alongside text, the same capabilities a bank, a telecom operator or a hospital needs from an AI agent.
All of those improvements flow back into our general models, and better general models make everything we build on top of them more capable, so a customer in one domain benefits from what we learned in another. That loop is why we build on all of these frontiers at once, and this funding round is designed to speed it up.
Europe has done this before
Whether a challenger can take on entrenched giants this way, with a different approach and allies building alongside it, is a question Europe has answered before. Half a century ago, the answer came from commercial aviation.
In the late 1960s, American manufacturers dominated the jet airliner market. Europe’s national aircraft makers were individually too small to challenge them. Britain’s government [pulled its funding](https://airbus.com/en/our-history/commercial-aircraft-history/trouble-and-strife-1968-1969) from the project that became Airbus in 1969. France and Germany pressed ahead. Airbus did not begin by matching Boeing aircraft for aircraft. It competed through a different design: the A300, the world’s first twin-engine widebody. Commercial success took years. A breakthrough came when Eastern Air Lines, led by former Apollo 8 commander Frank Borman, agreed in 1977 to [trial four A300s](https://www.airbus.com/en/our-history/commercial-aircraft-history/technology-leaders-1977-1979) and subsequently ordered more. A decade later the A320 brought [fly-by-wire controls](https://airbus.com/en/our-history/commercial-aircraft-history/fly-by-wire-1980-1987) to airliners. In 2025, Airbus [delivered 793 aircraft](https://flightplan.forecastinternational.com/2026/01/15/airbus-and-boeing-report-december-2025-commercial-aircraft-orders-and-deliveries/) to Boeing's 600.
The lesson is that an apparently settled market can be moved by a serious competitor with patient investment, a differentiated approach, and partners willing to build. Airbus builds jets in Mobile, Alabama, and [spends more than $15 billion a year](https://www.airbus.com/en/about-us/our-worldwide-presence/airbus-in-americas/airbus-in-the-united-states) with over 2,000 American suppliers. Its A220 [began life](https://www.cbc.ca/1.4740345) as Bombardier's C Series, designed in Quebec. Many of its engines come from [CFM International](https://www.geaerospace.com/propulsion/commercial/leap), a fifty-fifty venture between GE and France's Safran whose LEAP engine also powers Boeing's 737 MAX. None of that makes Airbus less European. Competition on the airframe and partnership on the engine made both sides of the Atlantic stronger.
That is the model we have in mind for AI. What we are building is a second option for the democratic world, and the United States benefits from it as much as Canada, Germany, and other allies do. The US frontier should not have to carry the competition with China alone. Building more frontier capability across the democratic world makes the entire alliance stronger.
Two decades of building
The foundation for this ambition already exists. AI has always been an international project, and Canada and Germany have been important contributors. In 2004, when neural networks were out of fashion almost everywhere, the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research [backed an AI program led by Geoffrey Hinton](https://cifar.ca/?p=59829) that brought him together with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun, the three researchers later honored with the Turing Award f

title: Security notice — malicious version of
body:
Security notice — malicious version of Anthropic.claude-code (2.1.312 and 2.1.313) identified in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace
Today we identified a security incident involving a specific extension in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace: Anthropic.claude-code version 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and MacOS. These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic. This does not impact other extensions downloaded from the cursor.com/marketplace, Grok Bot, Grok or our other SpaceXSI products.
What happened
Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace. The extension runs malicious code that attempts to install a persistent SSH backdoor. Specifically, it:
- Collects and reports host and user information: hostname, username, OS, architecture, home directory path, environment variable names, working directories, configured Git email, and public IP.
- Attempts to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to
authorized_keys
, enable the local SSH service, and open a reverse SSH tunnel. Outside of highly unusual circumstances where Cursor was started with administrator privileges, due to errors in the malicious code, this step would fail. - Attempts to make the reverse SSH tunnel persistent via a LaunchAgent (macOS), or a scheduled task that attempts to run as SYSTEM with a Startup-script fallback (Windows). Background scripts retry the tunnel roughly every 60 seconds.
Note: The attacker server no longer functions.
- We worked with the cloud provider that was hosting it to take it offline, so the reverse shell and host detail POST are not functional.
- These findings concern the identified package. We have no evidence that other versions of the extension or the official distribution are affected.
- Additionally, turning on the local SSH service requires admin rights, which the malicious extension does not have on most macOS and Windows hosts. On those hosts the step fails and the attacker could not have logged in through the tunnel. The extension added the attacker’s SSH key, installed persistence, and sent host details to the attacker. Follow the remediation steps below regardless.
What we did
- Removed the malicious version from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace immediately upon detection and blocked further distribution. We followed with a full shut down of the marketplace out of an abundance of caution.
- We audited access and confirmed no other extensions were tampered with.
- We rotated our keys, rebuilt the marketplace, and brought it back online.
- We worked with the hosting provider to take the malicious server offline, disrupting the attack by blocking the connection to that server.
What you should do
If you installed or updated to Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 from the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace on macOS or Windows between 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT on October 29, 2026:
- Run the attached script to validate if you are impacted (see below).
- Search across endpoint, network, and extension-installation telemetry for the indicators below.
- Isolate hosts showing evidence of payload execution or backdoor installation.
- Remove the unauthorized SSH key, persistence mechanisms, and running tunnel processes, and assess whether the host should be rebuilt. Uninstalling the extension may not be sufficient — the payload drops standalone persistence scripts that keep running.
- Rotate credentials and sessions accessible from affected hosts, from a trusted system. The limited env-var collection does not rule out later credential access over the backdoor.
Check whether you are impacted
The malicious extension appends the attacker's public key, labeled svc-telemetry
, to your SSH authorized keys. To check for it:
On macOS, run:
grep -qs svc-telemetry ~/.ssh/authorized_keys && echo "svc-telemetry key found" || echo "No key found; machine not impacted"
On Windows, run in PowerShell:
$files = "$HOME\.ssh\authorized_keys", "C:\ProgramData\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys" | Where-Object { Test-Path $_ }
if ($files -and (Select-String svc-telemetry $files)) { "svc-telemetry key found" } else { "No key found; machine not impacted" }
If the key is found, your machine is impacted. Follow steps 3 to 5 above, and run the remediation script for your platform below.
Remediate affected machines
These scripts remove the malicious extension, the persistence mechanisms, the running tunnel processes, and the attacker's SSH key. They exit with a non-zero status if anything remains.
On macOS, download [remediate-macos.sh](/static/security/claude-code-extension/remediate-macos.sh) and run it as the affected user, not as root, from the folder you saved it to:
bash remediate-macos.sh
On Windows, download [remediate-windows.ps1](/static/security/claude-code-extension/remediate-windows.ps1) and run it from PowerShell opened with Run as Administrator, in the folder you saved it to:
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\remediate-windows.ps1
Indicators of compromise
Package version 2.1.312
- Modified VSIX SHA-256 (darwin-arm64): fcbb327e38e61c4fec795e0d0591f52cd1014b813d20a5912104953c3a17c364 (MD5 e0d64d53e802a0217ba6f0e656ed2f20)
- Modified VSIX SHA-256 (win32-x64): 3de1722901165769893bef57c72594e9a54459faa23f3091b136b79966edd081 (MD5 bd3b71ddf3d0cc3af76249afd2c0eda1)
Package version 2.1.313
- Modified VSIX SHA-256 (darwin-arm64): 80402fdcad8799285fd93044976973ca000da7995fb93363f819bb8e4f84ee6c (MD5 34e491161e056c9b899a79b602ac73b9)
- Modified VSIX SHA-256 (win32-x64): 6786ec90cbd45949695bd7805c9fbb26cfc91bc5fc897de0183d9bcb9cb21731 (MD5 7838a3be2ca0ff08c1bdb160ef516d39)
Payload
- Modified code: extension.js in package versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for both Darwin and Windows in the extension folder contains 134[.]209[.]82[.]225 and svc-telemetry
- SHA-256: ecb58cb29078d9646ad1dcdbe51526f2d9cfea06be5fb2ab183e8ecc3ab6bf15
- MD5: f49bcd657ef1e626e85ce858958c1769
Network
- Attacker endpoint: 134[.]209[.]82[.]225
- Reverse SSH: tunnel@134[.]209[.]82[.]225, TCP 22
- External beacon: hxxp://134[.]209[.]82[.]225:8099/beacon (HTTP POST)
- Local beacon attempt: 127[.]0[.]0[.]1:8099/beacon (HTTP POST, loopback)
- Public IP lookups to ifconfig[.]me / api[.]ipify[.]org — legitimate services; access alone is not an indicator
SSH
- Unauthorized public key:
ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAIDdvylCEJ/k2TpezcTfedrkHyFSK9IZ3vmP6vhY4Ss0P svc-telemetry
- Unauthorized key fingerprint:
SHA256:0Z6R+DF64Do2nwQic8a7kkfDLNNk4IiK+2U2Rci4htk
- Reverse-tunnel key fingerprint:
SHA256:KOAU57+ZG6u3MG4WwzPzPX2O5YEe9qdOC1Bl+6MVyDQ
- Key comment:
svc-telemetry
Files and persistence
- Linux / macOS: unauthorized key in
~/.ssh/authorized_keys
;~/.config/.smt
,~/.config/.smtk
- Linux:
/tmp/.stk_<10 hex>
; cron@reboot /bin/sh "<HOME>/.config/.smt"
- macOS:
$TMPDIR/.stk_<10 hex>
;~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist
(labelcom.apple.sysmond
) - Windows:
%USERPROFILE%\.ssh\authorized_keys
,%USERPROFILE%\.config\smt.cmd
,%USERPROFILE%\.config\smtk
,%TEMP%\.stk_<10 hex>
; scheduled taskSysMon
(attempts to run as SYSTEM); fallback%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup\sysmon.cmd
Process / command-line
ssh -N -R '*:0:localhost:22'
,autossh -M 0
- SSH options:
StrictHostKeyChecking=no
,UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null
,ServerAliveInterval=30
,ServerAliveCountMax=3
,ExitOnForwardFailure=yes
,IdentitiesOnly=yes
schtasks /create /tn SysMon
systemsetup -setremotelogin on
Add-WindowsCapability -Online -Name OpenSSH.Server~~~~0.0.1.0
If you have further questions, reach out to [security@cursor.com](mailto:security@cursor.com).

title: Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready
body:
🌡 4
Protostar Challenge: Climate Risk Intelligence
Manage competition registration, data access, and submissions
Published
October 29, 2026
An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
Today, we're announcing [Project ProtoStar](https://huggingface.co/project-protostar), an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/), opens on November 2. See [How to Participate](#the-first-challenge-climate-risk-intelligence) below.
The initiative's founding partners include [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/), [Purdue University](https://www.purdue.edu/), [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://www.gatech.edu/), [Arizona State University](https://www.asu.edu/), and [The George Washington University](https://www.gwu.edu/), all working through the [Open Forum for AI (OFAI)](https://www.openforumai.org/) as the university coalition partner; the [Astera Institute](https://astera.org/); [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) as the infrastructure partner; and the [Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA)](https://orcaopen.org/), through its [Fostering Innovation Network](https://orcaopen.org/work/fostering-innovation-through-open-science-fin), as the community partner.
Participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to [protostar@orcaopen.org](mailto:protostar@orcaopen.org).
The U.S. federal government invests approximately [$190 billion annually in research and development](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48694), and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the [National Institutes of Health (NIH)](https://www.nih.gov/) and [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the [ten generalist repositories listed by NIH](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/NIHbmic/generalist_repositories.html) for sharing research data.
But making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.
Project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the [National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge](https://datacommons.cancer.gov/news/nci-crdc-artificial-intelligence-data-readiness-aidr-challenge) and [Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI](https://huggingface.co/blog/evijit/public-org-data-ai). The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.
The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/) hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.
The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.
Figure 1. New public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. [Explore the data](https://huggingface.co/spaces/evijit/hf-science-growth).
When organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's [National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while [NASA IMPACT's](https://huggingface.co/nasa-impact) 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an important part of making these resources useful: [90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13822).
Publicly available genomic data has proved important in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from [HuggingFaceBio](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceBio) such as [Carbon-A](https://huggingface.co/blog/HuggingFaceBio/carbon-annotator-genbank-genome-annotation) and [Carbon-X](https://huggingface.co/spaces/HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X-Release). By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support new research that others can build upon.
This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.
[Making scientific artifacts AI-ready](https://huggingface.co/blog/evijit/public-org-data-ai) is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.
A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?
To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:
- Demonstrate scientific reuse. Produce concrete examples of researchers and developers building on publicly funded scientific artifacts, including applications that combine resources across institutions or disciplines.
- Learn what makes reuse possible. Identify technical barriers, documentation gaps, interoperability challenges, and successful practices that can inform future research infrastructure, funding decisions, and public policy.
The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.
Hosted by [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/) | November 2–13, 2026
The inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on [research by Carnegie Mellon University](https://doi.org/10.1184/R1/7890488.v6), teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.
Participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.
Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.
Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.
[Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge](https://huggingface.co/spaces/CMU-OSPO/protostar-challenge-climate-risk-intelligence)
The CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be announced through the [Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/project-protostar).
Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or company building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.
We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to [protostar@orcaopen.org](mailto:protostar@orcaopen.org).
Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

title: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
body:
Automatic Speech Recognition • 0.8B • Updated • 464k • 93
[
](#introducing-anyspeechrecognizer-and-anydecisionmodel-open-models-for-speech-and-decisions-on-apple-platforms)
Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/anydecisionmodel.md)
Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.
Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.
In our [AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap](https://huggingface.co/blog/anylanguagemodel-1-0),
we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift.
With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases,
we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions:
familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.
Today we're announcing two packages:
[AnySpeechRecognizer](https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer)implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when.[AnyDecisionModel](https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel)answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama.
Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.
[
](#anyspeechrecognizer)
AnySpeechRecognizer
Computers have been transcribing speech for decades,
and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it.
Apple platforms already have an API for it.
macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer
,
Apple's new speech-to-text API.
You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber
and SpeechDetector
to an analyzer,
give it a file or a stream of audio buffers,
and read results from async sequences as they arrive.
AssetInventory
installs the models,
so your app decides when downloads happen.
It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:
- import Speech
+ import AnySpeechRecognizer
The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer
, SpeechTranscriber
, DictationTranscriber
,
SpeechDetector
, and AssetInventory
,
with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine.
If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough.
To use Parakeet instead,
change only how you create the transcriber:
let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
model: ParakeetSpeechModel(variant: .v3),
transcriptionOptions: [],
reportingOptions: [.volatileResults],
attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
)
The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer,
and reading results stay the same.
The [README](https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer#transcribe-a-file)
has a complete example
and [lists the differences](https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer#differences-from-apples-speech-framework)
from Apple's framework.
[
](#meet-the-models)
Meet the models
Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's [Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3).
It's a polyglot:
it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing,
so you don't pass a locale.
Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's [post-trained take on v3](https://huggingface.co/moondream/parakeet-ultra).
It was more accurate in most of our measurements.
Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's
[English-only Parakeet](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b).
All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.
Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model,
in [0.6B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf)
and [1.7B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf) sizes.
It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects,
including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover.
It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:
let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
model: QwenSpeechModel(variant: .large, language: Locale.Language(identifier: "yue")),
transcriptionOptions: [],
reportingOptions: [],
attributeOptions: []
)
Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.
To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel
for its configuration
and SpeechRecognitionExecutor
for one module's session.
The README includes a [small provider](https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer#custom-providers)
that reports placeholder text to help you get started.
[
](#core-ml-models-on-the-hub)
Core ML models on the Hub
To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:
| Model | Core ML conversion | Original checkpoint | License |
|---|---|---|---|
| Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3 |
|
[nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3)[mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/parakeet-ultra-coreml)[moondream/parakeet-ultra](https://huggingface.co/moondream/parakeet-ultra)[mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coreml)[nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b)[NVIDIA Open Model License](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/agreements/enterprise-software/nvidia-open-model-license/)[mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coreml)[Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hf)[mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coreml)[Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hf)[mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coreml)[nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2)[mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml](https://huggingface.co/mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coreml)[nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1)[NVIDIA Open Model License](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/agreements/enterprise-software/nvidia-open-model-license/)Each repository records its source checkpoint
and a checksum for every file,
and the package pins it to a fixed revision.
The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input,
which cuts live analysis time by about a third
at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate.
The repository also has the conversion workflows,
most of which follow FluidInference's [mobius](https://github.com/FluidInference/mobius) scripts,
and checks each conversion against the original model.
Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.
[
](#speaker-diarization)
Speaker diarization
When you transcribe a conversation,
you often want to know who said what.
That's speaker diarization,
and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it,
so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one.
SpeakerDiarizer
runs NVIDIA's
[Streaming Sortformer](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2)
on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber,
on the same timeline:
let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer(model: SortformerDiarizationModel())
if let request = try await AssetInventory.assetInstallationRequest(
supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) {
try await request.downloadAndInstall()
}
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [transcriber, diarizer])
The diarizer tracks up to four speakers,
even when they talk over each other.
A SpeakerTimeline
collects its results
and attributes each timed word to a speaker,
so you can print a transcript by speaker turn.
Like image support in AnyLanguageModel,
this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.
The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default.
You can also choose [v2.1](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1),
which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data
and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.
[
](#how-well-does-it-work)
How well does it work?
We measured the package with its hear
command-line tool
on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1.
Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:
| Transcriber | test-clean | test-other |
|---|---|---|
| Parakeet v3, file | 1.55% | 2.78% |
| Parakeet v3, live | 4.73% | 4.29% |
| Parakeet Ultra, file | 1.66% | 2.55% |
| Parakeet Ultra, live | 2.65% | 3.28% |
| Parakeet Unified, file | 1.43% | 2.19% |
| Parakeet Unified, live | 1.45% | 2.42% |
| Apple's transcriber, file | 2.12% | 3.97% |
Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.
These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets,
so measure with your own hardware and audio.
hear evaluate
works on your own files,
and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py
tool
[reproduces these measurements](https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer#accuracy-and-performance).
So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.
Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.
[
](#anydecisionmodel)
AnyDecisionModel
AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.
It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France; otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.
What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.
Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.
Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:
import AnyDecisionModel
enum Department: String, Choosable {
case billing, technical, sales
}
let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund."
let model = MLXDecisionModel(modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit")
let session = DecisionSession(model: model, state: .text(ticket))
let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?")
let team = try await session.choice("Which team?", from: Department.self)
let anger = try await session.score(
"How frustrated?",
levels: ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
)
urgent
is a Double
.
team
is a Choice<Department>
containing the selected case,
a probability for each option, and a confidence value.
anger
is a Score
containing the expected level,
a probability for each level, and a confidence value.
Because Department
conforms to Choosable
,
team.value
is a Departmen

title: Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
body:
Image-Text-to-Text • 1T • Updated • 1.08k • 10
[
](#welcome-le-chonk-mistral-large-4-on-hugging-face)
Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/mistral-large4.md)
Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.
The model is released in two official variants:
There are also [GGUFs](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org) created by [Unsloth](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF) and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).
Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!
[
](#table-of-contents)
Table of Contents
[
](#what-is-new-with-mistral-large-4)
What is new with Mistral Large 4
[Mistral Large 4](https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/mistral-large-4) combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a [Pixtral](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/model_doc/pixtral) vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.
You can find all the checkpoints in the [Mistral Large 4 collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/mistralai/mistral-large-4).
[
](#cybersecurity-capabilities)
Cybersecurity Capabilities
Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.
Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.
For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with [TRL you could fine-tune](#fine-tuning-with-trl) smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.
In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.
We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model,
[you can watch it here].
[
](#architecture)
Architecture
Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.
For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.
The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.
Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.
[
](#vision-encoder)
Vision encoder
Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.
[
](#benchmark-results)
Benchmark Results
Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.
On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.
Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.
Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:
- Artificial Analysis Cyber Index: ML4 ranks among the top five models globally on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities.
- Vulnerability reproduction and patching: It achieves 82%, the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation.
- Cybench: ML4 solves 93% of a suite of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions, demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems.
Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.
[
](#inference-support)
Inference Support
Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the [llama.cpp team](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF). We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.
[
](#transformers)
Transformers
The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM
, with AutoProcessor
preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low
, medium
, high
as reasoning effort. The default is high
, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort
: none
would still use high
.
To run the model, upgrade the transformers package
pip install --upgrade transformers
import os
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig
distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)
model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
model_id,
distributed_config=distributed_config,
)
# only text
text_messages = [
{
"role": "user",
"content": "Who are you?"
}
]
# text + image
multimodal_messages = [
{
"role": "user",
"content": [
{
"type": "image",
"image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg",
},
{
"type": "text",
"text": "How many cats are in the image?",
},
],
},
]
for messages in [text_messages, multimodal_messages]:
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
messages,
add_generation_prompt=True,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
return_tensors="pt",
reasoning_effort="medium",
).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
if int(os.environ["RANK"]) == 0:
print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))
You can run the script above by saving it in a python file script.py
and then run
torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py
[
](#vllm)
vLLM
vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this:
vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
--config-format mistral \
--load-format mistral \
--tensor-parallel-size 8 \
--decode-context-parallel-size 8 \
--enable-expert-parallel \
--dtype bfloat16 \
--max-model-len 131072 \
--max-num-seqs 16 \
--max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
--enable-prefix-caching \
--enforce-eager \
--mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0
Once the server is up and running, you can run the following.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
-d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}'
[
](#llamacpp)
Llama.cpp
Llama.cpp and [Llama App](https://llama.app/) already support Mistral Large 4.
You can install Llama App with the following command:
curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh
Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID:
llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K
[Here’s the repository](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF) with the quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and [this is the NVFP4 one](https://huggingface.co/ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4-GGUF), converted from the official NVFP4 repo.
Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.
You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out [the API reference](https://llama.app/docs/serve) for multimodality, tool calls and more.
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{
"messages": [
{"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
{"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
]
}'
You can run image-text inference as follows.
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
-d '{
"model": "muse-spark-open",
"messages": [
{
"role": "user",
"content": [
{
"type": "text",
"text": "What is in this image?"
},
{
"type": "image_url",
"image_url": {
"url": "data:image/png;base64,..."
}
}
]
}
],
"temperature": 0
}'
The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS
, Q2_K
, Q4_K_M
, NVFP4
, Q8_0
, and BF16
for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.
Running Q2_K
on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results:
- NVFP4: 32K context si

# Credit Saison achieves 954% ROI in a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot

Credit Saison’s ChatGPT Enterprise pilot delivered 954% ROI. See how leaders and employees helped turn the results into companywide adoption.

- [Transforming the company with assistive intelligence](#transforming-the-company-with-assistive-intelligence)

Credit Saison’s business centers on credit cards, with approximately 31.16 million cardholders. The company also operates financing and international businesses.

In September 2025, Credit Saison rolled out ChatGPT Enterprise to all employees. A pilot had exceeded its targets for time savings, giving the company the confidence to approve a companywide rollout just one month after the pilot ended. The rollout gave every employee access to AI at work. That shift began with the pilot.

## A pilot across the business delivers 954% ROI

With many employees in generalist roles, Credit Saison wanted to understand how AI could improve everyday work and deliver tangible results. Kazutoshi Ono, Credit Saison’s Senior Managing Executive Officer, CDO, and CTO, set a clear direction: “We won’t know until we really put it to work.”

Working with OpenAI, the company ran a ChatGPT Enterprise pilot with 315 participants for a little over a month, from late June to early August 2025. The group brought together volunteers, employees nominated by the project team, every executive including the president, and representatives from every department. It accounted for just under 10% of the company’s approximately 3,700 employees in Japan.

The results? Credit Saison reports a 954% return on investment (ROI) and 14 hours saved per employee each month, equivalent to approximately 169 hours annually. Both figures significantly exceeded the company’s initial targets of 500% ROI and 7.5 hours saved per person per month.

In a survey after the pilot, 75% of managers and 70% of nonmanagerial employees said they could not do without ChatGPT Enterprise. Approximately 80% of respondents in the legal department felt it improved their ability to do their jobs, while more than 80% in the IT department reported greater job satisfaction. The benefits extended beyond time savings to how employees felt about their capabilities and their work.

## Building adoption through employees and leaders

The pilot’s results reflected both the support in place and the people involved. Credit Saison’s CoE, which leads AI adoption, used a dedicated Slack channel to share successes and failures openly. Individual experiences became lessons the whole organization could use. OpenAI supported the effort with training for executives and practical workshops for beginners, helping participants apply AI to their work.

One highlight of the pilot was a custom GPT designed to simulate shareholder meetings. Using voice mode, employees could rehearse realistic, interactive exchanges that mirrored an actual shareholder meeting. The GPT drew particularly strong interest from Credit Saison’s senior leadership, and requests to share the prompt soon followed. This enthusiasm helped drive broader adoption of voice-based AI across the company.

Leadership’s engagement went beyond showing interest. Ono encouraged Katsumi Mizuno, Credit Saison’s representative director, executive president and COO, to lead by example: “It’s not enough to encourage employees to use it. Leaders need to use it regularly themselves.” Mizuno embraced this approach, creating his own custom GPT for company research and incorporating it into his daily work.

Executives were using AI themselves while employees were finding practical applications. Together, those efforts connected the decision to invest with everyday use, helping Credit Saison approve a companywide rollout within a month of completing the pilot.

## Three ways Credit Saison employees put ChatGPT to work

Across Credit Saison, employees are finding practical ways to incorporate ChatGPT into their everyday work, as these three use cases illustrate.

Retail sales: capturing daily team debriefs

- At counters in shopping malls and other locations, Credit Saison employees help customers sign up for and use credit cards. A custom GPT for store performance reporting helps these teams document their meetings at the end of each day.
- Using audio from the regular debrief, the GPT automatically summarizes each employee’s results, meeting notes, handover items for the next day, and areas to focus on. Teams keep running their meetings as usual while spending less time on documentation and compiling results. The familiar workflow makes it easy to adopt even for employees new to AI, and it is now used at every location.

Corporate sales: turning business challenges into better proposals

- Corporate sales teams use a custom GPT for company research to analyze customers. It helps them identify business challenges and assess where Credit Saison’s services could help.
- In one company analysis, it surfaced challenges that employees themselves had not fully recognized. By streamlining research and analysis before sales meetings, the GPT is helping teams improve the quality of their proposals.

Inside sales: giving new hires more opportunities to practice

- Inside sales teams needed to give less experienced employees more opportunities to practice without taking experienced colleagues away from selling.
- A custom GPT for prospect roleplay helps address that challenge. The AI plays the prospective customer, allowing employees to rehearse sales conversations by voice and receive feedback afterward. Teams value the chance to gain practical experience before speaking with real prospects.

**Results at a glance**

- 954% ROI achieved in a pilot with 315 participants
- 14 hours saved per participant per month, equivalent to approximately 169 hours a year
- 75% of managers and 70% of nonmanagerial employees said they could not do without ChatGPT Enterprise in the post-pilot survey
- Approximately 80% of legal department respondents reported an improved ability to do their jobs, and more than 80% of IT department respondents reported greater job satisfaction in the same survey
- A decision to roll out ChatGPT Enterprise companywide within one month of completing the pilot

## Transforming the company with assistive intelligence

Credit Saison sees AI transformation, or AX, as having three dimensions. The first, “Employee AX,” changes how employees work and enables things they could not have done without AI. That extends beyond the use of ChatGPT in sales. In engineering, for example, Credit Saison reports that Codex saves an average of 850 hours of work each month.

The company is also looking toward “Customer AX,” which focuses on improving customer experiences, user interfaces, and user experience, and “Corporate AX,” which rethinks organizational structures and roles around AI.

For Customer AX, Credit Saison is developing an AI call center in-house. Corporate AX is at an earlier stage, with the company identifying specific applications. It is also considering ChatGPT Work as part of its ambition to help employees focus on higher-value work. As AI takes on tasks autonomously, the company plans to take an even more careful approach to security, with the protection of customer information as a prerequisite.

> “We can’t stop at Employee AX. The challenge ahead is how far we can progress toward Corporate AX, redefining our organizational design and the division of responsibilities with AI as a starting point.”

—Kazutoshi Ono, Director, Senior Managing Executive Officer and CDO, CTO, Credit Saison

Credit Saison sees its relationship with OpenAI as important to that progress. By staying informed about the latest capabilities, it plans to evaluate how new technologies can improve its operations and create value for customers, then deploy them quickly once it has established that they can be used safely.

Leaders using AI themselves and employees finding ways to make it useful in everyday work have sustained adoption at Credit Saison. The next step is to build on those small, practical improvements and extend them to customer interactions and the way the organization works. The company aims to turn “Assistive Intelligence,” its approach to helping people do more, into transformation across the business.

title: Quoting Ted Sanders
body:
28th October 2026
In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:
Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra
[
[...]] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.
— [Ted Sanders](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50248124#50249160), explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions
