title: Thinking about the evolution of forward-deployed engineers over the last 24 months
body:
Published Time: 2026-10-28T21:08:40+00:00

Markdown Content:
The rapid pace of AI model development and technology maturity is changing the definition of forward-deployed engineering.

By [Kevin Shatzkamer](http://commandline.microsoft.com/author/kevin-shatzkamer)CVP, Forward Deployed Engineering, Microsoft[Website →](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kshatzka/)

2026.10.28

Forward-deployed engineering (FDE) isn’t a new term. Popularized by Palantir circa 2009, the concept of FDE was simple: apply a product model to custom solutions. Companies leverage empowered software engineers with direct access to users and data to discover what produces the desired customer outcome and then help the platform organization generalize those findings into durable products. The practice succeeded where traditional product requirements gathering failed—at the execution layer, where products and platforms intersect with operational realities. Product discovery, design, integration, and iteration happened against real operations rather than hypotheticals.

Being pedantic, I held onto this terminology for too long. I defined “forward-deployed engineer” as a job title, rooted in software engineering, that occupied a much different space than sales engineering or solutions architecture or consulting. I held onto the “hero FDE” who made technology work and made products better. I even held on to “deltas” (engineers on the frontlines) and “echoes” (domain deployment and adoption strategists) as a two-in-a-box execution structure, with both “gravel roads” revisited with “paved highways.” Much of this is still relevant, but I think there is clear nuance.

Customers needed this definition of the FDE when the core priority was to build foundational data layer integrations and analytics layers around a common semantic layer. Customer workflows were tacit, data was fragmented or sensitive, operational stakes were high, and users often couldn’t specify the right solution in advance. They still need this definition of the FDE, because there is much work to do to establish these foundations.

But like many other job functions, the rapid pace of AI model development and technology maturity is changing the definition of forward-deployed engineering. In fact, FDE is increasingly being used to describe capability—not just job function. Across model providers, cloud providers, and SaaS companies, forward-deployed engineering is getting institutionalized as a deployment operating system for high-ambiguity, high-value AI transformation. The signal here is that the hardest problems in AI have shifted from the model to deployment, with technical patterns showing up first, and being proven first, in production—then fed back to the tools and platforms. What I’ve observed:

1.   **The definition has widened.** What began as a customer-embedded, transformational software engineering role has increasingly become an end-to-end delivery function, spanning process redesign, production engineering, data science, governance, customer capability transfer, and measurable business outcomes.
2.   **“Engineer” remains non-negotiable.** The common denominator remains hands-on engineering embedded close to the customer’s real work. Execution still requires production code, systems architecture, integrations, evaluations, observability, security, and operational—not advisory—ownership. The feedback loops into product roadmaps (and models) are still critical.
3.   **The unit of deployment is a pod (or a squad, or a crew).** The “hero FDE” gives way to small, multi-disciplinary teams of domain experts, software engineers, data scientists, process engineers, and designers, augmented with coding assistants and deployment agents, deployment frameworks, and ecosystem partners.

![Image 1](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/fde-evolution-command-line-v3-1024x683.png)
## The mission, technology center, and responsibilities all changed

Over the last several years, we’ve seen the bottleneck in successful AI programs shift from use-case identification and prioritization to engineering talent. We saw PoCs get stuck at business validation or on security, observability, or compliance requirements. We also saw pilots stall before production scale and quality. The constraint moved from value determination to software development capacity. Then we saw rapid improvement in AI coding tools and the maturity of the agent harness, unblocking the path to production scale, quality, and trust. Now, we’re entering a new phase where the bottleneck becomes transformation capacity, or an organization’s ability to take an idea to production and measurable value, then to a scaled capability for the next team to reuse. Most organizations have never had to build this muscle, let alone build it at a pace that matches the AI technology curve. This is both a mindset shift for most organizations and a critical foundation to successful FDE projects: durable return on value.

As the constraints changed, the mission needed to change. The mission changed from:

*   Pre-2025: Make a platform work in a complex operating environment
*   Mid-2025: Close the identified AI prototype to production gap
*   **Today: Redesign and operate critical workflows around AI and agents**

And as the mission changed, so has the technical competency, tooling, and delivery responsibility. The technology center has changed from:

*   Mid-2025: Data integration, applications, and platforms to full-stack applications, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), APIs, and models
*   **Today: Multi-agent systems, the agentic harness,****MCP/tool use, evals, observability, identity, security, state management, cost/latency, CI/CD, and AI-assisted development**

The delivery responsibility has changed from:

*   Mid-2025: Build (and potentially operate) to prototype and then facilitate production handoff
*   **Today: Stable production development, post-launch tuning, governance, incident readiness, and capability transfer**

Success is measured through workflow impact, production adoption, and ROI. Success is also measured in the structural capability leave-behinds: an observable system, knowledge graphs, tuned models, eval frameworks, and trained experts.**At the conclusion of any FDE project, the goal is to transfer operating capability to the customer—not manufacture continuous dependence. This happens with three best-practices for FDE:**

1.   **Co-Engineering:** Similar to pair programming, for the entire engineering discipline (testing, CI/CD, continuous evaluation, written records of design decisions, code review)
2.   **Formalized transfer:** Knowledge transfer sessions running in parallel to final engineering sprints
3.   **Customer ready to operate**: The transfer is dependent on the customer’s ability to run it; a named customer owner, support team, and documented deployment and run-state processes

| **Dimension** | **Early formulation** | **Shift 1** | **Shift 2 (current)** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Mission** | Make a powerful platform work in a specific, complex institution | Close the prototype-to-production gap for generative AI | Redesign critical workflows for operational scale and production around AI and agents, with measurable outcomes |
| **Unit of delivery** | Individual FDE plus strategist; small customer team | Small specialist FDE team | Multidisciplinary pod: software/AI engineers, domain experts, TPM/delivery lead, security/governance, sometimes change/adoption specialists, augmented by AI agents |
| **Technical center** | Data integration, applications, infrastructure, proprietary platform | Full-stack applications, APIs, RAG, model integration | Multi-agent systems, MCP/tool use, evals, observability, identity, compliance, security, state management, cost/latency, CI/CD, and AI-assisted development |
| **Deployment responsibility** | Build and sometimes operate the solution | Prototype through production handoff | Stable production, post-launch tuning, governance, incident readiness, and capability transfer |

### A new working definition of FDE

A quick recap of the changes:

*   **Early FDE:** Put an unusually capable engineer next to a difficult customer problem and connect field reality to a reusable platform
*   **Mid-2025 FDE:** Use that engineer to bridge the widening gap between an impressive AI prototype and production quality, scale, and adoption
*   **Today FDE:** Deploy an AI-accelerated, multidisciplinary capability that discovers the right business problem, redesigns the workflow, builds and governs the production system, proves measurable value, changes the product roadmap, and leaves the customer stronger

This leads me to a single way of expressing FDE when asked in the future: a small, multidisciplinary team deployed directly against a measurable business outcome, combining product, engineering, AI, data, operations, and transformation capabilities to move an AI opportunity from problem identification to production and measurable value.

# Evernote turns AI-driven discovery into paid subscriptions

Evernote used ChatGPT Ads to reach people working with AI and followed new users from free trial to first subscription payment.

## Giving new users a reason to start

[Evernote ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://evernote.com/) helps people capture, organize, and retrieve the knowledge they build over time. For longtime users, that collection of notes and ideas becomes a “second brain,” growing more useful as they add to it.

> “The challenge is helping new users see enough value to become paying customers. We need to show people what Evernote can do for them and give them a clear reason to start using it.”

– Claudio Di Blasi, Data Analyst at Bending Spoons

That challenge is also a question of relevance. Many people already know Evernote by name, but may not know how the product has evolved. As it develops AI capabilities, the company wants to show prospective users how its approach to capturing and organizing knowledge fits the way they work today.

ChatGPT Ads offered a way to introduce that evolving product to people already using AI to create and work with information.

## Connecting AI workflows with a place to keep knowledge

Evernote’s starting point was a practical need: keeping information useful after it has been created. People working with conversations, notes, and transcriptions may want a place to organize that material and find it again. The team saw a natural role for Evernote in that workflow.

Its initial ads highlighted Evernote as a place to save and organize notes and transcriptions, drawing on messaging from strong-performing search campaigns. That gave the team a practical starting point for testing how those use cases resonated in ChatGPT.

Ads directed people to Evernote’s website, including its homepage, with conversion campaigns optimized for new-account registrations. Using its own web analytics and subscription records, Evernote could follow that initial interest through to a free trial and a first subscription payment.

## Seeing interest carry through to subscription

Evernote built its core campaigns—its primary group of ChatGPT Ads campaigns—around a single product feature. In the first month, around 25% of desktop visits from those campaigns resulted in a new account, giving the team an early indication that people were willing to try the product.²

Evernote also saw promise in the step that mattered most to its subscription business. New users from those same campaigns converted from free trial to paid subscription at a rate about 10–20% higher than the historical average earlier this year across its paid acquisition channels.¹ For a team focused on helping new users discover enough value to subscribe, that was a meaningful early finding.

Evernote is treating those first-month results as encouraging and directional while it tests whether the performance can hold as the channel grows.

## Helping more users discover where Evernote fits

Evernote’s next step is to make the connection between its product and AI workflows more tangible. The team plans to explore additional use cases and develop creative and dedicated landing pages that show people how Evernote can fit into their own work.

> “We saw a natural fit between people using ChatGPT and what Evernote offers. What stood out in the early results was how well new users converted to paid subscriptions. For us, that was an encouraging sign that we were reaching people who found real value in the product.”

– Claudio Di Blasi, Data Analyst at Bending Spoons

Source: Evernote’s first-party web analytics and subscription records. Evernote attributed a new account to ChatGPT Ads when the user’s first tagged visit came from a ChatGPT ad click.

¹ Trial-to-paid conversion. Evernote compared the share of free trials that reached a first subscription payment. Trials from the featured ChatGPT Ads campaigns started August 28–September 12, 2026. Trials in the historical paid-acquisition benchmark started March–August 2026. The comparison does not establish incremental lift.

² Desktop registration. Evernote divided new accounts from the featured campaigns by desktop visits from those campaigns during September 14–28, 2026.

title: Gemini 4 Carbon: Our next frontier model
body:
Gemini 4 Carbon: our next frontier model
Today, we’re announcing the next frontier model: Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
Carbon ranks #1 on the recently updated v5.0 of [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/artificial-analysis-intelligence-index) at 59. It shows significant gains across coding and agentic tasks as well as across key capabilities critical for cybersecurity defense, landing a firm lead in SEC-bench Pro (88.2%) for finding vulnerabilities, ExploitGym (54.8%) for exploitation, and CWE-bench (71.0%) for patching. On internal benchmarks, Carbon drives a strong uplift in generating secure code, and in live coding environments with our own teams it shows reduced misalignment and fabrication rates.
Building on [Gemini 4 Argon](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/introducing-gemini-4-argon/), which was launched two weeks ago, Carbon illustrates the pace at which we’re pushing the frontier forward. Our researchers and models are working hand in hand to advance capabilities faster, while strengthening our safeguards in tandem.
We're taking a deliberate approach to rollout and are actively engaged in the U.S. government’s voluntary process for pre-release model testing. Starting this week, we will make Carbon available to a subset of cyber defenders and will gradually phase access to additional trusted partners through our [Fairwind Program](https://deepmind.google/fairwind-program/). We’re continuing to gather feedback and iterate on guardrails before making Carbon available to developers, businesses, and consumers via our product surfaces as soon as possible.
Gemini 4 Carbon will launch at the same introductory price
[1](#footnote-1)
as Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced at 95% off input token price.
Improving coding and reasoning for challenging, long-horizon tasks
Designed to take on much harder, long-horizon engineering problems, Carbon is built for sustained agentic workflows. Internally, our teams have seen Carbon run for days to persist through dead ends to tackle complex, multi-step engineering tasks like root-causing and patching subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.
Building on user feedback, we focused on improving model performance across a variety of domains, including coding, agentic, and scientific tasks, as well as full-stack web development and multimodal understanding. With improved quality of output and artifacts in web development, Carbon jumps +89 elo points to land at #4 (1768) on [WebDev Arena](https://arena.ai/leaderboard/code/webdev).
State-of-the-art cybersecurity performance to help build secure systems
Gemini 4 Carbon delivers a significant leap in cybersecurity capabilities. It achieves state-of-the-art performance across the cybersecurity defense lifecycle — vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation.
Our teams are already seeing strong gains in cyberdefense. On internal benchmarks, Carbon achieves more than 2x uplift in success rate for generating secure code over Argon. As another example, the Chrome team has reported that Carbon performed more than 10X better than another lab's large frontier model when generating high quality patches. Wiz, our leading Cloud security platform, also observes Carbon leading on benchmarks for web penetration testing, a core capability for [Wiz's Scan for Good](https://www.wiz.io/blog/scan-for-good-critical-ai-exposures) initiative.
Carbon excels across key external benchmarks (evaluated without guardrails):
- Finding real vulnerabilities: Core to cybersecurity defense is finding real vulnerabilities. Carbon achieves a state-of-the-art 88.2% on
[SEC-bench Pro](https://sec-bench.github.io/), autonomously uncovering complex flaws buried in real-world software.
- Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate first or remediate at all, cyber defenders increasingly rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. Carbon sets a new state-of-the-art on the popular exploitation benchmark
[ExploitGym](https://github.com/sunblaze-ucb/exploitgym)(54.8%).
- Patching at the root cause: Ultimately after identifying the vulnerabilities, fixing the root cause is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Carbon reaches 71.0% on Collinear’s
[CWE-bench](https://cwe-bench.com/#leaderboard), turning validated findings directly into working code fixes.
Advancing frontier model safety & security
Gemini 4 Carbon builds on the same multi-layered safety and security stack of Argon — combining model training, real-time misuse defenses, prompt-injection resilience, and chain-of-thought monitoring. In particular, we made significant strides in model alignment with Argon, and reported its propensities to behave in an aligned way in our [Safety and Security report](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_safety_report.pdf). With Carbon, we challenged ourselves to go a step further on alignment, and trained the model to respond to complex or high-pressure tasks in the right way.
- Reducing shortcuts and loophole exploitation: With Carbon, we further mitigated shortcut attempts in training while ensuring high-quality coding performance. Carbon reduced successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 to 0.0%, with attempts to cheat dropping to 0.4% — all while improving overall accuracy. In live coding environments with our internal teams, we observed that high-severity misalignment alerts dropped by almost 80%.
- Greater transparency and honesty: In our internal testing, Carbon cuts unsupported claims by approximately 2x over Argon. It puts methodological caveats directly into the deliverable or withholds blocked actions with a clear list of what remains required, rather than fabricating or hedging around missing evidence.
- Improved collaboration with the user in the face of ambiguity: Rather than guessing or forcing a path forward, Carbon retrieves the relevant sources and surfaces discrepancies to the user before acting — as a result, users should observe a much better collaborative experience with Carbon.
- Following through without overstepping: Carbon simultaneously reduced overreach by 26% and under-service by 29% resulting in much more reliable execution of multi-step plans end-to-end while respecting project constraints and staying strictly within scope.
- Resisting prompt injection: While Argon previously led the Gray Swan’s Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) Benchmark in prompt injection resistance with a very low 0.7% attack success rate, Carbon achieves 0.0% — resisting every evaluated attack attempt.
Coming soon to developers, businesses, and consumers
Pushing the frontier forward requires moving fast while remaining deliberate about deployment. With Gemini 4 Carbon, our goal is to deliver meaningful leaps in software engineering and cybersecurity defense without compromising on safety or reliability. We’re eager to see how the initial cohort of cyber defenders use this model and we look forward to bringing Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers soon.

title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
body:
28th October 2026 - Link Blog
[GitHub Octoverse 2026](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-commits-pushes-reach-new-highs-in-2026-as-developers-build-with-agents/). I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:
This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.
The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The [methodology section](https://github.blog/news-insights/octoverse/octoverse-commits-pushes-reach-new-highs-in-2026-as-developers-build-with-agents/#h-methodology) includes notes about how they did this:
Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]
Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]
Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

title: Thin, Light and Built for Everything: NVIDIA RTX Spark Windows Laptops Gain New Models, Agent Tools and Games
body:
[NVIDIA RTX Spark](https://nvidianews.nvidia.com/news/nvidia-rtx-spark-pcs-available-today-a-new-beginning-for-windows-pcs) powers thin and light laptops built for everything that developers, creators and gamers do.
RTX Spark laptops are now available from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. These powerful systems combine an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU in a single superchip with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That puts the NVIDIA CUDA platform, RTX graphics and the capabilities of a personal AI supercomputer inside premium Windows laptops built to go anywhere.
New and expected RTX Spark updates, coming soon, include:
- NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe, an open weight speech model for transcription, speaker attribution and translation is available on RTX Spark.
- The LFM3 family of open models with day-zero support.
- Resource management controls in NVIDIA App to allocate GPU resources between foreground apps and background agents.
- Phantom Blade Zero, S-GAME’s highly-anticipated action role-playing game, launches with ray tracing and NVIDIA DLSS 4.5.
- Experience Minecraft with path tracing and DLSS with RTX Remix1.6, available now for RTX Spark.
Turn Recorded Audio Into Useful Information With NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe
Introduced today, [NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B) is a new, open weight speech model that turns recorded conversations into useful information. Instead of needing multiple models for transcription, speaker labels and translation, developers can use one promptable model that handles all three, plus questions about the audio. It transcribes 40 languages, including seven Indic languages.
Developers guide the model with plain-language prompts. For example, for a single recorded meeting, users can ask it to:
- “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.”
- “Translate this audio into English.”
- “List what decisions were made in this meeting.”
Prompts can also include product terms and formatting conventions, which helps the model handle specialized vocabulary in fields like healthcare, financial services and customer service. Because the weights are open, developers can choose where audio is processed, from a desktop to the cloud.
Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks No. 1 on the [Hugging Face Open ASR](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_asr_leaderboard) and No. 2 among open weight models on Artificial Analysis — delivering leading accuracy with approximately 4.3 billion active parameters, 80% fewer than the No. 1 open weight model, making high-quality, intelligent transcription more practical on local hardware.
It’s available today on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B). Quantized versions are coming soon, so developers can run Transcribe locally onNVIDIA RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, Jetson AGX Thor devices or scale up on NVIDIA Blackwell data center GPUs. NVFP4 versions will be deployable through NeMo-Speech.cpp or vLLM.
Learn more in the [NVIDIA technical blog](https://huggingface.co/blog/nvidia/nemotron-transcribe-granary/).
Control How Agents and PC Apps Share GPU Resources
On RTX Spark, users can have long-running agents working alongside their favorite applications. Both share the system’s GPU compute, and the right balance of resources depends on what matters to users at that moment.
With the new resource management feature in [NVIDIA App](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/software/nvidia-app/), users can now choose how GPU resources are shared. They can prioritize their foreground app for the best performance, or give their background-running agent more resources to get work done faster.
Access control resource sharing from System > Advanced in the NVIDIA App. This feature requires hardware-accelerated GPU scheduling to be enabled in Windows Settings.
Liquid AI: One Model Family, Many Ways to Work
Liquid AI’s [LFM3](https://huggingface.co/collections/LiquidAI/lfm3) provides a new generation of Liquid Foundation Models designed for specialized tasks. The family spans text, vision, audio, omni and decision models built on one shared backbone, with base and post-trained models available as open weights. The models are compact and fast: Liquid AI’s new 1.7-billion-parameter base model outperforms its previous 2.6-billion-parameter base model.
These models support local workflows such as agents running in Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenClaw to triage inboxes and manage calendars, read documents and app screens, transcribe and translate speech, answer spoken questions about handwritten math, and route support tickets or voice requests.
Developers can run LFM3 models on RTX Spark with native support through llama.cpp and vLLM, and fine-tune the models locally.
‘Phantom Blade Zero’ Launches With DLSS 4.5
S-GAME’s [Phantom Blade Zero](https://pbz.s-game.com/en-US/) launches tonight, Oct. 28, at 7 p.m. PT on [Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/4115450/Phantom_Blade_Zero/) and the [Epic Games Store](https://store.epicgames.com/p/phantom-blade-zero-e78a35?lang=en-US). Players can take on the role of Soul, a swordsman framed for his master’s murder, as he travels the martial world to uncover a conspiracy.
NVIDIA worked with S-GAME Studio and S-GAME Publishing to add ray-traced effects to the title. On RTX Spark laptops and GeForce RTX GPU-powered PCs, ray tracing adds more accurate bounced lighting, detailed reflections and realistic shadows on foliage and terrain. The NVIDIA DLSS Dynamic Multi Frame Generation feature boosts frame rates with up to 6x frame generation, or adjusts the multiplier on the fly to hit a player’s target frame rate.
Read more on [GeForce.com](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/phantom-blade-zero-path-tracing-dlss-4-5-ray-reconstruction).
RTX Remix Breathes New Life Into Classics
[NVIDIA RTX Remix](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/rtx-remix/), the modding platform for remastering classic games with path tracing and DLSS, released version 1.6 last week. This update brought RTX Remix to the world’s largest gaming community: Minecraft. Both creators and players can render [Minecraft Java Edition 1.21.1 through RTX Remix](https://github.com/NVIDIAGameWorks/rtx-remix-minecraft/releases/tag/v0.1.0) with DLSS-accelerated path tracing and take full advantage of realistic lighting and materials in their future creations.
The update also adds DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering, up to 6x Multi Frame Generation, native RTX Spark support and agent-assisted workflows. Starting today, those upgrades come to [Portal with RTX](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2012840/Portal_with_RTX/) and the [Half-Life 2 RTX](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2477290/HalfLife_2_RTX/) demo. Both now support RTX Spark, with DLSS 3D-Guided Neural Rendering for more lifelike lighting and materials, a new Performance Mode for DLSS Frame Generation and new options that speed up path tracing.
RTX Remix 1.6 also makes AI-powered modding simpler. A redesigned ComfyUI workflow lets modders generate physically based materials directly inside RTX Remix, with no application programming interface setup, batch processing for full projects and presets for less technical creators. Plus, with NVIDIA agent skills, compatible AI agents can work directly with RTX Remix to help speed up remastering projects.
Learn more in the [RTX Remix blog](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce/news/remix-1-6-dlss-5-comfyui-2-0-minecraft-rtx-beta).
RTX Spark Laptops: Beautifully Designed, Built for Everything
RTX Spark laptops come in a range of designs, so users can choose one that fits how they work and play. Options include different screen sizes, colors, touchscreens, pen support and two-in-one convertibles. RTX Spark laptops are as thin as 14mm and as light as three pounds, with all-day battery life.
Such slim designs are possible because RTX Spark places the GPU, CPU and up to 128GB of unified memory on one power-efficient superchip. Creative projects and AI models draw from the same memory pool, so a laptop can take on work that used to call for a desktop workstation, even when unplugged.
Here’s what this means for:
- AI developers: Run models and agents locally on
[NVIDIA CUDA](https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda)— the same platform that powers AI in the cloud — with a path to deploy across more than 150 million NVIDIA RTX AI PCs and NVIDIA GPUs in the cloud. - Creators: RTX Spark can edit camera native 4:2:2 video and render 3D scenes of up to 90GB. Adobe Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases.
- Gamers: Hundreds of games run on RTX Spark, with NVIDIA DLSS, ray tracing, Reflex and G-SYNC delivering sharper visuals and smoother, more responsive gameplay.
RTX Spark laptops are available now from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI, starting at $2,599, with 128GB configurations on shelves. Find a laptop on the [RTX Spark product page](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/products/rtx-spark/).
#ICYMI: More Updates From NVIDIA Local AI
🦆Microducks learn to walk with help from RTX Spark: During the GTC Berlin keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed how AI agents running on RTX Spark can help train [Hugging Face’s Microduck robot](https://pollen-robotics.com/microduck/). A new NVIDIA technical blog walks through the workflow: Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt plan an obstacle course on RTX Spark, Astra builds the 3D assets, NVIDIA Isaac Lab trains the navigation policy and RTX Spark validates it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Watch the [demo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VvJai6HGfyE) and try the [playbook](http://build.nvidia.com/rtx-spark).
⚡[NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-E4B-4GB/) is now available, enabling natural conversations and multistep agent tasks with as little as 4GB of memory. The model powers local voice assistants, game characters and embedded interfaces on RTX Spark, DGX Spark, GeForce RTX GPUs and NVIDIA Jetson devices. It supports llama.cpp, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and LM Studio, and works with Hermes and OpenClaw. For more demanding agent workloads, [Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Bolt-74B-A9B-24GB) is designed to run local agents on RTX Spark.
🖼️Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6-billion-parameter open weights model that lets users generate and edit images locally. [NVIDIA-optimized versions](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/local-ai-gtc-rtx-dgx-spark-station-sync/) run on RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM. Developers can also fine-tune the model on RTX Spark using an [NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel recipe](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Automodel/blob/main/docs/model-coverage/diffusion/black-forest-labs/flux3-image-klein.mdx) to customize it for specific creative workflows.
🖥️NVIDIA DGX Spark 64GB is now available to purchase from manufacturer partners, giving developers and researchers another way to build and run AI locally. Powered by the GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip, it combines 64GB of unified memory with DGX OS and the NVIDIA AI software stack for agent development, inference and fine-tuning. [Learn more and explore purchase options](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/local-ai-dgx-spark-64gb-sync/).
Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on [X](https://x.com/NVIDIARTXSpark), [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/nvidiartxspark/), [TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@nvidiartxspark) and [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/NVIDIARTXSpark) — and stay informed by subscribing to the [NVIDIA Local AI newsletter](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/ai-on-rtx/?modal=subscribe-ai). Follow NVIDIA Workstation on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/showcase/3761136/) and[ X](https://x.com/NVIDIAworkstatn).
See [notice](https://www.nvidia.com/en-eu/about-nvidia/terms-of-service/) regarding software product information.

title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
body:
Automatic Speech Recognition • 34B • Updated • 4.28k • 314
[
](#nvidia-nemotron-35-transcribe-and-granary-v2-intelligent-multilingual-transcription-you-can-prompt-and-adapt)
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
[Enterprise + Article](/blog)
[
](#one-open-model-for-multilingual-transcription-speaker-attribution-translation-and-audio-qa-with-top-leaderboard-results-plus-the-open-granary-v2-data-pipeline-and-fine-tuning-recipes-to-adapt-it)
One open model for multilingual transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio Q&A, with top leaderboard results, plus the open Granary v2 data pipeline and fine-tuning recipes to adapt it.
A transcript can capture every spoken word and still leave users or applications wondering who said what, how to translate it, or how to format domain-specific jargon. Multilingual calls, fast-paced meetings, and medical dictation each need different output: a translation, speaker labels, or correctly spelled medical terms.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text, now available on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B) and [ModelScope](https://modelscope.ai/collections/nv-community/Nemotron-35-Transcribe). It brings transcription, speaker attribution (diarization), translation, and audio question answering into one checkpoint: it transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers. Developers can guide output with natural language, choose where their audio is processed, and adapt recognition to domain vocabulary and accents.
Transcribe is first among open-weight models on the [Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_asr_leaderboard) for English and sits on [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text/non-streaming?error-rate=word-error-rate-vs-active-size)’s accuracy–active-parameter frontier. For speaker attribution, it posts the lowest error rate on [David AI’s 21-language diarization leaderboard](https://research.withdavid.ai/blog/dai-asr-i18n#leaderboard) and ranks first in [VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison](https://voicearena.com/diarization-bench/methodology). Quantized versions are coming soon, so you can run Transcribe locally on your RTX Spark, DGX Spark, or Jetson AGX Thor—or scale up on Blackwell data-center GPUs.
Granary v2’s multilingual data (available on [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Granary-v2) and [ModelScope](https://modelscope.ai/datasets/nv-community/Granary-v2)) and reusable curation pipeline, together with [NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/tutorials/speechlm2/finetuning/README.md), extend prompt-level control to training: developers can define the written form they need and adapt the model to the speech their applications encounter. In a [medical case study](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/examples/speechlm2/finetuning/docs/medical-asr-synthetic-data.md), fine-tuning cut word error rate (WER) on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt.
[
](#guide-transcription-and-analysis-with-natural-language)
Guide transcription and analysis with natural language
The same checkpoint can turn one meeting recording into different outputs, depending on the instruction:
- “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.”
- “Translate this audio into English.”
- “What decisions were made in this meeting?”
Experience the model in action in the video below, where it tackles a classic scene from the 1940 screwball comedy His Girl Friday—a film famous for its rapid-fire, heavily overlapping dialogue.
Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe captions a scene from His Girl Friday (1940) and labels speakers, including overlapping dialogue.
For unfamiliar terms, try context before training. In a healthcare setting, for example:
Transcribe this medical discussion in the original language. Possible terms: HbA1c, metformin. Use these terms only when supported by the audio. Preserve standard medical spelling and write numbers in conventional written form.
The [model card](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B) has recommended presets, including reasoning for audio questions, plus the full prompt guide and a task-by-language matrix: language support differs by task, and audio question answering is trained in English. Word-level timestamps are also supported. As with any speech model, spot-check names, speaker changes, and answers against the recording.
From live classes to lasting lessons. Agora, whose real-time voice and video platform powers live conversations in apps, used word-level timestamps in a classroom demo: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe turns a recorded class into a transcript shown alongside the replay, so students can see what was said and when. [Agora’s blog](https://www.agora.io/en/blog/how-live-teaching-can-become-a-lasting-learning-resource/) walks through how they built it.
[
](#leaderboard-wins-from-transcription-to-speaker-attribution)
Leaderboard wins from transcription to speaker attribution
Among open-weight models, Transcribe leads on what was said; on who said it, it tops two speaker-attribution benchmarks outright.
Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard. The leaderboard measures transcription accuracy as word error rate (WER) on public test sets, in three tracks:
- English: first among open-weight models at 5.33% average WER (Figure 1).
- Multilingual: 4.62% mean WER across seven languages, the lowest among evaluated open-weight models in the model card’s Open ASR comparison.
- Long-form: 10.98% mean WER, also the lowest in that comparison.
Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the [Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard](https://huggingface.co/spaces/hf-audio/open_asr_leaderboard) (English) at 5.33% average WER, with API models excluded. Lower WER means fewer transcription errors.
Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Text Leaderboard. Artificial Analysis independently ranks speech-to-text models by AA-WER, its word error rate index. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ties for first among open-weight models at 2.8% AA-WER, with about 4B active parameters versus 24B for the model it ties. On AA-AgentTalk, the held-out voice-agent speech set that makes up 50% of the AA-WER index, Transcribe scores 1.8% WER, versus 2.3% for the next-best open-weight model. Transcribe pairs its speech encoder with a hybrid Mamba–Transformer mixture-of-experts language model, so only about 4B of its 30B parameters are active per token. That puts it on [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text/non-streaming)’s open-weight Pareto frontier of accuracy versus active parameters. On AA’s all-model chart, it ranks ahead of several widely used proprietary speech APIs.
Figure 2. [Leading AA accuracy](https://artificialanalysis.ai/speech-to-text/non-streaming) at about one-sixth the active parameters: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe achieves 2.80% AA-WER with approximately 4B active parameters.
Speaker attribution across languages and overlap. Sortformer speaker cues reach the language model with the acoustic features, so Transcribe can tag each turn during generation instead of relying solely on a later step to attach speakers to words.
David AI DAI-ASR-I18N Leaderboard. On [David AI’s DAI-ASR-I18N combined transcription-and-speaker-attribution track](https://research.withdavid.ai/blog/dai-asr-i18n#leaderboard), Transcribe ranks first among evaluated open-weight models and second overall. On the benchmark’s diarization track, which scores who spoke when across 21 languages, it has the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems tested, slightly ahead of NVIDIA’s dedicated [Nemotron 3 Diarization](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization) model.
Figure 3. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots on [David AI’s multilingual diarization leaderboard](https://research.withdavid.ai/blog/dai-asr-i18n#leaderboard): Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe posts the lowest overall diarization error rate (DER), 18.26% across 21 languages, followed by [Nemotron 3 Diarization](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization) at 18.38%. DER measures speaker-time errors; lower is better.
VoiceArena Diarization-Bench. On [VoiceArena’s English full-session benchmark](https://voicearena.com/diarization-bench), Transcribe posts the lowest concatenated minimum-permutation WER (cpWER) of 14 systems and ranks first in both in-person and online settings. It also drops the fewest words: deletions are 8.32% of reference words, versus a median of about 31%.
Figure 4. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots in [VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison](https://voicearena.com/diarization-bench): Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe leads at 32.4% cpWER, followed by NVIDIA Multitalker Parakeet with Nemotron 3 Diarization at 34.2%. Diarization-Bench v1 covers English full sessions, overlapping speech and 2–8 speakers. cpWER counts word errors after matching speaker labels; lower is better.
More evaluations. Ocular AI’s Converse-STT evaluation ranks Transcribe the top open model. Josh Talks’ [Voice of India](https://voiceofindia.ai) leaderboard reports Transcribe’s results across Indian languages.
High-throughput transcription. In benchmarking, Transcribe processed 100 hours of audio in under three minutes on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, using the forthcoming NVFP4 quantized version. Results were measured on 30-second clips at high concurrency.
Serve the available checkpoint with [vLLM](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/docs/source/speechlm2/vllm_serving.rst) today. Local deployment with [NeMo-Speech.cpp](https://github.com/NVIDIA/NeMo-Speech.cpp) is coming soon alongside the quantized versions. Transcribe is built for recorded audio, not live streaming.
Specialized recordings can still call for adaptation to domain vocabulary and transcript conventions. Granary v2 and NeMo Speech fine-tuning address that, starting with the data behind Transcribe.
[
](#granary-v2-the-open-data-curation-pipeline-behind-transcribe)
Granary v2: The open data curation pipeline behind Transcribe
A promptable speech model requires training data with unambiguous formatting targets. [Granary v2](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Granary-v2) is part of the [Nemotron speech collection](https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-speech) on Hugging Face and [ModelScope](https://modelscope.ai/collections/nv-community/Nemotron-Speech). Built with [NVIDIA NeMo Curator](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Curator), its reusable pipeline prepared multilingual speech used in Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe’s training, producing aligned transcript variants, task labels, and inspectable quality metadata. The public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in [Granary v1](https://huggingface.co/datasets/nvidia/Granary). These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.
Granary v2 generates three transcript forms for each recording (Table 1), the same verbatim and clean styles developers can request from Transcribe with a prompt. Beyond transcription, the pipeline produces short audio captions, code-switching restoration of loanwords, speech-grounded Q&A pairs, contextual ASR biasing terms, and translations with automatic quality scores.

| Text-normalized, verbatim | I paid, uh, twenty-five euros. |
| Inverse text normalization, with disfluencies | I paid, uh, €25. |
| Inverse text normalization, without disfluencies | I paid €25. |

title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
body:
The October inflection point for vibe game development
28th October 2026
I’ve written before about how November 2025 was [an inflection point for coding agents](https://simonwillison.net/tags/november-2025-inflection/)—the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we’ve reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it’s for vibe coding computer games.
[Tree Appreciator](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#tree-appreciator)[Emberwick](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#emberwick)[Battle Drones](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#battle-drones)[Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#pumpkin-farmer-aka-quarter-sun-cove)[Four times as insulting](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#four-times-as-insulting)[What happens if someone actually puts the work in?](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#what-happens-if-someone-actually-puts-the-work-in-)[You should build a game!](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/28/vibe-game-development/#you-should-build-a-game-)
Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:
- 3D modeling
- Music generation (see
[Scrimshaw Jukebox](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/6/scrimshaw-jukebox/)) - Game design (!)
That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in [my previous experiments](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Aug/7/moonlight-mayhem/). The challenge has been getting to a game that’s actually fun to play.
Game design is a deep subject area. I won’t pretend to be well versed in it—I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn’t think the models could do it.
Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun”... [and it did](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/20/battledrones/#v4-the-fun-update).
In the past few weeks I’ve vibe coded (in the [classic sense of the term](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Mar/19/vibe-coding/)—no looking at the code at all) four games that I’ve genuinely enjoyed playing.
I attended [Foo Camp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foo_Camp) in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn’t exist without AI assistance.
I haven’t done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn’t quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn’t match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.
Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.
Tree Appreciator
The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is [Tree Appreciator](https://tools.simonwillison.net/tree-appreciator). I used the regular Claude chat interface for this—it didn’t even need Claude Code.
I built this on a whim while we were driving along [Skyline Boulevard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_Route_35) looking at trees. My prompt was:
Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.
I’ve found that telling models to use [three.js](https://threejs.org/) works really well. Claude doesn’t have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.
This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all—I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can [play that here](https://tools.simonwillison.net/tree-appreciator). Here’s [the chat transcript](https://claude.ai/share/ee7de555-f85c-4ff0-96cb-d51ed5e479e9) that built it.
It’s pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a “herbarium” provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.
Emberwick
This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:
Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening
Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great
Here’s [that first version](https://simonw.github.io/emberwick/v01/emberwick.html). It worked really well!
I was inspired to increase my ambitions:
Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that
Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village
Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll
Here’s [that version](https://simonw.github.io/emberwick/v02/emberwick.html).
When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:
Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good
We’re back to prompts like “make it really good” here! Asking for a plot that “isn’t too cliche” seemed to work too—it’s a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.
Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems—things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.
Here’s [that final game](https://simonw.github.io/emberwick/v11/emberwick.html). It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.
There’s even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.
Once it was all working (and I’d iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I’m somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game—the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog—came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just “it’s a fantasy village and there’s a troll asleep in a cave”.
Here’s [the full shared Claude chat](https://claude.ai/share/840e0bc0-a68e-4894-8eec-8f83bd6ade26) in which I built this game.
I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here’s [the transcript](https://chatgpt.com/share/6ae176eb-1eac-83e8-ae54-729281fbdb70) and [the finished game](https://lantern-hollow-rpg.simonw.chatgpt.site) for comparison. It looks great, but I don’t think it plays nearly as well.
Battle Drones
This is by far my most successful project, which I [wrote about last week](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/20/battledrones/). It’s a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four [as of Saturday](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/24/battledrones/)) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.
This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what “fun” is.
The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn’t great to play.
I prompted Opus 5.5 to “Make it a LOT more fun” and then later to “Port this game to three.js” and the game was transformed. There’s a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in [my write-up](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/20/battledrones/).
Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of “mutators” that add variants of the rules.
It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here’s a replay of [Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna](https://simonw.github.io/battledrones/v11/?replay=battles/showcase/2026-10-14-frostbite-42-claude-haiku-5.5-vs-gpt-6-luna.json):
Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5’s ability to create 3D models. This page lets you [browse all of the models in the game](https://simonw.github.io/battledrones/models.html).
I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released [Panache](https://github.com/menufactory43/panache/) ([screenshots here](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/21/panache/)), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!
Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
I live in [Half Moon Bay, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_Moon_Bay,_California), home of the annual [Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_Moon_Bay_Art_and_Pumpkin_Festival), which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.
I decided to try building a game that wasn’t just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.
I called it “Quarter Sun Cove”.
I’m still iterating on this project, but it’s shaping up quite nicely. It’s a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.
Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.
It’s absurdly cute.
You can [play the latest version here](https://simonw.github.io/pumpkin-farmer/). I’m not convinced by the game mechanics yet—it’s actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.
Here’s the [initial brainstorming session](https://claude.ai/code/cshk_01V63sUyETi6UNbGUyjSYbHd13Mq93U6ty824Ha4eAxF4i), which resulted in [this spec file](https://github.com/simonw/pumpkin-farmer/blob/cdcf12083f403946b5c2a9e04312bbb42359bf58/SPEC.md). Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.
I told Claude to “surprise and delight the user frequently” and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.
This isn’t my best game yet—it’s not as fun to play as Battle Drones—but it represents the

# OpenAI and ServiceNow expand partnership across enterprise workflows

ServiceNow will bring OpenAI models and agents into workflows from development to security, and expand ChatGPT Work and Codex to employees.

Working with ServiceNow through ChatGPT

OpenAI and ServiceNow are expanding our partnership to bring more of our models and agents into ServiceNow products and connect ServiceNow workflows with ChatGPT and Codex. Together, we’re making it easier for businesses to build applications, resolve IT requests and address security issues using AI.

The expansion builds on our partnership [announced](https://openai.com/index/servicenow-powers-actionable-enterprise-ai-with-openai/) in January, bringing OpenAI into more of the work ServiceNow does for its customers and within its own business.

## Working with ServiceNow through ChatGPT

A new ServiceNow integration will bring business context and workflow actions directly into ChatGPT, helping teams investigate issues and take the next step in the same conversation. An IT team member will be able to find similar incidents, assess the risk of a change and update a ServiceNow record without leaving ChatGPT.

Customers connect ChatGPT to their own ServiceNow instance and choose which capabilities to make available. ServiceNow’s Action Fabric applies existing business rules and permissions, so the actions people can take reflect their organization’s configuration and access.

ServiceNow is also previewing interactive experiences inside ChatGPT. In one example, an on-call engineer will be able to review linked monitoring alerts, recent changes and affected services, then assign the right team and work toward a fix within ChatGPT.

> “AI becomes more useful when people can put it to work in the systems their businesses depend on. By bringing our models together with ServiceNow’s workflows and business context, we’re helping teams build software, address security risks and put AI to work across their organizations.”

*—Greg Brockman, President and Co-founder of OpenAI*

> “When two industry-defining innovators come together, a new chapter of business reinvention begins. OpenAI is pioneering the frontier of artificial intelligence. ServiceNow is the Super Intelligence Control Tower that orchestrates, secures, and governs AI across the enterprise. Together, we are unlocking extraordinary value for our customers by turning world-class reasoning into trusted execution at global scale.”

*—Bill McDermott, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of ServiceNow*

## Powering more ServiceNow products with OpenAI

We also plan to develop new capabilities across three areas:

- **Application development:** A planned Codex integration in ServiceNow’s AI Workflow Factory will help developers build applications using ServiceNow’s business context and platform capabilities. OpenAI models will also power Build Agent and Autonomous Engineer to support application development and modernization.
- **Cybersecurity:** A joint security solution will combine OpenAI’s cybersecurity capabilities with ServiceNow’s asset, identity and business context to help teams investigate vulnerabilities, prioritize risks and coordinate remediation.
- **Voice:** An OpenAI-powered experience in ServiceNow’s Super Intelligence Control Tower will let people describe an AI use case aloud, helping populate assessment fields and gather missing information through follow-up questions.

## Bringing ChatGPT Work and Codex to all ServiceNow employees

ServiceNow plans to give all employees access to ChatGPT Work and Codex, expanding beyond its engineering organization. Engineers can use Codex to explore codebases, make changes and run tests, while teams across the business can use ChatGPT Work in their day-to-day work. ServiceNow also plans to use OpenAI capabilities in its internal security work. OpenAI is also using ServiceNow workflows in our own operations, supported by the Super Intelligence Control Tower.

## Availability

The ServiceNow MCP plugin is available in the OpenAI marketplace today, with enhanced capabilities expected by the end of 2026. Voice capabilities in the Super Intelligence Control Tower are expected in the first quarter of 2027. The OpenAI-powered security capabilities are expected to enter early access in January 2027, with general availability planned for the second quarter of 2027. Codex in AI Workflow Factory is expected to be available in 2027.

title: The future of the firm
body:
***Authors’ note:**** This is the second essay in our series on the next economy, part of a **new platform** to host independent voices exploring an AGI future. It reflects our views, not those of OpenAI or our colleagues.*

The two of us were twenty-four when we started managing our own teams here at OpenAI. That is less impressive once you meet our teams.

We’re supposed to be grunts. At twenty-four, you’re at the bottom of the corporate ladder. You take the meeting notes and write a few memos. After years of drudgerous work, you are (hopefully) granted a broader remit.

Our path—and the path of many young people today—is looking different. We enter the workforce already with “employees” at our behest. These deputies work day and night, weekends and holidays. They are great at the grunt work. We even have math olympiad gold medalists on staff to advise us. Our new reports still make their share of mistakes. But they are getting better, learning our needs, and we are learning how to manage them.

Neither of us climbed the corporate ladder. Management has instead come down to our rung. This essay is about our promotion, and the other ways firms might reorganize as we enter the intelligence age.

When AI enters the firm, where does it go? We present three illustrative scenarios:

None of these scenarios will play out exactly as we describe, but we think aspects of all three will come true. All three are already happening in subtle ways.

Our focus here isn’t total automation but a transitioning economy. We are interested in what chimeric firms will look like as AI improves and laces itself into existing organizations.

We believe the hybrid firm is conceptually important because productive adoption of AI isn’t instantaneous. When the models only do a subset of tasks, adoption may be easiest by ground-level employees familiar with the work. Once the models perform broad functions end-to-end, higher-ups can use them directly. In our view, more capable AI is more adoptable: firms must learn technologies, but labor learns the firm and can onboard itself.

We’ll dissect the three new classes of org chart, then examine what they mean for the future of red tape, worker agency, firm size, and pay disparity.

Our first scenario seems least disruptive. Here, people stay in the same seats with the same reporting lines, ostensibly doing the same jobs as before. The human org chart looks unchanged between today and this future.

The difference is below us. Beneath each individual contributor, a new AI labor force reports up to each of us. Our org chart gets a basement, and we all become managers.

At first, this basement is unfinished. We start with one or two agents apiece, less as seasoned employees, more as eager interns we must supervise and readily forgive. Our expectations are low: send an email here, draft a memo there, reply to Slack messages everywhere. Like junior human employees, they begin with little autonomy and trust.

But as models improve, our agents take on more tasks with less supervision. They coordinate with each other. There might be manager AIs and grunt AIs, accountants and lawyers, all working together at your behest. Far from handholding an intern, your operation eventually looks like a small firm in its own right, with its own org chart and you as its board of directors.

Notice how this scenario doesn’t imply layoffs. Here we adopt AI without automating ourselves. We instead automate *our past selves*, and we move up in the hierarchy. AI takes on more and more of what we used to do. Our jobs remain because there is more to manage, and we gain responsibility for a greater sum of output.

Jobs aren’t static. Suppose that AI can do ninety percent of what you did before. You might conclude you’re left with only ten percent of the work. The other possibility is that you’re still doing a full job, just a different one—now focused on an objective ten times larger. That is the classic gift of technology: productivity rises, ambition rises to meet it, and wages can rise with the ambition.

This all depends on whether we still add value to production. This essay focuses on the coming years where automation isn’t universally capable or adopted. Even if AI could do it all, we might still value something more because a person made it, or insist that a person have the final say.

It also depends on our appetite. If, as consumers, we don’t care for ten times more output, the equilibrium will shift toward fewer workers or fewer hours worked. Historically, increases in output have not satiated us. We have a lot more but work only a little less. Should our appetite continue to grow as output multiplies—and we remain additive to production—we will choose to keep trading our labor for more consumption. If instead production becomes so abundant that we are satiated, we might volunteer a smaller labor force.

There are more objections we discuss later (e.g. whether we’ll have a larger number of smaller firms). We still think this scenario is important because adoption has to start somewhere. Firms need a way to stably evolve from their current org structures. Bolstering the work of existing employees may be an easier first step than wholesale restructuring. We see this in action today: one worker after another delegating to AI, without an organizational revolution so far.

This scenario relies on the front line hiring first. Ground-level workers—not managers and executives—lead on AI adoption. That appears likely, so long as the person who best gets AI to do the work is the person who used to do it themselves.

Models can already automate many data science tasks, but a department head unfamiliar with the methods and minutiae will struggle to leverage the tools. Until AI becomes proactive enough to tell you what you don’t know (see our next scenario), it will probably work best for those already familiar with how the work is done.

The biggest change in this scenario is for entry-level workers. There would no longer be a lowest rung, at least not for humans. When we hire young people, it won’t be to place them at the drudgerous bottom of the firm. Those positions will be filled by something that doesn’t mind.

With that, we lose some traditional routes to educate young workers: the apprenticeship, the learning-by-grunt-work, the earning of stripes. These are genuine costs, but we mostly see this as a privilege. The greenest hire with a good idea has resources to experiment. The oldest excuse in the building, *we just don’t have the manpower*, is dying. A junior employee with a great video game in her head and no path to the headcount can now simply build it.

In our view, this “promoting” scenario still has much for junior workers to learn—judgment, taste, the muscles of management and creative vision. We will be incentivized to cultivate these skills because they show up in our work product. We will still learn by doing, but at a higher level of scope. Firm elders remain incentivized to help us as responsible stewards (with equity stakes in our success). The opportunity here is a more stimulating role for everyone at every rung. Any worker can showcase their talents with a bigger remit, which matters most to entry workers who had no remit at all.

AI’s second way into the firm weaves through the existing org chart. Here the agents aren’t dregs but colleagues. A traditional manager hands a slice of the team’s work to a model the way she might delegate to any employee. AI inserts itself next to humans, not just under them.

The key difference from the first scenario: here, productive AI is adopted by *existing human managers*, not only by current individual contributors. To do so, it must be competent enough to be a fully fledged team member.

Humans are generalists. A hammer helps with one task; a human does a whole lot more. AI’s journey from tool to labor is a widening ambit: automating the task, then the job, then a team, and finally a firm. Every step up in scope requires broader competence.

A job is a suitcase full of many tasks. For a whole team, that suitcase is crammed with all sorts of diverse work. More tasks in the remit mean more potential chokepoints. If even one essential task in the team involves physical labor, a whole new set of peripherals is required. To be a slot-in substitute for an entire team, the AI must be capable across all its varied responsibilities.

AI that can handle bigger scope is harder to build. But for firms—and this is the central asymmetry of the whole transition—*bigger scope is easier to adopt*.

An end-to-end automated team or broad function can be directly adopted by an executive. A tool with narrower capabilities can’t so simply be implemented from on high. The simpler tool relies on widespread buy-in and retraining across the workforce.

New technologies traditionally make it cheaper to do a confined set of tasks. Then the burden shifts to the buyer. The firm must figure out how to leverage the new tool, and must retrain, reorganize, and rebuild its processes around it. Spreadsheet software didn’t install itself into the accounting department—the accounting department reshaped itself around the software.

Labor is the opposite. An intern, an employee, and a good team figure out how to be useful to *you*. They interrogate you, absorb your context, notice your needs. They tell you what you didn’t even realize you didn’t know. The best labor onboards itself.

The more AI becomes like labor in this sense, with initiative and adaptability, the less the firm must learn how to harness it and the more it figures out how to be useful to the firm. An executive probably won’t sit through a design software 101 lecture to learn a new tool. But he will happily entertain an offer that sounds like: *say the word, and I’ll set up your whole marketing function*.

Too often, we name the holy grail of AGI as automating a job. Granted, we haven’t even reached that yet. Jobs are so extraordinarily complicated because we are so impressively capable. Even so, very little of our economy’s output comes from lone-wolf workers. Productive jobs contribute to teams, teams to firms, and firms produce most everything we consume.

The “job” standard for AGI doesn’t give us humans enough credit. Labor isn’t just about the tasks, or even handling the non-routine components: our labor is also about prodigious *coordination*, our plasticity to do small parts of bigger outputs. Selling us as mere sacks of tasks is pennies on the dollar. Human capacity is in our organizations more than the individual. An economic AGI must reach the standard of *people*, not *person*.

As a result, the “interleaving” scenario may be quite inefficient if the AI is still tool-like or even worker-like, instead of team-like or firm-like. A model wedged beside every worker means a thousand seams and handoffs. This piecemeal setup may slow adoption.

We see a race between earlier, less capable implementations and later, more capable models. The victor hinges on whether adoption of future models is so much faster that it overcomes the extra time it takes to reach those competencies.

This “interleaving” scenario can coexist with the first “promoting” scenario. We may see firms shrink their human footprint as AI automates certain functions, while the remaining humans get much broader mandates aided by their agent workforces. Importantly, by itself this scenario doesn’t imply lower overall human employment. We could find ourselves with more firms, each with a lower headcount.

Our third scenario is the most confounding. Here, AI enters the firm *above* people. The stack is no longer humans over machines but human, AI, human: an automation sandwich. Some people “report” to an AI.

It sounds far-fetched, especially as a starting point for firm adoption. But we think, in less radical ways, this has already begun.
