title: Claude for Financial Advisors
body:
Claude for Financial Advisors
Financial advisors can now connect Claude to the custodians, portfolio platforms, CRMs, and planning tools they depend on, along with new skills tailored to the daily work of a financial advisor.
Today we're releasing Claude for Financial Advisors, a suite of connectors and workflow skills designed to help with research, prep, and documentation tasks that occupy an advisor’s time and keep them from client-facing work.
Time is scarce among financial advisors. A typical advisory practice spends only a sixth of its time in client meetings, according to [Kitces research](https://www.kitces.com/kitces-report-how-financial-planners-actually-do-financial-planning/). The rest goes to work around those meetings, piecing together information across systems to prepare, plan, and
document what was discussed. Meanwhile, over four in 10 American workers say they don't know who to go to for good financial or retirement planning advice, according to [EBRI's 2026 Retirement Confidence Survey](https://www.ebri.org/docs/default-source/rcs/2026-rcs/rcs_26-fs-3_prep.pdf). Time an advisor saves on prep and paperwork can go to a current client or new household they don’t yet have capacity to serve.
Claude for Financial Advisors includes:
- Connectors, which let Claude access the custodians, asset managers, and wealth technology providers advisors rely on most, so an advisor can work with a client’s information in one place.
- Skills, which use that information to help with specific tasks, like meeting prep, portfolio analysis, and compliance checks, always in service of the advisor's own judgment and style.
Connectors to the tools advisors already use
New connectors bring in the CRM, custodian, portfolio reporting, financial planning software, estate tools, and meeting capture that advisors rely on.
- Addepar brings investment intelligence into Claude, giving advisors governed access to portfolio data, analytics and workflows across public and private markets.
- BlackRock brings its portfolio construction expertise, model portfolios, and institutional analytics into Claude through Advisor Center, so advisors can deliver holistic advice across public and private markets.
- CAIS opens its alternative investment platform to advisors in Claude, so they can query fund data, review manager and fund performance, and see a client's public and private holdings together.
- Charles Schwab connects Claude to Schwab Advisor Services custodial data, including balances, positions, transactions, cost basis, alerts, and money-movement status, so advisors can review client information, see which clients need attention, and prepare for reviews.
- Conquest Planning brings its Strategic Advice Manager planning engine into Claude so advisors can create new client plans, review and apply strategies, update existing plans and prepare for client meetings all in one place.
- Envestnet lets advisors summarize Tamarac accounts and households in natural language, with a financial plan snapshot from MoneyGuide.
- FactSet brings multi-asset class content including funds and ETFs, news, company fundamentals, analyst estimates, and market data to Claude, so advisors can research the companies and securities in a client's portfolio.
- FINNY, the growth and prospecting platform, connects Claude to an advisor's campaign results by channel and sequence step, and lets advisors enrich prospect lists from their CRM, or upload new lists directly in Claude.
- Flourish connects Claude to financial advisors’ books of business, enabling them to work with client information, check rates, manage invitations, and prepare for client meetings, all within Claude.
- Franklin Templeton provides publicly approved fund and share-class information in Claude, including performance, fees, NAV, holdings, distributions, and fund documents, along with its published market and investment insights.
- iCapital brings a client's alternative investment holdings into Claude, enabling advisors to view NAV, commitments, unfunded capital, recent capital activity, and performance, while more easily connecting those insights to the client's broader portfolio.
- Invesco brings portfolio intelligence and practice management insights into Claude through its Invesco for Advisors connector.
- J.P. Morgan Asset Management (55ip) extends tax transition technology to Claude, so advisors can evaluate the tax impact of moving a client's holdings into a new portfolio.
- Jump, an AI platform for financial professionals, gives Claude client context (meetings, documents, tasks) and Jump-built skills that prepare next steps for the advisor’s review.
- MSCI brings its proprietary data and analytics into Claude, so wealth firms can assess investment options across public and private markets, monitor performance, and evaluate rebalancing opportunities.
- Nevis, the AI platform for wealth management, draws on client information from meetings, documents, and communications to support meeting prep and follow-up in Claude.
- Orion brings portfolio reporting and Redtail CRM insights into Claude for household reviews, opportunity analysis, meeting prep and follow-up.
- SS&C Black Diamond brings portfolio, performance, holdings and rebalancing data into Claude, so advisors can review their book, spot clients out of tolerance, surface tax loss harvesting opportunities, and generate client reports, tasks and rebalance sessions with their approval.
- Wealthbox connects Claude to client records and meeting history to power onboarding, meeting prep, and follow-up.
- Wealth.com gives Claude a structured view of each client's estate and tax picture, including trust and will summaries, tax return insights, and the full balance sheet, so advisors can begin planning with an organized summary of available information instead of documents spread across multiple systems.
- Vanguard brings information on its model portfolios and advisor investment solutions into Claude, so advisors can draw on Vanguard's trusted research, portfolio construction, and asset allocation expertise when making decisions for clients.
- Zocks, the AI meeting assistant for financial advisors, brings Claude the client intelligence it captures from every conversation, including profiles, goals, life events, and commitments.
These join other [connectors](https://claude.com/connectors) already available in Claude, including Microsoft 365, Salesforce, DocuSign, Box, S&P Global, Morningstar, and more.
The Claude for Financial Advisors plugin, which bundles advisor skills and connectors into a single install, works with BlackRock, Charles Schwab, Addepar, Envestnet, iCapital, Orion, Wealthbox, Wealth.com and Zocks, and advisors choose which of these to connect during guided setup. Some partners also offer their own plugins: BlackRock is launching one for Advisor Center, joining existing plugins from S&P Global and LSEG.
Skills built around an advisor’s day
Each skill in the Claude for Financial Advisors plugin supports a specific moment in an advisor's day, from prepping for a client meeting to explaining a drifted portfolio, and routes to tools the firm already uses to run their business. Firms can adopt these skills as is from our Claude for financial advisors [skill repository](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-for-financial-advisors), or adapt them to their own workflows, service model and house style.
- Advisor onboarding connects a firm's tools and runs the first meeting prep automatically, helping a new advisor be productive on day one instead of week three.
- Alternative investments brief pulls a household's alternative investments from iCapital or Addepar into a meeting-ready summary, shown alongside the rest of the portfolio, instead of an advisor reconciling separate statements by hand.
- Compliance and AI policy highlights content that may warrant additional compliance review based on user-configured criteria, assists firms in documenting review workflows, and supports AI-governance documentation processes.
- Estate and tax brief checks a client's estate plan against actual account titling and beneficiaries, looks back at the prior year's taxes, and can create CRM follow-up tasks, so mismatches surface for the advisor to review.
- Portfolio rebalance review flags drift and concentrated positions against a client's target allocation, and creates a first draft explanation an advisor would otherwise write from scratch.
- Post-meeting notes and follow-up turns a transcript into a client summary, a recap email, and CRM tasks in one pass, instead of an advisor doing each by hand after the call.
- Pre-meeting prep consolidates information from connected systems (including a client's holdings, recent account activity, and open items from prior meetings) into a single brief for the advisor to review, so they can prepare for and walk in ready for a conversation about that client's specific situation instead of reconstructing context from three systems.
- Prospect intake organizes what a prospect shares into a summary, an analyst handoff, and a what-to-expect memo, so the first meeting starts with the basics already in place.
Together, the skills gather information, summarize it, and draft client communications across the advisor’s day. Investment recommendations, client communications, compliance determinations, and other regulated activities remain subject to human review and approval.
Built for regulated professionals
Claude for Financial Advisors is designed so that the advisor stays in control, with approval required on critical tasks. Claude prepares briefs, summaries, and drafts analyses for advisor review, and stages administrative actions like CRM updates or draft client communications for the advisor's review and approval. The compliance skill screens client-facing language against the SEC Marketing Rule to flag potential issues, helps firms document review activities within their existing governance and recordkeeping processes, and includes a self-guided AI-policy workflow that helps firms document their use of AI under SEC rules. Workflow activities can be documented to assist firms in maintaining appropriate records and oversight processes.
More households served well
When Claude handles administrative tasks like meeting prep, follow-up drafts and pipeline review, advisors can spend more of their time serving clients. Practices can expand their customer base, and offer more of the services they need, like tax, estate, insurance, and retirement planning.
Here’s what customers and ecosystem partners have told us about working with Claude:
“Advisors are navigating increasingly complex client needs while facing an accelerating pace of change across markets and technology. Our work with Anthropic is an important step in our broader effort to bring BlackRock’s portfolio intelligence and asset allocation expertise to more advisors to help them scale their business and build better portfolios. By making our institutional-quality portfolio analytics more accessible, we are helping more advisors leverage our portfolio intelligence so they can spend more time focused on client relationships.”
“Anthropic builds AI aligned with human values. Mercer Advisors builds family offices aligned with client interests. That shared obsession is core to both firms and anchors our partnership. Claude helps our teams to work seamlessly across clients’ financial lives, while judgment and accountability stay with the advisor. That is how AI should work in any profession built on trust.””
“We are pleased to see Anthropic’s continued investment in capabilities tailored to the unique needs of financial advisors. Our collaboration is rooted in a shared belief that technology should support advisors, not replace them, helping them navigate complexity and more efficiently serve clients while keeping human judgment and discretion at the forefront.”

title: Manage costs and demonstrate ROI for Claude Code on Google Cloud
body:
Manage costs and demonstrate ROI for Claude Code on Google Cloud
Best practices for managing costs and measuring return on investment for Claude Code on Google Cloud.
As organizations delegate more work to Claude Code, spend grows with it, and platform teams need a way to both control costs and understand impact. Inspired by [a recent webinar (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/webinars/how-to-control-costs-and-show-roi-for-claude-code-on-google-cloud) with Google Cloud, we share how organizations using Claude Code can better track and optimize these considerations on Google Cloud, including three core levers: control, track, and prove.
Controls for managing Claude Code spend
Claude on Google Cloud has consumption-based pricing, so your bill is a readout of how much your developers are using Claude in your Google Cloud environment. Adoption drives usage; usage is what you pay for, and it’s also where the value shows up.
Your Claude Code bill is a product of how many tokens tasks consume and the models that handle them. Token consumption scales with task complexity and conversation length. Chat is a Q&A conversation. An agentic tool like Claude Code spends more tokens per task relative to chat because it's doing multistep work: reading files, running tools, and reasoning across a whole task. Meanwhile each model has its own price per token, so [matching the model to the task](https://claude.com/blog/claude-model-and-effort-level-in-claude-code) is the other major cost control.
Visibility into the tokens and model choices impacting your organization’s bill each month is available through the [Claude apps gateway](https://claude.com/blog/introducing-the-claude-apps-gateway) and Google Cloud services. You can govern the spend and manage costs via three independent levers:
- Control. Creating guardrails that guide usage without over-restricting access and unintentionally blocking people.
- Track. Granular oversight of where the spend is happening, and where it will continue to go, before the bill arrives.
- Prove. Identifying the value your org is getting from spending these tokens and attributing exactly where it’s coming from.
Here’s how to apply this control -> track -> prove framework to your own Claude Code on Google Cloud deployment.
The governance toolbox
Claude on Google Cloud comes with tools and capabilities for controlling, tracking, and proving the value of your spend.
Google Cloud already gives you many native capabilities you can apply to tracking and controlling your Claude spend:
- Per-project billing. Allows you to host a dedicated project for Claude Code as a clean way to track costs.
- Billing budgets and alerts. Allows you to set budget alerts and get notified as actual spend crosses thresholds you define.
- Spend caps (Preview). Allows you to enforce a service-level Google Cloud spend budget with ability to manually lift the cap.
- BigQuery exports. Lets you analyze Claude spend alongside the rest of your cloud costs.
- Quotas. Claude models on Google Cloud have per-minute limits on requests, input tokens, and output tokens for each model family and endpoint location.
- Provisioned throughput. Pay a fixed fee for reserved capacity instead of pay-as-you-go.
Claude Code and Claude apps gateway add their own tracking and control capabilities. The gateway is a self-hosted service, shipped in the same claude
binary your developers already use, that runs in your Google Cloud project between Claude Code and Claude on Google Cloud. Developers sign in through your identity provider, such as Google Workspace, so every request carries a verified identity. That lets you set model allowlists per IdP group, and spend caps per user, IdP group, or organization, by day, week, or month.
Here's how to choose and combine capabilities to manage the three levers measuring the cost and ROI behind your organization’s AI investments with Claude on Google Cloud:
Lever 1: Control
The control lever is all about providing guardrails that guide developers in their Claude Code use, instead of restricting them with arbitrary caps.
Guiding rather than restricting is important because high cost sessions are not necessarily bad — in fact, they're often high value, especially in Claude Code. Those sessions are generally your power users that are at the forefront, using new workflows and getting a lot of value from Claude and getting a lot of work done.
Waste tends to sit in the long middle of heavy spenders. For example, they're using Fable for a daily routine that Sonnet can easily handle. Or maybe they have forgotten some scheduled task they no longer care about, but it keeps on running automatically anyway.
There are four features that give you the guardrails to guide your users instead of restricting them:
[Spend limits (opens in new tab)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway-spend-limits). The Claude apps gateway allows you to set spend caps per user, per IdP group, or organization-wide, by day, week, or month. Group and organization caps are per-developer defaults that each member inherits, not a shared pool.- Threshold alerts. When used with Claude apps gateway, Claude Code on Google Cloud warns developers as they approach their cap, first past 75% and again past 95%. These are in-CLI warnings for developers, whereas Google Cloud Billing alerts are meant for admins. At the cap, the gateway returns 429 until the period resets or an admin raises the cap, and you can script cap increases through the gateway's admin API.
- Model defaults and allowlists. Specify which models are available, per IdP group, via the Claude apps gateway which enforces the allowlist server-side on every request. We have found that setting a model default works really well, because most people will stick to the model default; if they want to switch models, they usually are switching for a reason. You can use model defaults in addition to or instead of model allowlists.
- Gateway Admin API. The gateway serves an
[admin API for spend limits (opens in new tab)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway-spend-limits), so you can set and change caps programmatically, for example using a ticketing workflow.
Combine these capabilities to control your overall bill, but remember that control is only the first lever. Price per token doesn't give you the full picture. The most important metric is the cost per task, which can be monitored and analyzed by tracking this usage.
Lever 2: Track
This lever is all about seeing where spend is going and how it’s being used. The good news is that you can track Claude Code usage, costs, and tool activity across your organization. Primary tracking strategies include:
- Usage and cost observability.
[Claude Code's OpenTelemetry metrics and events (opens in new tab)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/monitoring-usage)report usage and estimated cost, broken down by skill, plugin, agent, and MCP server. Send them over OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) to tools you already run, such as Google Cloud Monitoring, through an OpenTelemetry collector or relayed by the Claude apps gateway (for centralized OpenTelemetry config). - End-user usage view. Developers see their own spend and get usage warnings right in Claude Code before they hit a limit.
- Data export to your existing systems. Google Cloud Billing exports to BigQuery let you filter to Claude SKUs by model and token type, putting Claude spend alongside the rest of your cloud and AI spend. OTel flows to your O11y stack, and the gateway Admin API can feed spend-limit status straight into your ticketing system.
Claude Code, whether running on developer machines or on cloud workstations, can export OpenTelemetry once you enable it, including sessions, active time, lines of code, commits, pull requests, tokens and cost, broken down by user, team, and model. The most recent releases of Claude Code also break usage down by skill, plugin, agent, and MCP server so you can see not just overall Claude Code usage but also which of your org’s internal skills and plugins get adopted. With the Claude apps gateway, you don't need to configure each machine. Set a telemetry destination on the gateway, and it turns telemetry on for signed-in developers. It also tags every export with the developer's verified email and IdP groups from their sign-in, rather than values configured on the client-side.
To attribute usage to your own cost centers and departments, set the OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES environment variable (for example, department=engineering,cost_center=eng-123). Claude Code adds these tags to every metric and event, so you can filter and aggregate by them. The metrics land in Google Cloud Monitoring (or other monitoring solutions like Grafana or Splunk) with those custom attributes.
A typical adoption view shows active developers, number of sessions over the last 24 hours, and total tokens consumed. The orange box shows blocked requests when developers hit their gateway-enforced spend caps. That metric pairs well with your existing ticketing system as a workflow that allows developers to request an increase.
For ready-made Cloud Monitoring dashboard, refer to the [Claude Code Monitoring template (opens in new tab)](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/monitoring-dashboard-samples/tree/master/dashboards/claude-code), which turns Claude Code’s OpenTelemetry metrics into a single view of adoption, coding activity, and token usage and estimated spend, so you can track usage and costs by user and model as you roll out Claude Code on Google Cloud. You can copy this template directly from within the Cloud Monitoring console.
To set up custom Claude Code telemetry on Google Cloud, start with the [Claude Code OTel quickstart (opens in new tab)](https://github.com/Google-Cloud-AI/partner-ai-anthropic/tree/main/01-quickstart/otlp-to-telemetry-api). Use it to configure s Claude Code to export OpenTelemetry straight to Google Cloud Observability suite including Cloud Logging and Cloud Monitoring. The quickstart also routes logs into partitioned BigQuery tables, one per event type (API requests, tool decisions, tool results, assistant responses, and completed hook executions), and ships SQL queries for spend per developer/model, tool success and latency, hook wait time, per-turn and per-session analytics.
Lever 3: Prove
The control lever governs and apportions usage and costs; the track lever allows you to visualize that spend. The prove lever is how you map usage to ROI for Claude Code on Google Cloud.
The metrics that platform engineers care most about measuring in Claude Code are contained within three dimensions: usage, developer satisfaction, and impact.
Adoption and usage metrics measure how people are using Claude in your organization, including your activated users and their weekly and daily usage. These reveal information like depth of use, user retention over time, and who your Claude Code power users are. These metrics are all derived via Claude Code OTel data.
Satisfaction metrics monitor the user experience for your engineers, including their happiness with Claude Code, perceived time savings, confidence in output, and any friction they might experience. Satisfaction metrics come from a short survey run before and after rollout, followed by ongoing user check-ins.
Impact metrics assess how Claude is delivering measurable engineering outcomes, comparing throughput, cycle time, and review speed against a baseline, plus qualitative measurements on specific bodies of work.
A starting set of impact metrics
Here's a starting set of impact metrics, grouped into three areas: time, effort, and volume.
Time measures how quickly work ships: PR cycle time from open -> merge, and code review turnaround.
Effort measures how much work each change takes: review iterations per PR, review comments and rework per PR.
Volume measures what the freed-up capacity delivers: PRs per engineer, deployment frequency, and named bodies of work: the

Check Point’s vulnerability research workflow used to take hours to complete. As part of the OpenAI Daybreak Defense Network, the company uses Daybreak to reduce that work to minutes, according to Jonathan Zanger, CTO of Check Point. Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI’s frontier cyber models that can analyze vulnerabilities, reason through attack paths, and identify security gaps in code and configurations.

Check Point helps secure over 100,000 organizations through its AI, workspace, cloud, and network security products. Check Point Research brings vulnerability research expertise to the company’s prevention-first approach, investigating emerging vulnerabilities and translating findings into protections for customers. Daybreak accelerates that research, shortening the path from understanding a vulnerability to developing a defense.

> “OpenAI is putting frontier cybersecurity intelligence in the hands of defenders and enabling companies like Check Point to turn this intelligence into threat prevention.”

—Jonathan Zanger, CTO, Check Point

## Turning vulnerability research into customer protection

“We’re seeing more cyber threats, and those threats are becoming increasingly sophisticated,” Zanger says. For Check Point, keeping pace means quickly turning information about newly disclosed vulnerabilities into protections for customers. “When a new vulnerability emerges, our job is to make sure our customers are protected against it as fast as possible.”

That work depends on expert analysts who investigate vulnerabilities and translate their findings into security signatures or indicators of compromise that Check Point’s systems use to recognize threats. This research requires specialized expertise, and the team’s capacity was previously constrained by the number of analysts available to do it.

Check Point uses OpenAI Daybreak to automate more of this workflow. “We leverage Daybreak to speed up and automate this process, and we can now do it in minutes instead of hours,” Zanger says. The value comes from the models’ ability to reason about security problems.

> “OpenAI Daybreak can understand vulnerabilities, analyze different attack patterns and scan the code to identify gaps.”

—Jonathan Zanger, CTO, Check Point

Zanger also points to advances in understanding complex code and configurations, and identifying how systems could be exposed to attack. Check Point now considers those capabilities mature enough to incorporate into its cybersecurity workflows. For vulnerability research, Daybreak supports the investigative work that informs the development of a signature or indicator of compromise, giving analysts a faster path from understanding a threat to developing protections.

## Developing autonomous network security with Daybreak

Check Point is also working with OpenAI to develop its Agentic Network Security Orchestration solution using Daybreak. The approach Zanger describes would combine continuous monitoring of customer environments with clearly defined operating boundaries and human approval for consequential actions. Customers would set their security objectives, and the system would explain its findings, recommended actions, and associated risks so they could decide how to proceed.

With vulnerability research now taking minutes to complete, Check Point’s next priority is remediation. The company is looking to use Daybreak’s capabilities to make it easier for their security teams to address the gaps they identify.

> “Combining OpenAI’s Daybreak with our existing security workflows unlocks a level of automation that can prevent threats in real time.”

—Jonathan Zanger, CTO, Check Point

For Check Point customers, faster research supports the development of protections against newly discovered vulnerabilities. With Daybreak, Check Point aims to extend that progress toward more autonomous defenses, with customers setting security objectives and approving consequential actions.

title: Auto repair for Together GPU Clusters: from GPU fault to healthy node
body:
At cluster scale, GPU faults are a reality. An Xid error, a double-bit ECC error, a GPU falling off the PCIe bus or a flapping InfiniBand link can stall a distributed training job or take an inference replica down. Spotting that something is wrong is usually the easy part. The hard part is everything between the fault and a healthy node again
Earlier this year, we announced the launch of our fully Automatic node remediation features. Our GPU clusters customers and our internal Inference platform has been using this capability to help drive workload resiliency and minimize down time. Our customers love this capability, and we wanted to take some time break the system down and explain how it works and why we designed it this way.
We first implemented “Passive health” checks system, that watches every node continuously, both inside your VM and on the host underneath it. When a check finds a fault, auto repair recommends the lightest action to fix and shows you supporting evidence behind the recommendation. You decide up front, fault by fault, whether a repair waits for approval or runs on its own. You also decide how long auto repair waits for running workload to finish. Your own detectors can open repairs through the same pipeline by writing a single annotation on a node.
Availability
Generally available today: passive health checks, repair recommendations, the auto-remediation policy (including per-fault and per-node consent), wait-for-idle controls, the escalation ladder, the safety rails, and API and console repair.
Preview: node-label based remediation contracts, which let you bring your own detection systems such as NVSentinel or custom controllers.
We are constantly adding new detection signals and remediation actions to ensure maximum coverage and minimum time to recovery.
Why NotReady is not enough
Most node auto-repair keys on a single signal: the node went NotReady
. That signal looks the same whether a node is broken or just briefly unreachable. When a storage or network event touches many nodes at once, every impacted node drops to NotReady. Our system has a circuit breaker built in to prevent mass replacement of nodes. NotReady also does not say why the node failed, so there's no basis for choosing between a reboot and a new machine.
So auto repair follows one rule: no node repair occurs without a failed health check behind it, and every repair carries its supporting evidence.
The pipeline
The pipeline has four stages: detect a fault, decide whether and when to act, repair the node, and re-validate the machine. The first three stages run against your cluster. The fourth runs on our side, on the physical host your node just vacated. Node-label requests from your own detection tooling enter at the decide stage and get exactly the same treatment as ours.
1. Detection from both sides of the hypervisor
GPUs in Together GPU Clusters are passed straight through to your VM for bare-metal performance. That means GPU faults are visible from inside the VM, while host and fabric faults are visible from the host. Detection therefore runs on both sides of the hypervisor and lands in one place.
Inside your VM, exporters watch:
- the kernel log, for Xid errors and GPUs falling off the PCIe bus
- DCGM, for ECC double-bit errors, row-remap failures, PCIe replay rate, and thermal throttling
- Node Problem Detector, for read-only filesystems, XFS shutdowns, kernel deadlocks, and repeated kubelet or containerd restarts
On Slurm, an exporter reports nodes marked DOWN or DRAIN.
On the host, we watch InfiniBand rail state and link flapping, attributed to the VM that owns those rails. We also watch host reachability, so a dead host shows up as a problem on your node rather than as silence.
Every alert ships a stable summary, a plain-language description, and a machine-readable evidence payload. For an Xid, that's each code and its NVIDIA mnemonic. For thermal throttling, it's the peak temperature and throttle count. The control plane passes those strings through untouched, so the console, the API (as linked_alerts
), and your notifications always say the same thing.
We keep observed separate from actionable. Every repair-relevant alert is recorded and marks your node Degraded. Only signals with an action mapping create a repair. Disk pressure, for example, shows up but doesn't trigger a reboot, because a reboot won't fix it. An alert with no mapping is counted and logged, never silently dropped, and routed to our support team for investigation.
2. Policy: we decide what, you decide whether and when
What is owned by the platform. Each signal maps to the lightest action that fixes it, so you never need to know which Xid means what:
Whether is yours to decide. In the Repairs tab, the Auto-remediation policy defaults to Approve before repair: every recommendation waits for a person, who can accept or override the action. You can switch the default to Fully automatic, but it isn't a blanket switch. The Repair actions checklist groups faults by the repair they trigger, and you select the ones you trust to run unattended. Inside the Xid group, you can set consent per code. A common setup auto-approves reboots for Xid 119 and 95 and keeps migrations gated. The Xid checklist also works under Approve before repair, if you want a short list of faults to run automatically while everything else waits for your review.
When is yours as well. A repair drains the node, so Wait for idle holds it until the node is actually idle. On Kubernetes, that means no running pod on the node is requesting a GPU. On Slurm, it means the scheduler reports no allocation on the node. Maximum wait bounds the hold, with a default of 2 hours and a cap of 24. Do not interrupt running jobs removes the bound entirely. Set the wait to at least your checkpoint interval. If the bound expires, the repair proceeds and the timeout is recorded.
Every repair records who requested it (Together Health Checker for automatic repairs), who approved it (a named user or Auto-Approved), which rule decided, and when.
3. Bring your own detector
Teams running large GPU fleets already have detection they trust: DCGM dashboards, NVSentinel, in-house scanners, job-level checks. Every repair, whatever its source, becomes the same record in our control plane. That gives capacity checks, audit, and safety rails exactly one home.
There are three ways in:
- API. Create a repair against an instance with a mode, an optional client-supplied ID for idempotency, and optionally the health check run or alert you're citing as evidence. You can also list, get, approve, reject, and cancel repairs.
- Console. The ⋮ menu on any node opens the Repair dialog with the detected issues and the recommended action.
- Node labels (Preview). Any detector with RBAC permission to write node metadata can open a repair by adding one annotation and one label to the node. The annotation carries the detector name, a stable request ID, the repair mode, when the fault was detected, and a human-readable reason.
Our cluster operator mirrors the node label
up to the control plane. The repair is recorded with the detector as an external requester, so it's always attributable and can never impersonate a user. Detector name plus request ID is the idempotency key across the cluster, finished repairs included, so a detector that re-asserts the same fault on every scan can't reboot a node twice. Authorization is your cluster's own RBAC, with no API key and no onboarding ticket.
Annotation requests can ask for Reboot, Quick reprovision, or Migrate. Remove stays human-only. Like a console click, these requests skip the approval queue, but they still pass the same evidence gate, capacity check, and budgets as everything else. A per-cluster cap means a buggy detector causes limited damage rather than a catastrophe.
4. Repair actions and the escalation ladder
Every repair follows the same lifecycle: cordon, wait (per your policy), drain, act, rejoin. The console shows the node moving through Cordoning → Draining → Repairing / Migrating → Joining → Running.
The actions, from lightest to heaviest:
- Reboot. Restarts the VM in place. Local
/scratch
and/tmp
data survive. - Quick reprovision. Rebuilds the VM from a clean image on a healthy host. Local data is lost.
- Migrate to new host. Rebuilds the VM on different hardware and sends the old host to re-validation.
- Remove. Pulls the node for RMA. Always human-initiated.
The same fix doesn't loop. If a fault comes back on the same machine after the same action has already run twice, the next recommendation moves one rung up. A third round of Xid reboots becomes a reprovision, and a third reprovision becomes a migration. The ladder is tracked per machine, cluster, alert, and Xid code. Attempts older than a week don't count, and neither do cancelled or self-resolved recommendations.
Migrations are evidence-gated. Migrate is the one action that consumes real capacity. It requires either a critical alert currently firing on the node or a critical alert on the same machine within the last ten days. A request that meets neither condition runs as a Quick reprovision instead.
Host power cycle (Preview). Some faults, Xid 79 among them, need the GPU to lose power, which a VM reboot can't do even though the hardware may be fine. Rather than consuming a new host, we can power-cycle the one you're on. No BMC credentials exist anywhere in the system. A boot-ID check prevents a retry from cycling a host that has already come back.
Clusters that need a guaranteed replacement window can reserve hot spare capacity, so migrations draw from that reserve rather than general availability. Ask your account team for details.
5. Rails that assume the alert storm will happen
A bad driver push, a storage outage, or a network partition can make dozens of nodes look sick at once. Node-level repair can't fix a cluster-level cause, so the rails are layered and independent:
- Persistence. A signal must hold for a per-signal duration before it becomes a recommendation.
- Cooldown. After any repair, a node gets roughly 30 minutes before a new recommendation can be generated.
- Concurrency budget. The budget is sized from cluster node count, and the operator runs one repair per node pool at a time.
- Circuit breaker. When one cluster generates a burst of correlated automatic repairs, the breaker trips. Many nodes failing at once points to a cluster-level cause, and repairing nodes one by one will not fix it.
- One target per repair. The schema enforces it, so a bug can't fan out across nodes.
- Auto-resolve. A recommendation whose alert clears before anyone acts disappears on its own.
The control plane is replicated, and every write is idempotent and checked against the state it expects. Two replicas racing on the same node produce one repair, not two.
6. The machine re-validates itself
When a node migrates off a machine, or is removed from one, that machine shouldn't go straight back into the pool, and it shouldn't sit in a queue waiting for someone to read diagnostics either. As soon as the old VM is gone, the machine moves into validation automatically. A test VM runs the same GPU, NCCL, InfiniBand, and storage checks that every brand-new machine passes before joining the fleet. No person touches the machine between your node leaving and the verdict landing.
There are three verdicts:
- Passed. The machine returns to the pool. No ticket is filed and no one is paged, so a transient fault stays transient.
- Failed. A hardware ticket is filed automatically with per-test results and logs attached. The machine stays out until it's fixed and passes again.
- Aborted. The checks couldn't run, for example because the host was reallocated or the test VM couldn't be placed. The machine is restored to its prior state, and nothing is condemned.
Only an explicit failure produces a ticket.
Built to extend past one accelerator
Repair decisions key on alerts, nodes, and machines, not on the GPU v

title: GPT-6.1 Terra
body:
26th October 2026 - Link Blog
[GPT-6.1 Terra](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-terra/) ([via](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50248124)) It's always interesting to note which aspects of a new model are emphasized in the release announcement.
In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, OpenAI went with visual reasoning and computer use:
We’re introducing GPT-6.1 Terra, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.
Terra sits in the same position as Sonnet in the Anthropic model collection - not the cheapest or the most expensive, making it harder to decide when to use it.
Computer use is a good example of a task that benefits from a less expensive model, since you might put it to work on automated, repetitive tasks.
OpenAI's Ted Sanders provided some useful advice in [a comment](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50248124#50249160) on Hacker News:
In the case of GPT-6.1 Terra, I'd say Terra is probably better than Astra and Sol at technical communication, similar on vision and computer use (but much faster!), and a bit worse on most other things. For API developers, it's a nice midrange option if you want something cheaper than Sol but a lot smarter than Luna (especially for vision / computer use / communication). For subscribers, it's not a bombshell release - if you're hitting usage limits, maybe it helps you go a bit further, and if you want clearer communication or faster computer use, it can be a nice option to select.
Here are [the pelicans](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F855d951d12c68eccca5374cd7d4f834e) for the different reasoning levels. This pelican [for "max"](https://tools.simonwillison.net/markdown-svg-renderer?url=https%3A%2F%2Fgist.github.com%2Fsimonw%2F855d951d12c68eccca5374cd7d4f834e#reasoning-2) cost [11.3161 cents](https://www.llm-prices.com/#it=16&ot=22629&sel=gpt-6.1-terra) and took 4 minutes and 11 seconds:
Here's [a new comparison grid](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/openai-pelicans-october-2026.html) showing pelicans for every reasoning level of OpenAI's current frontier lineup: GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra, and GPT-6 Luna.
GPT-6.1 Terra is priced at $1/million input tokens and $5/million output - almost half the price of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, and around 10x the price of GPT-6 Luna.

- Rust toolchain.
- Xcode command line tools and Metal toolchain.
- CMake, pkg-config, and Opus.
brew install cmake pkg-config opus
xcodebuild -downloadComponent MetalToolchain
From this repository:
git submodule update --init --recursive
cargo build --release --no-default-features --features mlx --bin pibot-tts-worker
Build all MLX binaries:
cargo build --release --no-default-features --features mlx
Pipi builds this submodule with:
npm run build:tts-rust
from the Pipi repository root.
Pipi currently defaults to the 0.6B Base 6-bit MLX model:
mlx-community/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base-6bit
The 1.7B Base 6-bit MLX model is also supported and was used for parity/performance testing:
mlx-community/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base-6bit
Dense BF16 Qwen/Qwen3-TTS models are still supported. Dense MLX linear weights and biases are intentionally cast to FP32 in this fork; this is required for good audio quality with the unquantized 0.6B model.
Example worker invocation:
target/release/pibot-tts-worker \
--serve \
--model-name /path/to/qwen3-tts-model \
--ref-audio /path/to/reference.wav \
--ref-text-file /path/to/reference.txt \
--language de \
--output-sample-rate 24000 \
--temperature 0.7 \
--top-k 30
The worker uses a binary stdin/stdout protocol and logs status/events on stderr. It emits streamed PCM chunks for low-latency playback.
Language names and short aliases are normalized by the worker, e.g. de
maps to german
. auto
remains supported.
Text-to-speech with a preset/custom voice model:
target/release/tts /path/to/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-CustomVoice \
"Hello world" Vivian english
Voice cloning with a Base model:
target/release/voice_clone /path/to/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-0.6B-Base \
reference.wav \
"Hello from a cloned voice." \
english \
"Transcript of the reference audio"
Reference audio should be mono 24 kHz WAV.
Generate Python MLX traces:
python3 scripts/trace_python_mlx.py \
--model /path/to/model \
--ref-audio /path/to/reference.wav \
--ref-text-file /path/to/reference.txt \
--text "Hallo" \
--language de \
--out /tmp/python-trace
Generate Rust MLX traces:
cargo run --release --no-default-features --features mlx --bin trace_rust -- \
--model /path/to/model \
--ref-audio /path/to/reference.wav \
--ref-text-file /path/to/reference.txt \
--text "Hallo" \
--language de \
--out /tmp/rust-trace
Compare traces:
python3 scripts/compare_traces.py /tmp/python-trace /tmp/rust-trace
The trace tools support forced/reference code paths used to isolate talker/code-predictor parity from audio-encoder drift.
MLX loads mlx.metallib
at runtime for Metal kernels. With Xcode 26.5 / Metal compiler metalfe-32023.883
, locally source-built MLX v0.31.2
can produce incorrect results for large-M transposed 6-bit quantized_matmul
/ qmm_splitk
calls. The official Python MLX wheel artifact does not show the same issue.
The vendored MLX-C wrapper in this fork works around the bad local Metal artifact by chunking large 2D/3D transposed quantized matmul calls into 16-token slices before calling MLX core. This keeps MLX's real quantized Metal kernels, avoids dequantization, and restores parity with Python MLX for Qwen3-TTS.
Standalone repro:
https://github.com/badlogic/mlx-qmm-repro
Upstream issue:
https://github.com/ml-explore/mlx/issues/3586
Apache-2.0
Based on the original Rust implementation from Second State and the Qwen3-TTS Python/MLX implementation from the Alibaba Qwen team.

title: Agents That Self Improve While You Sleep - Fuad Ali, Arize AI
body:
In this workshop, Fuad Ali of Arize AI shows how to build a self-improvement loop for AI agents: trace everything, let Signal (an always-on agent) read your traces on a schedule and file deduplicated issues, turn failures into evals and living regression datasets, run experiments to prove a fix works, and keep humans at the highest-leverage points: eval design, dataset curation and reviewing fixes. He demos the loop on a toy-shopping agent with a planted bug and takes questions on evaluating qualitative output, decision models and cost.

# Greptile takes bug detection beyond code review with GPT‑6 Astra

How Greptile uses GPT‑6 Astra to test user workflows, Daybreak to strengthen security, and Codex to reduce rework.

- [Looking ahead to faster development with Ultrafast](#looking-ahead-to-faster-development-with-ultrafast)

[Greptile⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.greptile.com/) builds AI agents that review and test code changes with full context of the codebase. “We are in the business of reducing bugs and making the world’s software more reliable,” says Co-founder and CEO Daksh Gupta.

For Daksh, that mission requires testing an application’s behavior as well as reading its code, and GPT‑6 Astra’s computer use gives Greptile a way to automate testing at scale.

> “For the first time ever, computer use is in a place where you can automate the experience of having a user try to break your application and allow large companies to ship much more confidently.”

*—Daksh Gupta, Co-founder and CEO, Greptile*

## Testing applications at scale with GPT‑6 Astra

Validating a pull request involves checking whether the code is logically correct, does what the developer intended, is secure, and avoids breaking existing functionality. For some of that testing, you need to actually run the application because reading the code alone might not reveal the problem.

Daksh gives the example of a button that disappears when a website is viewed on an iPhone. With GPT‑6 Astra, Greptile can start a development server for a pull request, resize the browser to an iPhone-sized viewport, and simulate a user moving through the application. The model’s visual understanding lets it inspect the screen and spot the hidden button.

“A QA firm testing all of your changes is just impractically slow considering how fast we’re able to ship code with these models,” he says. With GPT‑6 Astra, Greptile can automate this kind of application testing at scale.

## Strengthening customers’ defenses with Daybreak

Daksh says more powerful models also make it easier for attackers to exploit applications, putting companies at risk, even those that previously would not have been typical targets.

“We want to make it very easy for even a startup to secure their systems,” says Daksh. “With Daybreak, we’re able to do this in a way that is very safe, and we can ensure that our customers have more sophisticated defense mechanisms than the adversaries have offense mechanisms.”

## Reducing bugs and rework with Codex

Greptile’s Knowledge Base indexes a company’s codebase and documents how it works in a form people and agents can read. The company makes that documentation available to Codex through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

This allows Codex to write code that follows the customer’s existing patterns, and thousands of customers have connected Codex to Greptile’s knowledge base, according to Daksh.

To measure the impact, the team tracks how often AI-generated code is reverted. “When we provide agents with context, fewer reverts happen and customers save time and save inference,” Daksh says. Customers can put those savings toward new work instead of reworking the same changes.

Greptile also uses Codex to build its own software and agents. “We are massive users of Codex,” Daksh says. “We have enormous amounts of usage across every single function, engineering in particular.”

## Looking ahead to faster development with Ultrafast

For Greptile, Daksh explains, the only real bottleneck is how quickly the team can turn ideas into working software. He says model intelligence is already sufficient for many tasks, so he sees Ultrafast as a way to speed up development.

> “I’m most excited about Ultrafast as a lever for us to move exactly as fast as we can come up with good ideas.”

*—Daksh Gupta, Co-founder and CEO, Greptile*

His longer-term goal is to make changing and shipping critical enterprise software as easy as shipping a side project, with OpenAI helping Greptile build the validation that requires.

# GPT-6.1Terra

From visual understanding to action

- [Pricing and availability](#pricing-and-availability)

## Delivering fast and capable computer use at scale

We’re introducing **GPT-6.1 Terra**, a fast, efficient model that combines detailed visual reasoning and precise computer use alongside clearer, more natural writing. A significant step up from GPT‑5.6 Terra, it excels at the communication and computer-based tasks that fill the workday, from drafting proposals and interpreting technical drawings to filling out forms and editing videos.

Terra continues to advance the cost-intelligence frontier across our model families, providing a new balance of speed, capability, and cost. Its standard API prices are 50% lower than those of GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol, making it practical for developers to automate high-volume work, like reading incoming invoices and entering their details into accounting software. In ChatGPT Work and Codex, your plan goes further with GPT-6.1 Terra—the same usage allowance covers more tasks than with GPT‑5.6 Terra and substantially more than with GPT‑6.1 Sol or GPT‑6 Astra.

## From visual understanding to action

We measured GPT-6.1 Terra’s computer-use capabilities on **Agents’ Last Exam,** a benchmark of professional tasks that includes turning architectural drawings into a 3D model and reviewing an animated film shot by shot to create a time-coded log for a restoration team. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra scores 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra at about one-third the cost. It even performs on par with GPT-6 Astra at only one-tenth its price per token. At max effort, Terra is over three times as token efficient as Claude Opus 5.5, and one-fourth its price per token, resulting in a \~9x lower cost per task. Terra is also much quicker, completing tasks **over three times faster** than both GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

On **MMMU-Pro**, a benchmark of visual reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra outperforms GPT-5.6 Terra at every reasoning setting. It even nearly matches the scores of our most capable frontier model, GPT-6 Astra, and GPT-6.1 Sol at much lower cost.

**OSWorld 2.1** tests how well AI agents use desktop apps to complete multistep tasks, such as building a 3D model from a technical drawing. At medium reasoning effort, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-5.6 Terra’s best score at a fraction of the cost per task.

## A significant step up on factuality and coding

This year, we’ve invested heavily in reducing hallucinations and factual errors produced by our models. On our internal benchmark of error-inducing prompts, the error rate at low reasoning effort fell from 53.6% with GPT-5.6 Terra to 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Terra, a drop of nearly 37 percentage points. At maximum effort, the error rate fell by 18 percentage points to 4.3%, nearly matching the rates for GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol.

GPT-6.1 Terra marks a substantial improvement over GPT-5.6 Terra for software engineering. **Terminal-Bench 4.0** tests how well coding agents solve problems from the command line, such as fixing a webpage whose layout shifts as it loads. At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6.1 Terra solves 50.3% of tasks, more than double GPT‑5.6 Terra’s published score of 21.5%. For the most complex coding tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra remain the better choice.

**Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1** tests how well agents use code to carry out scientific research tasks, such as tracking cell divisions in a time-lapse video. At max reasoning, GPT-6.1 Terra surpasses GPT-6.1 Sol at lower cost, coming within five points of Opus 5.5 at less than one-fifth the estimated cost.

## Safety and alignment

As we make powerful AI more efficient and accessible, we continue training, testing, and refining our safeguards. GPT‑6.1 Terra meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, and maintains the protections developed for GPT‑6 Astra.

GPT-6.1 Terra brings with it the alignment improvements of the GPT-6 series. According to our evaluations, GPT-6.1 Terra is more likely to stay within scope and honestly disclose limitations and potential blockers to the user compared to GPT-5.6 Terra. In our prompt-injection tests, GPT-6.1 Terra also showed strong resistance to malicious instructions designed to divert it from the user’s task. More detail is available in the [system card ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-1-terra).

## Pricing and availability

Starting today, GPT-6.1 Terra is available to all Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users in ChatGPT Work and Codex. Developers can also access it through the OpenAI API as `gpt-6.1-terra`.

Standard API pricing is $1 per million input tokens, $0.05 per million cached input tokens, and $5 per million output tokens.

title: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox
body:
26th October 2026
[Research](/elsewhere/research/)
[webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox](https://github.com/simonw/research/tree/main/webframe-evaluation#readme)— An evaluation of webframe found it to be a fast, lightweight browser-JavaScript runner suitable for scraping, with performance comparable to shot-scraper, but with important rough edges including CSP failures, a 0×0 viewport, hanging loads, missing HTTP metadata, and limited browser controls.
[webframe](https://github.com/tractordev/webframe) is a neat little project from Jeff Lindsay which lets you "run a web page like a program" - you point it at a URL or file and it executes it in a hidden headless web view and outputs console.log()
to standard output and any exceptions to standard error.
It's written in Go on top of the [glaze](https://github.com/crgimenes/glaze) library, which provides access to a system browser ("WKWebView on macOS, WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows") so it doesn't need to bundle its own browser engine.
It reminds me of my own [shot-scraper javascript](https://shot-scraper.datasette.io/en/stable/javascript.html) tool, albeit in a much smaller package that doesn't depend on Playwright.
I had Claude Opus 5.5 [put it through its paces](https://claude.ai/code/cshk_01MX3aJH8vDGmGSj1xH9BYhj2HviVvLDaJbiELHyDoReYT) and prepare a research report for me. Here's the prompt I used:
Explore https://github.com/tractordev/webframe try running it and put it though its paces, build a few exploratory prototypes, then evaluate it as a potential sandboxing tool and as a tool for scraping web pages using the same patterns encouraged by the "shot-scraper JavaScript" command (see simonw/shot-scraper on GitHub, docs directory)

title: Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain
body:
Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain
Today, we’re launching “Polar Peaks”, our third quest in the [AI Quests](https://research.google/ai-quests/intl/en_us) series, created by Google Research and the [Stanford Accelerator for Learning](https://acceleratelearning.stanford.edu/) to teach students [how AI works and how to use it responsibly.](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/education/ai-quests/%5C) AI Quests invites students ages 11 to 14 to step into the shoes of Google researchers to tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges.
More than 400,000 quests have been completed to date, localized to 10 languages. Alongside the new quest, we’re also releasing training modules for teachers.
Polar Peaks: A journey to map the human brain
In the first two quests, students tackle flood forecasting and eye disease detection, inspired by Google Research’s [Flood Forecasting initiative](https://sites.research.google/gr/floodforecasting/) and AI model for [diabetic retinopathy](https://blog.google/company-news/inside-google/around-the-globe/google-asia/arda-diabetic-retinopathy-india-thailand/) screening. Our newest quest, “Polar Peaks,” has students travel to the frontiers of neuroscience and see how AI can speed up scientific research.
With the guidance of in-game mentors, students scan and map the neurons in the brain to better understand the game character’s memory loss. They complete tasks like data cleaning and model testing, learning firsthand that AI requires careful human oversight and critical thinking.
The quest is inspired by over a [decade of our research](https://research.google/blog/ten-years-of-neuroscience-at-google-yields-maps-of-human-brain/) in connectomics: the science of mapping neural networks in the brain. Upon completion of the quest, students hear from two researchers behind our real-world breakthroughs, including the recent mapping of the complete [fruit fly](https://research.google/blog/a-connectomics-milestone-mapping-the-complete-male-fruit-fly-brain/) brain, the largest brain map by number of neurons to date.
Training modules: Tools for teaching AI literacy
Teachers play a critical role in bringing the quests to life and fitting them into their existing classroom curriculum. We’re rolling out new dedicated teacher training modules to help educators reinforce key AI literacy concepts and use AI Quests for learning and discussion. These are launching within the [Google AI Educator Series](https://edu.google.com/learning-center/google-ai-educator-series/). The modules for Quest #1 and #2 are accessible [here](https://educertifications.google/google-ai-educator-series/47). The training module for Quest #3 will follow next month.
Earlier this year, AI Quests won a [2026 Webby Award](https://winners.webbyawards.com/winners/ai/ai-experiences-applications/education-learning-training?years=0) for AI Education, Learning & Training, and Best Global K–12 Learning Solution at the ETIH Innovation Awards. We’ll continue working with educators and partners to bring more quests to more classrooms this school year.

# Working with academic communities to build scientific understanding

Loading…

Share

Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture

- [Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture](#local-smoothing-and-the-kakeya-conjecture)
- [The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false](#the-exponential-time-hypothesis-is-false)
- [Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model](#existence-of-quantum-chromodynamics-and-completions-of-the-standard-model)
- [Supporting scientists](#supporting-scientists)

- [Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture](#local-smoothing-and-the-kakeya-conjecture)
- [The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false](#the-exponential-time-hypothesis-is-false)
- [Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model](#existence-of-quantum-chromodynamics-and-completions-of-the-standard-model)
- [Supporting scientists](#supporting-scientists)

We are announcing three new discoveries in mathematics, computer science, and physics about harmonic analysis, complexity theory, and quantum field theory.

Our release process continues to evolve in response to feedback from the associated academic communities. In our view, these manuscripts are best understood as a form of raw research data. To convert this raw research data into scientific understanding, in this release we are experimenting with a new approach. We reached out to external experts and asked them to act as shepherds, organizing groups to understand the new results. They advised three different release strategies:

- For the math result, release the AI output, leaving researchers free to organize their own efforts to explain the result.
- For the computer science result, form an external group of collaborators to explain the result, while making the AI output publicly available for anyone to examine and build on.
- For the physics result, form an external group of collaborators and defer to them on the release of materials.

We do not yet know which of these three approaches will be most useful, and we welcome feedback on what works and what we can improve.

The external collaborations will follow four principles:

1. **Transparency.** We are transparent about the existence of our collaborations. Participants will not be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements and will be free to discuss the work, share intermediate products, and publish their conclusions.
2. **No Academic Credit.** We do not seek academic credit for the discoveries produced by our internal models. Inviting a researcher to help steward a collaboration also does not imply that they or their working group made the original discovery.
3. **Recognition.** This group should receive recognition for the understanding they develop, the writeups they author, and the other materials they create. The group will also help ensure that the work appropriately credits researchers, techniques, and ideas that it draws on.
4. **Independence.** Participation is voluntary and unpaid. Working-group members participate independently, and their conclusions are their own. They do not speak on behalf of OpenAI, and OpenAI does not speak on their behalf.

We will turn over materials and artifacts related to these results to the collaborations. For the computer science collaboration, the group has decided to make the natural language proof and Lean formalization public immediately, and we are publishing them directly to our GitHub repository. For the physics collaboration, the group has decided to hold off on releasing the AI-produced artifacts and instead work on writing it up themselves.

All of these approaches involve tradeoffs. On the one hand, the collaborations empower experts to foster unpacking the results and contextualizing them in the broader academic community. On the other hand, choosing initial shepherds necessarily shapes who gets involved first and creates asymmetry of information. We welcome feedback on how to broaden participation and make this process more useful.

## Local smoothing and the Kakeya conjecture

The result in mathematics concerns harmonic analysis. In 1991, Sogge proposed the local smoothing conjecture, which concerns the behavior of waves as they become focused. In particular, the conjecture states that the most extreme focusing must be short-lived. The amount of focusing at a typical random time is always much smaller than what can happen at the worst-case time. This is a familiar pattern throughout mathematics: what can happen in the worst case is more extreme than what is observed after averaging. Because of how fundamental this conjectured phenomenon is, it also has wide ranging implications throughout mathematical analysis. For instance, it implies the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture.

In 2019, [Guth, Wang, and Zhang⁠(opens in a new window)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2020/192-2/p06) proved the local smoothing conjecture in two spatial dimensions. In 2025, [Wang and Zahl⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.ias.edu/news/once-century-proof-settles-maths-kakeya-conjecture) proved the Kakeya conjecture in three dimensions. Our models produced a proof of the local smoothing conjecture in every dimension and therefore also resolve the Kakeya conjecture and Stein’s restriction conjecture in all dimensions. The new proof is based on a novel auxiliary partial differential equation.

We obtained our AI output on October 18th, 2026, which was formalized in Lean the following day, and then we reached out to an expert to discuss forming a collaboration around this result. Following their recommendation, we decided to release the AI output publicly, following the same strategy for this result as our October 6th, 2026 [release⁠](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/). We have released both an [AI natural language output writeup⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Local-smoothing-for-the-Euclidean-wave-equation-October-25-2026/paper.pdf) produced by our models and a  [Lean proof ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/docs/079.md)in our public GitHub repository.

## The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false

The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem. The ETH has been widely believed to be true, and has been used in hundreds of papers to derive conditional computational hardness results across a wide variety of fields including graph theory, computational biology, databases, computational geometry, and more. Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean. The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.

This work will be verified and shepherded by a group led by Russell Impagliazzo (UC San Diego), Ramamohan Paturi (UC San Diego), and Ryan Williams (MIT). All three are experts in algorithm design and complexity theory.

- Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and have authored a [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcss.2001.1774) [number⁠(opens in a new window)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcss.2001.1774) of [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcss.2000.1727) [influential⁠(opens in a new window)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcss.2000.1727) [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-11269-0_6) [papers⁠(opens in a new window)](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-11269-0_6) on the [topic⁠(opens in a new window)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1663742) over the last 30 years.
- Williams has refuted [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2016.2) [strong⁠(opens in a new window)](https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.CCC.2016.2) [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11859) [versions⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.jair.org/index.php/jair/article/view/11859) of the ETH, used ETH for [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611973075.86) [hardness⁠(opens in a new window)](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/1.9781611973075.86) [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397505005438?via%3Dihub) [results⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304397505005438?via%3Dihub), and connected [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/10080703X) [algorithms⁠(opens in a new window)](https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/10080703X) and [⁠(opens in a new window)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2559903) [lower bounds⁠(opens in a new window)](https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2559903).

We have agreed to the group’s requests that all raw data of the results be made public to facilitate independent verification by the community, and that OpenAI commit to funding a conference to understand the implications of this work on the field as a whole. The group invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.

Our AI found its natural language disproof for the ETH on October 16th, 2026 and then subsequently we formalized the result in Lean on October 17th, 2026, which led us to develop the collaboration described here. To that end, we have released both an [AI natural language output writeup⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Exponential-Time-Hypothesis-is-False-October-25-2026/paper.pdf) produced by our models and a [Lean proof ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/docs/378.md)in our public GitHub repository.

Computational complexity has many open questions and conjectures, whose proofs or refutations have so far eluded the best efforts of scientists. We hope that humans with AI can provide new understanding in this field, and shed light on the inherent capabilities and limits of efficient computation.

## Existence of quantum chromodynamics and completions of the Standard Model

The physics collaboration will understand and explain a result that gives a mathematically rigorous existence proof of certain interacting quantum field theories containing gauge fields and fermions in four dimensions, including Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. Our work builds on [Balaban’s approach⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0129055X13300100) in constructive quantum field theory. As a subproblem, this work also includes a proof of the existence of pure Yang–Mills theory, which is part of the [Quantum Yang–M

# GPT‑6.1 Sol helps CodeRabbit strengthen security across complex codebases

Loading…

Share

As AI accelerates software development, engineering and application-security teams need ways to investigate code changes and address vulnerabilities while keeping people in control. CodeRabbit is using [GPT‑6.1 Sol](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-sol/) as the primary model in its security agent to extend review beyond individual changes and help developers understand risks across complex codebases.

A pull request can affect shared libraries, dependencies and safeguards elsewhere in an application. GPT‑6.1 Sol helps CodeRabbit connect behavior across files and components to surface potential security issues. CodeRabbit’s review is independent of the agent that wrote the code and complements established scanners. Its system also uses other frontier models and security tooling.

During pull-request review, Sol helps analyze changes as developers work. In Deep Scan, it supports broader investigation across repositories, including dependencies and how components interact. CodeRabbit Secure extends that investigation to linked repositories, such as a shared authentication library, to help teams understand how a weakness could affect the wider system.

CodeRabbit reports using GPT‑6.1 Sol to flag security-related issues across thousands of repositories and organizations. These findings feed into the pull-request workflows developers already use to review and improve their code.

CodeRabbit Secure connects investigation to remediation. For user-selected findings, it can attempt exploit verification in an isolated sandbox without testing production systems. For supported issues, it can draft a pull request with a proposed fix for a person to review and approve.

This work shows how frontier reasoning can support software security: understanding risks beyond an individual change, helping validate findings and turning them into proposed fixes. Human reviewers remain responsible for deciding which changes to ship.

Learn more about GPT‑6.1 Sol [here](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-1-sol/). Learn more about CodeRabbit Secure [here⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.coderabbit.ai/security).
