title: LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
body:
[
](#litpivot-developing-research-ideas-through-dynamic-contextualization-within-the-literature-landscape)
LitPivot: Developing research ideas through dynamic contextualization within the literature landscape
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
📄 [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02600)
Encountering a new paper can change a research idea's trajectory. The researcher may discover that someone has already addressed their proposed contribution, or find an unresolved problem in the paper that inspires a new direction of inquiry.
We call this process a literature-initiated pivot: a change in research direction prompted by reading prior work. It connects two activities that researchers often have to manage separately: developing an idea and deciding which literature to measure it against.
With collaborators at the University of Pennsylvania, we developed [LitPivot](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02600), a system that helps researchers navigate these pivots. Using papers retrieved through [Asta Paper Finder](https://asta.allen.ai/), LitPivot organizes literature around the part of a proposal being edited, offers critiques supported by excerpts from selected studies, and suggests revisions that researchers can accept, edit, or reject. LitPivot is intended to be used for early-stage research ideation, but the idea could possibly extend to longer writing tasks (i.e., writing the introduction section of a paper).
In a study with 17 researchers, domain experts rated research ideas developed with LitPivot as better grounded in the literature than those developed with a text editor and an AI chat tool. Participants also perceived their revised research ideas as more novel and useful, and reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature.
LitPivot will be presented at UIST 2026 in Detroit. Read the paper [here](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02600).
[
](#why-pivoting-is-hard)
Why pivoting is hard
Research ideas evolve through engaging with the literature. In our analysis of meeting notes from four completed computer science research projects, we identified 21 literature-initiated pivots across all four projects. These fell into two types: differentiating an idea from existing work to establish an idea’s novelty, and aligning an idea with existing work to build on it. This project itself went through two pivots before we settled on its contributions.
These changes can be difficult to navigate. In a formative study, five researchers developed proposals using a text editor and standard search tools. They struggled to develop their ideas while critically evaluating them against the literature. When a paper challenged an idea’s novelty, they wanted concrete suggestions for how to revise it, supported by prior work. These findings shaped LitPivot’s assessments, which pair literature-supported critiques with specific suggestions for revising the selected part of an idea.
[
](#how-litpivot-works)
How LitPivot works
In LitPivot, a researcher starts by writing a short proposal in an editor and enabling what we call facet highlighting, which segments an articulated idea into different facets (i.e., a problem, contribution, and evaluation). To check a proposed facet, the researcher clicks that segment in the draft. An adjacent panel groups related papers based on the selected facet (e.g., grouping papers by the evaluation methods they use when the evaluation facet is selected) and highlights the most relevant groups. The researcher selects papers, requests an assessment, and reviews a suggested revision alongside excerpts supporting the critique. The literature is then reranked based on relevance to the revised facet.
In particular, LitPivot separates a research idea into its problem, proposed contribution, and evaluation plan. Each facet has its own set and relevance ranking of related literature. LitPivot groups retrieved papers around the facet being edited, letting the researcher choose which ones the system should use to assess the draft.
Alongside scientific-writing environments such as Prism and agentic assistants such as Claude Code, LitPivot explores a new workflow for developing an early research idea: choosing literature to assess it against, using that evidence to revise it, and reconsidering which papers matter as the idea changes. Its paper groups and linked critiques make those steps explicit for each part of the proposal, while researchers control both the draft and the evidence used to assess it.
For a problem statement, LitPivot looks for evidence that the problem exists and reasons it matters. To assess a proposed contribution, it compares what the selected papers have already addressed with the limitations and future work they describe, looking for remaining gaps. For an evaluation plan, it checks whether the proposed tests address the research question and how similar work has been evaluated. The system then suggests a rewrite with supporting quotes attached.
Changing one facet of an idea can leave another out of date. LitPivot flags passages that may need revision, such as an evaluation plan that no longer adequately evaluates a revised contribution. Researchers can accept, edit, or reject suggestions, and request new papers or refresh the literature ranking as their proposal develops.
Paraphrased example from one study participant.
[
](#our-findings)
Our findings
In our lab study, 17 researchers each developed one assigned idea with LitPivot and another with a baseline tool—a text editor and an AI tool for asking questions about selected papers. Both conditions used the same collection of papers. Two domain experts, unaware of which system had been used, rated the resulting proposals on a single criterion: how well they used relevant literature to support and justify the idea. Proposals developed with LitPivot received higher ratings.
Participants in the same study also reported a stronger understanding of the surrounding literature and greater self-reported improvements in their ideas’ novelty and usefulness with LitPivot than with the baseline. Domain experts also reviewed the participants’ ideas and rated the ideas revised using LitPivot to be significantly better grounded in relevant literature.
One participant in our lab study started with a proposal to generate consistent, factual synthetic medical notes. LitPivot identified consistency across multiple hospital visits as a potential gap in the selected literature. The participant reviewed abstracts and removed papers about single-visit notes. After another assessment, they narrowed the proposal to detecting contradictions across notes from multiple visits. The example shows how revising an idea and choosing the literature used to assess it can inform each other.
In a follow-up study, five researchers used LitPivot on their own ongoing projects during 30-minute sessions. Participants used LitPivot across multiple project phases, not just at the beginning. Two used it to vet new ideas against the literature, while three used it to refine the framing of more mature ideas. One researcher highlighted how seeing parallel concepts from different domains helped them reframe their contribution.
These studies suggest that LitPivot can support both early exploration and the refinement of an existing research direction.
[
](#supporting-scientific-discovery)
Supporting scientific discovery
At Ai2, we’re developing AI to help researchers formulate testable ideas and examine the evidence behind them. [Asta](https://allenai.org/asta) supports that effort through [theory generation from published findings (Theorizer)](https://allenai.org/blog/theorizer), synthesis, and [hypothesis generation and testing on data (AutoDiscovery)](https://allenai.org/blog/autodiscovery), while [HARPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.00620) generates promising hypotheses informed by emerging research trends. [Scideator](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3786335.3813161) lets researchers recombine elements of prior work into new ideas and assess [their novelty,](https://aclanthology.org/2025.sdp-1.9/) and [IdeaSynth](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04025) supports iterative refinement with feedback grounded in the literature.
Our recent study, [Old Ideas, Novel Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02022), examines the limits of automated novelty evaluation, showing how small prompt changes can alter an AI judge’s verdict on the same ideas. LitPivot extends this line of work by making the choice of relevant literature part of the revision process. Researchers can change which papers they use to assess a proposal as their idea develops, then use critiques and supporting excerpts to decide how to revise it. The system connects those decisions across the proposal’s problem, contribution, and evaluation plan.
We hope insights from LitPivot help scientists build on existing knowledge and turn early ideas into new contributions to their fields.

# Securing our frontier model training environment

We’ve strengthened containment for internal frontier-model training and evaluation and used our strongest models to red-team the boundaries.

Our new approach to model containment

- [Resuming frontier training with stronger defenses](#resuming-frontier-training-with-stronger-defenses)

*This post describes how we secure the environments that we use to train and evaluate frontier models. These research settings differ from those in which customers use our released models: models in development may not yet have completed safety and alignment training, and we deliberately test them under adversarial conditions to expose weaknesses. Before making models available for broader use, we conduct safety and alignment assessments and put production safeguards in place.*

In order to work with software, AI models need computing environments: digital workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and attempt different approaches to solving problems. These environments allow models to practice these skills, while also restricting what they can access or do—helping contain the consequences when models make mistakes or exhibit misaligned behavior.

But as models become more capable, they become better at finding ways around those limits. A sophisticated model might exploit a software flaw or misconfiguration to escape a sandbox, exploit an internal service to reach the live internet, or find unauthorized ways to communicate with agents in other sandboxes. The [Hugging Face incident](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/) in July, as well as [other examples of model misalignment⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/) that we’ve observed, demonstrates how models with sophisticated cyber capabilities can bypass containment during their training and evaluation.

In response to those incidents, we’ve substantially hardened the security of our research environments. Working closely with cloud providers, we’ve added new controls throughout our infrastructure, reduced the attack surface that agents can exploit, and improved our methods for detecting misaligned behavior and attempts to cross security boundaries. These protections overlap, so that containment can hold even if an individual control fails—a strategy known as *defense in depth*.

**Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access. We’ve implemented this policy and will maintain it until advances in these safeguards justify broader internet access.**

These investments have allowed us to detect and stop sophisticated misaligned behavior before it causes damage. On September 20, for example, an internal research model [exploited a misconfiguration in a DNS resolver to gain limited access to the live internet during a training run⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/). Although we contained the incident, it exposed weaknesses that required further work. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models and used that pause to further harden our infrastructure, strengthen our monitoring, and improve the systems that automatically stop runs when we detect activity that poses a serious risk.

But increasingly capable models can find vulnerabilities or misconfigurations in even the most secure systems. To ensure the resilience of our research environments against even the most powerful models, we launched a high-compute red-teaming campaign to probe weaknesses in our infrastructure. Teams of frontier-model agents were tasked with finding vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that could allow them to take unauthorized actions—like accessing the live internet, escaping security boundaries, or conducting unauthorized communication with other agents.

These red-teaming experiments discovered previously unknown software vulnerabilities, as well as misconfigurations in our research infrastructure. We’ve remediated weaknesses our red-teaming agents discovered and—where these issues were present in open-source software—have worked with the relevant maintainers, under our [Patch the Planet](https://openai.com/index/patch-the-planet/) initiative, to disclose and fix them.

As our red-teaming experiments continued, the number of vulnerabilities and misconfigurations that our agents identified declined significantly. While we view this as an encouraging signal about the strength of our infrastructure, we expect that future models will be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities of which we’re not yet aware. We therefore view continuous red-teaming as a core part of our long-term strategy for strengthening the security of our research environments. Accordingly, we’ve made high-compute red-teaming part of the [safety cases](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/) we use to evaluate whether our frontier training and evaluation runs can proceed securely. With our assessments completed and enhanced controls put in place, we resumed reinforcement learning (RL) training and internal inference of our frontier models on October 1.

In this post, we discuss how we’ve strengthened the environments we use to train and evaluate our models, and how we use our most powerful models to find and repair weaknesses in our systems.

## Our new approach to model containment

Our approach to containment starts with a paramount requirement: the limits on what an agent can access must hold even when the agent tries to circumvent them. We define a strict security boundary around the resources the agent is authorized to use and design the surrounding infrastructure to enforce that boundary—even when agents make sustained, sophisticated attempts to breach it.

Inside the security boundary, agents can have access to browsers, code execution environments, computer-use tools, and other services they might need for their tasks. Agents that are explicitly authorized to communicate can also share particular resources within the same boundary. Everything else—everything that the agent is not explicitly authorized to access—must remain out of reach. If agents can access the infrastructure that hosts them, communicate with agents outside permitted channels, or reach external systems, that constitutes a failure of containment.

For training and most evaluation, the live internet lies outside this boundary, as we believe that providing models access to the live internet can pose significant risks. Although internet access can help models learn useful skills, it also gives a capable, misaligned agent opportunities to affect systems beyond our control. We’ve therefore designed the security architecture for our research environments with one overriding principle: *we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet*.



### Building an offline world

While we want to prevent models from gaining arbitrary access to the live internet, it’s also important that they learn how to browse, search for information, and work with web applications. To help them develop those skills without providing unfettered access to the live internet, we’ve built an “offline world”—a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems. All of our frontier RL runs use this offline mode of interaction.

### Enforcing isolation with defense in depth

Offline environments provide resources agents can use without accessing the live internet, but we also need to prevent agents from reaching beyond those environments. Training environments impose restrictions on what agents can access or do, but sufficiently capable or determined agents can search for ways around them: they can systematically probe their environments for weaknesses and exploit those weaknesses to take actions they were never authorized to take. As models become better at finding and exploiting these weaknesses, we need defenses that can maintain containment, even when models manage to defeat individual controls.

We address this challenge through defense in depth, with layers of protection that overlap and reinforce one another: sandboxes that restrict what our agents can access and execute, lightweight virtual machines (microVMs) that isolate agents’ execution environments from the computers hosting them, monitoring systems that detect unauthorized activity so that we can intervene in time, and network and cloud perimeters designed to maintain containment if all the preceding controls fail.

For code execution and computer-use tasks, containment begins with the environment in which the agent works. On Linux, we run restricted containers inside lightweight microVMs. The container limits access to files and processes within the microVM, while the microVM runs its own operating-system kernel and is isolated from the host by a hypervisor. We also use virtualized environments for macOS and Windows, and GPU-backed containers with user-space sandboxing for tasks that require accelerators.

The surrounding network and cloud controls are designed to maintain containment even if an agent escapes its sandbox and gains control of the host. Completely air-gapping this infrastructure—that is, disconnecting it entirely from external networks—isn’t currently feasible, since we need external connections in order to run and monitor experiments. We therefore restrict outbound internet traffic and unauthorized movement between systems, while preserving the necessary external connections. These restrictions extend to services that are reachable from the host machines, either direc

title: A Bank Trained Its Own Foundation Model to Catch Fraud — Freddy Lecue, Wells Fargo
body:
Freddy Lecue explains how Wells Fargo pre-trained its own transformer from scratch on billions of customer transactions instead of words. The model learns to predict the next transaction, and that one backbone can then be fine-tuned for fraud detection, credit line decisions, anti-money laundering and marketing. He covers the hardest part, turning tabular data like amounts, timing, merchants and zip codes into tokens, plus the model's size and training setup. On fraud, it caught more fraudulent transactions with fewer false alarms than the production XGBoost model, while staying fast enough for real-time card approvals.

title: Ultimate | Daniel Griesser
body:
Hey, a quick note before you start. Like my last posts, I dictated this one, an LLM helped me put it into structure, and we went over it together until it worked both to read and to listen to. The words are mine, the voice is not. The written version has a lot of screenshots, so whenever one matters, Iâll describe whatâs on it.
Working on [Ultimate](https://github.com/HazAT/ultimate) is the fastest Iâve ever iterated on software.
Before you ask what Ultimate is: itâs an experiment, a toy project built on [Pi Durable](https://earendil.com/posts/pi-durable/). Iâm trying to create the most malleable coding agent, or agent harness, Iâve used to date.
In essence, itâs an agent harness you talk to. It orchestrates coordinators that implement and fix small to large features: prototypes, throwaway experiments, fixes to its own core. They use worker, reviewer and scout subagents, or not, and they can do it completely hands-off. If you want to. You can also be very involved.
This is what a normal evening looks like. On the left, seven features are in flight, each with its own coordinator, workers and reviewers. In the middle, one of them is just going through the lander. On the right, the list of everything that branched off over the last few days.
How it started
I always had this idea to do something like this, but I felt like the durability layer wasnât good enough. Certainly there are others out there, but they all felt too complex, too involved and too integrated. Pi Durable made it possible, because I think it has the right balance between complexity, simplicity, and solid APIs and building blocks.
When I started Ultimate, it was literally a Claude Code session one-shotting the first version, and it was already usable with Opus 5.5. Not one sentence, though. It was a very thorough prompting and planning session, really thought through and planned out. Then I went to bed, came back, and the first version of Ultimate was already open.
And I was really surprised how well it already worked. A fully functioning web agent, with persistence, hot reloading and everything else I had asked for.
About twenty commits in, I started building Ultimate with Ultimate itself, and from that point on it evolved while I was using it. Iâm constantly adding, experimenting, testing, going back and forth on what feels good to me and what doesnât. And not just on Ultimate itself, Iâm also trying it out in different projects to find new things to polish, improve or iterate on.
It rebuilds itself while it runs
Ultimate is self-aware. It can build, analyze and test any feature itâs building on itself, and keep going while it reloads its own core.
How itâs built: the front end refreshes constantly while you build web components. On the server side, a supervisor holds the port. A new process starts and checks that it boots. If it does, the supervisor hands the port over, the browser just reconnects, and everything keeps going as it was.
That makes iteration quick and relatively safe. I think it broke maybe once, and that was because I did something weird.
Here a change just landed on main. The agent tells me the running app already picked it up without a restart, and the âReloadedâ line in the middle is the moment it happened, in the same conversation that built it.
You can even change the model in the middle of a run. Nothing really gets interrupted: everything is persistent, because Pi Durable just provides these nice primitives.
A team, not an agent
I often work on four to six features, polish passes, fixes or core changes at the same time, because the iteration loops and guardrails I built work so cleanly.
The coordinators are the real heroes of Ultimate. They do all the work. They investigate, build, design, review and ship, from mock prototypes to completely finished features.
Ultimate is worktree-based. Every feature gets its own worktree. That way, even while Ultimate itself is being built, different features can work on the same UI components. Each one tests its variation by spawning its own test server, then drives it with a browser and takes screenshots. You can see one fail a step below, read the error and simply try again.
So I say what I want fixed, I get a couple of questions, and I get back a fresh Ultimate instance at its own URL and port that I can fully interact with. I can even talk to an agent in it. And since every coordinator is just another chat, I can go in and iterate with it directly, without going through Ultimate, and then say: okay, now itâs good, ship it.
Sometimes coordinators go for quite a while and do several iteration cycles, because theyâre instructed to test and verify the work. They investigate, the workers implement and run the tests and checks, then the reviewers check. This is one coordinatorâs tree after a few rounds: three scouts, a designer, three workers, a reviewer with three specialist reviewers, and a new designer and worker already fixing what the reviewers found.
Sometimes the coordinator already sends me off to click around in the UI while the reviewers are still going. And if the reviewers find something the coordinator thinks is worth doing right away, it does it.
When I say merge, the lander takes over. Itâs an agent built into Ultimate: a coordinator tells it âthis worktree is ready to mergeâ, and the lander runs all the tests and checks and merges it into main. All of it runs on my machine, and only a green result gets pushed. And when something else landed in between and there are conflicts, it resolves them. Here it merged two features that touched the same code, fixed a test that broke in the process, and only landed once all 407 tests passed.
The lander is a standing agent, built into Ultimate. A standing agent is always there: it never gets concluded, so it keeps its conversation and everything it learned about the project. And thatâs how Ultimate is meant to be used. You create standing agents for your project that are specific to it and solve the tasks you want solved there, and you work with them interactively. Besides the lander, I have a Cloudflare standing agent that deploys.
Notes
Agents can talk to each other, and they can leave each other notes. A note is a message that doesnât trigger an agent turn. Itâs just there when the agentâs next turn starts, like giving it a hint about what happened.
For example, when a worker is deep in its task and something lands in main, its coordinator leaves it a note. The workers get these whenever something lands, when the plan changes, or when conversations affect each other. So they adjust their course on the fly towards something thatâs easier to merge and doesnât break or conflict. More or less, I have multiple engineers working on the same codebase at the same time.
This turned out to be a super helpful primitive for agents to communicate effectively and actually achieve the results I wanted. Really, the only thing I need to pay attention to is my chat with Ultimate itself. Everything else either keeps going on its own, or escalates to me with a question.
An example: side chats
The idea Iâm currently playing with is a side chat. The main Ultimate conversation just keeps going, and when I press Tab, I switch into a side chat that forks off the Ultimate conversation. There I can do some cleanup: conclude old conversations, clean up memory, use code mode to modify Ultimate itself. Or if itâs just a random question, I can ask it with the warm context of the main conversation. When Iâm done, I either summarize and inject what happened back into the main conversation, or discard it.
Ultimate didnât start by building it. It came back with an assessment and a questionnaire, five decisions with its own picks marked, like the layout or whether the summary wakes the main agent. Next to it, the first preview it built: the main conversation on the left, the side chat on the right, with âDiscardâ and âSummarize & injectâ at the bottom.
Only when I give the go does it hand the coordinator the instructions to implement it.
And when I read the replies, I sometimes uncover things that donât really make sense, or could be simpler. Since Ultimate knows exactly which conversations are ongoing and whatâs going on, it can immediately interject and steer all of them in parallel. Here I asked whether we could take something out of the system prompt and inject it instead. Ultimate found it cleaner than its own plan and told the side-chat branch to do it my way. Underneath, the arrow points at a note from that branch: FYI, no action, so it didnât wake anyone.
This chart is a fun little experiment, visualizing the actual flow and tool calls on a timeline. Ultimate is on top, the side chatâs coordinator below it, and its designer and worker at the end. The dashed lines show how often the side chat reported back to Ultimate because it needed something, and when it just left a note and didnât wake it, because there was only a progress update. The visualization isnât ideal yet, I havenât spent enough time polishing it, but it gets the idea across.
Everything is on record
With Pi Durable itâs easy to keep perfect context. The agent can read any action of any conversation of any subagent, which makes it super easy to analyze behaviors and codify them.
Regularly, we go back and ask Ultimate itself to inspect tool calls and failed tool calls, so we can codify tools, remove the ones we donât use anymore, and just get rid of old stuff. Here Ultimate read through the onboarding of my blogâs instance and explained the two things that went wrong, a failed first memory write and some guesswork in code mode, each with its cause and the fix it had already started.
I also throw away features way more often now. Very often I think something is a good solution to a problem, realize it doesnât really add anything, and remove it again.
The small things
Then there are all the small things you build when you live in a tool every day.
If I review code, itâs usually after Iâve merged something to main. But occasionally I want to check how something actually works before we land it, and give better guidance, so I quickly built myself a review tool that is fully integrated into the agent: a diff where I can leave a comment on any line. The small labels and titles, and sometimes even the state, come from a small summary model that any part of Ultimate can ask.
Thereâs also an API, and I use [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) to reach any running Ultimate on any machine I have. The cool thing is that Ultimates find each other and can talk to each other. So when I change Ultimate itself, I can tell another instance what changed and what to do, and it reports back to the main one with any bugs it uncovers.
Since I already use Ultimate in more projects than Ultimate itself, I obviously also built an updater: it shows whatâs new on main and the other instances pick up new prompts and extensions live. And because I donât want to lose any conversation, I built my own database backup. I can move a project to a different machine, restore it with a single command, and have the perfect context back.
Ultimate on my blog
Of course I also started an Ultimate instance for my blog, and primed it with previous conversations I had with Pi about it.
It creates subagents and services on the fly. I work with it, it keeps building the UI, and I iterate with it. It took me about ten minutes until I had my own personalized agent on my blog that does exactly the flow I wanted. That agent is the writer, a standing agent that helps me write and polish my posts and takes care of everything around the narration, from the spoken script to the audio you might be listening to right now.
It finished with a full assessment of my project and my past conversations, and came up with really good suggestions for what to build and how. Seven questions, from a standing writing agent to a confirm dialog before anything costs money, each with its pick already marked. Very often I just take what

title: How to Let AI Agents Sign Up for Your App Safely — Isabelle Williams, WorkOS
body:
Isabelle Williams, a product manager at WorkOS, uses a travel app she built to show how to make an app ready for users who arrive as agents. She covers auth.md, an open file that tells agents how to get access; an anonymous mode where an agent can try the app before a person claims its work; and ID-JAG identity assertions, which let the agent's provider vouch for the user so nobody has to fill in a signup form. In a live demo, an agent signs up, plans a trip and books dinner on its own. She then shows how to give an in-app agent its own scoped token so it can be audited, limited and revoked without touching the user's access.

title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
body:
Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment.
The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications.
Together, the ecosystem announcements below point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing — along with its growing demand for what comes next.
On Friday, Oct. 23, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang visited Astana, meeting with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev at the Akorda Presidential Palace and joining Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev — Kazakhstan’s minister of AI and digital development — for a public fireside chat at the [Alem.AI](http://alem.ai) program.
Jensen Huang and Kazakhstan’s AI Minister Speak at Alem.AI
In their fireside chat at Alem.AI, Kazakhstan’s international center for artificial intelligence, Madiyev and Huang discussed the country’s push to become an AI nation — building the energy and computing infrastructure to support homegrown AI and applying it across the economy.
Madiyev said Kazakhstan wants AI that reflects its language and culture. “We want AI that understands and speaks Kazakh and captures cultural contexts and cultural specifics,” he said, describing the country’s work on Kazakh-language models.
Huang said Kazakhstan could turn its energy resources into a foundation for AI production — and a new kind of export. “Instead of just exporting energy, in the future, you could transform energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” he said.
He also argued that local data is central to that ambition: it embodies a country’s culture, history and values. “Your country’s data is your natural resource. It belongs to you.”
The conversation also turned to physical AI. Madiyev pointed to Kazakhstan’s factories, mines, agriculture, transport and logistics as potential areas for development, asking how the country could become a hub for training models for robots and other physical systems.
Huang called the idea “fantastic,” saying physical AI could transform industries from mining and mineral processing to agriculture.
Huang said AI and robotics can help people do more, but ambition will shape how fully they seize that opportunity. He applied the idea to Kazakhstan, saying AI could help lift the country and its people.
“If you have ambition, and I believe you do, AI will lift your nation,” Huang said. “AI will lift your people.”
Huang also praised the founders of Higgsfield AI, the Kazakhstan-founded startup, and it was announced NVIDIA is making an investment into the startup during the event. “The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” he said, describing the founders as visionary and pointing to their effort to compete globally.
Asked about AI security, Huang said the technology must be developed and deployed responsibly. He described NVIDIA’s OpenShell as a way to contain AI agents by limiting their access to files and tools and monitoring their activity.
For young people entering a fast-changing field, Huang recommended learning how AI works — not just how to use it. He said aspiring AI programmers should understand the technology’s principles, strengths and weaknesses, combining technical knowledge with the ability to work effectively with AI.
“I envy being 18 years old today… because the world is changing so rapidly, and there’s a complete reset because of technology.”
The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling
The visits coincided with a signing ceremony marking Firebird’s investment agreement with the government of Kazakhstan, held at the presidential palace.
Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027.
A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships.
Firebird cofounder and CEO Razmig Hovaghimian attended the signing ceremony at the Akorda Presidential Palace alongside government officials.
“What began as a seed of an idea 180 days ago has grown into a major investment in Kazakhstan’s AI future,” said Razmig Hovaghimian, co-Founder and CEO of Firebird. “President Tokayev’s vision gave us the confidence to think bigger about what we can build together. With Jensen Huang here today, that ambition feels more tangible than ever. We’re building the infrastructure for Kazakhstan’s talent and ideas to reach the world.”
Kazakhtelecom, the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty.
Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale.
AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute
The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them.
Higgsfield is expanding its AI infrastructure with NVIDIA Vera Rubin running on cloud service providers, giving the company additional capacity as models, products and customer demand for its generative media applications grow.
More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute.
Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications.
Today’s announcements represent different layers of that stack — infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale.
Watch the fireside chat between Jensen Huang and Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, [streamed live from Alem.AI in Astana](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=d0j58QNeRmc).
Watch NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s [GTC Berlin keynote in replay](https://www.youtube.com/live/PvFjbPYEOZI?si=ZeL5KIaqxfXgrI8z).

title: An alignment assessment of the UK AISI cybertesting incident
body:
On August 4, 2026, the [UK AI Security Institute (AISI)](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/incident-report-unsanctioned-agent-behaviour-during-cyber-testing) published a report that detailed some concerning behavior it observed from Claude Mythos 5 during its testing of the model’s cyber capabilities. In AISI’s evaluation, Mythos 5 was given a capture-the-flag (CTF) cybersecurity challenge, in which it was asked to retrieve a protected piece of data (the “flag”) from a simulated network. Internet access was deliberately enabled (this was standard for AISI’s cyber testing at the time, but is no longer). The cyber safeguards we deploy with general release models like Fable 5 were disabled. In nine of AISI’s 43 evaluation runs, Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions (i.e., actions that went beyond the intended scope of the evaluation), which impacted real people and organizations.
In this post, which is being published alongside an [independent report](http://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/investigating-alignment-failures-in-aisis-incident) from AISI, we investigate these behaviors from Claude Mythos 5 further, to understand what they reveal about the model’s alignment. Like AISI’s report, we concentrate on the transcript (the complete record of the model’s reasoning and actions) from a single evaluation run. In this run:
- To capture the flag, Claude Mythos 5 was tasked with breaking into a small network of computers that AISI had built for the test, designed to resemble a real organization’s systems.
- It attempted—unsuccessfully—a range of approaches that targeted these systems using the methods that the evaluation intended.
- However, it also quickly found evidence that one of these machines periodically contacted GitHub, which hosts code repositories.
- After its initial, within-bounds attempts failed, Mythos 5 searched GitHub for a repository that it believed one of the machines downloaded software from automatically. This repository, however, actually belonged to unrelated human developers.
- Mythos 5 attempted to submit malicious code to the repository, reasoning that doing so would infect the CTF's machine when it next downloaded the code, and, therefore, could compromise the machine.
- The model then created fake user identities that contacted the maintainer of the repository in an attempt to pressure them into approving the code change. These identifies claimed, falsely, that the code was safe and helpful.
- The maintainers refused to accept the code change, and Mythos 5’s run eventually timed out.
This behavior would have been flagged immediately by our production safeguards on Fable 5, had they been enabled. Nevertheless, this behavior is important to study because the underlying failures here are not necessarily specific to cyber incidents like these. They speak to wider issues with the model’s conduct in evaluation settings; our models’ desired behavior remains a critical part of how we intend to ensure they behave responsibly.
The other eight transcripts were similar to the one described above. In each case, Claude Mythos 5 departed from the intended method for completing a CTF task, and took actions that impacted the real world. From an alignment perspective, we judge the primary transcript (above) to be equally severe or more severe than these other eight. In particular, the primary transcript showed the greatest degree of deception, in the form of Mythos 5’s attempts at social engineering to get its code change approved. Given this (and the degree of the transcripts’ similarities otherwise), we focused on completing one more exhaustive review of the primary transcript, and reviewed the other eight transcripts in less detail. This allowed us to run a large volume of experiments on the primary transcript, and thereby understand the root causes of the issues in more detail. We replayed the transcript from various points, and experimented with altering parts of the model’s prior context to examine how new information would have impacted the model’s behavior.
We judge Claude Mythos 5’s misalignment in the primary transcript to be comparable in severity to the Mythos 5 incident we [discussed on September 9](https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents), in which the model uploaded a malicious package to PyPi during another CTF task. This assessment is based on our judgment of the model’s behavior in two respects: overreach, or how far the model went beyond the intended scope of the task, and dishonesty, or the extent to which the model misrepresented its actions or intentions.
On overreach, the misalignment in this incident was somewhat less severe than in the PyPi incident. Here, before it turned to an attack, Claude Mythos 5 tried several approaches that would have been within the intended scope of the task; a task misconfiguration made it difficult (or potentially impossible) for the model to pursue those within-scope solutions successfully.
On dishonesty, however, Mythos 5 went further than in the PyPi incident. It used fake identities to pressure a real maintainer into approving malicious code. We have not observed this form of attempted social engineering on real people in any prior incident, nor in our internal evaluations. We interpret this as a severe form of dishonesty, rather than some new form or category of misalignment: as in the September 9 incident, Mythos 5 used these tactics exclusively in pursuit of its assigned task, and did not pursue any goals of its own devising.
On both overreach and dishonesty, we consider the primary incident to be more severe than any of the cases described in our [October 9 post](https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-unintended-model-actions). And, for context, this incident is of a very different nature to the OpenAI–Hugging Face incident that was recently investigated by OpenAI and METR. That incident saw several unique misaligned behaviors (like very large-scale coordination between agents to attack a production system), though it did not see a model trying to deceive an individual human in the same way.
Newer models appear substantially less likely to initiate the attack described here. We replayed the incident transcript with Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Opus 5.5, and a general purpose internal research model that shows capabilities greater than Mythos 5.1. Those three models began the attack between 0% and 13% of the time, relative to 83% for Mythos 5. Our newest models also proved to be much less likely to continue the attack once they realized it was causing real-world harm. Across our testing, in the immediate next few turns of the transcript, Mythos 5 never once decided to stop its attack, and Mythos 5.1 did so only very rarely. But Opus 5.5 and our internal research model stopped spontaneously 10% and 67% of the time—and we expect these rates to understate the true likelihood that these models would have ceased their attacks, since our tests only examined the model’s next few turns. Although we can’t be sure, we suspect that improvements to our alignment training have helped to mitigate Mythos 5’s behaviors in subsequent models.
We worked with AISI to complete this analysis of Claude Mythos 5’s alignment. A small number of researchers at both organizations were permitted to analyze the full, unredacted transcripts; a larger group accessed versions with sensitive information redacted. We provided AISI with regular updates on the progress of our assessment, held joint research meetings, and, to assist them in their analysis, shared information not otherwise available to AISI, such as the outputs of our interpretability tooling. We timed our publication to align with AISI’s own report into this incident. Their independent report is available [here](http://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/investigating-alignment-failures-in-aisis-incident).
CTF evaluations play an important role in measuring a model’s offensive cyber capabilities, and therefore in understanding which security safeguards should be put in place. AISI has [publicly committed](https://www.aisi.gov.uk/blog/building-a-more-secure-environment-for-evaluating-dangerous-capabilities) to running these evaluations without internet access until it has developed stronger internet access controls that would prevent models from causing real-world harm during their attempts to complete them.
The remainder of this post is structured as follows. In the first section, we summarize our overall findings about the alignment of Claude Mythos 5 in these transcripts. In the second, we describe our assessment’s methodology in more detail, before turning to our full analysis of the primary transcript. Then, we briefly address the other eight transcripts, before concluding with a wider discussion of how this incident compares to the others that we’ve recently documented.
Alignment assessment summary
In this section, we summarize our findings in more detail. As described above, Claude Mythos 5 turned to attacking a GitHub project after its in-scope (that is, within the rules) attempts to complete the CTF had failed. Its attack unfolded over nine “compaction cycles”—points at which the model summarized its progress and wrote notes to guide its next stretch of work. The figure below divides these cycles into four phases. In the first two cycles (“pre-attack”), the model mostly worked within scope, but began considering a GitHub attack increasingly seriously. At the start of cycle 3 (“starting attack”), it began scouting for a specific GitHub project to target. Later in cycle 3 (“early attack”), it took its first actions that affected real third parties, though even at this stage it potentially could have changed course. From cycle 4 onward (“mid-to-late attack”), it took its most serious actions and became very unlikely to change its trajectory in response to signs it was causing harm.
To better understand the model’s behavior during this incident, we replayed (resampled) it many times, each time without granting the model access to the real internet or tools. In each replay, we varied parts of the transcript or varied which model we used for sampling. We also asked the model targeted questions about its behavior. We describe our assessment techniques in more detail in the following section.
We sought to address three questions in relation to this incident:
- Why did Claude Mythos 5 begin the attack?
- Why did Claude Mythos 5 not stop the attack once it began?
- Would newer models behave differently than Claude Mythos 5?
A summary of our findings is as follows.
Why did Claude Mythos 5 begin the attack? Our experiments suggest that Mythos 5 only began the attack after attempting approaches to solve the CTF that were in-scope. However, due to a misconfiguration in the task’s instructions, solving the task using in-scope routes would have been very difficult, if not impossible. Given this, the key alignment failure we observed was that Mythos 5 disregarded signs of potential harm when it subsequently pursued out-of-scope approaches to the task. This failure is most clearly evidenced by the fact the model rarely mentioned harm in its chain of thought (CoT). Before the attack, only one of the 19 points where Mythos 5 discussed solving the CTF by accessing GitHub mentioned the possibility of causing harm to real people. When we edited Mythos 5’s CoT around these points to note this possibility, and then continued the model’s work from a later point, Mythos 5 went from pursuing the attack on 83% of occasions to 13%.
Why did Claude Mythos 5 not stop the attack? In our replays of the transcript, it proved very difficult to shift Mythos 5 away from the attack once it began, unless we offered some other, clearer path toward completing the challenge. When we resampled Mythos 5 from points in the middle or late periods of its attack, the model only stopped on its own in 2% of trajectories. Even when we edited the transcript to include evidence that it was on the incorrect pa

title: Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
body:
Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
Claude Duet is a proactive agent that works for you, even while you’re away. It builds on two layers of protection: safety training in the Claude model itself and the safeguards that exist in products like Claude Code and Claude Managed Agents. On top of those, we added new protections for working across your accounts and acting on your behalf.
[Claude Duet (opens in new tab)](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-duet) is an agent, currently in research preview, that uses a cloud-based computer to do work for you. It can use all the apps and services you've chosen to connect to Claude, and it runs continuously even after you close the app. It can read your inbox, draft replies, book things, and run routines while you are away. Our team runs Claude Duet on our own accounts and we use it for work every day.
We built Claude Duet on three principles to guide the agent's behavior:
- Your information, and what other people share in your connected apps, is handled with discretion, using a new classifier that checks messages Claude Duet drafts before they go out.
- You stay in control of what it does on your behalf.
- Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, sign-in tokens, or other credentials.
Claude Duet is new but the thinking behind it is not. In 2025 we [published our framework for safe and trustworthy agents (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/news/our-framework-for-developing-safe-and-trustworthy-agents), which puts people in control and treats privacy and secure interactions as basic requirements. Since then, we have written about why [no single defense is enough (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/research/trustworthy-agents) and why [protection inside the model can’t stand alone (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/how-we-contain-claude). We also build and operate the infrastructure businesses use to run agents in production through [Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents), and Claude Duet keeps credentials separate from the agent in the same way. It builds on this work, adding the protections that an agent acting for you needs. This post walks through what we added and what we’re still working on.
You approve important actions
An agent that acts while you’re away has to know when to stop and ask for permission before proceeding, and to do it at the right cadence. Before Claude Duet does something like sending a potentially sensitive message, paying for something, or deleting anything, it shows you the action, the destination, and the content, including every recipient. It then waits for you to approve the action.
A separate, automated check runs alongside each action, built on [the auto mode classifier from Claude Code (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-auto-mode) and extended for Claude Duet. It assesses whether the action matches your intent. The check runs outside the model doing the work so instructions hidden in a page cannot affect the outcome.
Some actions stay off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities, banking actions such as moving money between accounts, and accessing someone else's account. Some other steps aren’t covered by a "don't ask me again" rule, however often you have approved them, like paying or sending money, deleting an order, or creating an account. The routines that run while you are away have the same safeguards.
We spent a lot of time calibrating how often Claude Duet asks for approval. Approval fatigue is a serious issue, because too many requests teach people to tap through them, sometimes without adequate consideration. We will continue to adjust this calibration over time.
For purchases, Claude Duet pays with a one-time card from a wallet like Link from Stripe, limited to that merchant and amount. You see the item and the total, and you approve the purchase in your Link app. Your real card number isn’t shared with Claude Duet or the merchant.
Your information is handled with discretion
An agent that reads your email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where different types of information should go. If you ask Claude Duet to send your team a weekly recap, it should include only things everyone on the team already has access to and never private details, like your performance review conversations.
To address this, we built a new safety classifier that runs separately from the main model and checks whether each message Claude Duet is about to send contains potentially sensitive information. We categorize this information into two tiers:
- Never share: We give the most sensitive protection to information like sign-in credentials, full card and bank account numbers, and government ID numbers. Claude Duet is instructed never to share these with anyone, even if you ask.
- Needs consent to share: Claude Duet will share other private information, such as health or finances, only if you’ve explicitly approved it. Your own request counts as consent, so “send a note to my dentist about my tooth pain” generally won’t need additional approval.
If Claude Duet is blocked for either reason, it can decide to rewrite the message without the sensitive information and share with you for approval.
Claude Duet is still in research preview and these safeguards will occasionally miss something or flag a harmless message. That’s why they work alongside the approval mechanisms above, which are designed to keep you in control of what Claude Duet sends on your behalf. We expect to continue iterating on our classifier as we learn more about how people use Claude Duet.
You have visibility into tasks and connected apps
You can see what Claude Duet has done and is doing in its task list, where each task has its own page, and steer it mid-task. Claude Duet keeps your conversation history and its memory so it can carry context between tasks, until you delete your history or reset it. Deleting your account wipes everything Claude Duet has stored.
The apps you have connected to Claude carry over to Claude Duet, and switching an app off in one place switches it off in both. Disconnecting an app stops new access from that moment, but what Claude Duet already learned from it stays until you reset its memory, which you can do anytime from the app’s settings. Claude Duet also uses the memory from your Claude account, so details Claude remembered from your earlier chats are visible.
Credentials and the browser are isolated from the model
Claude Duet never sees your passwords, browser cookies, or the sign-in tokens for your connected apps, and it can’t save them to its memory. They only ever pass through separate machines the model can’t access, and the approvals and safety checks that govern what it does run there too.
Passwords
When a site asks for a password, you type it into a form inside the Claude app. The form encrypts it with a single-use key that exists only on our secure cloud browser machine, for that one single use. It passes the encrypted password unopened to the browser, which types it into the site. The model doesn’t see the password and can’t save or repeat it. Soon you will also be able to sign in with 1Password; Claude Duet will ask for a credential, you will approve that request in 1Password, and the credential will go to the browser without passing through the model.
An agent that signs in for you changes phishing in two ways. On one hand, Claude Duet doesn’t hold credentials for you so it can’t be phished for a password, and no hidden instruction can make it reveal a secret it doesn’t have. On the other hand, the sign-in form is itself a target, because anything that asks for a password can be imitated. So Claude Duet’s sign-in form only appears inside the app, during a sign-in you asked for. It never arrives as a link, a text message, an email, or a website other than claude.ai. If something that looks like Claude Duet asks for your password anywhere else, it’s not legitimate.
Sign-in tokens
When Claude Duet works in a connected app, it follows [our Claude Managed Agents design (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents) so credentials stay out of reach of the agent’s work. Credentials that the agent uses on your behalf, such as a sign-in token for a connected service, never enter the machine where the agent works. A placeholder for the credential sits there instead and a proxy outside that machine puts in the real value only as a request is made.
The browser
Your browser in Claude Duet runs in its own dedicated virtual machine in the cloud, separate from the model and from the cloud computers the agent works on. The agent drives the browser only through a fixed set of commands: open this page, click here, type this. Whatever a site runs [stays on the browser machine (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/managed-agents). The site’s code and cookies don’t reach Claude Duet’s memory or your connected apps, and none of the agent’s commands can read cookies out of the browser. What does come back is the page's text and downloads, because the agent has to read them to do its job. That’s why the other checks exist, and why Claude Duet also uses the prompt-injection safeguards described in our [browser-use research (opens in new tab)](https://www.anthropic.com/research/prompt-injection-defenses). Files it uploads through the browser get the same sensitive-information check as its messages.
Claude Duet is also designed to identify itself as an agent. Today, requests that its web browser sends include a distinct User-Agent header, and we publish the public IP addresses it browses from, so sites can recognize it and decide how to treat it. Before launch, we also contacted several large websites and gave them the option to prevent Claude Duet from visiting their sites, and some chose to. We’ll keep refining how Claude Duet identifies itself as we learn from the research preview.
How we tested Claude Duet
Testing started well before the research preview and continues now. Our Safeguards team built evaluations from routine-shaped tasks, each in three variants: an innocent version, one with injected instructions, and one that tempts the agent to do more than it was asked. Those run alongside shadow traffic from real use.
Red teams further tested whether Claude Duet would leak information, act without approval, or follow malicious prompts. We built a threat model of the whole system, across the repositories and trust boundaries it touches. An external penetration-testing firm tested Claude Duet with access to our source code, and a follow-on engagement covering the cloud browser and the sign-in form is running now. Each new credential feature is red-teamed on an isolated rig before it ships to anyone.
Claude Duet is also in scope of Anthropic’s public bug bounty program, which rewards valid reports and offers safe harbor for good-faith research, under our responsible disclosure policy. If you find a security vulnerability, we want to hear about it: report it through Anthropic’s bug bounty program on [HackerOne (opens in new tab)](https://hackerone.com/anthropic).
Building this with you
We’re releasing Claude Duet as a research preview because we want to learn what you value in a personal agent, including the protections and controls you’d like to see next. Some of what’s described here is still changing: how often it asks for approval, how you sign in, and how well the sensitive-information checks tell what’s private from what’s harmless. Tell Claude Duet in plain words what you’d like to see or what went wrong, and it will file a report for our team.

title: Claude Cowork and chat come together for Enterprise
body:
Claude Cowork and chat come together for Enterprise
Chat and Cowork first [came together](https://claude.com/resources/articles/cowork-is-now-claude) for Pro and Max plans in September. The same unified Claude experience is now generally available for Claude Enterprise plans.
Chat and Cowork are now one Claude on web, desktop, and mobile, so your team can ask a quick question or hand over a full project in the same conversation. Agentic work runs in a cloud environment that Anthropic manages, and Claude Enterprise admins control access by role and manage usage with a new Efficient mode.
One Claude for every task
Team members no longer choose between chat and Cowork before they start work with Claude. Conversations begin as a chat, and a simple question still gets a quick answer. When a task needs to run code or work with files, Claude continues in the cloud and returns the finished document, analysis, or deck. Because the work runs in the cloud, it keeps going after someone closes their laptop, and they can pick it up on the web, desktop, or mobile. Chats, projects, connectors, skills, and plugins carry over to the new unified experience.
Organizations are already seeing value from the unified Claude experience across their teams:
“Work at Carvana doesn’t happen only behind a desk. The unified Claude experience lets employees start a task on their computer and pick it up on their phone, with notifications when Claude has results or needs their input. It fits the way our teams work, whether they’re at their desks or visiting a site.”
“Before chat and Cowork capabilities were unified, they were separate experiences that had to be used and managed independently. Bringing them together has made everything simpler, both for our users and administrators. The transition was seamless, nothing broke across our connectors, skills or MCPs, and we’re confident rolling it out more broadly.”
“We no longer have to choose between chat and Cowork. With under ten minutes of prompting, Claude worked through stacks of county, state and federal budgets and public meeting documents, mapped how the funding streams connect, and produced a comprehensive report that would have taken our team weeks. I never had to decide which tool to use for which step. That report will shape our strategic plan and upcoming budget process.”
“Bringing chat and Cowork together answers what clients kept asking us, ‘which Claude should I use’ and ‘which one does what’. It adapts to how and where you work across mobile, desktop and browser. At Quantium, it’s helping us scale our own AI ambitions and what we can do for our clients.”
Maintaining security
If your organization has already approved Claude chat, this builds on the enterprise controls you already use, including single sign-on (SSO) and the Compliance API. Anthropic still encrypts data in transit and at rest and doesn’t use it for model training by default.
Claude does agentic work in cloud sessions, each running in its own isolated virtual machine with network egress off by default for Claude Enterprise and connector credentials kept outside the sandbox. Because that work runs in one environment that Anthropic manages, your security team gets central visibility and controls over it. The [security best practices guide](https://trust.anthropic.com/resources?s=3puokpm2aa1nn24nbcp0l&name=unified-claude-security-best-practices) on the Anthropic Trust Center covers the full architecture.
Managing cost
Claude Enterprise pricing stays usage-based. The newest Claude models are more efficient than their predecessors: billed through usage, Claude Opus 5.5 costs 40% less to run than Claude Opus 5 on typical workloads, and Claude Sonnet 5.5 costs up to 30% less than Claude Sonnet 5 for most work.
Depending on the task, agentic work can use more tokens than a quick chat. Claude Enterprise admins have four controls for managing this usage. Efficient mode is a new setting that keeps the unified Claude experience on Sonnet and Haiku models. Model entitlements set which models each role can use. Spend limits apply at the organization, group, and member level, and pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly amount to draw from.
Getting started
The unified Claude experience is generally available today for Claude Enterprise plans. Admins can manage the rollout in Organization settings. Organizations that use zero data retention for Claude Code, a HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys stay on their current configuration.
See the [admin setup guide](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/17444462) for details. If you're an existing Claude Enterprise customer, you'll receive an email about the rollout for your organization.

title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
body:
Updated • 60 • 1
[
](#does-your-model-run-on-aws-trainium-look-it-up)
Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
[Update on GitHub](https://github.com/huggingface/blog/blob/main/torch-neuronx-model-support.md)
In a [previous post](https://huggingface.co/blog/hf-torchneuron), we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx
package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?
The [torch-neuronx model support](https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support) Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.
[
](#look-up-a-model)
Look up a model
The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.
To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc
) and of Transformers to look at.
At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to
text-generation
andimage-text-to-text
models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.
[
](#run-it-yourself)
Run it yourself
Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py
script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the [TorchNeuron announcement](https://huggingface.co/blog/hf-torchneuron): it loads the model with from_pretrained
, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron")
.
On a Trainium2 (trn2
) instance with that stack, for example in the [AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container](https://github.com/aws-neuron/deep-learning-containers#torch-neuronx), install the packages, then run:
python3 run.py
No need for torchrun
: the script launches its own torch.distributed
ranks when the model is sharded.
A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public [NEFF cache](https://huggingface.co/buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache) bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:
hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache
[
](#what-runs-means)
What "runs" means
Each test loads the model on a trn2
instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.
At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS
says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.
[
](#the-results-are-a-dataset)
The results are a dataset
Everything the Space shows comes from the public [ aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support](https://huggingface.co/datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support) dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of
neuronx-cc
and library versions.Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py
that ran. You can query it directly:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_parquet("hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data")
df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B"][["neuronx_cc", "library", "library_version", "neuron_cores", "result"]]
The [dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support) gives the exact meaning of each result.
Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, [look it up](https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support).

# Anima helps clinics cut call waits by 75% with GPT‑6 and GPT‑Live

Anima expands what care teams can do with OpenAI models, giving them more capacity to respond to patients.

[Start building with OpenAI](https://openai.com/startups/)

- [Helping patients’ calls get through, and helping care teams serve them](#helping-patients-calls-get-through-and-helping-care-teams-serve-them)
- [Clearing 100,000 documents within days](#clearing-100000-documents-within-days)
- [Drafting clinical notes in seconds](#drafting-clinical-notes-in-seconds)
- [Building capacity for care that follows need](#building-capacity-for-care-that-follows-need)

Patient requests, clinical letters, and consultation notes all create work that care teams must review and act on. When that work builds up, patients can wait longer for a response, and important information can sit in queues.

[Anima⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.animahealth.com/) brings these workflows into one platform, with specialized AI teammates that gather patient histories, process documents, and draft clinical notes for care teams. Its vision is personalized healthcare for everyone, guided by the conviction that care should follow need.

Anima began in the UK, where it now serves over 14 million patients across more than 1,000 clinics and processes more than 800,000 cases a month. It’s expanding into the US, Australia, and beyond. The company uses GPT‑6 models in its document workflows and GPT‑Live for calls, selecting OpenAI after benchmarking all closed-source and open-source models, according to Shun Pang, Anima’s CEO and co-founder.

> *“We chose OpenAI for Anima’s mission-critical workloads because of superior intelligence, intelligence per dollar, and steerability with in-context learning.”*

—Shun Pang, Co-founder and CEO, Anima

## Helping patients’ calls get through, and helping care teams serve them

Before he started Anima, Shun had gone through clinical training, where he saw a patient miss potentially life-saving care because abnormal test results sat in a queue for six months. He came to believe that the problem with healthcare wasn’t about medicine, but about how information moved through the system. He built Anima to give care teams more capacity to respond to patients’ needs. The platform brings patient requests, clinical documents, and follow-up work into one place.

Anima’s AI receptionist, Andi, is built on GPT‑Live. Patients can describe their symptoms over the phone to Andi, while Anima’s proprietary policy engine guides the conversation through deterministic, clinically approved intake workflows. GPT‑5.4 mini then selects the appropriate questionnaire, and the completed medical history appears as a structured case in the clinic dashboard. Doctors and clinic staff can review the case and take action from there.

Anima reports that clinics using Andi have reduced phone waits from 40 to 50 minutes to 10 minutes, a reduction of at least 75%. In Anima’s patient surveys, 86% said they would use Andi again. Anima found that people in their 80s and 90s were among its happiest users. “They’re very happy to talk to a voice agent,” says Shun. “It’s infinitely patient and very polite.”

## Clearing 100,000 documents within days

Anima’s Documents product uses GPT‑6 models to extract information from incoming clinical documents such as the sender, recipient, document type, and event dates. A multi-stage pipeline then matches each document to the correct patient, identifies the appropriate clinical codes, and suggests the next action for clinic staff to review.

Clinical coding proved to be one of the hardest technical problems to solve. “There are around 800,000 possible SNOMED codes,” says Michael Skupien, Engineering Lead at Anima. “Only a fraction are used regularly, but different practices still make different decisions about which codes to use.”

Rather than ask clinics to configure the system or fine-tune separate models for each customer, Anima uses in-context learning to adapt model decisions to each practice. This approach requires models that can follow instructions consistently.

> “All of OpenAI’s models are really good at following instructions, easy to steer, and reliable in that steering.”

—Michael Skupien, Engineering Lead, Anima

According to Anima, practices that used to process about 15 documents per hour typically process 30 to 45. Top-performing clinics process 45 to 60. “We’ve seen clinics clear document backlogs of more than 100,000 documents within days of adopting Anima,” says Shun. “That means important updates and medication changes reach clinicians promptly instead of sitting in a queue for months.”

## Drafting clinical notes in seconds

As patients share critical information, doctors need to split their attention between listening and taking notes for the medical record. Anima built its Scribe product with GPT 5.6 Luna to turn consultation transcripts into structured clinical notes, and then reuse that same clinical context to draft referral letters and patient follow-up messages.



Instead of typing throughout the appointment, a doctor can give more of their attention to the patient. Anima reports that consultation notes that once took several minutes to write are drafted in seconds for the clinician’s review. Referral letters that often required 5 to 15 minutes to produce can also be drafted within seconds from the consultation and patient record, ready for the clinician to review.

“Patients receive clear follow-up messages shortly after the consultation, reducing anxiety and improving recall,” says Shun. “We often hear that doctors now finish their day on time instead of working until 8 or 9 p.m.”

## Building capacity for care that follows need

Anima’s vision is personalized healthcare for everyone. That requires care teams to have the information, time, and capacity to understand each person’s needs and act on them across the whole patient journey.

Its work with OpenAI models supports practical steps towards that vision. Andi gathers information over the phone and turns it into structured requests for staff to act on. Documents helps teams process incoming clinical information. Scribe drafts notes and follow-up communications for clinicians to review.

Anima reports that most cases across its platform are resolved within 24 hours, with a median resolution time of approximately 3.5 hours. “We’re having a huge impact on 14 million patients in the UK supported by OpenAI’s models,” Shun says. “It’s really mission-critical for the patients and the clinics.”

Anima gives teams more room to care today, and helps them build pathways and services for the future.
