# OpenAI and Poland’s NASK partner to advance AI safety and security

Loading…

Share

OpenAI and Poland’s NASK National Research Institute have signed an agreement to explore collaboration on AI safety, security and technical research. The partnership will bring together expertise from both organizations to better understand emerging risks, strengthen safeguards, and explore how advanced AI can contribute to a more secure and resilient digital ecosystem.

As AI systems become more capable, international collaboration between developers and public research institutions will be essential to understanding their risks and building stronger safeguards. OpenAI’s existing work with the US Center for Advancing Standards and Innovation for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), UK AI Security Institute (AISI) and other public research institutions around the world has already helped strengthen safeguards, identify and fix security vulnerabilities in AI agents, and advance frontier AI safety.

Through the agreement, NASK’s AI Safety Research Center – serving as the Polish Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute (AISI) – and OpenAI will collaborate on AI safety research, exploring ways to evaluate increasingly capable AI systems, identify potential vulnerabilities and strengthen safeguards.

> “Collaboration with OpenAI is a natural step for the Institute and its AI Safety Research Center, which is actively involved in AI safety research. This work spans developing safeguards against emerging risks, detecting synthetic AI-generated content, and understanding both its malicious uses and the multilingual aspects of these challenges. AI safety cannot be achieved in isolation. It is a collaborative effort, and only through active cooperation between public AI Safety Institutes and frontier AI developers can we ensure that AI becomes truly reliable and safe to use. By combining our research expertise with OpenAI’s technical capabilities, we can better anticipate risks, strengthen safeguards, and build public trust in these transformative technologies.”

*—Radosław Nielek, Director of NASK*

> “Poland is home to exceptional scientists and technical talent, many of whom have helped lead OpenAI’s own research. As AI becomes more capable, it’s vital that we draw on expertise beyond our own organization to challenge our assumptions, test our systems and strengthen safeguards.This agreement with NASK opens the door to doing that together, bringing Poland’s research expertise into the international effort to make AI safer.”

*—Tom Duff Gordon, VP and Head of EMEA Policy at OpenAI*

OpenAI has [called](https://openai.com/index/building-standards-next-phase-ai/) for the US to work with countries around the world on international technical standards for frontier AI, drawing on the expertise of AI safety institutes and standards bodies. Common approaches to evaluating capabilities, assessing risks, testing safeguards and reporting incidents can help countries compare evidence and respond to risks that cross borders. The collaboration with NASK reflects the value of bringing national expertise into this wider effort.

In NASK’s case, this expertise rests on extensive research in AI safety, applied directly to protecting public services and Poland’s digital information ecosystem. Without national partners like NASK, global AI safety standards may remain detached from the realities in which AI is actually used.

The agreement also builds on OpenAI’s existing work with cyber defenders in Poland. In July, CERT Polska, which operates within NASK, [gained access⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.nask.pl/aktualnosci/nask-z-przelomowym-narzedziem-od-openai?utm_source=chatgpt.com) to OpenAI’s cyber capable models through Daybreak. The team used OpenAI models to help discover six vulnerabilities in MikroTik RouterOS, including flaws that could be combined to take control of affected devices without authentication. The vendor released fixes, which CERT Polska confirmed prevented the attacks it observed.

title: recommended reading. the "harness" is hilarious.
body:
jailbreaking the switch 2
ns2jb is a software-only jailbreak of the switch 2 for the current latest firmware 23.0.1
October 18, 2026
cs
You can get a copy of the exploit from the [ns2jb](https://gitlab.com/pepsipu/ns2jb) repository.
ns2jb is a software-only, tethered jailbreak for the Switch 2. It allows running arbitrary native code as any ordinary sysmodule, and as the built-in fs
sysmodule. This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2.
To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World. Thanks to my friends in [Dabney House](https://dabney.caltech.edu/) who helped me choose characters to add and playtest the game.
The very first thing I did was set up a harness around the Switch 1 and 2 so Codex could, ideally, jailbreak the Switch 2 without me:
Edit: Many people have been asking me if I actually used this prompt. No, it’s just a silly caption. I set a /goal for userland code execution, but that didn’t succeed. The jailbreak itself took substantial effort for ~2 weeks. The Mario Kart World, however, was entirely vibecoded in a day, and was just for fun.
The JetKVMs allow Codex to send controller inputs to the Switches over USB and receive video output over HDMI. We also need a way to press the power button—when the Switch 2 crashes, it needs a button press to restart.
That’s what the Bluetooth light switch flicker from Amazon is for. When the lever comes down, it presses the power button. Once the power button is fully pressed, the rest of the lever’s torque lifts the mechanism.
WebKit is a popular target for console jailbreaks, so it’s unsurprising that Codex has picked it for initial code execution.
It claims to have “native control-flow hijack” by taking advantage of a WebKit n-day loaded via a custom Wi-Fi captive portal.
We’d like to get code execution in microkernel services (or “sysmodules” on the Switch), so we can run homebrew, mod games, download saves, etc. Unfortunately, this approach of replacing one JavaScript function object with another doesn’t generalize beyond existing functions—we’d need a new way to make arbitrary IPC calls. That looks difficult.
Why?
- WebKit has execute-only memory, or XOM, so even with arbitrary memory RW, we don’t know where a gadget that could perform arbitrary IPC calls is.
- Even if we did, perhaps by parsing relocation data, it’s not clear how we’d construct a signed pointer for it because of PAC.
- And even if we could, with some signing gadget, it’s not clear how we’d call this pointer, since CFI type-checks most call sites.
Codex has reset the goal to complete these steps. It’s a side bet; it may succeed[1](#user-content-fn-1), but let’s be real: the accessibility of WebKit and the Nintendo BBP reward have probably incentivized many before me to look here[2](#user-content-fn-2).
While that runs, let’s explore other options.
My idea was to target Switch 1 games, for two reasons:
- They’re built by developers. It’s less likely we’ll need to deal with PAC and CFI, especially because the Switch 1
[does not support PAC](https://developer.arm.com/-/media/Arm%20Developer%20Community/PDF/Learn%20the%20Architecture/Understanding%20the%20Armv8.x%20extensions.pdf#page=10). - Since the Switch 1 root of trust is owned, we can decrypt the code and read it.
Maybe we can still get the upsides of the browser attack surface—orchestrating from JavaScript, using existing n-days, etc—while avoiding the downsides of WebKit mitigations by finding a Switch 1 game that embeds a browser? Something analogous to Electron, but for games, so we could pull off an exploit like this [Discord RCE](https://blog.electrovolt.io/posts/discord-rce/). I can’t disclose this approach’s findings publicly at the moment, but luckily, there are other Switch 1 games.
In particular, I’m interested in [SmileBASIC](https://www.nintendo.com/us/store/products/smilebasic-4-switch/). This is because it’s been pwned before, in [smilehax](https://plutooo.github.io/smilehax), giving userspace code execution on the 3DS. It’s a giant C++ codebase; surely, if there was an exploitable memory corruption in the BASIC interpreter, there can be another.
Codex found a useful 32-bit integer overflow in the interpreter. When removing items from an array, the interpreter checked position + count <= array.length
, but the sum could wrap and become negative. To fill the gap created by removing elements, it’s supposed to shift the remaining elements left, like so:
memmove(
backing + position * 8, // start of the gap
backing + (position + count) * 8, // elements after the gap
(length - position) * 8 // bytes to copy
);
Say we have a string array R
of length 4, and we run REMOVE R,&H60000000,&H3FFFFFFF
. position + count
wraps to 0x9fffffff
. As a negative signed 32-bit integer, it’s less than array.length
. The multiplications by 8 also wrap, so we end up performing memmove(backing, backing - 8, 32)
, pulling the previous 8 bytes into the array. The command does report an Out of memory
error, but it doesn’t matter, since the copy has happened already.
This is useful because the 8 bytes preceding any array in SmileBASIC contain a pointer to the array itself! After the REMOVE
, operations on R[0]
will treat the array backing as if it were a string.
Since a pointer occupies what would be the length field of R[0]
, the string length is enormous, and we can perform reads and writes out of bounds. We read and write to memory by copying to and from substrings of R[0]
.
This was a Switch 1 game, so the SmileBASIC agent could work on the exploit on my Switch 1, while the WebKit agent worked on the Switch 2. After some time, it got ROP.
Okay, now we need to compromise a more privileged process. We’re interested in [ordinary sysmodules](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Switch_System_Flaws#System_Modules) and [built-in sysmodules](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Switch_System_Flaws#BootImagePackage_System_Modules).
Which sysmodule should we pursue? We don’t have their code, so it’s unclear which sysmodules have which privileges.
I gave a few Codex instances the goal of getting sysmodule code execution. Most chose to focus on [audio and ldn](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Switch_System_Flaws). I think that’s because audio and ldn have had bugs on the Switch 2. Codex also looked at the [NV service](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/NV_services), probably because GPU drivers are generally fruitful?
fs
sysmoduleIn the meantime, I started looking at the [built-in fs sysmodule](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Filesystem_services), because:
- The Switch 1 code shows that it’s
[able to serve decrypted code](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Filesystem_services#fsp-ldr). - There’s a lot of code.
- It’s probably similar to the
fs
module in the Switch 1, since the filesystem API didn’t change very much.
The first reason is the most attractive to me. Even if we can’t get a useful jailbreak from fs
, we can at least decrypt some of the other sysmodules so Codex can find bugs in them.
Other sysmodules like [ ldr](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Loader_services) and
ro
An [IFileSystem handle](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Filesystem_services#IFileSystem) has an IPC command, [GetEntryType](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Filesystem_services#GetEntryType). This takes a path string, normalized with Path::Normalize
.
Paths containing a parent-directory component with a backslash, like /..\
, call into a helper that allocates a temporary heap buffer of 0x301 bytes. Our path is copied in, but it can be larger than the buffer, causing a buffer overflow. lol
We’ll need a good victim allocation to overflow into. Codex found that the BufferedStorage
object allocates a cache entry for its files. If that entry has its dirty bit set, reads and writes to the file follow a pointer to cached data.
We can hijack that for arbitrary read/write[4](#user-content-fn-4).
From here, I scanned through memory to find SmileBASIC’s connection object and set the [saved PID to 1](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Filesystem_services#Permissions:~:text=If%20the%20processID%20is%20%3C%3D%206%20%28which%20happens%20only%20for%20built%2Din%20sysmodules%29%2C%20it%20will%20use%20a%20hardcoded%20registration%20data%2E%20The%20default%20mask%20in%20this%20case%20is%200x8000000000000000%2E).
Now, my process has “FullPermission”, meaning I can perform privileged filesystem actions. I dumped internal storage and all ordinary sysmodule code, so Codex could perform offline analysis and I could understand where to go next.
Homebrew and modding typically rely on executing our own native code. Looking at the dumps, the only ordinary sysmodule with permission to map executable code is [ ro](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/RO_services). All these sysmodules have CFI, PAC, and XOM. The
ro
directly.Let’s revisit that first point about fs
serving decrypted code. This was useful for dumping the code for ordinary sysmodules. What’s the intended functionality of this interface? Loading programs?
Games and ordinary sysmodules are distributed as [Nintendo Content Archives](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/NCA), or NCAs, containing a filesystem image called ExeFS. This contains a file for the main executable, main
, and program metadata, [ main.npdm](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/NPDM).
To load a program, the built-in [ ldr sysmodule](https://switchbrew.org/wiki/Loader_services) asks
fs
to open ExeFS, and fs
replies with an IPC handle to the filesystem. fs
also provides two pieces of cryptographic information about the NCA header: the header’s SHA-256 hash and the developer’s signature of that hash. The loader uses this information to perform two signature checks:- Is Nintendo’s signature of
main.npdm
’s process permissions and the developer’s public key valid? - Is the developer’s signature of the NCA header hash valid?
Seems cryptographically sound to me, because, in theory:
- the NPDM signature fixes the process permissions and developer key;
- the key fixes the NCA header’s signature;
- the signature fixes the NCA header’s hash;
- the hash fixes the NCA header’s contents, including its filesystem hashes;
- those hashes fix the executable content.
In practice, however, I’m doubtful of that last claim, because it’s the responsibility of the fs
module to ensure the served filesystem matches the NCA header’s filesystem hash, and we have ARW in it.
Indeed, with ARW, we can replace the ExeFS object behind the loader’s IPC handle with our own temporary filesystem. This filesystem still needs to serve a valid developer main.npdm
for the loader’s first check, but the executable main
itself can be arbitrary.
The second check will pass because, by the time the loader opens the filesystem, fs
has already submitted the valid NCA header hash and signature for the original filesystem.
There are two writes we perform:
- The first puts a temporary filesystem object we’ve made into the domain-table entry for the loader’s ExeFS. This temporary filesystem contains the original
main.npdm
and our replacementmain
. - The second puts the loader’s ExeFS object into the domain-table entry for our temporary filesystem. It’s just to keep refcounts consistent and prevent
fs
from crashing.
These writes must happen after the loader requests the ExeFS filesystem but before fs
processes the subsequent file requests. How do we ensure this?
The fs
process maintains a list of its IPC connections. When a connection has a new IPC message, fs
processes it.
Using our arbitrary read/write, we can replace the handle fs
waits on for the loader’s IPC connection with an event handle we control from SmileBASIC. That lets us control when fs
processes a loader message.
With this, we can execute arbitrary code as any program we have a main.npdm
for!
What main.npdm
s do we have? Well, all of them. With ARW, we can use to the loader’s fsp-srv

title: Why AI Startups Will Disappear Without Compute Markets — Evan Conrad, San Francisco Compute
body:
Evan Conrad explains how San Francisco Compute, which began as an AI lab that had to sublease its own GPU cluster to stay alive, ended up both operating clusters and running a market for them. He walks through the chain of problems a new lab or inference company hits: everyone is sold out, the deposit eats the bank balance, clusters arrive late and break, and demand is nearly impossible to predict. He argues these are all one risk problem, that AI companies run into credit limits before power limits, and that without a working compute market the price of entry keeps climbing until no new startups can get in.

title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
body:
Viewer • Updated • 513 • 326 • 16
[
](#turning-database-grading-into-rl-rewards-post-training-agents-with-thinkingbox)
Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
This is the follow up to our first blog post,
[The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.]ThinkingBox-Training is now available on[GitHub].
We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.
Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
[
](#this-is-a-joint-blog-by-microsoft-and-hugging-face-special-thanks-to-mirco-milletari-and-xiang-jiang-from-microsoft-sergio-paniego-from-hugging-face-and-our-former-intern-zhuochun-li-university-of-pittsburgh-for-co-authoringreviewing-efforts)
This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.
We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.
Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. [In the first post](https://huggingface.co/blog/microsoft/thinkingbox), we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.
Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+
So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.
Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.
We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.
[
](#what-happened-after-training)
What happened after training
We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.
Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.
| Metric | Base | RL fine-tuned | Change | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Observed 20/20 | 38 (7.50%) | → | 107 (21.10%) | +69 tasks |
| pass@1 (successful attempts) | 5,242 (51.70%) | → | 6,163 (60.78%) | +9.08 pt |
| pass@20 (tasks solved at least once) | 453 (89.35%) | → | 446 (87.97%) | −7 tasks |
Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.
What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.
Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.
[
](#contents)
Contents
[What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds](#what-the-benchmark-found-in-sixty-seconds)[Results: the dependability column moved](#results-the-dependability-column-moved)[Where the gains landed](#where-the-gains-landed)[What dependability costs](#what-dependability-costs)[The training loop](#the-training-loop)[Offline policy-relative difficulty](#offline-policy-relative-difficulty)[What earns a reward](#what-earns-a-reward)[Run the training stack](#run-the-training-stack)[Where this goes next](#where-this-goes-next)
In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in [Run the training stack](#run-the-training-stack).
[
](#what-the-benchmark-found-in-sixty-seconds)
What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds
[ThinkingBox-Bench](https://huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench) grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.
[In our first post](https://huggingface.co/blog/microsoft/thinkingbox) we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.
And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.
If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.
The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.
[
](#results-the-dependability-column-moved)
Results: the dependability column moved
After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.
Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from [our first blog's Table 2](https://huggingface.co/blog/microsoft/thinkingbox) and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.
| Model | Retail | Auto insurance | Travel | Neobank | Consulting | Overall | Observed 20/20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Claude Opus 5.5 | 80.97 | 68.40 | 54.28 | 71.25 | 61.58 | 67.16 | 241 (47.53%) |
| Claude Opus 5 | 80.71 | 65.80 | 49.95 | 70.62 | 66.19 | 66.50 | 241 (47.53%) |
| GPT-5.4 | 76.33 | 62.65 | 68.12 | 65.34 | 54.60 | 65.36 | 128 (25.25%) |
| GPT-5.6 Sol | 67.65 | 65.30 | 60.34 | 59.09 | 57.52 | 61.91 | 82 (16.17%) |
| Qwen3.8-27B RLFT | 67.91 | 56.45 | 62.69 | 62.40 | 54.51 | 60.78 | 107 (21.10%) |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 72.35 | 54.40 | 58.94 | 56.39 | 54.31 | 59.19 | 102 (20.12%) |
| GPT-6 Astra | 71.73 | 46.55 | 55.87 | 60.87 | 56.83 | 58.31 | 231 (45.56%) |
| Kimi-K3 | 82.24 | 50.80 | 61.83 | 41.35 | 51.63 | 57.37 | 68 (13.41%) |
| Qwen3.8-27B | 64.03 | 47.85 | 53.41 | 47.88 | 45.69 | 51.70 | 38 (7.50%) |
The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.
Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.
The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with [prior work](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13837). One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.
Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.
[
](#where-the-gains-landed)
Where the gains landed
Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.
Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).
[
](#what-dependability-costs)
What dependability costs
The [first post](https://huggingface.co/blog/microsoft/thinkingbox) priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.
Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20
Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:
Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.
| Measure | Base | RL fine-tuned | Change | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Campaign cost, 20 runs | $925.80 | → | $855.58 | −7.6% |
| Cost per successful attempt | $0.177 | → | $0.139 | −21.4% |
| Tasks passing 20/20 | 38 | → | 107 | 2.8× as many |
| Cost per dependable task | $24.36 | → | $8.00 | −67.2% |
At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.
[
](#the-single-attempt-view)
The single-attempt view
Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.
Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.
The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in [our paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19741) fall outside the plotted range.
The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cos

title: Better AI Models Won't Fix Your Engineering Team — Nicholas Arcolano, Jellyfish
body:
Nicholas Arcolano, head of AI and research at Jellyfish, uses data from about 50,000 engineers at 447 companies to ask how much the model really matters for AI coding output. When Cursor pushed many of its users onto Grok, merged PRs barely moved. Breaking down what drives throughput, the tool explains under 1%, skill use about 3% (heavy skill users see roughly a 30% bump), token usage about 9%, company and team about 12%, and the individual engineer most of the rest. The engineers who were top performers before AI are mostly still the top performers now. His advice for leaders: focus on the people, skills and environment you can control.

Applications and agents make many small decisions throughout a workflow: how to classify an input, where to route a request, or which action to take next. Individually, they are simple. At scale, their latency and cost add up.

Today, we’re making the Decisions API generally available. Built with [GPT‑6 Luna](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-sol-and-luna/), the Decisions API focuses Luna’s intelligence on questions with bounded answers, helping applications and agents make near real-time decisions from text, images, and structured inputs up to 10x faster than GPT‑6 Luna through the Responses API.

Since public beta, we’ve added a native GPT‑Live integration, prompt caching for reused context, and inference residency in the US and EU. Developers can also pass native JSON inputs, include images in question instructions, and ask up to 400 questions per request, twice the previous limit. We’ve also continued to improve latency, including additional capacity in several regions in Asia.

## How teams are using the Decisions API

Early adoption of Decisions has shown its applicability across a variety of use cases.

Across OpenAI, teams are applying the Decisions API across product and business workflows. The dots team is using it to reduce response times and improve interactivity. Our Personal Finance team is using it to categorize transaction descriptions, while our Communications team is using Decisions to classify coverage by the themes and scores whether it reinforces or challenges key narratives—helping identify what warrants closer review.

These early examples show how fast, structured decision-making can turn incoming information into useful action across a wide range of use cases. Customers are applying the Decisions API just as broadly, from accurately attributing AI costs to making language-learning experiences more interactive.

1 of 5

> “*With Box Extract and* *the* *Decisions API, we classify business documents and route them to the right next step. In our evaluation,* *the* *Decisions API delivered \~5x faster route selection on 30 certificate of insurance cases, with the same accuracy as* *the* *Responses API—automating routine work and sending lower-confidence cases to reviewers.*”

**—Biswaroop Palit, VP, Product Management Platform and Integrations, Box**

> “*The* *Decisions API is helping us score the risk of agent-generated \[*[*rshell commands*⁠(opens in a new window)](https://github.com/datadog/rshell)*] before executing them to autonomously remediate issues. Compared with available frontier models, it delivered 40x faster p95 with comparable accuracy—making it possible to place Decisions* *in the hot path of a remediation action.*”

**—AJ Stuyvenberg, Staff Engineer, Datadog**

> “*The Decisions API has made it 4x faster and 30% cheaper to attribute our AI costs to the actual work when compared to GPT‑6 Luna, without sacrificing accuracy.*”

**—René Sultan, Research Engineer, Ramp**

> “*At Sierra, we use** the** Decisions API to choose the right next action during parts of our orchestration in live customer conversations. It runs at under 280 ms p95, about 3× faster and 90% lower cost per call than our previous approach, with no drop in customer outcomes.*”

**—Ajeet Grewal, Engineer, Sierra**

> “For language learners, timing matters. In our testing, the Decisions API integration in GPT‑Live was able to reduce the time to next action by over 90%, from 1.4s to 0.13s, creating a much more interactive learning experience.”

*—Andrew Hsu, CTO, Speak*

## Select the type of decision your application needs

Using the Decisions API is simple: developers define a question and its allowed answers, then provide context as text, images, or native JSON. The API returns one of three supported answer types—a probability, choice, or score—that applications can use to determine what happens next. The variety of answer types allows Decisions to be applicable across a wide variety of use cases.  
  
Decisions API supports three answer types:

| Type | Use it to | Main result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| predicate | Estimate the probability that a condition is true, such as whether a product has visible damage. | probability: an estimate from 0 to 1 that the condition is true. |
| choice | Select one of your predefined options, such as whether an agent should continue, retry, or ask for clarification. | choice: one of your supplied values. The response also includes probabilities and confidence. |
| score | Rate an input against ordered levels in a rubric, such as the severity of damage. | score: the probability-weighted average of the level indices. |

## Build real-time voice experiences with the Decisions API and GPT‑Live

With [GPT‑Live](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-live-1-in-the-api/), you can bring natural, expressive conversation to your voice applications, with smooth interruption handling that keeps conversations flowing. Decisions API now [integrates natively with GPT‑Live⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions-voice), helping applications make fast, focused decisions during live conversations. A customer support agent can decide whether to ask a clarifying question, route a request, or escalate an issue. An avatar can adjust its facial expressions as a user speaks to it, and based on the user’s words, respond with a wink or a smile to create a more interactive experience.

The example below uses transcript updates to select an avatar’s expression. Add this configuration to `session.triggers` in an existing GPT‑Live session.

``` ````

Live emits a `decision.event`; the application reads the selected `reaction` and animates the character accordingly. [Learn more about connecting voice to Decisions API. ⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/decisions-voice)

title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
body:
Image Feature Extraction • Updated • 157 • 10
[
](#olmoearth-v13-state-of-the-art-embeddings-for-the-whole-planet)
OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
[Enterprise Article](/blog)
🤗 [Models](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OlmoEarth-v1_3-Base/) | 📄 [Tech Report](https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth-v1-3) | 📊 [Data](https://source.coop/olmoearth/olmoearth-v1-3-embeddings) | 💻 [Code](https://github.com/allenai/olmoearth_pretrain) | 🌎 [Embeddings Explorer](https://olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings) | 🗺️ [Interactive story](https://narrative.allen.ai/olmoearth-embeddings)
Today, we’re releasing [OlmoEarth v1.3](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OlmoEarth-v1_3-Base/), a state-of-the-art satellite embedding model. Alongside OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re sharing precomputed, annual embeddings for the whole planet (10m, 64- and 128-dimensions), plus a new browser-based tool to explore and customize maps based on those embeddings — the [OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer](https://olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings). This means anyone can put OlmoEarth v1.3 to work right away, from tracking change over time to finding similar places—no sign-in, and no advanced technical knowledge required.
Until now, the primary way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio: training a model for each task and running it over satellite imagery to make a map. That requires GPU access and the ability to download and store the [imagery](https://allenai.org/blog/olmoearth-infrastructure). Embedding models compress satellite data into ready-to-use features that can be reused cheaply for many tasks.
With OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re excited to give users more ways to explore and engage with planetary artifacts in whatever way suits them best.
[
](#compute-once-reuse-everywhere)
Compute once, reuse everywhere
An embedding represents what the model learned from millions of images. OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a year of radar (Sentinel-1) and multispectral (Sentinel-2 and Landsat) satellite time series and produces one 128-dimensional vector for every 10-meter pixel on Earth; the first 64 dimensions also work on their own as a smaller embedding.
Foundation models and global embeddings are expensive to produce, and to make sure everyone is able to access the benefits, we’ve computed these embeddings for the entire planet and shared them with the community on [Source Cooperative](https://source.coop/olmoearth/olmoearth-v1-3-embeddings). From there, a crop map, a land-cover map, or a change analysis becomes a lightweight modeling problem: train a small classifier on top and run it locally.
How OlmoEarth v1.3 makes an embedding: a vision transformer reads the satellite data, an Attention Pooler pools it into one vector per patch of land, and a linear layer reduces it to 128 numbers.
[
](#state-of-the-art-embeddings)
State-of-the-art embeddings
We evaluated OlmoEarth v1.3's embeddings against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2 across 27 evaluations, covering six continents and many different tasks. OlmoEarth’s 128-dimensional embeddings score highest on 20 of 27 evals and rank highest overall. The 64-dimensional version, at half the size, still leads on 18 of 27 evals. As part of this evaluation, we introduce [PLANTEUR, a new crop-type benchmark for tropical farming](https://allenai.org/blog/planteur), and the embeddings generalize best to places a classifier has never seen (PLANTEUR technical report is available [here](https://allenai.org/papers/planteur)). Everything behind them is fully open: the model weights, the pretraining data, and the pretraining code.
In practice, this means a small classifier trained on the OlmoEarth embeddings is enough to map what’s on the ground: think classifying smallholder crops in Kenya, detecting brick kilns west of Dhaka, assessing fire damage in Indonesia, and tracking gold mining in the Peruvian Amazon.
Compared to previous generations of OlmoEarth models, OlmoEarth v1.3 was also our cheapest model to train. It took 53% of the computing time of our last version (v1.2) and 18% of our first (v1), with 50% and 22% of the carbon emissions. And it also remains a strong fine-tuning model, matching v1.2's performance across research and partner labels. Our latest model builds on the same foundation as earlier OlmoEarth versions, tuned so the embeddings stay lightweight without giving up accuracy across tasks, and that efficiency work carries forward into the versions ahead.
Full results and methodology are in our [technical report](https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth-v1-3).
If you wanted to reproduce it, pre-training OlmoEarth v1.3 Base would cost roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, data, and code are all open.
[
](#one-place-nine-years)
One place, nine years
How much each pixel’s embedding changed between 2017 and 2020 (left) and 2020 and 2025 (right). Magenta is the largest change. Left: mining spreading southeast, the big patch at lower right. Right: that corner has gone quiet; the change now sits in the older mining zone to the west, part regrowth, part renewed digging. Explore it yourself in the [OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer.](https://olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings#map=11.38/-12.9486/-69.9637&s=zdY7bCoJAFEX_ZT0fh3GycTy_Ij5MJnaxm4Ug4r9HJfRSb5vFXrAmBtQJd5R8uBX2gHBCqXfx3DYIW9RnwhhRK4yb970eUK5x3yMca9QLFzQVIjrRo2VZJrk11qdrSdKVsc77SsrEFya4LPxhzoQ8hBf7ur_Y4lbVJ7xv6gdCt8x4bruGeX4C)
In Peru's Madre de Dios region, illegal gold mining around La Pampa peaked in 2017 and 2018, clearing more than 1,200 hectares of forest in the buffer zone of the Tambopata National Reserve, [according to Amazon Conservation's MAAP monitoring program](https://www.maapprogram.org/lapampa_opermercury/). In February 2019, Peru's Operation Mercurio shut most of it down. The question ever since has been, did it stay down?
The embeddings help answer that. Compare each pixel's vector across years, no model training required, and the 2017 to 2020 pair lights up where the mining was spreading to the southeast. Run the same comparison from 2020 to 2025, and the signal shifts. The crackdown is visible in the embeddings.
The more interesting part is what the second map still shows. It is not dark. According to [MAAP](https://www.maapprogram.org/gold-mining-peru/), pockets in the northwest kept operating, and the old mining zone keeps changing as the land recovers. The embeddings register that too. The reprieve was brief, and the pressure is building again. In August 2026, the [Associated Press](https://apnews.com/article/illegal-mining-peru-military-operation-amazon-gold-mercury-navy-728d312a5687ecc6a1e6c6d6798965fe) reported, Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve after prosecutors found mining had crossed into Tambopata itself.
Our [interactive story](https://narrative.allen.ai/olmoearth-embeddings) opens on this stretch of Madre de Dios, and walks through several other examples from there.
[
](#the-olmoearth-embeddings-explorer)
The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer
The [OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer](https://storage.googleapis.com/ai2-olmoearth-embeddings-us-central1/explorer-global/index.html#s=zdY9BDoIwFETvMutv09_SAP8qTRe1EjRBRDAkSLi7sbhwobvJS-Ylb8UMYcIEQTvdu-EBwhWCdI5924BwgrCpCAni2VhVszN0MLWyheVAeEJYq5IJS4RownLMxjRDMMTLCMItkwhZMUK8z6LSOZtFhbEukGdTKK0r_susdjv7-v5i-RvCHjU26Z3UfWbs267Btr0A) is an interactive analysis tool built from the embeddings themselves, rendered as a false-color map of the planet. Pan anywhere, flip between years to see how landscapes have changed, and pull up the underlying Sentinel-2 imagery to check the map against the real thing. Then start asking questions: click a place to find others that look similar, or drop a few labeled points and train a small classifier on the spot, then export the result as a GeoTIFF. No account, no setup required.
For many teams, testing an idea against OlmoEarth has meant a fine-tuning run, on the order of hours. In the explorer, a first pass takes seconds. You can analyze entire regions from a handful of labels, no GPU needed. When a task calls for fine-tuning, the embeddings can help you decide whether it deserves the compute, and where the model falls short.
The archive behind the Explorer holds embeddings at 10-meter resolution, roughly 150 TB per year, covering land and adjacent coastal waters. At launch, 2025, 2024, and 2023 are global, and 2017 to 2022 cover select countries, with more coverage on the way. You can retrieve the embeddings in the full 128-dimensional version or the lighter 64-dimensional version. Every embedding also comes with a record of where it came from. For each 20-kilometer tile and year, open provenance tables list the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat scenes the model read, with links to the public catalogs that host them, so you can trace any pixel back to the imagery behind it.
[
](#get-started)
Get started
This release includes the OlmoEarth v1.3 Base model, the precomputed global embeddings, the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, and the technical report. If your work needs a specific time window, OlmoEarth Studio runs the same model over the dates, modalities, and resolution that you choose, and a [tutorial](https://github.com/allenai/rslearn/blob/master/docs/examples/OlmoEarthEmbeddings.md) shows how to generate embeddings on your own compute. These tools work together: explore in the Embeddings Explorer, fine-tune in Studio when a task calls for it, and take your map from there. Everything is published under the OlmoEarth Artifact License, the same open license as v1 and v1.2.
Pull the embeddings for a place you care about, put your question to them, and show us what you find.

title: NVIDIA Unveils Minerva to Bring End-to-End Observability for AI Factories
body:
Launched today, [NVIDIA Minerva](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/software/minerva/) is an AIOps platform built to help teams find problems earlier and keep AI factories productive. It brings together telemetry from infrastructure and AI workloads, then applies purpose-built AI models to turn that data into timely, actionable insight.
AI factories are among the most complex operations in the world, with vast numbers of GPUs working across high-speed networks to train models and serve AI applications. At that scale, a single degraded component can slow an entire job. The warning signs may be easy to miss, such as a GPU running hotter than its peers or an NVMe drive losing performance under load.
The platform focuses on AI factory yield, a measure of the useful work infrastructure produces through GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime and token production.
Delivering a Dynamic View of an AI Factory
Traditional monitoring tools often divide the data center into separate views. Networking, compute, site reliability and machine learning teams each see a different part of the operation. Minerva connects those signals across NVIDIA GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers and workloads.
With these signals, Minerva builds a dynamic knowledge graph that logically maps the infrastructure — GPUs, SuperNICs, switches and cables — and the jobs running on it. This context helps operators trace a slow training job to the component affecting it, even across a factory with hundreds of thousands of GPUs.
It analyzes billions of data points per hour using supervised and unsupervised machine learning. It learns normal behavior, detects previously unseen anomalies, predicts emerging failures and correlates related events based on the factory’s topology. Instead of sending every symptom to an operator, it can group an event storm into a focused incident with a likely root cause.
Minerva comes with a native AI assistant and connects to external agentic AI tools. This adds a natural-language interface grounded in live telemetry. Operators can investigate cluster health and receive recommended remediation through conversation. Teams can keep a person in the loop to manually implement fixes or connect Minerva to automation through infrastructure application programming interfaces and external systems.
Results That Maximize AI Factory Yield
The ability to correlate workload and infrastructure issues along with its agentic AI capabilities help simplify AI factory operations. Instead of dealing with a blizzard of alerts, Minerva aggregates related problems into a single actionable item. This allows AIOps teams to move from reactive to proactive maintenance. And all of this helps AI factories maximize GPU uptime.
Minerva delivers value for the key metrics AI factories focus on:
- Longer time between interruptions: Minerva spots trouble before it happens, so jobs run longer without incident.
- Faster time to repair: When an incident does happen, Minerva pinpoints the problem, leading to a significantly quicker resolution.
- Greater insight: Modern AI infrastructure generates a flood of data; Minerva filters it out, leaving only the handful of alerts that actually matter.
IREN is among the NVIDIA partners using Minerva to optimize its AI factories.
“As we scale our AI factories, the key to providing the best service for our customers is maximizing the productivity of our GPUs,” said Denis Skrinnikoff, chief technology officer of IREN. “NVIDIA Minerva gives our operations team one view across the network, the GPUs and the jobs running on them, so we focus more on proactive maintenance rather than troubleshooting. That visibility strengthens our operating model for the infrastructure we’re building next.”
Joining IREN, Aolani, [Bitdeer AI](https://www.bitdeer.ai/en/blog/nvidia-minerva/), IBM, Jio, Lambda, Quake AI and Tesla plan to deploy Minerva.
In addition to Dell Technologies, [Lenovo ](https://news.lenovo.com/europes-ai-moment-gtc-berlin-26)and [Supermicro ](https://learn-more.supermicro.com/data-center-stories/supermicro-nvidia-minerva-supercloud-ai-factory)will offer Minerva as part of their AI factory operations portfolios.
Learn more about [NVIDIA Minerva](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/networking/products/software/minerva/).
See [notice](https://www.nvidia.com/en-eu/about-nvidia/terms-of-service/) regarding software product information.

title: Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types
body:
Beyond tree cover: mapping the worldâs forest types
A new 10-meter resolution map shows which of the world's forests are natural, planted, or farmed, and how they are changing over time
Protecting the planet's forests starts with a simple question: what type of forest are we looking at? From space, an old-growth rainforest, a eucalyptus plantation, and an oil palm estate can look like the same patch of green. But they hold very different amounts of carbon and biodiversity. Telling them apart, and knowing how each patch has changed over time, shows us where conservation is working and where natural forests are being converted into plantations and farms.
Today, Google DeepMind and Google Research, together with the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), are releasing[ Forest Typology (ForTy) 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41597-026-08299-5), a global map that categorizes every 10-by-10-meter patch of land on Earth into six distinct forest and land-use types, a key baseline for the EU's deforestation regulation. Alongside it, we're sharing an early time series that tracks how these forests changed each year from 2017 to 2025, including where natural forests were replaced by plantations or farms. For the first time, users can see at 10-meter detail worldwide, year by year, not just where forest was lost, but what replaced it: a timber plantation, a tree-crop farm or other land.
Why "tree cover" isn't enough
All forests store carbon and, together, forests are home to most of the world's land-based plant and animal species. But a forestâs ecological value also depends on its history: a primary forest that has never been cleared holds far more carbon and biodiversity than a single-species timber plantation that is harvested every decade or two.
Most global maps only indicate whether trees are present. That's a challenge for those trying to protect natural forests. The European Union's regulation on deforestation-free products (EUDR), for example, requires that products like coffee, cocoa or palm oil do not originate from land that was forest in 2020 and has since been converted to agriculture. Similarly, wood products, such as furniture, must also be free of forest degradation: they can't come from primary forests that have since been converted into plantation or planted forests, or from naturally regenerating forests that have since been converted into plantation forests. As a result, companies and regulators need to know not just where trees are, but what kind of forest they form (primary or regrowing, planted or plantation, forest or farm) and what replaces that forest after a harvest.
Last year, we jointly released [Natural Forests of the World 2020](https://research.google/blog/separating-natural-forests-from-other-tree-cover-with-ai-for-deforestation-free-supply-chains/), a 10-meter resolution global map that separated natural forests from all other tree cover. It offered a starting point to help companies and regulators implement the EU Deforestation Regulation, and to support commodity producers in meeting their commitments not to convert natural forest. That map answered one question for every patch of land: was it natural forest in 2020 or not? ForTy goes further, showing what kind of forest is there, from primary forest to timber plantation to tree crops, and, with the new time series, how that changes each year.
How ForTy classifies the world's forests
Specifically, ForTy sorts land into six categories based on definitions from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO):
- Primary forest: native forest with no visible signs of human disturbance.
- Naturally regenerating forest: forest that grew back on its own, for example after logging or fire.
- Planted forest: forest that people planted or seeded, and managed over long cycles.
- Plantation forest: fast-growing, intensively managed tree farms, often of one species.
- Tree crops and agroforestry: farms that grow things other than wood, like oil palm, rubber, cocoa, or fruit.
- Other land: everything else, from grassland and cropland to cities and water.
Training our ForTy model was challenging because these categories depend in part on how land is used, not just how it looks. To teach our model the difference, we built a large-scale collection of forest-type examples with about 1.7 million labeled locations drawn from expert surveys, national and regional datasets, and targeted reviews of places where the model struggled. The model uses a custom architecture designed for the challenges of remote sensing data, and takes as a key input [AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/GOOGLE_SATELLITE_EMBEDDING_V1_ANNUAL), data-compact summaries of years of satellite observations for each 10-meter pixel, so it can spot subtle clues like planting patterns, growth cycles and harvest rhythms.
Putting the map to the test
A map is only useful if people can trust it. So, with IIASA and WRI, we validated ForTy against more than 9,000 randomly chosen sites around the world. At each site, two trained experts studied high-resolution imagery and years of satellite records to determine which type of land was really there. ForTy picked the right forest type 90% of the time, and told forest apart from non-forest land 95% of the time, outperforming other global forest maps.
Beyond accuracy, we know that global conservation is not one-size-fits-all. Instead of giving a yes-or-no label for a specific patch of land, ForTy provides a probability score for each class, enabling users to adapt the classification to regional contexts and application-specific precision trade-offs. For example, a company assessing deforestation risk under EUDR might set a strict threshold, only accepting pixels the model is highly certain about to avoid regulatory risks. Meanwhile, a researcher estimating total forest extent might use the full spectrum of probabilities to get a fuller picture of the potential landscape.
From a single snapshot in time to a story of change
A map of a single year is a useful baseline, but forests change. Our [new early-release time series](https://nature-trace.projects.earthengine.app/view/forest-typology) applies a similar approach to every year from 2017 to 2025. It shows not only where forests disappear and where they grow back, but also what kind of change happened: a natural forest turned into a timber plantation, for example, or abandoned land slowly regenerating into forest.
This differentiation matters because some of the most important changes are hard to see from space. When a natural forest is logged and replanted as a plantation, the land soon looks green again, so standard tree-cover maps might not pick up the change. ForTy's time series makes these hidden changes visible, both losses and gains.
What's next
The Forest Typology 2020 map [described in Scientific Data] and the new time series are now freely available on Google Earth Engine under an open license. We hope governments, companies, conservation groups and scientists will use them to help build deforestation-free supply chains, direct forest finance where itâs needed, and protect the natural forests that matter most. Over the coming months, we'll keep improving the time series with our partners and users, and we'd love to hear how you use it. ForTy is part of our [portfolio](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/publisher/nature-trace) of research on [AI for Nature](https://deepmind.google/blog/mapping-modeling-and-understanding-nature-with-ai/), which includes mapping the drivers of forest loss, forecasting deforestation risk, modelling global species distributions, and monitoring biodiversity in the field. FortTy is also the latest addition to [Google Earth AI](https://ai.google/earth-ai/), Googleâs collection of geospatial models and datasets designed to help tackle the planet's most critical environmental challenges.
Acknowledgements
This work was co-developed by Google DeepMind and Google Research, with the World Resources Institute and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis. title: Cloud Deployment Incoming: ‘Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’ Arrives on GeForce NOW
body:
Lock in and load out this GFN Thursday. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives on [GeForce NOW](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/?ncid=pa-srch-goog-673352&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24109411186&gbraid=0AAAAAD4XAoFI7HGI1e1ouyUf4Z1vqL6Yj&gclid=Cj0KCQjw5vLVBhCiARIsAD56SFLLXG-prLkw0jX3AoX_rJn-CLfJKlNygVblhTr8HBpxVWSPe9WUkusaAvP1EALw_wcB) at launch, bringing a new campaign, multiplayer action and DMZ, high-stakes extraction mode to [supported devices](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/system-reqs/#windows-pc). The campaign also gets an enhanced look: GeForce RTX 5080-class performance arrives for Ultimate members, bringing support for ray-tracing features in the cloud.
There’s a new way to join the cloud, too: Existing supported Fire TV Stick users can now purchase one-month Performance or Ultimate memberships directly through Amazon, making it easier to sign up and start streaming on the big screen.
Plus, Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE brings cinematic pixel art and strategic battles to the cloud, and The Elder Scrolls Online’s Echoes of Skyrim Season adds the entire Greymoor Chapter free for all ESO Standard Edition owners.
It’s all part of six games joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) this week.
Deployment Without the Downloads
Squad up and answer the call on the cloud.
Activision and Infinity Ward’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launches today on GeForce NOW. Members can drop into the trenches in Korea, close-quarter combat in New York, high-octane chases through Paris, night raids in Mumbai and city-wide engagements to reclaim occupied territory.
Fight as Private Park, a young South Korean soldier facing live combat for the first time alongside his squad as a routine patrol turns into a desperate fight for survival. Beyond the front lines, operator-turned-outlaw Captain Price is operating outside the system he once served, pursuing revenge through covert missions as the conflict spreads.
Multiplayer pairs precise combat with fluid movement, a dozen core 6v6 maps from around the world and battlegrounds that are shaped by the campaign’s global conflict. The DMZ extraction mode sends players into contested territory to recover valuable technology, weigh objectives and decide when to get out. Loot, fight, negotiate, betray and extract — it’s all fair in the cloud and battleground.
[Ultimate members](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) can now experience the campaign with ray tracing, powered by newly added GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, supported TVs and more. With game downloads and installs handled by GeForce NOW, members can spend less time preparing a local rig and more time preparing the next loadout.
A New Way to Play
GeForce NOW in-app purchase is rolling out to existing supported Fire TV Stick users, making it possible to purchase a [membership](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/premium-memberships/) directly through Amazon using an existing account. Transactions are processed through Amazon’s billing system, creating a more seamless path from setup to gameplay.
GeForce NOW transforms Fire TV into a powerful PC gaming rig in the cloud. Members can stream supported PC games they already own or purchase new titles from digital stores including Steam, Epic Games Store, Ubisoft Connect, Xbox PC Game Pass, GOG and EA.
The library includes thousands of ready-to-play games, including many of the world’s most-played titles and more than 100 free-to-play games. No downloads, installs, patches or updates stand between a new game and playtime. An Amazon Fire TV Stick, the GeForce NOW app and an Ultimate membership are all it takes to level up the living room with GeForce RTX 5080-powered gaming.
A Pixel-Perfect Fantasy
Classic roots. A new adventure.
Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE launches today on GeForce NOW, bringing the series’ classic roots into a cinematic pixel-art world.
Travel with companions bound by fate and uncover the truth behind a force threatening to bring everything to ruin. Strengthen the party with Visions of beloved FINAL FANTASY characters, each bringing unique skills and abilities to battle. Dynamic camera angles and pixelized 3D models give familiar fantasy a fresh perspective.
Exploit enemy weaknesses to stagger foes, break their defenses and seize extra turns before finishing the bonus phase with powerful Resonance attacks. Airships, crystals, espers and moogles bring familiar series favorites to a world filled with secrets to discover.
GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage in the cloud, leaving more space on supported devices for everyday essentials. Save the inventory management for potions and Phoenix Downs.
Step Into a New Season in Tamriel
Familiar lands. Fresh reasons to return.
The Elder Scrolls Online’s [second season](https://www.elderscrollsonline.com/en-us/news/post/70213), Echoes of Skyrim, launched Wednesday, Oct. 21, free for all ESO players and ready to stream through GeForce NOW.
Season Two gives everyone who owns ESO Standard Edition access to its Skyrim content and the Antiquities treasure-hunting system. The Markarth downloadable content follows Monday, Nov. 9, rounding out the additions with two classic zones to explore.
The Season also introduces Solo Dungeons, reimagining challenges previously designed for groups. Moon Hunter Keep and March of Sacrifices have been redesigned and rebalanced for players ready to tackle their dangers alone. Earn new rewards and take on new challenges at your own pace without needing to find a group.
A new Tamriel Tome also launched Oct. 21, offering both free and premium battle pass reward tracks.
In addition, members can look for the following titles joining the [GeForce NOW library](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/games/) this week:
- We Were Here Tomorrow (New release on
[Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/2315050?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), Oct. 20) - FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE (New release on
[Steam](https://store.steampowered.com/app/3259780?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), Oct. 22) - Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 (New release on Oct 23, available in the Call of Duty app)
- CONTROL Resonant (
[Epic Game Store](https://www.epicgames.com/store/p/control-resonant-3568d3?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now)) - Crimson Desert (
[Epic Games Store](https://www.epicgames.com/store/p/crimson-desert-6d6135?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now)) - Planet Zoo 2 (
[Xbox app](https://www.xbox.com/games/store/planet-zoo-2/9nb4jf6b6vsf?utm_source=nvidia&utm_campaign=geforce_now), supports XBOX Play Anywhere)
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.
Gamers who want to test out high-performance GeForce NOW cloud gaming can start with a [day pass](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/geforce-now/?ncid=pa-srch-goog-673352&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24109411186&gbraid=0AAAAAD4XAoGPVGKakiCteqkRtoF1Q-KSI&gclid=CjwKCAjws_DTBhB_EiwAXZknGUBjXpM5vNQvnwLXUGilFsIHBSkbKPfllg7RGpFFuQZv2GFityJC6BoCq8MQAvD_BwE) to try premium cloud gaming before committing to a membership. Better yet, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward a first monthly membership — making it easy to try GeForce RTX-powered cloud gaming with the latest releases, then level up for more.

title: Automate CSV to Parquet with Hugging Face Buckets, Webhooks & Jobs
body:
Files keep landing in your Hugging Face Storage Bucket. Here is how to process each one automatically, without downloading anything.

In this live-coding video we set up a webhook on a bucket that triggers a Hugging Face Job whenever a new file arrives. The Job runs the `optimize-parquet.py` uv script, converts the new CSV to optimized Parquet, and writes it to a second bucket. We upload a 10,000-row slice of the NYC taxi dataset, and the triggered Job finishes in about 8 seconds. For data engineers already using Buckets who want to automate what happens next.

Topics covered:
- Hugging Face Storage Buckets with the hf CLI
- Running a uv script as a Hugging Face Job
- Webhooks that trigger Jobs on bucket changes
- Converting CSV to Parquet automatically
- Checking Job status, logs and output

Resources:
- Webhooks guide (bucket to Jobs): https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/webhooks-guide-bucket-jobs
- optimize-parquet.py script: https://huggingface.co/datasets/uv-scripts/data-processing/raw/main/optimize-parquet.py

title: 1,368 AI Failures and What They Teach About Evals — Vishal Srivastava & Tanmay Sah, New York Life
body:
Vishal Srivastava and Tanmay Sah studied 1,368 incidents from a public AI incident database to ask what real failures say about how AI systems should be tested. They sort failures across three areas (technical strength, deployment controls and business impact) and 13 sub-areas that cover about 98% of incidents. Weak deployment controls, such as human review and monitoring, are the most closely tied to harm. They show how to rank use cases by how much is at stake, why the evaluator itself needs checking, and a build-break-fix loop that tries to prove a system wrong instead of right, applied to a real airline chatbot that gave a customer the wrong refund policy.

title: How to Test AI Agents When No Benchmark Exists — Nathanael Weill, Air Canada
body:
Nathanael Weill leads a team building AI agents at Air Canada, where tasks are so specific there's no public benchmark and domain experts have little time to grade results. His fix is to write the answer first: start from a known answer, generate the input from it, and check whether the agent finds its way back. He shows how that took a past RAG project from one expert-graded test a week to dozens of automated tests a day, then applies it to a supplier-contract review agent with five ways to build a test set: past decisions, planted rule violations, removed clauses, changes that shouldn't matter, and contract templates with filled-in blanks. He also explains why he avoids LLM judges whenever code can check the answer.
